“I wouldn’t call it a war. Right now, there is no active shooting,” Vance said, before clarifying. “I recognise there have been places where this has flared up.”
His remarks come after days of intense fire between the US and Iran. Still, Vance argued that major combat operations only lasted “about six weeks” and that the US has succeeded in degrading Iran’s defence production capabilities.
He also sought to turn attention to the Strait of Hormuz, a focal point of the war, accusing Iran of preventing the flow of traffic through the vital trade route.
“When you ask, ‘When will this end?’, you’re asking me a question like: When will the Iranians stop shooting at ships?” Vance told reporters.
“I think the reality is, I don’t know the answer to that question. You’d have to ask the Iranians.”
Prior to the outbreak of war on February 28, traffic flowed freely through the strait. But after the US and Israel launched an initial volley of attacks that month, Iran closed the waterway to commercial vessels, in a blow to the global fossil fuel trade.
Roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and gas flowed through the Strait of Hormuz prior to the war.
Vance, however, argued that US military operations against Iran were helping create the conditions for increased oil shipments through the strait.
He also asserted that a new deal transferring control of 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves to the US would help lower global oil costs.
“When will the Iranians shooting at ships stop having an effect on world energy markets? The answer is it has less effect day by day,” Vance said.
Vance also chided US allies for not doing more to contribute to the war, crediting US President Donald Trump with singlehandedly preventing a larger energy crisis.
“What we’re doing right now is protecting commercial shipping in order to ensure that we don’t have a worldwide energy crisis,” Vance said.
“The only reason we don’t have an energy crisis is because of the leadership of the president but also because of the fine work of our military.”
When asked about a US attack that reportedly struck a wedding party in the coastal Iranian city of Sirik, Vance said the military was investigating the incident. But he added that he was “extremely sceptical” of accounts about the attack from the Iranian government.
“We’re investigating it because obviously we care. We want to know,” Vance told reporters at the White House. “When our military makes mistakes, they learn from them to try to get better from them.”
The attack is reported to have killed at least five people, including children, and injured nearly 70 more.
Human rights advocates, however, have pointed out that the US has denied responsibility for past attacks that have killed civilians around the world. Victims have few ways of seeking accountability.
The US military has said of the incident that it “never targets civilians”.
The Trump administration also denied responsibility for an air strike on an Iranian elementary school in Minab that killed more than 150 people, most of them schoolchildren, on the first day of the war.
Evidence reviewed by US media and international observers suggests the use of a US Tomahawk missile.
Thousands of people have been killed in Iran since the war began, as well as around the Middle East, in places like Lebanon.
Some 18 US service members have also been killed, with 750 more wounded, as of August.
But at the White House briefing, reporters pressed Vance about reports that at least one widow of a fallen service member was not receiving the full benefits given to the families of those who die on active duty.
Libby Klinner, the widow of the late Air Force Major John “Alex” Klinner, posted in August that the benefits were withheld because “we haven’t officially declared war” on Iran.
Vance, a veteran himself, pledged to reach out to her directly after the briefing. “Our heart breaks for every single person who lost their lives in this operation,” he said.

Estonian defense minister quits after wasting €70 million on faulty shells for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Estonian defense minister quits after wasting €70 million on faulty shells for Ukraine
Estonian Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur has announced his resignation after it emerged that Tallinn had paid some €70 million ($81 million) in advance for artillery shells for Ukraine to a company with no track record of producing such ammunition.
The scandal erupted on Wednesday after the Eesti Ekspress newspaper reported on the botched procurement and the ensuing legal dispute. In August 2024, Tallinn signed a contract with Italian-registered Datasel, owned by Indian company Neco Defence Munitions, to supply artillery ammunition for Ukraine. The government paid €15 million upfront despite neither company having any previous record of manufacturing artillery shells.
A second deal followed in October, with Estonia paying another €10 million in advance. The first batch was due to reach Ukraine in November, but Datasel reported problems and repeatedly delayed delivery.
Despite the setbacks, Estonia signed two more contracts with the company, eventually bringing total advance payments to around €70 million. The money came from the EU’s European Peace Facility, which has been extensively used to fund weapons and other military assistance for Kiev. Tallinn is now disputing the contracts in a case before the European Court of Arbitration in Strasbourg in a bid to get money back.
The government acknowledged the blunder, with Pevkur proclaiming the readiness to take the “political responsibility” and announcing his resignation. The outgoing minister, who will stay in the role until a replacement is picked, however, appeared to shift the blame for the affair on the country’s procurement authority, the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK).
“The defense minister does not conduct contract negotiations. The defense minister does not count socks and ammunition. The defense minister makes the fundamental decision to support Ukraine,” Pevkur explained.
The RKIK boss, Elmar Vaher, acknowledged that his agency was to blame for the scandal, yet shifted responsibility to his predecessor, Magnus-Valdemar Saar.
“I have been familiar with the matter since January. I cannot see inside people’s heads to know how they were thinking and what the main arguments behind their decisions were,” Vaher told the ERR broadcaster. “The decision was made by RKIK’s former director general.”
It remained unclear to what extent the contracts remained unfulfilled, since Estonian officials provided conflicting accounts on the matter. Pevkur said that “tens of millions of euros’ worth of the ammunition” were delivered and are currently sitting “in a warehouse in a European country.” The shells, however, were “not of sufficient quality” to send them into Ukraine, according to the outgoing minister. The defense ministry’s secretary general, Kaimo Kuusk, described the consignment as “wholly incomplete,” while the Eesti Ekspress report called the munitions “useless” and faulty.

A preliminary US military inquiry reportedly found that strike resulted from a targeting error, after outdated coordinates identified the school as part of an adjacent Revolutionary Guard naval base. The Pentagon said at the time it was investigating; a full report has not been made public.

Defence lawyer Kevin Reddington made that statement shortly after the jury sent Judge William Sullivan in Plymouth, Massachusetts, a note that prompted him to reinstruct jurors on what would constitute “reasonable doubt”.

The jury sent Sullivan a note a day earlier that said: “After much deliberation, we are still unable to come to a unanimous decision.” They sent a similar note on Tuesday. But on both days, the judge instructed them to continue deliberating.
If the jury does not reach a verdict and Sullivan declares a mistrial, prosecutors would need to decide whether to retry the case, which has included more than 80 witnesses and more than 300 exhibits.

France has recorded its hottest summer ever in 2026, joining Belgium, Britain and Ireland as temperatures soar in Europe, the globe’s fastest-warming continent.
“We have just lived through the hottest summer ever recorded since measurements began in 1900,” French Environment Minister Monique Barbut said on Thursday at a presentation of the summer climate report.

France has endured multiple severe heatwaves this year, including one in late June that set a new intensity record.
The country saw an unprecedented 2,025 excess deaths recorded during the heatwave, with a particular increase in deaths among people aged over 45, said French Health Minister Stephanie Rist.
Another heatwave stretched from late July into August, matching a 23-day record previously set in 1983.

“The summer of 2026 will go down in history,” Barbut said.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu tasked Barbut in late July with presenting new measures to speed up implementation of France’s national climate change adaptation plan.

Millions in France, Italy, Spain, the United Kingdom and elsewhere in Europe experienced extreme temperatures this summer.
Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent, with temperatures increasing at twice the speed as the global average since the 1980s, according to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service.

OpenAI begins rollout of new powerful AI model GPT-6 Astra to select clients

06:00:16 KST

ChatGPT maker OpenAI has said it has begun rolling out its newest and most powerful artificial intelligence (AI) model to select customers, saying it has built in safeguards to mitigate security risks.
"At this level of capability, safety has to become our top priority," OpenAI President Greg Brockman told reporters on Thursday about the release of GPT-6, also known as Astra.
Just over a year has passed since OpenAI launched the previous version of its flagship model, GPT-5.
Concerns about the capabilities of advanced models have grown since then, following incidents involving systems built by OpenAI and rival developer Anthropic.
OpenAI paused some model development for two weeks this summer after two models it was testing were involved in a security breach at AI platform Hugging Face.
The San Francisco-based company said Astra was developed with stronger safeguards after that incident, though Astra itself was not involved in the hack.
Some cybersecurity customers will get access to the new model Thursday, the company said, with a wider rollout to other paying customers to follow. Users on the free tier or the cheapest paid plan will not get access.
In a blog post, OpenAI said Astra can autonomously handle a wide range of "tedious" computer tasks, including website creation, scientific analysis, game development, cybersecurity and coding.
To illustrate the time savings of building autonomous AI agents with Astra, the company said the model could cut apartment hunting from six hours to under 10 minutes.
"It's not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era," Brockman said on the call, referring to artificial general intelligence, a hypothetical stage at which AI systems match human intelligence across most tasks.
OpenAI previously had an agreement with Microsoft, one of its earliest and largest investors, under which an exclusivity clause would end once OpenAI reached AGI. Those terms were scrapped in April.
'Limited window'
OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki acknowledged there was still uncertainty about how a new model behaves once released.
"A model can become very good at achieving a goal, and it can still act in ways that go against what the person intended," Pachocki said on the same call.
"We also have to be willing to slow down or withhold further scaling when our confidence in safety is not sufficient," he added.
OpenAI, Anthropic and more than 100 other organisations signed an open letter last week calling for a coordinated global response to AI-related cybersecurity risks, warning that the window to strengthen cyber defences was limited.
Anthropic went further on Monday, calling for industry-wide coordination on safety and on the pace of developing increasingly capable models.
"I believe that shared safety standards and international coordination on further AI development need to be prioritized now," OpenIA's Pachocki said on Thursday.
The US state of Alabama opened an investigation into OpenAI last week over the Hugging Face breach, his office citing what it called the company's complete lack of oversight and adequate safeguards.

Farage pledges to slash UK energy bills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

BIRMINGHAM, England — Nigel Farage's Reform UK has promised to use its first 100 days in government to ditch a string of policy costs from energy bills, a move the party claims would save people £250 per year.
The announcement will be made by Reform’s Deputy Leader Richard Tice in a speech at the party’s annual conference in Birmingham on Friday.
The proposal would reduce costs for voters partly by scrapping levies already directly applied to household bills and partly by reducing costs for gas generators, savings which the party says will be passed on to consumers.
Advertisement
The cost of energy “represents a national crisis,” Tice said. A cap on energy costs, expressed as the average household's bill and set every quarter by the Ofgem regulator, is set to jump 4 percent next month. The hike is principally driven by the impact of the Middle East conflict on global gas markets.
In a statement, Reform said it will remove charges levied on gas generators, including through the U.K. Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS). The ETS is designed to force down harmful greenhouse gas emissions by the most energy-intensive manufacturers.
The Labour government has made attempts to link emissions trading systems in London and Brussels central to ongoing “reset” talks between the U.K. and EU, arguing that will cut industrial costs and ease trade barriers. Both sides are targeting a deal at the next EU- U.K. summit, expected this fall.
Tice will also pledge to scrap Carbon Price Support (CPS), a tax on power generators introduced by former Conservative Prime Minister David Cameron. The Labour government under Keir Starmer had already pledged to remove CPS costs from bills from 2028.
The party said removing those two levies would shave £90 per year from energy bills.
Reform pledged to scrap other policy costs currently added to household bills, including the remainder of the Renewables Obligation scheme, used to fund legacy net-zero projects. The majority of levies associated with the scheme were shifted into general taxation by former Chancellor Rachel Reeves last year.
Advertisement
Removing that cost, as well as charges to pay for the so-called Feed-in Tariff, used to encourage take-up of renewables, and for the Warm Home Discount, which funds help with electricity costs for struggling households, would save another £80, the party said.
Reform said it would also make permanent Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s decision to scrap VAT on household electricity bills, a policy the government has forecast will cost £850 million over the next year. Farage's party said it would also remove VAT on gas.
Tice pledged Reform would “take extraordinary measures to bring costs down, restore fairness to the energy sector, and take urgent action within 100 days of taking office to put an extra £250 a year back into your pockets.”

Not only will the states and territories pile on the pressure at a health ministers' meeting today by raising concerns the change will strain their public hospitals even further, but day two of the Senate inquiry into the issue is also happening.
ICYMI: Health Minister Mark Butler is proposing to wind back the rebate those aged 65 and over get on their private health cover to bring it into line with other age groups.
It'll mean more than 3 million older Australians will pay hundreds of dollars more a year, but it is expected to save the federal budget $3 billion over four years, which will be invested into aged care.
The Council on the Ageing, which appeared at the inquiry yesterday, said 1.2 million pensioners would be affected.
Shadow Health Minister Anne Ruston tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast it is important to encourage people to use the private system to avoid adding more pressure to already-stretched public hospitals "at a time when their health costs are going, by the very nature of their age, to be higher".
'Nothing has changed': Chalmers sticks by housing tax changes
So, would Treasurer Jim Chalmers consider tweaks to the housing tax changes down the line if the market downturn was sustained?
It doesn't sound like it.
"From our point of view, nothing has changed our view that this is a really important reform because for far too long Australians, particularly young Australians, were locked out of the housing market," he tells ABC's News Breakfast.
Chalmers stands by Treasury house price forecasts amid downturn
Treasurer Jim Chalmers is standing by his department's forecasts about the impact the May budget's tax changes will have on house prices.
The budget wound back capital gains tax discounts for investors in established housing and limited negative gearing to existing investments and new builds. Treasury forecast the measures would reduce house price growth by 2 per cent.
But an uptick in interest rates, paired with the changes, have been credited for prices falling in almost every capital city in August, according to Cotality.
Chalmers tells ABC News Breakfast the Treasury forecast was based on a "two-year assumption".
"I would encourage people to understand that it's a two-year assumption, not something about the last couple of months. It's about the next couple of years," he says.
"Even if you look at some of the more dramatic forecasts that some of the banks have put out, for example, about house prices, even in some of those forecasts they expect house prices to return to growth next year."
New ACTU chief's Hanson warning
The new secretary of the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) has told 7.30 there needs to be stronger guardrails and consultations in place to protect workers' rights with the arrival of AI.
Melissa Donnelly, 44, is the youngest secretary in decades to take over the influential ACTU at a time when workers are bracing for the arrival of artificial intelligence in Australian workplaces.
"Workers absolutely deserve and should have a say on AI in their workplaces," Donnelly said.
"That's not necessarily a veto. But workers are really worried about what it means for their jobs, what it means for their job security, what it means for their kids' jobs into the future.
"We have creative workers who are having their work stolen. There has to be a broader discussion, and workers deserve to have a seat at that table and have a say on what happens."
Donnelly said one of the priorities of her mandate was to ensure wages rise to help with the cost-of-living crisis, but warned Australians she did not think One Nation was the answer.
She reminded the public about One Nation's record when it comes to workers' rights, as Pauline Hanson's party seeks to capitalise on discontent amongst working Australians in a tough economy.
"One Nation says one thing and does another," Donnelly said.
"The reality is that Pauline Hanson's track record is voting against penalty rates, voting against rights for casual and gig workers. She's opposed the minimum wage. She's most recently suggested it should be easier to sack workers.
"If you're worried about cost of living, Pauline Hanson is going to make it worse."
'Serious concerns' for 36 unaccounted-for Australians in flood disaster
Australia still has very "serious concerns" for the safety of the 36 citizens yet to be located after the Nepal-Tibet flood disaster.
Two more Australians were confirmed safe overnight, revising the number of missing citizens down to 36.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers welcomed the news, but stressed the government still held concerns about the safety of the remaining 36.
"I can confirm two more Australians were located overnight. That would be a huge relief to the loved ones of these two Australians who've been located," he tells ABC's News Breakfast.
"But we still have very serious concerns for the 36 Australians that we haven't been able to locate yet.
"There are thousands of people still missing in Nepal and in Tibet. Good news that two Australians have been located overnight. We are concerned for the 36 who are still unaccounted-for."
Chalmers says Australia has sent "some of its best people" to assist in the search and rescue and recovery.
States fume over private health changes
The states and territories have set the stage for a showdown with the Commonwealth over its proposed private health insurance rebate changes, with some demanding the federal government ditch the plan amid new warnings it will worsen the strain on public hospitals.
Health ministers will discuss the proposal to remove the higher rebate for Australians aged 65 and over at a meeting in Sydney today.
The federal government says the change will bank $3 billion in savings over four years, to be spent elsewhere in the aged care system.
But states like New South Wales, South Australia, Victoria and the Northern Territory have all raised concerns over the proposal, while the Queensland LNP and Tasmanian Liberal governments have gone further, demanding the plan be ditched.
"This is, I think, robbing Peter to pay Paul – and Paul hasn’t been paid yet," Queensland Health Minister Tim Nicholls told the ABC.
"We think that the Commonwealth has not yet got a full understanding of the impact … if we see more people dropping out of private health insurance, then we'll see more people turning up in our public health institutions, including our public hospitals."

ICE agent charged with lying under oath about Minnesota shooting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
20:55:49 UTC
05:55:49 KST

ICE agent charged with lying under oath about Minnesota shooting
Authorities say agent fired into home with people inside, lied about circumstances.
Federal prosecutors in the United States have charged an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer accused of lying under oath to investigators regarding the shooting of a Venezuelan man during an immigration crackdown this year.
Prosecutors alleged that Christian Castro lied to federal investigators about the events that led up to him firing on 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis through the door of a Minnesota home in January.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Mother and daughter detained by ICE in hospital after car crash
- list 2 of 3US judge declines Minnesota’s effort to force Texas to extradite ICE agent
- list 3 of 3Ex-ICE agent charged over shooting is freed by Texas authorities
The Associated Press news agency and The New York Times reported the indictment, quoting a person familiar with the matter who was not authorised to discuss the investigation publicly. It was expected to be unsealed when Castro is detained.
Castro, a former Department of Homeland Security agent, also faces multiple state felony charges in Minnesota related to the nonfatal shooting, including assault with a dangerous weapon.
Authorities in the Midwestern state had sought to extradite Castro from Texas to face trial. Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican and President Donald Trump loyalist, declined to cooperate with the request.
The ensuing standoff left Castro detained in Texas for 90 days before his release last week. Under Texas law, the state cannot hold the subject of an extradition order for longer than that. His whereabouts were unclear as of Thursday.
The charges mark a rare move by the Department of Justice under Trump.
Trump’s top officials have repeatedly argued that immigration agents maintain broad protections while conducting enforcement, a position rejected by many legal experts.
For example, no one has been charged in the fatal shootings by immigration agents of Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis in January.
An Associated Press review conducted in February found about two dozen ICE employees and contractors had faced criminal charges since 2020.
An American Civil Liberties Union report released in July documented instances of violent tactics or other civil rights violations in about a third of 1,200 immigration enforcement incidents reviewed in 2025 alone.
Video evidence contradicts statement
The Trump administration distanced itself from the Castro case after video emerged contradicting the agent’s initial accounts of the confrontation.
Castro told investigators that Sosa-Celis had attacked him, which the surveillance footage showed did not happen.
Todd Lyons, then acting head of ICE, said at the time that the footage “has revealed that sworn testimony provided by two separate officers appears to have made untruthful statements”.
Castro and a fellow agent chased Alfredo Aljorna, a Venezuelan national, after a traffic stop, according to charging documents.
Aljorna fled to the home he shared with Sosa-Celis. After a brief scramble, the two men ran inside. Castro then shot through the closed door, “knowing [the home] was occupied by several people”, the documents said.
One witness said there were two children in the house when Castro opened fire. Sosa-Celis was hit in the leg.
Federal authorities have since suspended Castro and dropped all charges against Sosa-Celis and his co-defendant, who were both initially accused of forcibly assaulting an ICE officer. The other agent involved in the incident was also suspended, but has not yet been charged.
Thursday’s indictment comes after ProPublica this week reported that Department of Justice (DOJ) officials had blocked prosecutors from pursuing more serious civil rights charges against Castro, including “deprivation of rights under color of law”.
However, a source close to the investigation told the AP the active investigation could still result in civil rights charges.
The Trump administration has scaled back the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division and dismantled several Biden-era police oversight initiatives since returning to office in January 2025.
That has come as the administration has revved up its mass deportation campaign across the country.
In August, immigration agents detained 50,925 people with the Department of Homeland Security hailing it as a new record for the “highest number of illegal aliens arrested in a single month”.

German police probing suspected arson attack against arms manufacturers
German police have launched an investigation into a suspected arson attack near the Munich premises of defense contractors Rohde & Schwarz and Helsing, detaining two Bulgarian nationals in connection with the incident.
Two incendiary devices were thrown from a car at a construction site around midnight on Thursday, Bavarian police said. One ignited and was extinguished by officers, while a bomb disposal team defused the second. No injuries or significant damage were reported.
Police shortly afterward detained a 28-year-old woman and a 38-year-old man, both Bulgarian citizens.
The motive remains unclear, although police noted that “several defense companies are located” at the site. Because a political motive cannot be ruled out, the Bavarian State Criminal Police Office and the Bavarian Central Office for Combating Extremism and Terrorism have taken over the investigation.
Die Welt later reported, citing a police spokesperson, that a letter claiming responsibility had appeared on a platform linked to left-wing extremists.
Several defense contractors are based near the site, including Rohde & Schwarz, which supplies radio and communications equipment to German security agencies and the military, and drone manufacturer Helsing.
Since the escalation of the Russia-Ukraine conflict in 2022, EU officials have repeatedly alleged Russian involvement in suspected sabotage and other incidents described as ‘hybrid attacks,’ although Moscow has denied responsibility and conclusive evidence has not been publicly presented.
In another high-profile case, an explosive-laden drone was discovered between Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said on Tuesday that authorities believe Russia was behind the incident.
Berlin subsequently announced the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin, along with other measures.
Moscow has rejected the allegations. Russian President Vladimir Putin accused Berlin of seeking to distract from its domestic economic problems by “planting the evidence” to implicate Russia.
Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova likewise dismissed the accusations as an “absolutely trumped-up and far-fetched” pretext for closing the Russian facilities.

The first Ozon facility hit was a logistics center in the Samara region, followed by warehouses in other regions.
Russia has also been striking warehouses in Ukraine. Ukrainian publishers say Russian attacks have destroyed more than 10 million books in recent months. A children’s book publisher in Kharkiv alone lost about 8 million copies to a fire after an August 1 attack.

Initially, men aged 27 to 60 were subject to conscription, but in April 2024, the mobilization age was lowered to 25. On May 18 of the same year, a law toughening mobilization requirements came into force. The authorities are doing everything possible so that draft-age men cannot evade military service. Videos of forcible mobilization and clashes with draft officers are regularly surfacing on Ukrainian social networks. Amid the understaffing problems in the Ukrainian army, territorial recruitment officers organize man-hunting raids in public places, seizing draft-age men by force. Such incidents often result in human deaths. However, even that's not enough to make up for Ukraine's shortfall of troops. The number of desertions and unauthorized abandonment of military units is constantly growing. From time to time, the country raises the topics of mobilizing women and lowering the mobilization age.

SC: BCI writ runs only over lawyers, not law students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
20:51:40 UTC
05:51:40 KST

Supreme Court Thursday ruled that Bar Council of India has no jurisdiction to discipline or regulate law students
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Thursday ruled that Bar Council of India has no jurisdiction to discipline or regulate law students and quashed its letters threatening to debar Nalsar University law graduates from registering as advocates for opposing an invitation to CJI Surya Kant as chief guest at the institute's annual convocation.Despite BCI chairperson Manan Kumar Mishra pleading for closure of the issue saying that the objectionable letters to the Hyderabad institute on Aug 13 were withdrawn within hours, a bench of CJI Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said the ambit of BCI's powers, as the statutory regulatory body for the legal profession, is required to be delineated."From an in-depth consideration of the issue, we are of the opinion that Advocates Act, 1961, whereunder BCI is statutorily created, does not confer any express or implied power on BCI or state bar councils to take any disciplinary or punitive action against law students. BCI has disciplinary jurisdiction over law graduates only after they have registered as advocates," SC said.The bench agreed with senior advocate K Parameshwar who, for former Nalsar law graduate petitioners, argued that BCI does not have jurisdiction over law students, and its Aug 13 letters amounted to making deep inroads into freedom of speech and expression of students.Only parent institution can take disciplinary action, says SCSo far as law students are concerned, it is the parent institution or the authority prescribed under laws and bylaws governing the institution who alone have the competence to take disciplinary action, if so required, against the students,” said the bench.
Parameshwar said while the letter threatened to bar the registration of the Nalsar 2026 batch of law graduates as advocates, a second letter, while withdrawing the threat, directed the university to identify the students who had given the call to oppose the invitation to CJI as chief guest at the convocation. The advocate added that both letters were without jurisdiction.On Aug 14, SC stayed the operation of both letters, terming them “absolutely uncalled for”, and shielded the students and faculty ag-ainst any action by the university pursuant to BCI’s letters.BCI chief Mishra said that both letters were withdrawn subsequently.The CJI-led bench said, “Having held so, we declare all the communications of Aug 13 or subsequent modified communications to be wi-thout any authority of law.”This indictment and clipping of wings of BCI come a day after the same bench entertained petitions alleging serious irregularities in its functioning and its composition without proper elections.
On Aug 14, the bench had also said BCI had nothing to do with the students’ protest against the invitation to CJI. “The students might have written a letter to me. It is a dialogue between me and students. Who are they (BCI) to unnecessarily create an issue? This action is totally uncalled for,” CJI had said.Trashing BCI’s threat, CJI had told Parameshwar to convey to the students “to get licences to practice at the earliest and begin their careers in Supreme Court. We will empanel them and give them legal aid cases. This will be our response to all those who intend to create impediments in their professional career.”

Tunisian Cassation Court upholds long sentences for opposition members

Tunisian Cassation Court upholds long sentences for opposition members
TUNIS, Sept 3 - Tunisia's Cassation Court on Thursday upheld prison sentences of up to 45 years imposed on opposition leaders, lawyers and businessmen on charges of conspiracy, their lawyers and families told Reuters.
The opposition said the ruling, which is the final stage of the three-year legal proceedings and cannot be appealed, reinforces President Kais Saied’s authoritarian rule.
Forty people were charged with conspiring to overthrow the president in one of Tunisia’s largest recent political prosecutions. Twenty fled abroad and were sentenced in absentia.
“The ruling confirms that the judiciary is not independent,” said lawyer Haifa Chebbi, daughter of prominent opposition figure and National Salvation Front leader Nejib Chebbi, who was sentenced to 12 years.
"Opponents entered prison by political decision and will leave when Saied falls,” she said.
Saied has said the judiciary remains independent and that he would not become a dictator. In 2023, when most of the defendants were arrested, he said the politicians were "traitors and terrorists" and that judges who would acquit them were their accomplices.
Tunisia's justice minister has said the defendants tried to destabilise the country and overthrow Saied.
Rights groups say Saied has controlled the judiciary since suspending parliament and seizing extraordinary powers in 2021, ruling by decree, dissolving the independent Supreme Judicial Council and sacking dozens of judges in 2022.
Prominent opposition figures Ghazi Chaouachi, Issam Chebbi, Jawhar Ben Mbarek and Ridha Belhaj were sentenced to 20 years in prison, while politician Noureddine Bhiri received 10 years. REUTERS

Near the Canary Islands, a boat carrying migrants suffered an accident — dozens of people, including an infant, died
Kyiv • UNN
A boat carrying 128 migrants traveled from Gambia for 27 days and suffered an accident near Gran Canaria. Around 80 deaths have been confirmed.
Around 80 migrants died after a boat carrying 128 people got into trouble off the southern coast of the island of Gran Canaria. Sky News reported this, citing Spain's Maritime Rescue Service, UNN writes.
Details
The boat departed from Gambia on August 7 and spent 27 days at sea. Rescuers received a distress signal on Wednesday and were able to reach the vessel around midnight.
By the time rescuers arrived, the bodies of five people who had died were on board. The survivors were taken to the port of Arguineguín in Gran Canaria, where they are being cared for by local authorities.
Women and an infant were among the dead
Helena Maleno, founder of the non-governmental organization Walking Borders, said, citing accounts from the survivors, that three women and an infant were among those who died during the crossing.
Spain's Maritime Rescue Service said that, as of the morning, it had confirmed around 80 deaths among the 128 people on board the vessel. The bodies of many of those who died could not be recovered due to adverse weather conditions.The Atlantic route from West Africa to the Canary Islands is considered one of the most dangerous migration routes. Every year, thousands of people attempt to reach Spanish territory by crossing long distances in overcrowded boats.

U.S. Navy’s newest Flight III destroyer to be commissioned in October
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
20:46:32 UTC
05:46:32 KST

- The U.S. Navy will commission the destroyer USS Ted Stevens (DDG 128) on October 3 in Whittier, Alaska, its first Alaska commissioning since 2013.
- The Flight III Arleigh Burke-class ship carries the AN/SPY-6(V)1 radar and Aegis Baseline 10 combat system and will homeport in Norfolk, Virginia.
The U.S. Navy will commission its newest guided-missile destroyer, the USS Ted Stevens (DDG 128), on October 3 in Whittier, Alaska, according to a release from Commander, Naval Surface Force, U.S. Pacific Fleet.
The ceremony will be the first Navy ship commissioning held in Alaska since 2013, when the USS Anchorage (LPD 23) was commissioned at the Don Young Port of Alaska, according to the USS Ted Stevens Commissioning Committee. Secretary of the Navy John Phelan approved the Whittier location earlier this year.
The Ted Stevens is a Flight III Arleigh Burke-class destroyer, the third of that configuration, built by Huntington Ingalls Industries’ Ingalls Shipbuilding in Pascagoula, Mississippi. The ship’s sponsors, Catherine Ann Stevens and her daughters Susan Stevens Covich and Lily Stevens Becker, christened the vessel there in August 2023. The Navy took delivery of the destroyer in December 2025, and it departed Ingalls in May 2026, arriving at its future homeport of Naval Station Norfolk on May 15.
The ship honors Ted Stevens, a decorated World War II Army Air Corps pilot who earned two Distinguished Flying Crosses and two Air Medals flying missions over “The Hump” in the China-Burma-India theater. Stevens later became a leading advocate for Alaska statehood and represented the state in the U.S. Senate from December 1968 to January 2009, serving as president pro tempore during the 108th and 109th Congresses.
“Equipped with cutting-edge systems and capabilities, USS Ted Stevens is ready to answer our Nation’s call to counter aggression and safeguard our interests by providing a powerful advantage at sea,” said Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao.
“USS Ted Stevens represents the combat-ready, lethal force our Navy needs to deter aggression and defend our nation,” said Adm. Daryl Caudle, Chief of Naval Operations. “With her advanced sensors, weapons, and air and missile defense capabilities, this ship will give our Fleet greater capacity to find, track, and defeat threats across the maritime domain.”
“That legacy now passes to the Sailors who will bring this ship to life, turn her advanced integrated air and missile defense into combat power, and carry Senator Stevens’ standard forward,” said Vice Adm. Joe Cahill, commander, Naval Surface Force, U.S. Pacific Fleet.
Flight III Arleigh Burke destroyers carry the AN/SPY-6(V)1 Air and Missile Defense Radar and run the Aegis Baseline 10 combat system, along with upgraded electrical power and cooling capacity to support the added sensor load. The class is built to handle air defense, ballistic missile defense, anti-submarine warfare and surface combat missions, including against advanced cruise and ballistic missile threats.
Following the commissioning ceremony, the Ted Stevens will sail to its permanent homeport in Norfolk, Virginia.

Diplomatic efforts to end Russia’s four-and-a-half-year war on Ukraine have stalled in recent months as the US has shifted its focus towards its war in the Middle East.
“We expect to see the envoys of the president of America here in Kyiv. We have confirmation from them,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly address.
“They will have meetings in Moscow and in Kyiv. We are counting on a meeting in the coming days,” he added.
Trump’s special envoys, Steve Witkoff and the president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, have been involved in shuttle diplomacy between Russia and Ukraine.
While they have travelled to Moscow multiple times, they have never been to Kyiv.
Zelenskyy said that “tentative dates have been set” for the envoys’ first visit to the Ukrainian capital.
In July, Zelenskyy said he had spoken with Witkoff and Kushner “to reinvigorate diplomacy and bring peace closer”.
Russia’s war on Ukraine has turned into Europe’s worst conflict since World War II, killing thousands of civilians and hundreds of thousands of troops since 2022.

"It also examines the extent to which the platform's own editorial and publishing systems participate in the generation, selection, circulation, amplification or monetisation of content," he said.The bench has asked whether a digital platform's legal position can continue to be treated merely as that of a passive intermediary when its systems actively generate, modify, curate, recommend, publish, amplify or monetise content.The commission has specifically asked the I&B ministry whether Meta falls within its regulatory purview as a publisher or publisher of online curated content under IT Rules, 2021 wherever the company's systems generate, modify, curate, recommend, publish or amplify content.Meta owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.Details have also been sought regarding the regulatory status and obligations of Meta and the action required to be taken by the ministry under the existing regulatory framework.

Leonid Slutsky was promised second place in the September elections, sources tell Meduza. Frustrated that the Kremlin stopped helping, he’s now saying LDPR belongs to the security services instead.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
20:39:49 UTC
05:39:49 KST

Leonid Slutsky was promised second place in the September elections, sources tell Meduza. Frustrated that the Kremlin stopped helping, he’s now saying LDPR belongs to the security services instead.
Leonid Slutsky, who leads Russia’s Liberal Democratic Party (LDPR), has begun casting it as a “party of security officials” rather than as a party of the Kremlin’s civilian staff. That is how Slutsky describes the party in private conversations with allies and with businesspeople close to the Liberal Democrats, and even in public campaign materials.
A post on LDPR’s Facebook page says security officials are running for the party in elections to the State Duma, Russia’s lower house of parliament. Slutsky made the same point on his VKontakte page. The party’s social media posts read (errors as in the original):
Our team is made up of heroes and builders. LDPR’s list of State Duma candidates includes 111 people who know firsthand what it means to defend the Motherland. They are veterans of the “special military operation,” volunteers, and security officials. Among them are brigade commander Alexey Vereshchagin and Sergei Antoshin, leader of “Bars-Bryansk.” Our guys on the front lines are correcting past mistakes today, strengthening the Russian World.
Two LDPR members and a strategist who works with the political bloc of Russia’s Presidential Administration told Meduza about the shift in positioning.
The party changed its image because Slutsky is unhappy with the work of the political bloc headed by Sergei Kiriyenko. The reason for his displeasure is the party’s declining ratings and the fear that comes with them — that LDPR will fail to take the coveted second place, or even third.
“[At the political bloc] they promised second place, but they’re not delivering. It didn’t work out in the presidential election, and they’re not helping in the Duma election,” said one party member, summing up Slutsky’s complaints.
The same member said Slutsky now coordinates the campaign not with Alexander Kharichev, head of the Social Monitoring Directorate, but with Andrey Yarin, head of the Domestic Policy Directorate.
Under the Kremlin’s informal division of labor, Kharichev — who is close to the head of the political bloc — oversees election campaigns; Yarin handles day-to-day “operational” matters with regional authorities. Yarin has always been seen as closer to the security officials than to Kiriyenko’s team.
After the full-scale invasion began and Vladimir Zhirinovsky, LDPR’s founder, died in 2022, the Presidential Administration’s political bloc did try to pull LDPR into second place in regional elections. It managed to secure that result only last year, when LDPR finished second in seven of the 11 regions electing legislatures.
In the 2024 presidential election, LDPR’s new leader finished only fourth, behind not just Russian President Vladimir Putin but also Communist Party (KPRF) nominee Nikolai Kharitonov and Vladislav Davankov of the New People party. That happened even though the political bloc had sent Andrey Polosin, an experienced political strategist close to Kiriyenko, to help Slutsky, and even though the leaders of KPRF and New People took no part in the campaign.
According to the strategist working with the political bloc, “that’s when the mutual grievances between Slutsky and Kiriyenko’s team began.”
“Andrey [Polosin] did good work, but Slutsky and [Maria Voropayeva, the head of the party’s staff] complained about him to Kharichev constantly. They tried complaining to Kiriyenko, too. At some point SVK stopped talking to him and handed Slutsky off to Kharichev — that stung as well,” the strategist said. “Though at a congress or a public event Kiriyenko will, of course, say hello and toss out a line.”
The political bloc’s complaint, which Meduza has reported before, is that Slutsky cannot pull off the role of a public politician and that he himself “doesn’t understand this,” according to the strategist who works with the Presidential Administration and another source close to the Kremlin. Even so, Slutsky is seriously trying to become the party’s frontman: he has led and continues to lead LDPR’s lists in regional legislative elections.
“In the Russian system, it’s not a problem for a loyal party to be run by an uncharismatic man — no,” said a political strategist who works with the Kremlin. “You can be smarter about it: push other, more public figures to the front. Or just work with slogans and branding and try to take second place that way, especially when your interests line up with the Presidential Administration’s. But that doesn’t suit Slutsky’s vanity.”
The party is repeating that mistake in the current campaign, he said: its leader takes part in debate after debate and puts himself front and center in LDPR’s campaign videos, in which he urges voters to “save Russia” by voting for the party.
Another prominent LDPR figure appears in one of those videos: Viktor Bout, an arms dealer convicted in the United States, whom Russia exchanged in 2022 for basketball player Brittney Griner, who had been detained at Sheremetyevo Airport with hashish oil for a vape pen. Bout is on the federal portion of the party’s State Duma list, but in this ad he, for some reason, plays an ordinary businessman.
A source in the party said the campaign built around Slutsky is aimed mainly at a loyalist, patriotic electorate, and he sees no problem with that. He acknowledged, though, that internal polling shows Slutsky’s name recognition is low even among LDPR sympathizers.
After Zhirinovsky’s death, LDPR continued to use his image in some regional elections, and it remained the centerpiece of Slutsky’s 2024 presidential campaign messaging. In the current State Duma campaign, though, the founder’s name is almost absent.
Under Zhirinovsky, LDPR eagerly played up the issue of “fighting migrants.” By the early 2010s, however, the party had scaled back its use of the “Russian question” in its messaging at the Kremlin’s prompting. Under Slutsky, LDPR returned to anti-migrant appeals, riding a wave of xenophobic sentiment that grew among Russians in the 2020s.
Now the party’s leadership is unhappy with the political bloc’s unspoken ban on flirting with nationalist ideas. Still, posts with xenophobic appeals continue to go up on LDPR’s social media accounts.
“It [the nationalist theme] would give us a good boost, but Slutsky apparently didn’t get the go-ahead. Maybe he couldn’t have. And yet he presented himself as someone the Presidential Administration supports and helps in every way!” said a party member critical of the LDPR leader.
Both he and the strategist working with the Presidential Administration believe that recasting the Liberal Democrats as a party of security officials, and Slutsky’s outreach to Yarin, who is close to the security officials, are meant to paper over, within the party, the evident lack of understanding between Slutsky’s team and the political bloc’s leadership.
“Slutsky came into the party leadership as the political bloc’s man. If something is wrong in his relationship with Kiriyenko, [Slutsky, for appearances,] needs a new patron — real or imagined — who will deliver the necessary result. The security officials and Yarin became just that. And Slutsky really does go to Yarin — on day-to-day party business. But it’s Kharichev who oversees the elections,” said the strategist who works with the Presidential Administration’s political bloc.
Meduza’s sources do not rule out that LDPR could finish not second but as low as fourth in the State Duma elections. Second place, by their account, will go to KPRF, and New People may contend for third.
The party A Just Russia, in their view, will make it into the State Duma only if the political bloc receives instructions to that effect from Putin. “In the polling, public and internal alike, they don’t clear the threshold. The story with [A Just Russia leader Sergei] Mironov will only push their ratings down. But there’s no clarity yet on whether they’ll be in parliament. If the president wants to keep the current lineup of Duma factions, A Just Russia will get help,” said the strategist working with the Presidential Administration.
In his view, the Kremlin will not put in the effort to pull LDPR up to second or third place: “If they get to third on their own — which is realistic — no problem. If they don’t, that’s their problem. They’ve been helped every way possible for years as it is.”
LDPR had not responded to Meduza’s request for comment at the time of publication.

Putin says the Russian stock market is just ‘slightly in the red.’ (It’s in its longest losing streak since 2008.)
The Russian stock market is “slightly in the red” but will gradually recover, Russian President Vladimir Putin said at the plenary session of the Eastern Economic Forum. Over the past six months, however, the Moscow Exchange index (IMOEX) has lost more than 22%.
What did Putin say?
“Yes, we understand that right now it [the stock market] is slightly in the red. But I’m confident everything will gradually recover, with macroeconomic indicators holding steady and strengthening,” Putin said. He said the Russian economy is in an “absolutely stable situation” and that the recent drop in investment is due in part to the anti-inflation policies of Russia’s Central Bank and the government.
What’s happening in the market?
The Moscow Exchange index has now fallen for six months in a row — its longest losing streak since the 2008 global financial crisis. The current decline is far smaller in scale, however: over six months in 2008, the IMOEX lost 68.25%. Analysts say Russia’s high benchmark interest rate and geopolitical uncertainty are weighing on the market, since high yields on deposits and bonds make riskier stocks less attractive to investors.
The debt market has been rocky, too. After Russia’s Central Bank meeting on June 19, investors began selling off government bonds because the pace of rate cuts fell short of market expectations. The RGBI government bond index hit a one-year low in early July, and Russia’s Finance Ministry canceled several auctions of federal loan bonds (OFZs) because of volatility. In July, Russians withdrew 90 billion rubles from bond funds — the most since record-keeping began — even as inflows over the same period exceeded 100 billion rubles.
The Finance Ministry’s pause in primary OFZ issuance, meanwhile, benefited corporate borrowers. Companies issued 875 billion rubles in bonds in August, 37% more than in July and 32% more than a year earlier — an all-time record.
What about individual stocks?
The calculations use closing prices for shares of VTB (VTBR), Gazprom (GAZP), and Yandex (YDEX) on the Moscow Exchange on March 6 and September 2, 2026. We calculated how the value of 100,000 rubles invested in each company’s shares would have changed in proportion to that company’s share price over the period. Inflation and dividends are not factored in. Over the period covered, Yandex and VTBpaid dividends on their 2025 results, while Gazprom’s shareholders approved a decision to forgo payouts.
Take the shares of three Russian companies: Gazprom, VTB, and Yandex. Over six months, 100,000 rubles notionally invested in VTB shares would have shrunk to 60,300 rubles, a drop of 39.7%. The same sum in Yandex would have fallen to 79,100 rubles, down 20.9%, and in Gazprom to 66,500 rubles, down 33.5%.

why japanese architects carve parking into tiny urban homes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
20:35:30 UTC
05:35:30 KST

carving a void in the home
At the corner of two narrow streets in Tokyo, an orange compact car slips beneath a white house that seems to have been cut around it. Atelier Tekuto’s Reflection of Mineral occupies an irregular 44.62-square-meter plot, where the client wanted as much living space as possible along with covered parking.
Three separate height restrictions pressed against the building from above, and the car claimed its space from below. Yasuhiro Yamashita and his team filled the available envelope and sliced into it until the house became a small polyhedron, with one deep cut at street level forming a sheltered pocket exactly where the vehicle needs to sit.
When seen from the street, the relationship feels strangely domestic. There is no broad garage door announcing a separate automotive room. The car just nestles into the underside of the house, close enough that the architecture appears to loom over it.
This condition turns up again and again across Japanese residential architecture. A bedroom projects above a hood. A living room spans the width of a parking bay. The ground floor recedes by a few meters and the rest of the house moves back toward the street overhead. Each version begins with the same fact, which is that a car occupies a large rectangle of space, and on a tiny urban plot that rectangle has to go somewhere.
Reflection of Mineral, Atelier Tekuto, Tokyo, Japan, 2006 | image courtesy Atelier Tekuto
WHEN PARKING BECOMES PART OF THE BRIEF
Japan gives a unique weight to the space reserved for the car. The country’s Act on Assurance of Car Parking Spaces and Other Matters dates to 1962, and Tokyo police currently define an eligible storage space as somewhere off the road, within two kilometers of the vehicle owner’s principal place of use, with access from a road and enough room to accommodate the entire vehicle.
The space can be rented elsewhere, so Japanese law does not force the car beneath the house. Yet for an urban homeowner who wants parking on the property, it introduces a fixed dimension into a site where almost every square meter is already so valuable.
Building regulations add another layer to the equation. Parking and bicycle-storage areas can be omitted from floor-area-ratio calculations up to one-fifth of a building’s total floor area, while road-height rules shape how high a house can rise beside narrow streets. In residential zones, Tokyo’s road-slant regulations generally establish an inclined buildable envelope from the opposite edge of the road.
A house can therefore be pressed from several directions at once: the street determines part of its profile, permitted floor area governs its size, and the parked vehicle removes a significant piece at ground level. The faceted geometry of Reflection of Mineral begins to look almost like a physical diagram of those forces.
Reflection of Mineral, Atelier Tekuto, Tokyo, Japan, 2006 | image courtesy Atelier Tekuto
TOKYO BUILDS UPWARD
More than forty years before Reflection of Mineral, Takamitsu Azuma’s Tower House offered an early and unusually pure version of the same urban negotiation. Completed in 1966, the reinforced-concrete house rose from a roughly 20-square-meter site in central Tokyo, a tiny piece of land acquired as the city was being reshaped around the 1964 Olympics.
Azuma chose the city center at a moment when suburban expansion offered Japanese families a more conventional path to home ownership. His response was vertical — six levels are stacked into around 65 square meters of floor area, and are all connected as a continuous sequence around the stair.
The scale of the plot makes the presence of a car especially impactful. Here was a piece of land comparable in area to a generous parking space, yet Azuma treated it as the footprint for an entire family home. A vehicle could still be tucked beside the base, while the rooms climbed upward above the street.
The house became one of the defining examples of Japanese urban dwelling because its smallness was tied to a larger position: living in central Tokyo could demand a different shape of home. Space would be stacked vertically and shared between functions, with the city itself taking on some of the territory a larger house might ordinarily contain.
Tower House, Takamitsu Azuma, Tokyo, Japan, 1966 | image © Lukas Gruntz / Architecture Tokyo
LEARNING FROM THE LEFTOVER
By the late 1990s, Atelier Bow-Wow was looking closely at exactly these urban fragments. Its research into Pet Architecture documented tiny ad hoc buildings squeezed into leftover pieces of Tokyo, from narrow gaps beside infrastructure to plots created by changing street patterns. Yoshiharu Tsukamoto described these buildings as forms of space production shaped through occupancy, where an awkward condition becomes something usable instead of being erased.
The practice’s Mini House, completed in 1999 on land connected to the planned Kan-8 Loop Road, extended its upper volume outward so a car could slide beneath it. The building’s name even referred to a miniskirt, with the house lifted above the open space below.
This way of reading Tokyo helps explain why these parking pockets feel so different from a typical garage. The awkward dimension becomes part of the architecture’s logic. Naomi Pollock’s survey Jutaku: Japanese Houses connects Japan’s unusual houses to high real-estate values and strangely shaped sites, along with regulations governing sunlight and off-street parking. These factors have led to a culture of small urban houses in which architects work closely with what the site gives them, including wedges and narrow strips.
Mini House, Atelier Bow Wow, Tokyo, Japan, 1999 | image © Shinkenchiku-sha
THE CAR ENTERS THE SECTION
Atelier Tekuto pushed the relationship into an especially strange place with OH House, completed in Tokyo in 2010. The irregular plot sits five feet below the road, and the client placed parking at the top of the brief. Instead of laying down a solid slab for the car, the architects formed its parking platform from mesh steel.
Daylight passes through the surface into the level beneath, where the entrance and bedrooms occupy the lower part of the house. Seen from below, the vehicle appears to float overhead. Parking has become part of the building section, with the underside of the car occupying the visual field of the rooms beneath.
The vehicle is thus given a role well beyond storage. Its platform admits daylight into spaces below and establishes the route into the house. The entrance sits beside the stairs leading from the parking area, so arriving by car and arriving home become part of the same compressed sequence.
The rest of the 88-square-meter house has to make its own economies around this choice. Furniture is suspended to preserve floor area, while the family spaces occupy the larger volume above. In a house designed for six people, the car keeps a major piece of the section for itself.
OH House, Atelier Tekuto, Tokyo, Japan, 2010 | image © Toshihiro Sobajima
THE GARAGE DISAPPEARS
Other houses reduce the maneuver until it becomes almost diagrammatic. In Denenchofu House by Junichi Sampei of A.L.X., a narrow reinforced-concrete base leaves room for a parked vehicle while the larger steel-clad residential volume sits above. The footprint changes from one level to the next because the automobile has claimed a portion of the ground.
Sou Fujimoto’s House NA has a similar relationship, just lightened. The beloved 2011 house is composed of 21 small floor plates connected at different heights within a transparent steel frame. At street level, the system begins with a covered carport beside the entrance, and the inhabited platforms accumulate above it.
Once the car pulls away, the opening reads as part of the larger porous structure. The garage has almost vanished as a recognizable room. There is a roof, enough clearance for a vehicle, and a direct line back to the street. Everything else belongs to the house.
House NA, Sou Fujimoto, Tokyo, Japan, 2011 | image © Iwan Baan
A VERY LARGE PIECE OF FURNITURE
With Japan’s unique regulations, the automobile brings a stricter element to residential design. It arrives with dimensions that the architect has limited freedom to compress, along with a turning radius and an required connection to the street. In Japan’s smallest houses, it acts even like a massive piece of furniture whose position can alter the entire plan.
The proportions of cars favored in Japan make this a bit easier. Compact cars occupy a major share of the market, and the country’s kei category has long encouraged vehicles with exceptionally small footprints. Yet the architecture tells a broader story than vehicle size alone.
In cities, less than 60 percent of households own passenger vehicles, compared with nearly 80 percent in regional areas (according to the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association). With this in mind, owning a car in Tokyo is a fairly unique lifestyle within a city that offers many other ways to move. For those who make that choice, the house sometimes has to absorb it to keep parked cars out of the way.
THE SPACE BETWEEN HOUSE AND STREET
Once the car leaves, the home is left with a carved-out void. Meanwhile, a typical garage remains a garage, defined by its walls and door. Many of these Japanese parking pockets open directly onto the street, so the vacancy produces a sheltered exterior space beneath the home. The car-sized hole therefore occupies both the domestic interior and a part of the city’s ever-changing sidewalk life. Across these houses, parking stops reading as an appendage. Instead, it becomes one of the dimensions from which the house itself is designed.
Roadside House, Raf Architects, Niigata, Japan, 2014 | image © Toshiyuki Yano

FIFA accuses UEFA of 'smear campaign' in fight over Gianni Infantino World Cup plan
In short:
FIFA has accused UEFA of a "smear campaign" against its president, Gianni Infantino.
UEFA said it was considering criminal proceedings against Infantino for his aborted World Cup sell off bid.
What's next?
Infantino is up for re-election for a fourth term as FIFA president in March 2027.
FIFA accused UEFA of waging a "smear campaign" against it and president Gianni Infantino, escalating a dispute over the abandoned proposal to sell a stake in the world governing body's commercial rights, according to a court filing seen by Reuters.
"While these applications are styled as legal pleadings with captions and docket numbers, they are little more than press releases in further support of UEFA's smear campaign against FIFA and its leadership," FIFA said in the filing.
Reuters has contacted FIFA and UEFA for comment.
UEFA said it was considering criminal proceedings against Infantino and other FIFA officials over FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), a proposed entity that would have held commercial rights linked to the men's and women's World Cups.
UEFA alleged the proposal was developed without adequate consultation with FIFA's governing bodies and 211 member associations.
In a motion to intervene seen by Reuters filed on September 1 by FIFA (AMERICAS) Inc. and FWC2026 US, Inc., FIFA asked the court to defer ruling on UEFA's application or allow it to oppose the request.
FIFA argued that UEFA was seeking discovery for "purportedly contemplated (but non-existent) Swiss criminal proceedings". The world governing body also alleged UEFA had sought to derail the FFE proposal from the outset.
The proposal was withdrawn on July 31 after opposition from UEFA and other regional governing bodies.
"Rather than participate in that democratic process, UEFA issued a press release, the beginning of a weeks-long smear campaign against FIFA and its leadership," FIFA said in the filing.
FIFA further argued that UEFA's opposition was motivated by a desire to preserve European football's dominance.
Infantino, up for re-election for a fourth term in March 2027, has been criticised since tabling the now-abandoned proposal, with several countries withdrawing their support for his candidacy.
The Swiss-Italian administrator is under pressure from three confederations to resign, including UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation and CONCACAF, which represents North and Central America and the Caribbean.
The regional governing bodies have discussed a potential vote of no confidence in Infantino.
Infantino, who retains support from the African and South American confederations, has sought to sideline the confederations and appeal directly to individual members.
UEFA, in a statement last week, said that it would work with partner confederations to ensure member associations are offered a "credible alternative" committed to reform, if Infantino seeks another term.
UEFA also provisionally suspended plans to boycott FIFA competitions, paving the way for all qualified teams to participate in next month's Under-20 Women's World Cup in Poland, the first major tournament that could have been affected by the stand-off.
However, the body said its members had unanimously mandated the confederation to pursue "every available institutional, political and legal avenue" to secure reforms and restore limits on presidential authority.
The confederation also called for "a genuinely independent external review" of the failed FIFA proposal, saying: "FIFA cannot investigate itself and expect the football community simply to accept its conclusions."
Reuters

Russian Ballistic Missiles Destroy Warehouse Holding Ai Weiwei Artwork Near Kyiv
A warehouse housing an installation by internationally renowned Chinese artist Ai Weiwei was destroyed during a Russian missile attack on the Kyiv region on July 19, the artist said.
He stated that the warehouse, located in the Bucha district on the outskirts of Kyiv, was hit by two ballistic missiles during the Russian attack.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The facility contained Ai’s installation Three Perfectly Proportioned Spheres and Camouflage Uniforms Painted White. The extent of the damage to the artwork itself remains unclear.
World-renowned Chinese dissident artist and sculptor Ai Weiwei presented his first major installation in Ukraine in fall 2025. Titled Three Perfectly Proportioned Spheres and Camouflage Uniforms Painted White, the work explores themes of war and concealment, as well as the tension between ideals of rational order and the realities of contemporary war.
Created specifically for its presentation in Ukraine, the installation was unveiled at Pavilion 13, a multidisciplinary cultural venue. The work reflects Ai’s longstanding humanist and pacifist perspective, shaped by his experiences with state repression and his broader artistic exploration of violence, displacement, and political power.
Ai Weiwei is widely regarded as one of the most prominent figures in contemporary art, combining artistic practice with outspoken criticism of authoritarianism and political repression.
His work has been exhibited at major international events and institutions, including the Venice Biennale, Documenta, and the São Paulo Biennial. Ai’s personal history has also been shaped by persecution by the Chinese authorities, beginning with the targeting of his family.
The reported destruction of the warehouse comes as Ukraine’s cultural sector continues to document the impact of Russia’s war on art and cultural heritage.
In May, an exhibition highlighting the work of photographers and documentary creators covering war and its human consequences under extreme conditions opened at the Cannes Film Festival, according to the Ukrainian Association of Professional Photographers.

Türkiye praises Syria’s efforts to address chemical weapons legacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
20:32:18 UTC
05:32:18 KST

Berk Kutay Gokmen
03 September 2026•Update: 03 September 2026
Türkiye’s UN Permanent Representative Ahmet Yildiz praised Syria’s determination to address the country’s chemical weapons legacy in close coordination with the international community.
Speaking at a UN Security Council meeting on Syria’s chemical weapons disarmament, Yildiz called the issue “one of the gravest legacies of the Assad era,” but said there is now “genuine cause for optimism.”
“We firmly believe that sustainable progress on the chemical weapons file can best be achieved through practical, gradual and well-coordinated cooperation with Syria, taking into account the realities on the ground,” he said.
Yildiz welcomed the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) Executive Council’s July decision to restore Syria’s rights and privileges within the organization, as well as recent agreements on the verification of chemical weapons facilities.
He also welcomed the deployment of an OPCW Technical Secretariat team to Syria to inspect the destruction of Category 3 chemical weapons and said Ankara looked forward to its report.
Yildiz acknowledged challenges in identifying, securing and preparing chemical materials for destruction, partly due to the clandestine nature of the former regime’s chemical weapons program.
“These challenges have been further compounded by Israeli airstrikes targeting potential chemical weapons-related sites, following the fall of the former regime,” he said.
He warned that such strikes could release hazardous materials, endanger civilians and destroy evidence crucial to establishing facts and ensuring accountability for past chemical weapons attacks.
Yildiz said Türkiye would continue supporting Syria’s efforts to strengthen its technical and logistical capacity in line with OPCW standards.
“We reiterate our strong support for the Syrian-led and Syrian-owned efforts to address the chemical weapons file,” Yildiz said, adding that the shared objective should be “a Syria that is permanently free of chemical weapons.”

Trump seeks repayment from Europe for past Ukraine aid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
20:30:18 UTC
05:30:18 KST

- President Trump said the U.S. has "virtually unlimited" munitions and is producing weapons "at levels never seen before" amid Iran war stockpile reports.
- Trump said he will seek repayment from European countries for Ukraine aid, though the U.S. already runs a NATO-backed program where allies pay for U.S. weapons sent to Ukraine.
President Donald Trump said Wednesday the United States has “virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition” and is manufacturing munitions “at levels never seen before,” pushing back against months of reporting that the war with Iran has strained U.S. weapons stockpiles.
Trump made the claims in a Truth Social post published at 7:56 p.m. on September 3, in which he also said the United States would soon resume munitions sales to allies after prioritizing its own stockpiles during the conflict.
“For the treasonous SCUM that refuses to accurately report on our Military Operation in Iran, we have virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition, far more than we could ever use for this, or for any other War (which is highly unlikely!), that could improbably take place,” Trump wrote. “In addition, we are producing Munitions at levels never seen before. We are stockpiling and preparing for any contingency that could happen. We are taking them for ourselves, the U.S.A., rather than selling them to others, but the sales to Allies will soon again, begin.”
The post is the latest in a series of denials Trump has issued since March, when reports first surfaced that the intensity of U.S. operations against Iran was drawing down stocks of key munitions. The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post reported in early March that Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine had raised concerns about depleted stockpiles ahead of the war’s start. Trump called those reports a “disgrace” at the time and said the U.S. had a “virtually unlimited supply” of certain munitions.
Similar reports resurfaced in July, when The New York Times, NBC News, CBS News and CNN reported that nearly two weeks of daily strikes on Iran had drawn down supplies of defensive interceptors, including Patriot and THAAD missiles, protecting U.S. bases in Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain. U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz disputed the reporting on NBC’s “Meet the Press” that month, saying anyone leaking such information “deserve[s] to be in jail.”
In August, Reuters reported that the U.S. Army had used “virtually all” of its inventories of Army Tactical Missile Systems and Precision Strike Missiles during the five-month conflict, citing people familiar with internal military data. Trump responded at the time by calling the U.S. munitions stockpile “massive” and vowing to hunt down “treasonous” leakers.
In Wednesday’s post, Trump also said the Biden administration had given Ukraine and NATO “far more Munitions” at no cost than the U.S. has used in Iran.
“Hundreds of Billions of Dollars was given to Ukraine and NATO, free of charge, that Europe would have paid for, If they were only asked, but we will be asking for that money, though somewhat belatedly!” Trump wrote.
U.S. military aid to Ukraine under the Biden administration totaled roughly $131 billion, according to figures compiled by the Atlantic Council, most of it disbursed in 2022. European countries have collectively provided more than $227 billion in total aid to Ukraine as of 2025, the same figures show, exceeding the U.S. contribution.
Since July 2025, the United States and NATO have operated the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, a mechanism under which European allies and Canada, not the United States, pay for U.S.-manufactured weapons shipped to Ukraine. The program was established through an agreement between Trump and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. As of October 2025, 26 countries had contributed more than $4 billion through the initiative, according to the Atlantic Council.

Kiev demands global flight ban over Russia
Kiev has demanded that the UN aviation watchdog effectively shut Russian airspace to civilian traffic after Vladimir Zelensky threatened that Ukraine’s expanding long-range drone campaign would make flying over the country increasingly dangerous.
Ukrainian newspaper Zerkalo Nedeli reported on Wednesday that Infrastructure Minister Nikolay Kalashnik had sent a letter to Juan Carlos Salazar, secretary general of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), calling for action against flights through Russian airspace.
The letter urged the watchdog to “encourage aviation authorities, air navigation service providers and airlines” operating in Russia to take measures to “protect” civilian aircraft, including a complete ban on flights through Russian airspace by carriers from ICAO member states. 
“The presence of civilian aircraft in Russian airspace may entail particularly high risks,” Kalashnik reportedly wrote in the letter obtained by the outlet.
ICAO later issued a general statement on aviation safety but mentioned neither Russia nor Ukraine and did not directly address Kiev’s demand. Instead, it appealed to all member states to “assess the safety of airspace controlled by them and take all appropriate measures.”
Kiev’s demand followed an explicit threat from Zelensky to foreign airlines, insurers and governments on Tuesday that continued Ukrainian drone attacks would put civilian aviation in Russia at risk. 
“The safe days in Russia’s skies are over,” he said, urging carriers to reconsider flights to Moscow, St. Petersburg and other major Russian destinations.
Russian President Vladimir Putin described Zelensky’s warning as a move toward “state terrorism” and vowed that Moscow would respond if Kiev’s threats resulted in tragedy. “Let no one doubt that,” he said.
Ukraine has intensified long-range drone strikes on Russia in recent months, repeatedly grounding flights and causing prolonged disruptions at airports as air defenses respond to incoming UAVs. The attacks have also targeted Russian ports, energy facilities and civilian infrastructure, including e-commerce warehouses.
Drones have also struck residential areas, including high-rise apartment buildings and houses.
An attack last month on the Black Sea resort of Gelendzhik in southern Russia killed at least eight people, including four children, and wounded dozens more. Another strike on industrial and civilian sites in Nizhnekamsk, in Russia’s Republic of Tatarstan, killed 13 people, while a July 18 attack on a Wildberries warehouse in the town of Kotovsk in Tambov Region left seven workers dead.
Moscow has described the intensified Ukrainian strikes as indiscriminate terrorist attacks intended to distract from Kiev’s battlefield setbacks and has responded with renewed long-range strikes on Ukraine. The Russian military maintains that it does not target purely civilian facilities, saying its attacks are directed at military, defense-industrial and dual-use sites.
