Scientech eyes 50% expansion in shipments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:41:05 UTC
01:41:05 KST

Scientech Corp (辛耘), which specializes in supplying advanced packaging equipment and reclaimed wafers, yesterday said shipments would expand 50 percent annually this year, benefiting from thriving demand for artificial intelligence (AI) applications and rapid technological shifts.
The company’s production lines are reaching full utilization through the end of this year and the growth momentum is expected to carry into next year based on the business prospects provided by customers, Scientech vice chairman M.T. Hsu (許明棋) said at the Semicon Taiwan trade show in Taipei.
“Order book visibility for critical semiconductor equipment now extends through 2028,” he said. “We are increasingly concerned about our inability to fully satisfy customer orders.”
Photo: Lin Yi-ju, Taipei Times
Scientech’s optimism is built on capacity surges of 80 percent in advanced chip-on-wafer-on-substrate packaging from 2022 to next year, forecast by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電), Hsu said.
Scientech also seeks to become part of the next-generation chip-on-panel-on-substrate (CoPoS) packaging supply chain, he said.
TSMC in July said that it was building a pilot line for CoPoS packaging and estimated that it would take another year to improve the yield rate before entering volume production.
Photo: CNA
The technological progress in advanced packaging is very dynamic, with new generation technology emerging every year, faster than the four years needed for microprocessor manufacturing, Hsu said.
With strong demand for advanced packaging equipment and reclaimed wafers, the combined revenue from the two segments is expected to outgrow its equipment distribution business for the first time this year, Hsu said. This uptrend is likely to persist over the next few years, he said.
Scientech has recruited 200 semiconductor equipment professionals this year, bringing the total to about 450, outpacing its local competitors, he added.
At the same event, Msscorps Co (汎銓科技) chairman Gino Leou (柳紀綸) said his company, which provides semiconductor material and failure analysis services, is targeting first-tier AI suppliers, foundry companies, outsourced semiconductor assembly and test companies, and optical transceiver makers as it begins making inroads into the fast-growing semiconductor equipment market.
Msscorps, which showcased its light leakage detecting equipment yesterday, aims to supply light leakage detecting photonic IC used in the copackaged optics (CPO) packaging technology, Leou said.
The company plans to sell 10 to 20 units of the new equipment next year to contribute up to NT$3 billion to its total revenue, he said.
Msscorps’ revenue rose 31.95 percent year-on-year to NT$254 million (US$8 million) last month, an all-time high, attributable to robust demand for material analysis linked to CPO and AI chips.
During the first eight months of this year, revenue expanded 22.67 percent annually to NT$1.71 billion, also a record high for the same period, company data showed.

Chiang Wan-an’s absurd moves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:41:05 UTC
01:41:05 KST

More than three years ago, Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) embraced the principle that “saying nothing means making no mistakes.” By not taking any positions or expressing opinions, he had little chance of saying the wrong thing and went on to win a three-way mayoral race.
After taking office, he continued with a similar philosophy of “doing nothing means making no mistakes” — by avoiding major municipal construction projects, he would have little opportunity to make mistakes. As a result, Chiang’s first term has been largely devoid of any memorable policy achievements. However, that has also allowed him to live up to his name, coasting along safely with no major scandals all the way to the next mayoral election.
Now, with the emergence of a new challenger — Democratic Progressive Party Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) — who has been earnestly studying how to improve Taipei’s municipal governance, Chiang is panicking. He has torn away his paper-thin facade of “say nothing, do nothing, make no mistakes,” forcing Taipei residents to witness a series of baffling statements and policies.
The Chiang administration installed eight artistic sunshades at five intersections in Taipei’s Xinyi District (信義) for a total cost of about NT$60 million (US$1.89 million). Not only have their designs been mocked as expensive “oyster mushrooms,” but their ability to provide shade is also highly questionable. And yet, these are not the only controversial “mushroom umbrellas” in Taipei.
In front of Muzha Park (木柵公園) in Taipei’s Wenshan District (文山), the city government built cylindrical roof bus shelters costing NT$4.13 million each. Those were even fitted with rooftop vegetation, but lacked adequate rustproofing and drainage. As a result, the structures began to rust, turning them into “red mushrooms.” Passengers waiting underneath have gotten their clothes soiled by dripping rust water, rendering the shelters virtually useless.
Local borough wardens had strongly opposed the project, but the Chiang administration was unmoved and charged ahead with its plan to “grow mushrooms.”
Another absurd policy that Chiang hastily introduced — and just as hastily scrapped — was the so-called “smoking cage” near Taipei’s Gongguan (公館) shopping area. It was intended to be an outdoor smoking area, but was just an iron cage where people could smoke, putting them on display like exotic circus animals.
What is even more ridiculous is that the main purpose of setting up outdoor smoking areas is to prevent exposure to secondhand smoke, which requires enclosed spaces equipped with ventilation systems. “Smoking cages” do nothing to serve that purpose.
The Chiang administration quickly removed the cage-like fences and replaced them with enclosed stalls equipped with handrails, but still lacking ventilation systems. If opened for use, they would quickly become steam rooms under Taiwan’s subtropical climate and scorching sun, leaving smokers at risk of fainting.
Many people joked: “No wonder they added handrails.”
Although handrails have been added to smoking areas, they have disappeared from MRT trains. The city government claimed it was intended to increase passenger capacity, but if more people are squeezed into trains while supporting poles and handrails are removed, would they not be thrown into one another should the train make an emergency stop?
What has infuriated Taipei residents most is that, whether he is questioned about one of the aforementioned issues or other shortcomings in city governance, Chiang consistently provides irrelevant answers.
More recently, a standard response has emerged: “Ask about Taipei, get an answer about Kaohsiung.”
No matter what he is asked, he always counters with: “What about Kaohsiung?”
Taipei has long been home to the central government’s many ministries and agencies. As Taiwan’s political and financial capital, it receives far more funding and resources for infrastructure than other cities and counties.
It was also the first city in Taiwan to build a metro system, which has fostered a longstanding sense of superiority in some Taipei residents, who look down on other cities and counties. Yet Chiang has now reduced Taipei residents’ status, forcing them to ask Kaohsiung about every issue. How humiliating is that?
Taipei residents, stop choosing mayors who bring shame upon your city.
Tommy Lin is chairman of the Formosa Republican Association and director of the Taiwan United Nations Alliance.

EDITORIAL: Standing firm on Taiwan’s dignity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:41:02 UTC
01:41:02 KST

The Gwangju Biennale, Asia’s oldest and most prestigious international exhibition of contemporary art, is to open tomorrow. A “Taiwan Pavilion” has been installed to showcase the works of Taiwanese artists at the exhibition, which runs until Nov. 15.
However, the pavilion’s name was a subject of weeks of dispute due to Chinese obstruction.
The organizer, the Gwanju Biennale Foundation, had approved the National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts’ application to join the exhibition using the name “Taiwan Pavilion.” However, in June, it unilaterally changed the name “Taiwan” to the museum’s acronym NTMoFA on promotional materials.
The organizer said that as it was an institutional pavilion, not a national one, Taiwan’s exhibition was named after the applicant.
Taiwanese curators and the Ministry of Culture said all documents and contracts signed during the application were made under the name “Taiwan Pavilion.” Taiwanese and international artists, as well as many biennale participants protested the change, calling it “political censorship.”
The name change is a betrayal of the biennale’s founding ideals of protecting freedom, human rights and democracy, artists said.
Gwangju is renowned as a “sacred ground of democracy” in South Korea, and the biennale was established in 1994 to commemorate the 1980 Gwangju Uprising — a democratic movement against military authoritarianism.
The renaming is a “threat to freedom of expression and to the global artistic community,” Taiwanese curators and participating artists said in a statement.
The Ministry of Culture issued an ultimatum demanding that the pavilion’s name be changed back to Taiwan. On Tuesday last week, the foundation conceded and restored the name Taiwan on promotional materials.
After the change, Chinese Ambassador to South Korea Dai Bing (戴兵) met with Gwangju Mayor Min Hyung-bae, expressing “regret and concern” over the decision to allow Taiwanese exhibitors to participate under the nation’s name. China also ordered all its artists to withdraw from the event, showing how it was manipulating and politicizing the art event.
Taiwan has long faced diplomatic oppression, exclusion and discrimination by other countries due to pressure from China. Beijing has over the past few years expanded that pressure from military and politics to the sports and cultural domains.
This time, the Ministry of Culture clearly expressed its stance: “If Taiwan is not respected, it would rather not participate.”
Such a tough stance has also been demonstrated in other cases, such as Taiwan withdrawing from the Pacific Islands Forum last year and from the WTO Ministerial Conference in March to protest the host countries’ downgrading of Taiwan, and to uphold national dignity.
Those actions showed that when it comes to sovereignty issues, the government no longer prioritizes “maintaining diplomatic peace,” but instead dares to bear the cost of withdrawing from international events.
Taiwan’s international visibility has also increased, thanks to its growing economic, democratic and geopolitical contributions and importance. Meanwhile, China’s attempts to pressure or interfere in international events are increasingly causing resentment and winning Taiwan more support.
The Gwangju mayor, for one, reportedly told the Chinese ambassador that “politics should not interfere with the arts.”
South Korean artists and art groups also issued a joint statement saying that Taiwanese artists and art community “have the right to name their own nationality identity according to their political freedom and convictions.”
Additionally, thanks to the support of Pacific Island ally Palau and like-minded nations such as the US, Taiwan has resumed participation in the Pacific Islands Forum, and would be able to work with Pacific allies on issues including digital resilience, renewable energy and smart healthcare.
The Gwangju Biennale’s restoration of Taiwan’s title is also a rare diplomatic victory for Taiwan.
Minister of Culture Li Yuan (李遠) thanked all local and artists, as well as the international community and the media for their support, saying: “Their efforts have demonstrated how art and culture could be used to resist authoritarians.”
On the eve of the biennale’s opening, Gwangju’s mayor vowed to investigate the Taiwan Pavilion controversy to safeguard the “Gwangju Spirit” of protecting freedom and democracy.
For Taiwan, the case could be a lesson that, regardless of whether China’s transnational repression continues, as long as Taiwan stands firm on national dignity, more people and like-minded democracies would stand on its side.

16:41:02 UTC
01:41:02 KST

The Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency yesterday released a documentary on a hundred-pace viper that had incubated 16 eggs, all of which hatched, but only a baby viper escaped after they were attacked by red-banded snakes.
The agency’s Taichung branch last year launched the viper reproduction monitoring project soon after forest rangers Lin Chun-yu (林俊佑) and Chou Chia-cheng (周家成) spotted a pregnant hundred-pace viper in a grass-covered burrow near a parking lot in Tbulan Village (松鶴部落).
The Atayal village, in Taichung’s Heping District (和平), is headed by Ecyang Yapu, who was positive about the project and assisted in access control and power supply.
Photo courtesy of the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency
Yapu named the viper “Yaway,” which means “a gentle, beautiful woman” in the Atayal language.
“I was so worried when I saw red-banded snakes sliding into the burrow, and wished I could drag them out and shoot them dead,” he said.
The viper family was also invaded twice by Asian marauder ants, which built trails on the eggs.
All the 16 eggs laid between Aug. 13 and 14 last year hatched between Sept. 20 and 22 that year.
Yaway stayed eight days to protect her young before leaving the burrow.
However, two of the babies were devoured by a red-banded snake two days after she departed, said Formosan Wild Sound Conservation Science Center Co CEO Lee You (李昱), the project’s principal investigator.
The branch reported the incident to the forestry agency, which decided not to intervene in the natural selection process on the advice of biologists.
More red-banded snakes visited the burrow and ate all but one of the babies, Lee said, adding that only the viper that had ventured into the woods might have survived.
Agency Director-General Lin Hwa-ching (林華慶) said he felt a sense of loss when he watched the film due to the slim survival rate.
Asked why the agency decided not to intervene even though the vipers — a rare and valuable species in Taiwan — were attacked by a non-protected species, Lin said that protected species is a human construct.
“It is a natural process. Even if the baby vipers had been protected by humans, they would still have to return to the wild and face the challenges posed by nature,” he said.
The forestry agency’s respect for natural processes aligns with the EU’s non-intervention guidelines for wilderness and wild areas, which prioritize the integrity of a functioning ecosystem over the needs of individual species, he added.
Branch Director Chang Hung-yi (張弘毅) said they hesitated about dedicating lots of resources to another viper monitoring project following the one in 2023.
“We soon decided that ... continued observation and data collection are required for ecological monitoring,” he said, adding that the second project resulted in many new findings.
The branch in 2023 and last year monitored a hundred-pace viper that guarded its eggs until they hatched — the second such in-the-wild recording of the species..
The documentaries have been published on the forestry agency’s YouTube channel.

Foreigners fueling Sudan war: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:41:01 UTC
01:41:01 KST

Foreign weapons, military technology, fighters and logistical networks are helping sustain Sudan’s conflict and expanding the warring parties’ ability to strike deep into civilian areas, a UN fact-finding mission said in a report published yesterday, warning that some attacks might amount to war crimes.
Sudan’s war erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between Sudan’s military and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) ahead of a planned transition to civilian rule. The conflict has devastated the country, displaced more than 14 million people and created what the UN has described as one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
The UN mission said investigators found reasonable grounds to believe that a transnational network involving individuals and entities in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Chad, Libya and Somalia supplied the RSF with weapons, military equipment, logistics, training and foreign personnel.
Photo: AP
The UAE, Chad, Libya and Somalia, the RSF and Sudan’s military did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The UAE rejected allegations that it had provided military, logistical, financial or political support to the RSF, while Chad insisted it remained neutral in the war and denied knowledge of weapons transfers through its territory, the report said.
The UN mission said it obtained evidence that Colombian contractors played a significant role in operating and maintaining drone systems and other advanced weapons used by the RSF.
It estimated that the total number of Colombian contractors involved could approach 2,000 and said some were present during operations around al-Fashir in Darfur.
Colombia told investigators it opposed mercenarism and was taking steps to address the participation of Colombian nationals in foreign conflicts.
Mass killings of non-Arab communities when the RSF captured al-Fashir bore hallmarks that point to genocide, the UN mission said in a previous report in February.
The RSF has denied such abuses, saying that the accounts have been manufactured by its enemies and making counteraccusations against them.
The mission said its investigation into external support for Sudan’s military was at an early stage, but had found evidence that foreign-supplied combat drones and loitering munitions — which can hover over an area before striking a target — had expanded the army’s long-range strike capabilities.
It said some of those weapons were used in attacks on civilian locations, including Yabus Market in Blue Nile State.
The report found that both sides committed serious violations of international human rights law and international humanitarian law in their drone operations, with some conduct amounting to war crimes.
Both sides have previously denied allegations of human rights abuses.
Expanded range, persistence and increasingly sophisticated capabilities enabled Sudan’s military and the RSF to strike far beyond immediate front lines, and evidence points to both sides carrying out drone attacks that killed civilians and hit hospitals, schools, markets and displacement sites.
More than 1,000 civilians were killed in drone strikes from January to May, according to figures cited by the report.
From May to July, RSF drone attacks damaged electricity and fuel facilities in the North Kordofan capital of El Obeid, which was under Sudanese Armed Forces control as RSF pressure intensified in June.
Strikes disrupted water supplies, healthcare, transport and other basic services in a city already under severe strain and partial siege, the mission said.
Among the cases highlighted in the report were SAF strikes on Ad-Da’ein Teaching Hospital in East Darfur that investigators said killed at least 70 people and left the facility non-functional.
The mission reiterated calls for enforcement of the Darfur arms embargo and urged the UN Security Council to extend it across all of Sudan.

Ministry touts safer sports environment amendments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:59 UTC
01:40:59 KST

People would soon be able to verify the qualifications of sports coaches through an online inquiry system after the Executive Yuan approved proposed amendments to the National Sports Act (國民運動法) yesterday.
The Ministry of Sports said that it proposed the changes to ensure that children are protected and to prevent unqualified coaches from entering schools.
The amendments would list sexual assault, serious bullying, corporal punishment and instructing athletes to use banned substances as grounds for disqualification, elevating the provisions to the statutory level, the ministry said.
Photo: Chung Li-hua, Taipei Times
The government should deny certification, withhold licenses or revoke certifications of coaches, referees and other sports professionals deemed unfit, the amendments state.
The online system would allow people to search for coaches, referees and other sports professionals by name or certificate number, helping distinguish between people with the same name or those who have changed their names.
“We will work with the Ministry of Health and Welfare and the Ministry of Justice to confirm and update the list of unfit coaches. Sports associations would be asked to investigate any isolated case first, and personnel involved in the case would be blocked from the investigation. Coaches would be removed immediately if it is ascertained that they broke the law,” Minister of Sports Lee Yang (李洋) said.
The amendments would transform specialized school programs for student athletes, too.
Students in such classes follow the regular school curriculum while receiving additional, and often intensive, sports training.
The system is intended to develop athletes for interschool, national and international competitions, but it has faced concerns about balancing athletic training with academic education.
Schools should have a proper oversight mechanism that ensures students in sports-focused classes receive a well-rounded education, and avoid excessive training and competitions, the amendments state.
Additionally, sports-focused classes would not be allowed at elementary schools, and all existing sports-focused classes at that level would be transformed into sports clubs or community sports, they say.
“The reform does not ask children to give up sports. Rather, we want them to participate in sports in a gradual and step-by-step fashion. We also want students in sports-centered classes to have a normal education,” Lee said, adding that it would communicate with the Ministry of Education over the details of the policy.
The amendments would also authorize government agencies to allocate budgets, and provide venues, sports equipment, assistive device support and professionals for people with disabilities, the sports ministry said.
Sports events organizers would be encouraged to create inclusive competition categories, it added.
The changes aim to promote the sports industry’s growth, raise Taiwan’s global profile through sports diplomacy and international events, bolster the financial transparency and governance of sports organizations, and ensure decisions better reflect athletes’ needs, it said.

Influencers and content creators armed with smartphones and ring lights have featured prominently in the stands at this year’s US Open, as they try to grab the spotlight away from the on-court action at one of tennis’ marquee events.
About 100 content creators were given credentials for the tournament, organizers said, with 20 of those dedicated to providing coverage of the food and beverage scene alone, where caviar-topped chicken nuggets and the famed “Honey Deuce” cocktail promise viral attention.
Thousands more amateur social media hounds could be found throughout the plaza and in the stands — after shelling out for their own tickets.
Photo: Reuters
“I feel like every slam kind of has their own identity and the US Open has kind of always been the ‘big-show Grand Slam,’” 2017 finalist Madison Keys said.
Celebrities have long been ubiquitous in the stands — from A-list stars to US President Donald Trump — as the ultra-wealthy shell out thousands of dollars for seats at the see-and-be-seen event of New York’s summer sporting calendar.
However, the growing love affair between influencers and the premier US tennis event has caused some growing pains.
A chair umpire on Monday was forced to reprimand a group of patrons for staging a disruptive photo shoot while twice champion Naomi Osaka was serving during her first round win against Anastasia Zakharova.
Another social media user attracted attention for all the wrong reasons when she posted a series of photos posing inside Arthur Ashe Stadium while Keys was in the middle of playing a point against Alina Korneeva, which breached basic tennis etiquette.
“I can appreciate the influencers coming and kind of showcasing the US Open experience,” 2024 runner-up Jessica Pegula said. “But I do think that it’s tough when you see videos like that when they’re taking pictures and using the selfie lights. People are down there trying to perform, and it’s their career and their job. It seems like a bit disrespectful. I think it’s gotten a little maybe too much.”
The trend is a direct result of the tournament’s popularity, with surging attendance leading organizers to expand the main draw action to 15 days. The tournament was further expanded with the mixed doubles competition being held as a standalone event the week before singles action kicks off.
The men’s ATP tour expanded its partnership with TikTok earlier this year, citing a more than 25 percent increase in posts under #tennis last year.
“The more we try to raise awareness about tennis, the better it is, the more popular the sport is,” 2021 champion Daniil Medvedev said.
“For sure, if it disturbs during the play, like if you see the light or something, well, you always say to the referee, can be sometimes challenging, like if during the point this happens,” he said.

Instead, injuries have foreclosed the possibility of a clash between the two champions in three of the four Grand Slams, with the Spaniard missing the French Open and Wimbledon due to a wrist injury and the Italian absent from New York because of a knee injury. Data at geothermal site show promise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:57 UTC
01:40:57 KST

Boring at CPC Corp, Taiwan’s (CPC, 台灣中油) second deep-geothermal exploration well in Yilan County has reached 3,361m and recorded temperatures of 200°C, raising hopes that the site in Dongshan Township (冬山) could host Taiwan’s first deep-geothermal power plant.
The company plans to drill two additional horizontal appraisal wells to determine the size of the heat reservoir and whether it can support commercial power generation, with work expected to be completed in 2028.
The development is part of the second phase of the government’s energy transition policy, with geothermal power offering a stable source of electricity that is less affected by weather conditions than solar and wind power.
Photo: Lin Ching-hua, Taipei Times
CPC began exploring deep geothermal resources in 2024 in cooperation with Academia Sinica, drilling a well near Yilan’s Yuanshan Township (圓山).
The Yuanshan bore reached 4,028m, but temperatures were insufficient to support a commercial-scale geothermal power plant, so it was converted into an observation well, CPC said.
The firm turned its attention to Dongshan, where it began drilling its first well in October last year, completing it on April 21, CPC spokeswoman Lin Ke-ju (林珂如) said yesterday.
The Dongshan bore, which was drilled vertically, reached 3,361m and recorded temperatures of 200°C, making it a potential target for geothermal power generation, Lin said.
CPC plans to drill two horizontal appraisal wells to expand the area of underground exploration, and conduct water injection and pumping tests to assess the heat reservoir and its ability to support commercial power generation.
However, the wells could extend beneath land owned by other parties, potentially infringing on their property rights.
CPC has asked the government to establish a legal mechanism to address the issue.
Energy Administration Director-General Wu Chih-wei (吳志偉) said that the agency is seeking to amend the Renewable Energy Development Act (再生能源發展條例) to address potential disputes over the drilling of appraisal wells.
The proposed amendment would say that landowners would not be able to refuse requests to drill geothermal wells deeper than 300m, Wu said.
The amendment has been approved by the Executive Yuan and sent to the Legislative Yuan for review.
CPC said the next stage would involve procuring drilling and related engineering services, with the procurement process expected to be completed by the end of this year.
If the site is found to be commercially viable, CPC would drill eight additional production wells over an estimated two-and-a-half to three years, with the work potentially completed by the end of 2031.
The firm could then begin work on establishing a deep-geothermal power plant.

Photo from the Taiwan International Youth Ambassadors Association Facebook

China has also issued a travel warning advising its citizens not to visit Palau.
Taiwan was excluded from last year’s PIF leaders’ meeting in the Solomon Islands, but participated in events surrounding this year’s forum in Palau, including the Pacific Prosperity Exhibit and the Taiwan/Republic of China-Forum Countries Dialogue.
The 55th PIF Leaders Meeting is being held in Koror from Sunday last week to today.

They said they were confused as to why China would take such an approach, when Taiwan simply wanted to build friendships.
International Youth Ambassadors have been sharing information about Taiwan with local people and making new friends in Palau, they said, adding that the exchanges had been natural and uncomplicated.

Executive Yuan approves record budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:56 UTC
01:40:56 KST

The Executive Yuan yesterday approved a record NT$607.63 billion (US$19.13 billion) supplementary budget, including NT$421.3 billion to stabilize the economy and NT$145.69 billion for weapons procurement.
The budget was carefully planned to have no effect on fiscal planning or the national debt, officials told a news conference, calling on the legislature to support the bill.
Measures to stabilize the economy amid conflict in the Strait of Hormuz accounted for the largest share of the budget, a Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) spokesperson told the news conference.
Photo courtesy of the Executive Yuan
The Cabinet would give state-run oil supplier CPC Corp, Taiwan (CPC, 台灣中油) a capital injection of NT$233.8 billion to offset its losses, the spokesperson said.
CPC has spent heavily on building the nation’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) infrastructure and supply chains, as well as keeping fuel prices down despite a heated energy market, putting the company in the red, they said.
The state-owned enterprise is key to enacting government plans to increase Taiwan’s energy resilience by securing LNG supplies, which justifies the heavy subsidies, they said.
The government also proposed NT$187.5 billion to offset inflation stemming from ongoing conflicts in the Middle East, they said.
That includes the costs of price controls on fuel, including household gas, and electricity, as well as subsidies for domestic air travel and taxi fuel, fertilizers, oil for the nation’s fishing fleet and harbor service fees, the spokesperson said.
Vice Minister of Economic Affairs Lai Chien-hsin (賴建信) said that energy prices have surged amid the US-Iran conflict, which started in February, with crude oil reaching a record US$144 a barrel.
Although crude oil prices fell in late June, CPC must enact measures to stabilize fuel prices while the fighting continues, Lai said, adding that Japan and South Korea have implemented similar policies.
CPC’s intervention has kept fuel prices in Taiwan lower than any of its neighbors, he said.
Without them, gasoline prices would have risen to NT$45 per liter at the pump, he said, adding that without the controls, monthly spending on gas by an average commuter would have been NT$1,000 to NT$2,000 more.
The proposed budget would also fund CPC price controls that kept bottled LNG prices under NT$200 per bottle, which helped rein in inflation, Lai said.
The government’s plan to keep household natural gas prices unchanged for the rest of this year would depend on the budget act passing, he said.
Supporting CPC’s investment in LNG infrastructure and supply chains is a national security issue, as Taiwan needs to increase storage capacity for its strategic reserves, Lai added.
Huang Wen-chi (黃文啟), director of the Ministry of National Defense’s Department of Strategic Planning, said the supplementary budget would also fund key capabilities that “Taiwanese armed forces should have had years ago.”
The budget is to allocate funds for seven types of missiles, including high-altitude anti-ballistic missile air defense systems, coastal surveillance uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs), attack drones, uncrewed one-way strike boats and two classified projects, he said.
The defense ministry considers the funding an imperative, as the military budget approved by the legislature funded only 10 out of 23 critical projects, he said.
The funding shortfall has led to yawning capability gaps and negative effects on the armed forces’ ability to fight, which must urgently be addressed, he said.
The defense ministry’s revised goal for building up a UAV fleet was to obtain 40,000 drones by next year, he said.
Asked whether the defense ministry is authorized to ask the legislature to fund next year’s spending items in this fiscal year, DGBAS official Hsu Yung-yi (許永議) replied in the affirmative, citing Article 72 of the Budget Act (預算法).
The article allows the Executive Yuan to propose budgets for special projects scheduled for implementation a year from the current fiscal year, which applies to the defense ministry’s requests, Hsu said.
Asked whether the Executive Yuan would countersign the legislature’s version of the defense budget, Cabinet spokeswoman Michelle Lee (李慧芝) did not give a firm answer, but said that Taiwan cannot leave its defenses unattended.
The Cabinet took receipt of the Legislative Yuan’s bill on Wednesday evening and is reviewing it before rendering a decision, Lee said.

How TV fell in love with female gangsters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:55 UTC
01:40:55 KST

Television loves a gangster story — and apparently so does the Duchess of Sussex. This week, Netflix’s The Gentlemen — Guy Ritchie’s latest addition to the gangster canon, which stars Theo James as a distractingly handsome aristocrat who becomes embroiled in the world of organized crime — returns for its second season. And last month, the show hit the headlines after rumors that Meghan was reportedly in early talks to join its third season when she and Prince Harry made their highly unexpected return to the UK.
At first, Meghan’s potential role seemed like a random pivot for the former Suits star, who now seems far more at home holding a jar of her Montecito-made jam than brandishing a gun. But really, these casting rumors are indicative of a wider shift in the traditionally machismo-fueled gangster genre, where it’s now more common to see women stealing the spotlight — and calling the shots.
When The Gentlemen premiered in 2024, it marked a departure from Ritchie’s previous work. Alongside James and Vinnie Jones, the show stars Kaya Scodelario, who is best known for portraying Effie in Skins, the seminal British teen drama. Scodelario plays Susie Glass, a sharp, impeccably dressed, ruthless head of an underground cannabis empire, who introduces Eddie (James) to her world following the death of his father. She isn’t the first female character in Ritchie’s crime shows, but she is the first woman who has parity with her male peers. She’s the polar opposite of a “damsel in distress” — in fact, wherever she leads, Eddie follows.
Photo: AP
“What I liked about her was that this isn’t a story about her learning how to be a criminal … She’s already at the top of the ladder,” said Scodelario when I interviewed her in 2024.
She told me that people initially assumed Susie would be “the girlfriend or the wife or the sidekick,” when really the opposite was the case.
Susie is part of a new wave of female characters in gangster shows who are intrinsic to the genre increasing its depth and scope. As a society, there’s a tacit acceptance that men will be involved in all kinds of criminal activity and violence, but female gangsters force us to take a much closer look at the characters’ motivations. These women create space for scenes that sometimes feel even more shocking and subversive, precisely because of their proximity to femininity.
On Netflix’s assassin series Black Doves, the professional killers are handled by the grudge-holding Lenny Lines (Kathryn Hunter), whose tiny stature only makes her more scary. The show’s most powerful organized crime boss is Alex Clark, played by Tracey Ullman, who runs a massive criminal enterprise that has connections reaching into the highest level of the British government.
Similarly, in the Paramount+ series MobLand, which also returns for its second season this month, the most hair-raising character isn’t crime boss Conrad Harrigan (Pierce Brosnan) or even his rough-around-the-edges “fixer,” Harry Da Souza (Tom Hardy). No, it’s Maeve Harrigan (Helen Mirren) — the mob family’s Irish matriarch, who is as bloodthirsty as she is protective.
Traditionally, women in gangster shows have tended to be either shallowly written objects of male desire, or cunning matriarchs like Maeve, who command respect and use family ties to control people. The latter category often operate quietly behind the scenes, holding the real financial or political power while the men in their families are front and centre. Think Polly Gray (Helen McCrory), the treasurer of the Shelby family in Peaky Blinders, or Youn Yuh-jung’s portrayal of a deliciously evil and corrupt country club owner in season two of Netflix’s Beef.
This year, we’re starting to see the archetype gradually evolve. In HBO’s Euphoria, drug queenpin Laurie, played by a chillingly deadpan Martha Kelly, is very much not a matriarch or a sexualized figure. (With the exception of doting on her beloved pet parrot, Paladin). And rather than fade into the background, she didn’t hesitate to go up against fellow drug lord Alamo Brown in a murderous turf war. In fact, right up until the grisly finale, there is nobody above Laurie, and her destiny is entirely in her own hands.
And in The Gentlemen, Scodelario’s character is the classic millennial girlboss — a fitting role for an actor who had her breakthrough on a show that defined 2000s youth culture. Susie loves red lipstick and an Instagram-ready outfit, making her simultaneously an object of desire and aspiration. She’s a gangster who doesn’t look like a gangster, but at the same time, her visual femininity isn’t her defining characteristic — it’s her ability to strategize and get things done.
In a show where the men are often held back by their status and the firmly set roles that they occupy — father, heir, fixer — Susie is a hyper-capable shapeshifter who can cut their egos down to size. In the heart-pumping season two premiere alone, we see her tweed-clad at grouse shooting, suited up at an art auction (to spend a cool ￡16 million on a Botticelli painting), covertly hatching plans in a steamy lakeside sauna (of all places), pursuing masked thieves on bikes in a classic high-speed chase, negotiating with a (terrifying) Italian mafia boss, and continuing her flirtationship (or is it?) with Eddie.
Really, it’s not surprising that The Gentlemen supposedly piqued Meghan’s interest, because its second season is a high-budget, twist-heavy affair. The series now boasts a prestige production value that feels more aligned with Netflix past mega-hits including The Crown and House of Cards. And crucially, it’s also a show where women take up more space than ever in the Guy Ritchie cinematic universe. In Susie’s world, aristocrats might be the original organized criminals, they are by no means the best — as long as she’s around.

NBA fines Clippers US$30m after probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:55 UTC
01:40:55 KST

The NBA on Wednesday came down hard on the Los Angeles Clippers, stripping the team of five first-round draft picks, imposing a US$30 million fine and suspending owner Steve Ballmer for a year over salary cap circumvention tied to Kawhi Leonard.
After a year-long probe, the NBA said in a statement that an independent investigation found a pattern of misconduct and multiple significant rules violations by the Clippers organization.
The league had launched an investigation into the Clippers following media reports that Leonard, a two-time NBA champion, was paid by a now-bankrupt environmental firm that had close ties to former Microsoft CEO Ballmer as a way to circumvent league rules that restrict the total amount a team can spend on its player payroll.
Photo: AFP
Leonard had a four-year, US$28-million endorsement contract with the firm, but the twice NBA champion was alleged to have provided no work as part of the deal, the reports said.
As part of the penalties announced by the NBA, Ballmer is suspended from all league and team activities for one year “for knowingly seeking to help Leonard obtain off-court income opportunities.”
“I am deeply disappointed by the flagrant violations of our rules and by the Clippers’ institutional and leadership failures that led to this misconduct,” NBA commissioner Adam Silver said in a statement. “The severity of the penalties reflects the seriousness of the violations.”
The Clippers said in a statement that they “vehemently reject” the NBA’s findings, calling them the result of a “biased” investigation seeking to justify a predetermined narrative rather than facts and evidence.
“What the league told us privately differs from what it announced today publicly, and they have not held themselves close to the standard commissioner Silver set at the start of this investigation to ensure its fairness and accuracy,” the Clippers said in a statement.
“We intend to vigorously challenge these findings and penalties through every avenue available to us and look forward to an ethical and impartial arbitration process,” it said.
The NBA said that Leonard, through the conduct of his then-business manager Dennis Robertson acting on his behalf, violated the circumvention rules by pressuring the Clippers to assist him in obtaining off-court income opportunities. Two-time NBA Finals Most Valuable Player Leonard is required to pay the league US$700,000 in connection with his violations.
During the investigation, the Toronto Raptors put their planned trade for Leonard on pause as the NBA told them that they would assume the risk of any potential outcome of the investigation affecting the player who led them to a championship in 2019 before leaving for the Clippers.
Leonard, in a separate statement on Wednesday, said he accepted full responsibility for what he called lapses in judgement by people within his inner circle, adding that he regretted the distraction the situation had caused his fans and family and that he looked forward to returning to the Raptors.
“I entered into my contract with the Clippers as well as the agreements in question in good faith, fully committed to fulfilling my obligations and with no knowledge of any intent on anyone’s part to circumvent the salary cap,” Leonard said.
“For 15 years, my priority has been giving everything to my family, the game, and those I share the court with. As I return to Toronto, I am focused on what I can control, closing this chapter, and moving forward with a clean slate,” he said.
The Clippers would forfeit first-round picks in each of the 2029, 2030, 2031, 2032 and 2033 NBA Drafts.
Clippers president of business operations Gillian Zucker was suspended without pay for one year for being “primarily and directly culpable for the impermissible endorsement arrangements,” the NBA said.
Lawrence Frank, the team’s president of basketball operations, was suspended without pay for six months for his involvement. The Clippers would also be subject to a compliance program overseen by the NBA for a period of five years.

KMT calls for DPP apology over nuclear power U-turn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:54 UTC
01:40:54 KST

The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) yesterday said that President William Lai (賴清德) should apologize for phasing out nuclear power, as regulators indicated they were close to approving the restart of Taiwan’s last operating reactor less than a year and a half after it went offline.
In a statement, KMT Culture and Communications Committee Director Chen I-hsin (陳以信) said the plans to return the Ma-anshan Nuclear Power Plant to operation showed that Lai’s pledge to achieve a “non-nuclear homeland” by last year without electricity shortages had failed.
Chen said nuclear power was essential to industrial competitiveness, artificial intelligence (AI) development and energy security and that Taiwan Power Co’s (Taipower) pursuit of Ma-anshan’s reopening vindicated the KMT’s calls for a more pragmatic energy policy.
Photo: Tsai Tsung-hsien, Taipei Times
In contrast, the Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) long-standing opposition to nuclear power was a “mistaken policy” that had cost Taiwan, Chen said.
The Nuclear Safety Commission (NSC) on Wednesday said that it had completed technical reviews of Taipower’s application to restart Ma-anshan, with approval pending final administrative procedures.
Taipower applied to restart the Ma-anshan and Guosheng nuclear plants in March, after amendments passed in May last year allowed for the licenses of decommissioned reactors to be extended for up to 20 years beyond their original 40-year operating limit.
Later yesterday, DPP caucus chief executive Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) questioned whether Chen would also seek contrition from opposition politicians who campaigned against nuclear power, including New Taipei City Mayor Hou You-yi (侯友宜) and Hou’s predecessor, Eric Chu (朱立倫), both former KMT presidential candidates.
Speaking at a news conference at the Legislative Yuan, Chuang said that the DPP’s “nuclear-free homeland” policy reflected public safety concerns when it was adopted.
While rising electricity demand from Taiwan’s booming AI and semiconductor sectors had made a policy review appropriate, Chuang said it was premature to conclude that the government had decided to restart nuclear power.
Chuang said that voters, not political parties, would ultimately decide the issue through a referendum on scrapping the “nuclear-free homeland” policy to be held alongside November’s local elections.
Even if the referendum passes, restarting the Ma-anshan plant would still require clearing multiple regulatory and safety hurdles, including resolving the issue of nuclear waste disposal, he added.
The Ma-anshan power plant, in Pingtung County’s Hengchun Township (恆春), shut down its last — and Taiwan’s last — active nuclear reactor on May 17 last year.
The Guosheng plant, in New Taipei City’s Wanli District (萬里), shut down and entered decommissioning in March 2023.

The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) on Wednesday accused the Control Yuan of halting the publication of civil servant property disclosures, while the watchdog blamed the stoppage on a lack of appointed members.
Writing in separate releases, the KMT and TPP caucuses accused the Control Yuan of stopping the publication of public disclosures in a bid to shield corrupt Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) officials.
The parties alleged that the Control Yuan suspended the publication to protect Overseas Community Affairs Council Minister Hsu Chia-ching (徐佳青), who it recently fined NT$100,000 for allowing her son to join a council-founded youth camp on the Pratas Islands (Dongsha Islands, 東沙群島).
Photo: Taipei Times
Since taking office five years ago, Hsu made 47 trips abroad for a total of 536 days, costing taxpayers NT$23 million (US$724,295), the KMT caucus said.
The Control Yuan in a news release said that it lacks legal authority to report on cases of corruption, as the legislature has not approved any new members to the constitutional branch of government.
It said the statements from the opposition parties are untruthful as the disclosure gazettes themselves are still being printed.
The gazette is a routine part of the Control Yuan’s operations, which is not affected by its lack of duly appointed members, the KMT caucus said.
“The Control Yuan was highly efficient in targeting [former] TPP chairman Ko Wen-je (柯文哲), but now excuses itself for not being staffed,” the caucus added.
The different treatment of Hsu and Ko shows that the body has a double standard benefitting DPP officials, it said, demanding that the gazette’s publication be resumed within the week.
The TPP caucus said that the lack of members did not affect the Control Yuan’s freezing of Ko’s assets.
The Control Yuan said that laws and regulations stipulate members must formally censure an official before the matter can be published in the gazette.
The Control Yuan has no members authorized to enable this process at the moment, it said.
The branch is legally designated to be in charge of enforcing the Political Donations Act (政治獻金法) and Recusal of Public Servants Due to Conflicts of Interest Act (公職人員利益衝突迴避法), which means it does not need appointed members to investigate Ko, it said.

Natalia Rjumin-Girardet, a Swiss national who narrowly escaped deadly flash floods in Nepal while making a spiritual journey to Mount Kailash in Tibet, said that “divine providence” saved her.
The 70-year-old yoga teacher was traveling by bus with a group of eight people of different nationalities along a road bordering the Bhotekoshi River when the disaster struck.
“Suddenly, I saw the [group’s] cook jump out of the bus window. Someone else opened the door and I saw a huge mountain ... in the fog,” Rjumin-Girardet told reporters by phone from a hotel in Kathmandu.
Photo: AP
Then she realized that the “mountain” was actually a “massive wave of water and mud.”
“I saw everyone start running, so I started running too,” she said, her voice trembling. “I think we had a minute, maybe two, to get out of the bus.”
The Russian-born woman with short, gray hair said that by luck, a small, concrete staircase stood right next to where the vehicle had come to a halt, allowing the group to get away.
Photo: AFP / Ludmila Yilmaz
After the stairs, “we ran” up a hillside, she said, adding that no one in the group remembered how they had reached higher ground, as they were all in a state of “shock.”
“Those stairs saved us,” she said. “We were incredibly lucky.”
Once she realized she was safe, Rjumin-Girardet said she turned around and saw the devastation below.
“I saw houses, cars and even buses being swept away by the wave,” she said.
“It was truly awful,” she said, adding that it was only later that the group understood the full scale of the disaster.
Their hotel and the entire village of Syabrubesi where they had spent the night had been completely destroyed.
According to the latest figures, rescue teams had recovered more than 1,100 bodies, while nearly 4,500 people were missing after the gigantic wave of freezing water, rocks and debris triggered by a glacial collapse roared down the China-Nepal border on Wednesday last week.
The members of the group that Rjumin-Girardet was with, who had been on their way to make a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, see their survival as a “miracle.”
“It was divine providence that allowed the group to stay alive,” she said. “If we had arrived two or three minutes earlier or later, we might not have been lucky enough to be saved.”
She described how the survivors spent the first night after the flash flood huddled in a small barn on a hilltop, in the cold and rain.
“We hardly slept,” she said.
The next morning, a helicopter evacuated them to an area where military personnel took charge of them, before transferring them to Kathmandu.
Having lost her phone on the bus, Rjumin-Girardet was finally able to notify her loved ones that she was alive thanks to a friend who had her sister’s number.
Today, the group remains very close.
“For us, August 26 has become an important date, [marking] a rebirth,” she said.
Rjumin-Girardet, who founded Art and Peace — a Swiss association using art and creativity as tools for dialogue — said she did not yet know whether she would return to Switzerland or continue her journey.
However, she said she hoped lessons could be drawn from the harrowing experience.
“I would like everyone to have more compassion for others,” she said. “Perhaps our world could change a little for the better.”

Legislature vows to scrutinize budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:50 UTC
01:40:50 KST

The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) yesterday vowed to strictly scrutinize the Cabinet’s NT$607.63 billion (US$19.13 billion) supplementary budget, blasting a massive bailout for CPC Corp, Taiwan as illegal and demanding the promulgation of the opposition’s drone industry act.
In response to the inclusion of military drone procurements in the supplementary budget, the KMT caucus called on the Cabinet and President William Lai (賴清德) to countersign and promulgate the opposition-majority legislature’s version of the drone budget.
For the government to request supplementary funds, it must first approve the regular budget allotted to the same projects, it said.
Photo: Wang Yi-sung, Taipei Times
This means the opposition’s National Defense Autonomy and Uncrewed Vehicle Industry Development Act (強化國防自主暨無人載具產業發展條例) must be countersigned before the lawmakers can discuss the supplementary budget, it said.
The NT$145.69 billion funding for arms, primarily drones, in the supplementary budget must be implemented in a manner consistent with the drone industry legislation passed by the KMT and the TPP, it said.
This means the Ministry of National Defense must prioritize domestically sourced systems and components to stimulate the rise of an indigenous drone industry fully supported by integrated domestic supply chains, the KMT caucus said.
The legislature is to scrutinize the government’s proposal for compliance with these conditions, it said.
The public and the Taiwanese drone industry overwhelmingly support the opposition’s drone act, the caucus said.
TPP caucus whip Jacky Chen (陳清龍) said that the Cabinet’s resort to proposing a supplementary budget proved that the government lied about the necessity of funding drones with a special budget act.
Using a supplementary budget to subsidize the CPC is not lawful under Article 79 of the Budget Act (預算法), which stipulates that such budgets can only be invoked if a major incident causes a state-run enterprise’s expenses to exceed the legal budget, he added.
No major incident caused the CPC to be in the red for six years straight other than its own unprofitability, he said.
The Cabinet is using 40 percent of its proposed supplementary budget on the CPC instead of funding defense or making meaningful increases to the salaries of police, firefighters and military service personnel, he said.

President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday paid tribute to Taiwan’s fallen military personnel and pledged that his government would provide better care for armed service members as the nation marked Armed Forces Day.
During a ceremony in Taipei, Lai laid flowers at the Martyrs’ Shrine, which honors nearly 500,000 soldiers who died fighting during World War II for the Republic of China.
Other senior government officials and descendants of the fallen soldiers also attended the Fall Martyrs’ Commemoration Ceremony in Taipei’s Zhongshan District (中山).
Photo: CNA
Earlier yesterday, Lai thanked all of the members of Taiwan’s armed forces for protecting national security and defending the nation’s sovereignty.
Over the past year, his administration has improved salaries and benefits for military personnel, including raising combat and professional allowances earlier this year, Lai wrote on Facebook.
From next year, military personnel, civil servants and teachers are to receive a 4 percent salary increase, he said.
The government will continue to improve living and training environments for the armed forces, while providing better support for service members’ families, including childcare, so that military personnel can focus on their mission of protecting the country, he added.
Armed Forces Day in Taiwan is celebrated annually on Sept. 3 to honor the armed forces and Japan’s defeat in World War II.

Canada’s battle to build a new global defense bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:42 UTC
01:40:42 KST

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has thrown his weight behind a new global defense bank intended to help allies rearm, but other major economies have yet to commit just weeks before prospective members are due to sign up.
The Defense, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB) has been seeking to raise about 100 billion euros (US$116 billion) and use the money to lend at low cost to governments and contractors for defense projects. It would also offer guarantees for lenders financing smaller firms seen as riskier borrowers. Alongside Canada, where the DSRB would be based, Albania, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania, Turkey and Ukraine have pledged their support.
Two officials from countries involved in the project said that the DSRB had secured about 5 billion euros in commitments by last month. It is aiming for about 20 billion euros in paid-in capital and a further 80 billion euros it can tap when needed, one of them said. However, Germany, Britain and other G7 countries have so far declined to join, raising questions over whether the DSRB can achieve the triple-A credit rating it wants to help secure the lowest funding costs.
“To make a good impression on the ratings agencies, they would need to have several other substantial governments participating,” said William Perraudin, managing director at Risk Control, an analytics firm specializing in multilateral institutions.
Reuters spoke to eight people with knowledge of the discussions to join the bank. Some said that whether the DSRB can offer cheaper financing than highly rated national governments was a stumbling block for some potential members.
The amount of capital countries would need to commit while public finances are strained, the bank’s governance and overlaps with existing initiatives were also cited as factors. Canada said it is talking with many countries ahead of a charter signing that its lead negotiator for the DSRB, Isabelle Hudon, said on the sidelines of July’s Farnborough Airshow was planned for the autumn.
“We are proceeding at pace, developing Articles of Agreement and working with allies and partners alike to form a group of founding nations,” Canadian Ministry of Finance press secretary John Fragos said.
Speaking at Farnborough on a panel dedicated to defense investment, DSRB founder Rob Murray said the lender would help countries rearm to counter mounting security threats.
“We need 10 of them, frankly,” the former British Army officer and NATO innovation chief said.
European countries are increasing defense spending after US President Donald Trump demanded that they take on more of NATO’s burden, although few are close to meeting the alliance’s latest targets. Carney earlier this year called for an alliance of “middle powers” to respond to what he sees as the fracturing of the US-led world order.
The DSRB would “ensure that Canada and our allies have the capacity to meet the challenges of a more dangerous and divided world together,” he said in July.
Perraudin said the DSRB could use financial leverage separate from the balance sheets of already indebted nations to boost defense investment. However, to become a significant player, it would need additional sovereign backing beyond current commitments, he said.
While big European economies can already borrow cheaply, membership would ensure their domestic contractors can access the DSRB funding, said Linus Terhorst of the Royal United Services Institute think tank.
Five of the people with knowledge of the talks about DSRB membership cited potential overlap with other financing efforts, including the EU’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program and Britain’s proposed Multilateral Defense Mechanism (MDM).
The EU launched its 150 billion euros SAFE defense financing program last year, while Britain is developing a MDM with the Netherlands, Finland and Poland focused on joint procurement.
One official also cited concerns about the upfront capital required from governments, as well as uncertainty over how projects would be selected. Larger countries have been asked to put forward about 1 billion euros, two people with knowledge of the plans said.
Murray said that this could be paid over three years and would in time return profits through dividends, while the DSRB would provide a more permanent institution for financing defense than SAFE and could work with any procurement method.
“If we do this properly, higher defense expenditure can generate technology, factories, skilled jobs, stronger supply chains and economic growth while simultaneously strengthening deterrence,” Murray said.
Canada hopes Britain could reconsider under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham, whose minister of defense, Wes Streeting, described the DSRB at Farnborough as a “really interesting and innovative mechanism.” He also said he did not see the proposed defense bank and MDM as being in competition. Britain previously declined to join, citing concerns over value for money. According to his Downing Street office, Burnham discussed the DSRB alongside the MDM scheme with Carney in July and with Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden during a visit last month to Kyiv.
“The UK joining would create pressure from German industry on the German government to join,” said Terhorst.
A German Ministry of Finance spokesperson said that its position on the DSRB had not changed since July, when it said it had taken part in DSRB talks as an observer and was reviewing the outcome. The Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that no decision had been made about participating.
British and German industry groups have lobbied their countries to join. Andrew Kinniburgh of Make UK Defense said companies risked being excluded from projects financed through the bank if Britain stayed out.
About a dozen banks, including JPMorgan and Deutsche Bank, have provided some US$10 million in funding or services in kind to help establish the DSRB, a person with knowledge of the matter said. The lenders, which could earn millions in fees arranging DSRB-funded projects, also backed an advertisement in the Financial Times newspaper saying the project had “the hallmarks of a future AAA-rated multilateral financial institution.”
JPMorgan and Deutsche Bank declined to comment.
Canada’s Hudon said at Farnborough that she was confident the DSRB could get a triple-A rating. Murray said a multilateral bank’s rating depends on many factors and often exceeds the average rating of members.
Ottawa is prepared to launch the bank with the current group of supporters, one person involved in the project said, with other countries free to join later. That could help cement the rating it wants.
“The creditworthiness of multilateral institutions is principally driven by the support of their core shareholders,” said Elisabeth Rudman, head of financial institution ratings at Morningstar DBRS.

Russia’s and Iran’s war efforts are being materially supported by Chinese supplies of drone components and missile fuels. Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:40:42 UTC
01:40:42 KST

American Cole Houshmand yesterday took the Fiji Pro title ahead of Gabriel Medina in pumping conditions at the Cloudbreak reef, while in-form Canadian teenager Erin Brooks earned a second straight world tour title.
Californian Houshmand had lost six times in the first round this year, but turned his season around by beating reigning world champion Yago Dora in the quarter-finals and Medina in the title-decider.
His victory in the final was all the more impressive as Brazilian Medina scored a perfect 10 with his first ride of the final in a 1.8m to 2.4m swell.
Photo: EPA-EFE
“I went on the first wave and when I turned back, he was just getting blown out of a perfect wave. I was thinking ‘what have I done?’” Houshmand said.
Three-time world champion Medina failed to back up his first ride, and Houshmand ran out a 16.87-15.17 winner to take his third title in three years on the elite tour.
“I’m pretty speechless. It never really goes the way you expect it,” Houshmand said. “But if you just put your head down and work hard, and have faith, it’ll all work out.”
Medina’s second place moved him up to fourth in the standings, 6,840 points behind compatriot and championship leader Italo Ferreira with five rounds of the season to go.
Texas-born Brooks also landed a 10-point ride when the eighth stop of the tour kicked off last week and she kept up her fine form to claim back-to-back titles after her win at the Tahiti Pro last month.
The 19-year-old beat five-times world champion Carissa Moore 11.84-9.97 in the semi-finals and clinched her second Fiji Pro title when Australian Isabella Nichols was unable to compete after suffering an injury.
“I love Bella like a sister and I was so [devastated] to hear she got injured,” Brooks said.
“It’s been unreal,” she added of her last two events. “I was having a real shocker [of a season]. I was having some disbelief in myself. I’m just so grateful to be where I am right now.”
The two straight wins moved Brooks up to eighth in the women’s rankings, which are led by Hawaiian Moore.
The world tour next moves on to southern California for the Trestles Pro from Friday next week to Sept. 20.

Russia is “actively” preparing sabotage operations against Denmark, particularly its defense industry, the head of the Danish intelligence service was quoted as saying yesterday.
The warning came after EU countries summoned Russia’s envoys and discussed fresh sanctions after an explosive-laden drone incident in Germany that the bloc’s foreign policy chief said bore the marks of “state-sponsored terrorism.”
Russia has in the past few months been accused of ratcheting up sabotage attacks against European backers of Ukraine.
Photo: Reuters
“The Russians are actively preparing sabotage operations targeting the defense industry in Denmark,” Emil Graesholm, head of counterintelligence at the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, said in an interview with newspaper Berlingske.
“It is fundamentally important that the defense industry, in the broad sense, take the necessary security measures so that it is able to protect itself,” Graesholm told broadcaster TV2. “Many actors in the sector are already actively working on this.”
Russian security services are seeking to recruit “completely ordinary Danes” for missions, he said.
The missions might, for example, involve taking photographs, and checking and reporting on access and security conditions around a facility, he said.
“We are talking about the methods, because they don’t need to look like a spy movie,” he told Berlingske.
Separately, Norwegian authorities on Wednesday seized a Russian vessel — the Professor Molchanov — in the Arctic archipelago of Svalbard at the request of Ukraine’s Naftogaz as part of a global effort to enforce a US$4.22 billion arbitration award stemming from Russia’s 2014 illegal annexation of Crimea and its seizure of Ukrainian energy assets.
In 2023, an arbitration tribunal in The Hague, Netherlands, ordered Russia to pay US$4.22 billion to the Ukrainian state-owned energy company for unlawfully seizing its assets in Crimea.
After Russia’s refusal to pay the award, Naftogaz has been petitioning national courts seeking court orders to seize Russian commercial assets.
“This is another important step towards restoring justice for Russia’s unlawful seizure of Naftogaz assets in Crimea. Russia cannot evade responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award. We will continue to pursue Russian assets around the world,” Naftogaz chief executive officer Sergii Fedorenko said.
The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs yesterday called the seizure “piracy.”
Russian Minister for the Development of the Russian Far East and Arctic Alexei Chekunkov said that Moscow would challenge the ruling, saying the seizure of the vessel was “another example of Western countries’ legal nihilism and lawlessness,” Interfax news agency reported.

Data center spending to reach US$31.6tn by 2050
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:38 UTC
01:40:38 KST

Global data center spending is set to reach US$31.6 trillion through 2050 to meet the world’s growing appetite for artificial intelligence (AI), an investment boom with no precedent in history, PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP (PwC) said in a report released on Wednesday.
Dwarfing projects such as the railways, Internet and electrification, spending on data centers could even hit US$50 trillion over the next two-and-a-half decades if AI adoption accelerates beyond PwC’s “central scenario” forecast, the firm said.
For comparison, US GDP is about US$30 trillion.
Photo: AFP
With consumers, companies and governments increasingly using AI, tech giants such as Microsoft Corp and Amazon.com Inc and smaller data center providers are setting up new computing facilities across the planet at a rapid clip. The bulk of the spending would go into what fills the data centers — hardware from companies such as global AI chip leader Nvidia Corp.
At the same time, the tech industry is trying to blunt a backlash against data centers that threatens to slow down the buildout.
At least 75 projects, worth about US$130 billion combined, were blocked or delayed by local opposition during the first three months of this year, according to research group Data Center Watch.
Protesters cite concerns about environmental impacts, resource consumption and more broadly how AI could upend employment and society.
The US would capture nearly half the projected data center spending, at US$15.1 trillion, PwC said.
The Asia-Pacific region would follow at US$8.2 trillion, Europe at US$5.6 trillion, the Middle East at US$1.1 trillion and Africa at US$255 billion of the cumulative capital expenditure, PwC’s inaugural Global Data Center Outlook showed.
“Railways. Electrification. The Internet. Each required enormous amounts of capital and defined an era,” the researchers said in the report. “The AI infrastructure cycle under way dwarfs all three. This one resets every four to six years — and shows no signs of ending.”
On an annual basis, global data center spending would increase from about US$800 billion this year to US$1.1 trillion in 2030 and US$1.8 trillion in 2050, PwC predicted.
China and India would drive the largest share of incremental demand, supported by large populations, rapidly expanding digital economies, and substantial headroom for AI to embed in business and consumer activity.
While global demand is strong, factors such as power availability, data sovereignty requirements and the flow of semiconductors would determine which regions capture the investments, PwC said.
Power would be the foremost factor that shapes where AI infrastructure investment occurs, it said.
Indeed, much of the forecast hinges on how fast reliable electricity supply for data centers can be established, the report said.
Affordable, reliable, and increasingly low-carbon electricity at scale is the hardest requirement for many markets to meet.
While the researchers’ projection assumes a fairly open trading system where chips move freely across borders, disruptions in semiconductor supply chains could cut global investment by nearly 20 percent, they said.
Meanwhile, a growing sovereignty push could redistribute, but not reduce, global investment.
“The US$31.6 trillion question isn’t whether the capital exists. It does,” the researchers said. “Nor is the question whether the demand is real. It is. The question is which regions, operators and institutions are positioned to capture it and which aren’t.”

Palau urges ‘unified’ China response
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:38 UTC
01:40:38 KST

Palau’s president yesterday called for a “unified” Pacific response to a missile test by China in July, while Taiwan and its Pacific allies a day earlier at the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) reaffirmed their commitment to peace, stability and prosperity.
China gave only a handful of nations short notice before test-firing an intercontinental ballistic missile in July, sparking condemnation from several Pacific leaders.
The 18-member PIF being held in Palau was expected to release a communique after press time last night, with a formal response to the test possibly included.
Photo: AFP
Palau, which invited Taiwan to attend sideline events as an aid partner, urged the region to send a strong message.
“That’s definitely something that we’ll be discussing today [yesterday], and a unified Pacific voice is critical in getting Beijing to respect sovereignty, to respect transparency, and to be a responsible partner,” Palauan President Surangel Whipps Jr told reporters.
“I think that’s the message that we should be sending to Beijing,” Whipps said. “So it’s important we have a unified position and we’ll work on that.”
He said that Beijing had “threatened and really disrespected” the region with the test of the rocket, which monitors said appeared to land in the ocean somewhere between the Solomon Islands, Nauru and Tuvalu.
“They never bothered to tell us that that’s what’s happening,” he said.
Beijing said the test launch was “a routine arrangement of China’s annual military training” and that “relevant countries were informed in advance.”
The PIF yesterday had a leaders’ retreat, during which officials were expected to hammer out the wording for a joint communique.
Meanwhile, Chinese Special Envoy for Pacific Island Countries Affairs Qian Bo (錢波) said that there would be “consequences” after Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) attended the PIF opening ceremony.
On Wednesday, Taiwan and its three Pacific allies reaffirmed their commitment to peace, stability and prosperity in a joint statement.
The statement — which was signed by Lin, Whipps, Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine and Tuvaluan Prime Minister Feleti Teo — also expressed support for the 2050 Strategy for the Blue Pacific Continent, a regional framework aimed at addressing shared challenges and promoting sustainable development.
The statement was signed during the 30th Taiwan/Republic of China Forum Countries Dialogue, hosted by Whipps alongside the PIF.
At the Taiwan forum, Lin exchanged views with the leaders of diplomatic allies on talent development and regional exchanges, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement.
Lin proposed integrating education, training, employment and skills assessment, drawing on Taiwan’s experience in vocational education to help its allies cultivate talent that meets the needs of their societies and industries, the ministry said.
The initiative aims to improve the employability of young people and build a stronger talent base for their countries’ long-term development, it said.
The leaders also explored the feasibility of using funds from allies to invest in Taiwan’s capital markets, and expanding cooperation in areas including finance, industry and economic development, the ministry said.
Although the international landscape has continued to change, Taiwan has remained committed to working with its Pacific partners in a pragmatic and mutually beneficial way to address shared challenges, Lin said.

MAC approves China travel for APEC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
16:40:34 UTC
01:40:34 KST

The Mainland Affairs Council (MAC) yesterday said that it had conducted risk assessments and contingency planning for all government officials scheduled to attend APEC ministerial meetings in China this year, and has determined that they can proceed.
The council made the remarks as Minister of Labor Hung Sun-han (洪申翰) is scheduled to attend the APEC Human Resources Development Ministerial Meeting in Nanjing on Sept. 21, making him the first minister to travel to China since President William Lai (賴清德) took office in 2024.
“So far, officials’ trips have gone smoothly. We think the overall risks this time would be manageable,” MAC Deputy Minister and spokesman Liang Wen-chieh (梁文傑) told a news conference in Taipei.
Photo: Chen Yu-fu, Taipei Times
Officials including Deputy Minister of Economic Affairs Chiang Wen-jo (江文若) and former chief trade negotiator at the Office of Trade Negotiations Yang Jen-ni (楊珍妮) have traveled to China to attend APEC-related meetings this year, Liang said.
Hung would enter China by presenting APEC’s invitation and following the organizer’s arrangement, without having to present a Mainland Travel Permit for Taiwan Residents, Liang said.
Hung’s participation and remarks at APEC already demonstrate the existence of the Republic of China (Taiwan), with no need for any additional declaration of sovereignty, he added.
Any interaction with Chinese officials during the meetings can proceed naturally, and Hung need not avoid or make a deliberate attempt to meet, he said.
“We hope that, as the APEC host, China will treat our delegation appropriately in accordance with existing practices and APEC rules,” Liang said.
Liang also responded to reports that a Taiwanese man was interrogated by Chinese immigration officers during a business trip to Shanghai due to his past work as an intern for Amnesty International.
China views international human rights organizations as engaging in anti-China activities, and Taiwanese who were participants of these groups risk being interrogated or persecuted, Liang said.
“This would cause people to censor themselves and avoid joining activities hosted by civil groups, constituting a major threat to Taiwan’s democratic system,” Liang said.
So far, about half of Taiwanese who were interrogated or detained during trips to China are current or retired civil servants, Liang said.
While China’s Taiwan Affairs Office tried to assure the public that they should not be concerned about its new entry and exit regulations, which are to take effect on Sept. 15, so long as they do not engage in criminal activities in China, the travel risks do not disappear, he said.
“They could still be interrogated for what they have done in Taiwan and elsewhere,” he said, adding that the best way to counter the problem is to disclose such incidents in public.
Liang said that the purpose of asking people to register trips to China is so that the government can provide timely assistance in case of emergencies.
