Another European country transfers gold out of US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:31:16 UTC
00:31:16 KST

Another European country transfers gold out of US
The central bank of the Netherlands has become the latest country to move gold holdings out of the United States, announcing on Wednesday that it had transferred 86 tons of bullion to London. The bank described the move as “crisis preparedness” during a time of “increasing geopolitical unrest.”
The transfer was carried out between March and August. The bulk of the gold was moved from New York, with the rest coming from Canada. Only about 27 tons were physically transported across the Atlantic, while the remainder was accomplished through sales in the Americas and repurchases in London. Prior to the transfer, the Dutch central bank (DNB) had held 313 tons in North America.
“With this relocation, we have improved the tradability of our gold reserves,” according to a written statement by DNB Governor Olaf Sleijpen. “We expect that we will never need to use them, but we do need to strengthen our resilience and preparedness.”
The DNB’s move comes after France’s central bank sold its remaining 129 tons of gold held at Federal Reserve vaults in New York between July 2025 and January 2026, leaving it with no bullion in the United States. The proceeds from the sale were used to purchase an equivalent amount of gold in Europe.
In 2017, under the first administration of US President Donald Trump, Germany’s Bundesbank announced that it had completed the transfer to Frankfurt of 300 tons of its gold held in New York. During Trump’s second term, several prominent German economists have called for the removal of the bank’s remaining holdings from the US.
Venezuela under President Hugo Chavez repatriated about 160 tons of its gold reserves from foreign banks, a move that was completed by January 2012. However, some 31 metric tons of Venezuelan gold are still held by the Bank of England. Efforts undertaken by then-President Nicolas Maduro to bring the bullion home were stymied by Great Britain, which did not recognize Maduro as the legitimate head of Venezuela’s government.
The DNB praised Bank of England-held gold as being “the world’s most easily tradable gold.” The Dutch central bank reported owning 612.4 metric tons as of the end of 2025, worth about €72 billion (about $84 billion).

Russia Church Official Wants Stalin-Era Divorce Rules Back as Demographic Fix
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:25:03 UTC
00:25:03 KST

- Category
- World
Russia Church Official Wants Stalin-Era Divorce Rules Back as Demographic Fix
A senior Russian Orthodox Church official proposed on September 2 reviving a Stalin-era Soviet decree to make divorce significantly harder in Russia, framing the move as a demographic necessity modeled after wartime policy, according to the independent Russian outlet Agentstvo.
Fyodor Lukyanov, chairman of the Patriarchal Commission on Family Affairs, Protection of Motherhood and Childhood, made the proposal at the Eastern Economic Forum during a session titled
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"The Family as the Foundation for Preserving the Spiritual and Moral Values and Sovereignty of Russia," Lukyanov argued that abortion and divorce must be made economically disadvantageous and pushed to the social margins through a coordinated effort by the state and business.
"All citizens who were in a de facto marital relationship were required to register their marriage, indicating the duration of their cohabitation. Passports introduced a 'marital status' field. Differentiated taxation was introduced—income tax rates fell as the number of children increased.
The divorce procedure became more complex: two stages, a mandatory statement of grounds, the summoning of the spouse, and the calling of witnesses. This is not today's online divorce in our country," Lukyanov stated at the forum.
Lukyanov explicitly invoked Decree No. 118/11, issued by the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR in July 1944, arguing that the Soviet experience offers "a great deal of good that can be drawn upon given the current situation."
He noted that the USSR lost 26 million people during the Second World War and that the Soviet leadership responded with demographic measures—measures he argued Russia must now "retrieve and use." Under the 1944 decree, divorce required a court ruling rather than a simple registry office filing, and proceedings could include interrogations by prosecutors. The decree's provisions on marriage and divorce remained in force until 1965.
Lukyanov also raised questions about the official statistics on abortion, suggesting that a reported decline in their number reflects a fall in the population of women of reproductive age and possible manipulation of data.
He pointed to Russia's rate of recorded miscarriages—44% of pregnancies with an abortive outcome in 2024—and implied that clinics have a financial incentive to reclassify abortions as miscarriages under the compulsory medical insurance system, since the reimbursement rate for the latter is higher.
"Is this what happened to our women? Or is someone changing the statistics? Yes, most likely," he told the forum. Agentstvo noted that the 44% figure is calculated not from all known pregnancies but from those ending in an abortive outcome, a measure distinct from the World Health Organization's (WHO) standard reference range of 10–15%.
The proposal comes amid a deepening demographic crisis in Russia, with senior officials increasingly pressuring young people to have more children. In July, Federation Council Speaker Valentina Matviyenko demanded that young Russians start families early and have at least three children before turning 35.
Russia recorded 1.178 million births in 2025, below the previous post-Soviet low of 1.215 million in 1999, while births fell by another 17,000 year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026.

Russia Threw Six FPV Drones at Ukraine’s Armed Robot—It Completed the Mission Anyway
Ukraine’s Droid TW-12.7 unmanned ground vehicle survived five FPV drone strikes and completed its combat mission before a sixth hit finally disabled the platform, according to a DevDroid press release shared with UNITED24 Media on September 2.
Soldiers from the fire support company of Ukraine’s 74th Separate Reconnaissance Battalion deployed the UGV during a remotely conducted operation against a concentration of Russian troops.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
As the Droid TW-12.7 approached the position, two FPV drones struck the vehicle almost simultaneously. One of the hits damaged its aiming module, but the platform remained mobile and continued the mission.
Operators adapted to the damage by aiming in the direction of the weapon barrel and opened fire on the target. Two additional FPV drones struck the UGV during the engagement, but it remained operational long enough to complete its primary task.
The vehicle then began withdrawing and survived a fifth FPV strike while continuing to move. A sixth drone eventually disabled it on the return route.
DevDroid said the Russian troop concentration was cleared and enemy forces suffered losses. The entire operation was carried out remotely, allowing Ukrainian personnel to avoid direct contact with Russian troops.
“In this engagement, the enemy was able to stop the Droid only with the sixth FPV drone, but they still failed to prevent it from completing the mission. For us, this is what survivability means in practice: after being hit, a system must not simply remain mobile—it must retain enough functionality for its operators to complete the mission and achieve the intended result,” DevDroid CEO Yurii Poritskyi said.
The Droid TW-12.7 is a Ukrainian reconnaissance-and-strike UGV developed by DevDroid. It is equipped with a remotely operated turret carrying a 12.7 mm M2 Browning heavy machine gun, as well as an integrated ballistic computer and AI-assisted targeting functions.
The platform is designed to engage personnel, vehicles, and lightly armored targets while allowing Ukrainian troops to conduct dangerous frontline missions from a safer distance.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukraine is expanding its fleet of unmanned ground vehicles, aiming to produce at least 50,000 combat and logistics robots this year to reinforce infantry units and bridge manpower shortages along the frontline.

PUMA Partners With Ukrainian Fashion Brand CHER’17 for First-Ever Collaboration
German sportswear company PUMA has partnered with Ukrainian fashion brand CHER’17, marking PUMA’s first collaboration with a local fashion label in the Ukrainian market.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the press release, the CHER’17 x PUMA collection is built around the concept of unexpected changes to everyday plans, reflected in the campaign’s central message, “No plan is a plan.” The collaboration reinterprets PUMA’s classic designs through details inspired by everyday accidents and imperfections.
“Modern life requires improvisation: so many things genuinely don’t go according to plan. We decided to dedicate our collaboration to this spontaneity and explore it through a new perspective on PUMA’s classic silhouettes,” says Tetyana Parfilieva, Creative Director of CHER’17.
The collection centers on a customized version of the PUMA Suede, one of the company’s signature footwear silhouettes. CHER’17 has reworked the model with prints and visual effects designed to resemble paint splatters, peeling surfaces, and traces of dirt.
Rather than treating these elements as imperfections, the collection incorporates them as intentional design features, reflecting its broader theme of adapting to circumstances that do not go as planned.
The collaboration also extends beyond footwear, with T-shirts featuring visual elements based on the same concept.
For CHER’17, the partnership represents another step in the Ukrainian brand’s development and its cooperation with international fashion companies. The project also adds to a growing number of collaborations between Ukrainian labels and established global brands.
“This collaboration was entirely an initiative of the local PUMA Ukraine team. We have a great appreciation for our brands and had long wanted to create a joint local project. CHER’17 was a perfect match for us in terms of values: it represents boldness, dynamism, and contemporary urban style,” Olha Tyshchenko, Brand Manager at PUMA Ukraine, said in a comment to UNITED24 Media.
She noted that in today’s reality, many circumstances are beyond people’s control and can unfold differently from what was expected, stressing that such unexpected changes should not be a reason to become discouraged or stop moving forward.
“Sometimes, it is precisely these unexpected turns that give rise to something truly exciting, authentic, and special—just like this collaboration,” Tyshchenko concluded.
The collaboration follows other recent milestones for Ukrainian fashion on the international stage. Earlier this year, Ukrainian fashion brand LITKOVSKA made its debut on the official Paris Fashion Week runway schedule, where it presented its Fall-Winter 2026/27 collection, FIREFLY.

Rights groups urge US lawmakers to drop provision to deepen defense ties with Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Rights groups urge US lawmakers to drop provision to deepen defense ties with Israel
WASHINGTON, Sept 3 - Dozens of civil rights and advocacy groups are urging Congress to scrap a defense bill provision that would deepen U.S.-Israeli military technology ties, according to a letter seen by Reuters, at a time of growing U.S. skepticism toward the longtime ally.
The provision would deepen cooperation between the U.S. and Israeli defense sectors by accelerating joint military technology development and other partnerships. The bill passed the House of Representatives in July and awaits Senate action.
The provision of the 2027 National Defense Authorization Act, known as Section 219, seeks to set up frameworks for joint ventures, licensing agreements and U.S.-based co-production partnerships with the Israeli industry.
In Thursday's letter addressed to leaders of the House and Senate Armed Services Committees, 56 groups said deeper integration with Israel's defense sector would be "exceptionally dangerous" and urged lawmakers to remove the provision.
The groups include Amnesty International USA and the civil rights network National Lawyers Guild as well as Arab and Jewish advocacy groups.
"At a time in which American interests are increasingly diverging from those of Israel, and American public opinion is turning increasingly against unconditional support to Israel, creating new points of influence for Israel in the U.S. defense-technology ecosystem is exceptionally dangerous," said the letter, which has not been previously reported.
Israel is one of Washington's closest allies in the Middle East, and the two countries cooperate extensively on defense and intelligence issues. Supporters say deeper ties could help speed military innovation and technology development.
A spokesperson from the Israeli Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment on this story.
But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a May interview with CBS that he hoped to wean Israel off U.S. military support within a decade. In a June letter to a U.S. congressman he wrote that the time has come for Israel "to move from aid recipient to partner."
Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen told Reuters that it was not in U.S. national interests to deepen such cooperation with the Netanyahu government.
"This provision ... threatens to compromise sensitive technologies and, based on our prior experience, risks giving the Government of Israel the ability to interfere in U.S. defense decisions," Van Hollen said.
U.S. PUBLIC SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL DECLINES
U.S. public support for Israel has fallen since the Gaza war began in 2023, particularly among Democrats. A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48% of voters and 66% of Democrats believe the United States is too supportive of Israel, up from 16% and 20% when the question was first asked in 2017.
Support for Israel among Democratic voters has plummeted, candidates critical of Israel are winning Democratic primaries and even moderate lawmakers are increasingly willing to challenge decades of U.S. support for Israel.
The Islamist militant Hamas group, in an October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, killed nearly 1,200 Israelis and foreign nationals and took hundreds hostage. More than 73,000 Palestinians have since been killed in Israel's subsequent assault on Gaza, according to Gaza health officials.
The letter criticizes Israel for its potential violations of international humanitarian law in its war in Gaza and rising settler violence against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. It says such developments should prevent any discussion of deepening military ties.
A memorandum of understanding that provides $3.8 billion annual U.S. military aid to Israel is approaching its expiration date in 2028 and conversations are under way on how Washington's assistance to Israel would evolve beyond that date.
Some members of Congress have already tried to strip the provision from the fiscal 2027 NDAA. Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky and Democratic Representative Ro Khanna of California introduced an amendment to block it, but it did not make it into the House version of the bill.
Once the House and Senate write their versions of the NDAA, members of the two chambers work out a compromise version of the bill, which must pass both chambers - typically near the end of the calendar year - before it can be sent to the White House for President Donald Trump to sign into law or veto. Pokémon Sleep and Japanese hospitality brand NOT A HOTEL are translating one of gaming’s most recognizable objects into inhabitable architecture. The collaboration borrows its premise from the fictional universe, where Poké Balls are conceived as comfortable places for Pokémon to rest. Here, the scale shifts from pocket-sized device to human retreat, with architecture and technology used to create an environment centered on calm, comfort, and a good night’s sleep. The idea also neatly extends the logic of Pokémon Sleep, the mobile game that tracks rest and rewards players for developing healthier sleeping habits.
the poké ball-themed hotel appears in hokkaido | images courtesy of NOT A HOTEL
A POKÉ BALL LANDS IN HOKKAIDO
For now, the structure remains deliberately mysterious. The first images reveal its unmistakable spherical exterior against Hokkaido’s open landscape, but the rooms, materials, internal organization, and sleeping experience have yet to be shown. The complete project will be unveiled on September 15, 2026, leaving a few important architectural questions unanswered — including how one furnishes a giant ball without everything rolling toward the middle.
The project sits comfortably within NOT A HOTEL’s broader approach to hospitality, which brings together design-led architecture, digital technology, and highly controlled stays. Founded in Japan in 2020, the company develops a network of distinctive residences by architects and creators, combining private ownership with hotel services and shared access across its properties. The Poké Ball may be its most pop-cultural experiment yet, but the conversion of an instantly recognizable image into a fully operational retreat follows the same appetite for architecture as experience.
the familiar sphere becomes a place to sleep
AN EXCLUSIVE NIGHT INSIDE THE ICON
The Poké Ball-Themed Hotel will not operate as a conventional property with rooms available through a booking platform. Instead, stays will be offered through a limited campaign, giving selected participants the opportunity to experience the one-off structure. Application requirements and further details will be announced alongside the full reveal on September 15 through the official Pokémon Sleep channels.
Until then, the project exists somewhere between architectural teaser, oversized collectible, and remote sleeping pod. Its success will ultimately depend on what lies beyond the circular entrance: whether the collaboration simply enlarges a familiar object or uses its unusual geometry to propose a genuinely memorable interior. The messaging here could hardly be clearer. By disclosing a test that had deliberately been kept secret, NATO was sending a direct signal to Moscow: European forces are developing longer-range strike options, and not every capability will be visible before it is ready.
NATO Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum said the test had been kept secret until after it was completed and involved a German frigate firing the missile in the North Atlantic.
The command stated: “Kept secret. Now revealed. The German Navy just tested the Israeli LORA ballistic missile from a German frigate in the North Atlantic — quietly, deliberately and with a range of 500+ km.”

It added: “NATO 3.0 looks like this: Europe is taking more responsibility, building serious capabilities and keeping a few cards close to the chest. Deterrence just got a little more interesting.”
Vice Admiral Jan Christian Kaack, Inspector of the German Navy, said: “With the successful launch of a ballistic missile last night in the North Atlantic, we made naval history. I am extremely satisfied with this achievement.”
Kaack added that the system “can be successfully deployed from our units, and the potential range exceeds anything we have known before.”
In his original statement, the German Navy chief said the trial opened a new chapter for maritime deterrence and readiness, stating that the system could be operated successfully from German units and that its possible reach exceeded previous German naval capabilities.
The test was conducted with Israel Aerospace Industries’ LORA, or Long-Range Artillery Weapon System. According to IAI, the missile has a range of around 400 kilometres and an accuracy of within 10 metres, while NATO’s public account of the German test referred to a range of more than 500 kilometres.
Israel Aerospace Industries said the missile was launched from an operational German vessel equipped with a command trailer and launcher. According to the company, the missile followed its planned trajectory, navigated to the target and successfully struck it, with both the weapon system and missile meeting the objectives of the trial.
Boaz Levy, Chairman of IAI, said: “This is an unprecedented achievement for IAI and the Israeli Ministry of Defense. The successful trial of the LORA missile, launched from a naval vessel and striking its target with exceptional precision, took place overnight in Germany – the country where the world’s first ballistic missile was developed.”
He added: “This trial demonstrates Israel’s technological strength and the unique cooperation between Israel and Germany. It marks another significant achievement alongside the deployment of the Arrow 3 system on German soil, further strengthening Germany’s defense and deterrence capabilities and deepening the strategic partnership between our two countries.”
IAI chief executive Guy Bar Lev said: “Israel Aerospace Industries is proud to take part in strengthening the strategic cooperation between the State of Israel and the Government of Germany. This significant milestone is underscored by the operational live-fire exercise (OPEX) of the LORA system, one of the world’s most advanced and combat-proven ballistic missile systems.”
The German Navy is using its OPEX initiative to trial technologies and operational concepts as part of its Marine 2035 and Beyond programme. The process is intended to allow new systems to be tested rapidly under conditions intended to resemble operational use as closely as possible.
The North Atlantic launch comes as Germany expands its investment in long-range strike and air and missile defence. The country has also begun fielding the Israeli-developed Arrow 3 ballistic missile defence system as part of its wider effort to strengthen national and NATO defensive capabilities.

US pressure on Iran starting to tell, as sanctions and blockade bite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:06:14 UTC
00:06:14 KST

US pressure on Iran starting to tell, as sanctions and blockade bite
DUBAI - A US campaign to throttle Iran’s economy by blockading its oil exports and stopping sanctions evasion is growing increasingly difficult to withstand, three senior Iranian sources said.
Washington has, in recent weeks, sought to ratchet up the economic pressure on Tehran, in an effort to extract concessions in any future negotiation that six months of conflict have so far failed to secure.
Although Iran’s clerical rulers managed to bypass sanctions for decades, the latest US moves have left them in a far more sensitive position, with few remaining channels to secure foreign currency or buy goods, the sources said.
In particular, the effort to stop Iran accessing international financing networks in other countries it has long used to keep its economy functioning poses a real and urgent threat, the sources said.
Any sign the economic campaign may break a months-long deadlock in the conflict will likely cheer US planners, though Iran has also warned it could respond to the pressure with military escalation, raising the stakes at a key moment.
Petrol stocks low as currency collapses
The war has erupted back into open fighting this week, with US attacks along Iran’s Gulf coast prompting retaliatory Iranian strikes at US bases in Arab states.
Neither side has yet signalled it is ready to make the concessions demanded by the other, leaving the war in a costly stalemate - though one that may be shifting.
While more energy is flowing to international markets through the Strait of Hormuz despite Iranian efforts to continue disrupting the seaway, the US blockade of Iranian oil exports has entirely cut off Tehran’s main source of revenue.
Adding to Iran’s problems, the economy was already deep in crisis before the conflict, with a cratering currency and spiralling inflation, while months of bombing have run up a massive bill to rebuild damaged industry and infrastructure.
Meanwhile, the country’s financial squeeze is itself biting into Tehran’s efforts to get around the sanctions regime, leaving less cash to pay the high premiums required to skirt sanctions illicitly, the sources said.
The rial has fallen to record lows over recent days and one senior source said Iran only has another two months’ supply of gasoline, which has to be imported despite domestic oil production because of limited refining capacity.
Iran’s rulers are keenly aware of the potential risks of an economic meltdown and the possibility of it reigniting the nationwide mass protests it put down in January by killing thousands of demonstrators.
“They are under very, very severe economic pressure. They’re losing control of the Straits. It’s really a question of if they choose to negotiate, and I think they’ll have to,” said Ali Ansari, modern history professor at St Andrews University in Scotland.
The war is also entering a new phase, with each side trying to influence each other’s politics.
Iran hopes the threat of inflation will deter the US administration before midterm elections in November, while Washington aims to push Iranians to revolt, a senior Iranian official said.
Blockade and secondary sanctions squeezing Tehran
The latest US measures expanded secondary sanctions that target countries doing business with Iran in a bid to stop it clearing dollar transactions needed for both oil sales and to finance crucial imports of goods and raw materials.
That effort is making Iran’s existing sanctions evasion networks - front companies, unregistered tankers and smuggling - too expensive to use, the three senior sources said.
Iranian crude loadings have fallen this month to about 260,000 barrels a day, from about 1.7 million a year earlier, according to data from commodity analytics firm Kpler, with only a trickle still moving off terminals for distribution by truck, train or smaller boats over the Caspian Sea.
Tehran says it still has tens of millions of barrels stored in tankers outside the blockade zone that it can sell, but the new sanctions mean intermediaries are stepping back or demanding more money, one of the officials said.
Total trade has fallen between 25 per cent and 35 per cent, with imports hit harder than exports, President Masoud Pezeshkian has said, one of several top officials warning in recent weeks about Iran’s rapidly deteriorating situation.
US pressure and Iran’s own attacks have meanwhile disrupted one of the main conduits for Iranian trade - the United Arab Emirates, which said on Aug 19 that all commercial exchange and financial dealings with Tehran were halted until further notice.
“If those channels stay closed, a supplier wants cash, a deal is routed through another country and a shipment arrives later and dearer,” said an Iranian trader in Tehran who deals in imported goods.
The currency has collapsed in value from around 1 million rials to the dollar a year ago to over 2.2 million rials now.
The internal impact is very painful. Official figures put 12-month average inflation at 69.9 per cent with food, beverages and tobacco prices rising at nearly twice that rate.
Official unemployment rose to 9.1 per cent in the spring, while the number of those in work fell by about 450,000 from a year earlier amid a wider fall in labour force participation.
Even for those still in work, the average monthly salary of around US$125 (S$158) a month comes nowhere near meeting basic household spending requirements that come to around US$450 a month according to official data.
“We are getting poorer every day,” said Mahnaz, a 34-year-old private-sector employee in Tehran who asked that her family name not be used. REUTERS

Belgium records nearly 3,000 deaths due to summer heatwaves
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
23:03:46 CST
00:03:46 KST

BRUSSELS, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Belgium recorded nearly 3,000 excess deaths during three periods of high temperatures this summer, according to data released Thursday by the national public health institute, Sciensano.
Data from Sciensano's Belgian Mortality Monitoring (Be-MOMO) system showed that 2,035 deaths were recorded during the first heatwave from June 18 to July 3, representing an increase in mortality of 48.8 percent. The second heatwave, from July 4 to 17, saw 535 excess deaths, a 14.8 percent increase, while the third period of intense heat, from July 28 to Aug. 16, saw a 7 percent spike in mortality, or 365 deaths.
Sciensano said the first heatwave had the most pronounced impact on mortality, with a significant increase in deaths among people aged 15 to 64. This marked the highest excess mortality levels, both in absolute numbers and as a percentage, among heatwaves analyzed in Belgium since 2000.
The institute said the severity of the episode was linked to a combination of factors: the duration of the episode, the intensity of the heat and ozone concentrations.
It also said that maximum temperatures in Belgium had hovered around 30 degrees Celsius for 10 consecutive days from June 18, including three days near 35 degrees Celsius, while ozone concentrations remained above 100 micrograms per cubic meter for 10 consecutive days.
Be-MOMO monitors mortality from all causes by comparing observed deaths with the statistically expected number of deaths. The latest figures may still be revised as mortality data are further consolidated, Sciensano said. ■

Also on Thursday, two Palestinians, including a 13-year-old child, were killed by Israeli army fire on tents housing displaced people in Beit Lahia in northern Gaza, according to local sources.
A source at Al-Shifa Hospital confirmed the fatalities.

LJUBLJANA, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Slovenia experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, with temperatures from early July through the end of August averaging 2.8 degrees Celsius above the 1991-2020 average, the Slovenian Environment Agency (ARSO) said on Thursday.
The previous record highs were recorded in 2003 and 2024, when average temperatures were 2.4 degrees above the 1991-2020 average, ARSO said.
This August was also the hottest August since temperature records began in 1950, while the country is currently experiencing an extremely severe drought that could become the worst on record, the agency said.
The Slovenian government has pledged financial assistance to farmers whose crops have been affected by the drought.
The country's Triglav glacier is also under severe pressure from the high temperatures. The Anton Melik Geographical Institute said last week that it expects the glacier on Slovenia's highest mountain, Triglav, to disappear completely by early October.
The glacier, located at an altitude of 2,864 meters, covered about 14 hectares in 1946 but had shrunk to just 0.2 hectares by 2023. ■

CONAKRY, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Guinean Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah presided over the opening ceremony of the 12th African Conference on Sexual and Reproductive Health and Rights in Conakry on Wednesday.
The conference, which will run through Saturday, brings together policymakers, researchers, health professionals, representatives of civil society, technical and financial partners, as well as young people from several African countries to discuss issues related to the sexual and reproductive health and rights of adolescents and young people.
Held under the theme "Sexual and reproductive health and rights of adolescents and young people in Africa in the face of multifaceted crises," the conference aims to promote the exchange of experiences and develop concrete responses to the challenges facing young people amid multiple humanitarian crises, the effects of climate change and declining funding for sexual and reproductive health services.
At the opening ceremony, Bah said that "Africa draws its greatest strength from its youth" and this strength "will only fully bear fruit if young people are educated, protected and healthy."
He noted that early pregnancy, unaddressed violence or delayed access to healthcare could lead to interruptions in schooling and undermine young people's prospects for the future.
"Sexual and reproductive health involves several dimensions of public policy: it concerns maternal health, education and the protection of women, equal opportunities and the quality of human capital," Bah said.
According to him, crises "amplify risks, disrupt services, keep young people away from health facilities and reduce intervention capacities," making prevention more difficult at a time when it is most needed.
He therefore called for concrete actions and policies capable of delivering tangible results in terms of the health and protection of young people.
Guinean Minister of Health and Public Hygiene Khaite Sall stressed that the rights recognized to young people should be translated into concrete actions and effective access to health services.
"Health is no longer considered a supporting expenditure, but a strategic investment in human capital and in the future of the country," she said.
According to Sall, the vision of the Guinean authorities is to advance the country toward universal health coverage while strengthening adolescents' and young people's access to local, confidential and respectful health services.
The minister also called for turning commitments into action so that sexual and reproductive rights would not remain merely principles enshrined in laws and policies, but could be effectively exercised by the people concerned.
According to the organizers, the 12th edition of the conference will focus in particular on sustainable financing for sexual and reproductive health services, adapting services to crises, combating gender-based violence, and strengthening young people's participation in decision-making. ■

China-Singapore security team claims breakthrough in hacking Starlink terminals
Darknavy gains full administrative control over SpaceX’s user terminal allowing research into the system’s security programmes
2-MIN READ2-MIN
5
 Listen
Zhang Tongin Beijing
A team of cybersecurity experts has announced they successfully compromised the latest Starlink user terminals, crossing the security boundaries of the world’s largest satellite constellation.
In a post on its social media account on Tuesday, Darknavy, an independent cybersecurity research institute headquartered in Singapore and Shanghai, said it had used sophisticated hardware attacks to gain full administrative control over the terminals, allowing it to run any custom code on the devices.
This gives researchers unprecedented freedom, according to the pot, by reopening a long-missing entry point for in-depth security studies of the Starlink satellite system.
Starlink, SpaceX’s low-Earth-orbit satellite internet service, works by connecting user terminals to satellites in near-Earth orbit, which then relay data through ground gateways to the wider internet.
As newer satellites are gradually equipped with laser links, some satellites can also communicate directly with one another via laser, reducing reliance on ground stations while improving transmission speeds and expanding global coverage.
In battlefield conditions like those in Ukraine, where no local ground gateways exist, Starlink terminals can still gain access to the internet by routing signals through satellites that connect to gateways in neighbouring countries.
The terminal acts as both an antenna and a router, making it a critical node for direct communication with the satellites.

A culprit for corrosion may have been operating under our noses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Water droplets can do their own version of the electric slide. But instead of tearing up the dance floor, they may be wearing away at our cars, infrastructure and cultural heritage sites.
Water drops that become charged by sliding along a surface can then transfer their charge when they land on materials with the right electrical properties, including metals. This eventually drives the material to corrode, even when covered by a protective coating, researchers report August 26 in Nature. Water may also pick up charge in clouds, thunderstorms and waterfalls, so this effect might be widespread.
This work could pave the way for better anticorrosion coatings, says Stefan Weber, a physicist at the University of Stuttgart in Germany who was not involved in the study. Earlier work had shown that sliding along many surfaces causes water drops to become charged, but looking to sliding electrification as a source of corrosion represents a step forward, Weber says.
It’s electric
As drops of water slid down common surfaces, including leaves and a commercial kind of glass called polystyrene glass, they can pick up an electrical charge. In an experimental setup (left), when thousands of these drops landed on the Teflon-coated copper, they caused damage visible by microscope (bottom row; scale bar represents 100 micrometers).
Corrosion’s impact on the global economy is not trivial. This broad category of damage that includes rust cost the U.S. automotive industry alone more than $30 billion in 1999. Corrosion costs are not consistently tracked, but estimates put the global cost in the trillions.
Previous work attributed damage to the physical impact of water droplets, as well as small amounts of corrosive compounds like acid that they might contain. At first, it was not clear whether these electrified drops caused damage, says Zhongyuan Ni, a physicist at the Max Planck Institute for Polymer Research in Mainz, Germany. In early experiments, he could find no damage to a surface after hundreds of drops. “One day, I just let the experiment [keep] running. I forget; I [went] to drink coffee or something,” he says. When he came back, he found signs of damage that prompted him and his colleagues to investigate further.
With knowledge that thousands — not hundreds — of drops were needed to create observable damage, the researchers continuously released drops of water onto Teflon-coated copper surface samples. They imbued drops with charge by sliding them along common surfaces like leaves and construction materials. Each surface was tilted to ensure that water drops would land on the coated copper. For comparison, the team also released water drops directly onto Teflon-coated copper with no sliding.
All of the samples hit with sliding drops appeared damaged when inspected under a microscope, but not a sample hit with direct drops. A different microscopy technique used on a damaged sample revealed that the charged water drops had not only penetrated the Teflon, but reached and corroded the copper. The team observed similar deterioration on samples of polystyrene glass–coated copper and gold, showing that the phenomenon is not unique to Teflon-coated copper.
While these charged water drops could be in the clouds or sliding along your windshield, they should not scare you, Ni says. Their effects are small. But they add up for monuments, machinery and infrastructure that are exposed to the elements for years. Small charges shouldn’t be ignored, Ni says. Even if they’re tiny, “sometimes they will play an important role.”

Additional costs for alternative logistics of agro-export amount to EUR 50-90 per tonne – UCAB head
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
17:57:35 EEST
23:57:35 KST

Additional costs for the delivery of Ukrainian agricultural products to alternative unloading points in the case of reorientation of exports from the sea route amount to EUR50-90 per tonne, said Oleh Khomenko, director general of the association Ukrainian Club of Agrarian Business (UCAB).
He stated this during a joint press conference of representatives of the mining and metallurgical and agricultural sectors entitled "Ukrainian export without sea: why ports have no alternative" at the press center of the Interfax-Ukraine news agency on Thursday.
"Logistics chains that are being rebuilt now cannot fully replace the Black Sea - neither in terms of complexity of the route, nor in terms of economy and throughput, nor in terms of cost. Because now the additional costs of delivering cargo to alternative unloading locations - the Black or Baltic Sea - amount to EUR 50 to EUR 90 per tonne," Khomenko said.
According to him, the increase in logistics affects the competitiveness of agricultural production and the financial condition of agricultural enterprises, as well as the receipt of foreign exchange earnings.
He noted that the current situation is especially critical with regard to the production cycle in the agricultural sector, since Ukraine is entering the autumn sowing period, when agricultural producers need to accumulate funds. At the same time, according to him, problems with places of grain storage and its shipment are piling up.
According to him, the period of December-January will be the most critical for the agricultural sector. If the Ukrainian seaports are not unlocked by this time, the spring sowing campaign, which will begin in March-April, may be threatened with failure due to a lack of funds among agricultural producers.
According to Khomenko, the increase in Ukrzaliznytsia tariffs by 30% additionally increases the cost of logistics for agricultural enterprises exporting products, so it should be temporarily canceled.
"This decision should be reconsidered. And for the time being, we should come to the conclusion that this increase in tariffs should be canceled at the government level or at the level of Ukrzaliznytsa, in order to alleviate the situation with liquidity and the cost of logistics for agricultural and other enterprises that export their products," he said.

====================================================================================================

Russia Is Paying for the War with Its Future Economy
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
17:56:26 EEST
23:56:26 KST

Andriy Dubas, President of the Association of Ukrainian Banks
For several years, massive government spending related to the war was one of the main drivers of the Russian economy. Military contracts ensured demand for businesses, supported employment, household incomes, and consumption. Now, this model is producing significantly weaker results: economic growth is slowing, the cost of capital remains high, and budgetary and production constraints are becoming more visible.
This is clearly evident from GDP trends. After growing by 4.9% in 2024, the Russian economy expanded by only 1% in 2025. In 2026, the Russian Ministry of Economic Development expects growth of just 0.4%, while the Bank of Russia forecasts growth in the range of 0–1%.
Government procurement supports demand; resources are concentrated in military sectors
The Bank of Russia explicitly identifies the consumer sector and the portion of the manufacturing industry focused on government procurement as key drivers of economic growth. This explains why significant government spending has long allowed Russia to sustain economic activity despite sanctions and other restrictions.
This model concentrates resources in sectors that serve government contracts. Meanwhile, parts of the civilian economy face more challenging conditions.
The need to maintain a balance between the military and civilian sectors is already being discussed within Russia itself. Putin’s special representative, Boris Titov, has warned against an excessive concentration of the economy on the needs of the military-industrial complex.
This is an important signal: while military demand remains significant, its ability to drive growth across the entire economy is gradually weakening.
High borrowing costs are accompanied by production constraints.
Another factor is the high cost of financing. Following a prolonged period of tight monetary policy, the Bank of Russia’s key rate stood at 14% in July. For businesses, this means expensive loans and more challenging conditions for new investments.
In August, the manufacturing PMI fell to 48.8 points. Companies reported declines in production and new orders, weaker demand, and rising costs for fuel and imports.
The Bank of Russia is already anticipating a further economic slowdown due to a “temporary loss of capacity” in manufacturing and logistics. This is a fundamentally important point: the issue is no longer just about demand or the cost of borrowing, but about the economy’s ability to produce and supply goods.
The consequences of Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy and logistics infrastructure are emerging as a separate factor. In particular, Russia has already revised its oil production forecast for 2026 downward, and Reuters cites the effects of the war and strikes on oil refineries among the reasons.
Budgetary pressure is becoming increasingly evident
The changes are most evident in public finances. According to preliminary data from the Russian Ministry of Finance, the federal budget deficit for January–July 2026 amounted to 6.455 trillion rubles, or 2.8% of GDP. The current annual plan calls for a deficit of 3.786 trillion rubles. The Ministry of Finance itself attributes a significant portion of the accumulated deficit to front-loading of expenditures.
Oil and gas revenues to the federal budget fell by 16.8% year-over-year over the seven-month period, to 4.595 trillion rubles. During the same period, expenditures rose by 14.5% to 28.567 trillion rubles.
Military and security spending remains substantial. The 2026 budget allocates approximately 16.84 trillion rubles for defense, security, and law enforcement combined.
The pressure is also evident at the regional level. According to Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service, in 65 of 85 Russian regions, real budget revenues at the end of 2025 were lower than in 2021. Among the reasons are reductions in federal transfers and corporate income tax revenues.
The Russian economy has so far managed to maintain its export revenues, large domestic market, and ability to reallocate significant budgetary resources. However, an ever-increasing portion of these resources is being directed toward the war effort, which limits opportunities for civilian investment, modernization, and regional development.
The cost of the war is becoming increasingly visible for Russia. In fact, it is already paying for it with its own future.

Trump congratulates Hegseth on ‘good job’ after deadly Iran wedding strike
US President Donald Trump has congratulated Secretary of War Pete Hegseth over the latest American strikes on Iran, despite one of the attacks hitting a wedding and killing several civilians.
Iranian authorities said two women and two children aged four and 16 were killed when a US munition hit a home hosting a wedding in Kuhestak, Hormozgan Province, on Tuesday. At least 67 others were wounded, many of them women and children.
According to weapons experts cited by AP and the New York Times, the fragments recovered at the site belonged to an American air-delivered guided munition, most likely a JSOW.
The Iranian Red Crescent has since asked the International Criminal Court to investigate the Kuhestak strike, while Iran’s UN envoy has urged the Security Council to condemn it.
US Central Command has said it is looking into the reports while insisting that American forces do not target civilians.
“You did a good job last night in Iran, by the way. You knocked the hell out of them,” Trump told Hegseth during an event at the White House on Wednesday. “We’re winning that one very big, by the way, in case you haven’t noticed,” he added, claiming that much of Iran’s naval and air capability has been destroyed.
Tehran responded to the latest wave of attacks by launching its own ballistic missiles and drones at US military facilities in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, and the UAE, as well as Erbil in Kurdistan Region, Iraq.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) later claimed to have killed “a number of enemy elements” and destroyed several drones in a missile and UAV attack on Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem Air Base.
Kuwait acknowledged that its air defenses had intercepted incoming missiles and drones but reported no casualties. Jordan said ten of 13 ballistic missiles that entered its airspace were intercepted.
Tuesday’s wedding strike follows several other incidents in which US attacks have caused heavy civilian casualties in Iran. On the opening day of the war in February, a US strike hit an elementary school in Minab, killing 175 people, most of them children. On the same day, a US strike also killed at least 21 civilians, including seven children, in the southern Iranian city of Lamerd.
Tehran has accused Washington of war crimes throughout the conflict, reporting up to 3,000 civilian casualties since the US and Israel launched their campaign against the Islamic Republic in February.

Berezhna: Current grounds for revoking Honored Artist title no longer meet today's requirements
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
17:49:15 EEST
23:49:15 KST

Ukraine’s Deputy Prime Minister for Humanitarian Policy and Minister of Culture, Tetiana Berezhna believes that the current grounds for revoking the title of "Honored Artist of Ukraine" are outdated and need to be revised.
"Indeed, the grounds for revoking this title [Honored Artist of Ukraine], as provided for in current legislation, no longer meet the demands of the present day. Therefore, it would likely be a good idea to review them and make them more suitable for a state of war, when a quick response is needed," Berezhna told Interfax-Ukraine on Thursday.
The deputy prime minister said that since the revocation of titles is regulated by law, changing the list of grounds for such revocation will not happen overnight.
According to the Law On State Awards of Ukraine, such awards may be revoked: upon a court conviction in which a person awarded a state honor is convicted of a serious or particularly serious crime, a criminal offense against the foundations of Ukraine’s national security, against peace, the security of humanity, and the international legal order, as well as a number of other criminal offenses; by a decision of the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine (NSDC) on the application of special economic and other restrictive measures (sanctions), enacted by a decree of the President of Ukraine, whereby a sanction in the form of revocation of a Ukrainian state award was imposed on a person who had been awarded a state award.
As reported, on September 3, a petition was posted on the website of calling for the initiation of proceedings to strip performer Oleksiy Potapenko (stage name Potap) of the honorary title "Honored Artist of Ukraine" reached the number of votes required for consideration.
According to the petition’s author, the grounds for revocation include: the public use and promotion of Russian-language cultural content; public statements and actions regarding the Ukrainian language that could be perceived as devaluing, ridiculing, or opposing Ukrainian national identity; public collaboration and the creation of joint media content with citizens of Russia and representatives of the Russian entertainment industry; and actual residence and professional activities outside of Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy awarded Oleksiy Potapenko the title of "Honored Artist of Ukraine" in June 2020.

Aussie expert says hope still exists for those trapped in Nepal tunnels
Australian tunnel safety and disaster expert Arnold Dix has urged rescuers in Nepal not to give up hope of finding survivors inside the tunnels in the Upper Trishuli-3A hydropower project, where scores of workers are feared trapped underground days after a flash flood. 
“The operation at Trishuli 3A is proceeding as a rescue, not a recovery,” Dix, who is remotely assisting the operation, wrote on LinkedIn. Footage recorded around the time of the August 26 flood shows around 30 people moving toward and seeking shelter in the power station tunnels, he said. 
Dix said tunnels can remain comparatively stable after devastation above ground and may preserve breathable air and survivable spaces. “Silence is not evidence of death. It is only the absence of a signal,” he wrote, citing past rescues in Chile, 
Thailand, and India where people survived underground for days without contact. Rescue teams are still trying to reach workers at more than a dozen hydropower sites along the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli corridor. At Trishuli-3A, a 93-member team is working with Chinese tunnel specialists, while teams from India and South Korea are assisting operations at other sites.

Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said on Thursday that 1,252 people have died and 4,216 remain missing. Around 900 people working at hydropower projects are among those still unreachable, while 11,993 people have been rescued. 
More than 21,000 security personnel have been deployed across the affected areas as rescue teams clear mud, rocks, and damaged roads. The flood swept away settlements near Nepal’s border with China, and the authorities estimate around 20,000 homes will have to be rebuilt in safer locations. 
Dix helped advise the 2023 Silkyara tunnel rescue in northern India, where all 41 workers trapped after a collapse were brought out alive after 17 days. He described the scale of Nepal’s current operation as being like “23 Silkyaras going on at the same time.”

She coordinated arson attacks on the cars of Ukrainian military personnel — an agent of the Russian GRU was sentenced to 15 years in prison
Kyiv • UNN
The court found an agent of Russian intelligence guilty of recruiting perpetrators and coordinating arson attacks on the cars of Ukrainian military personnel. Her handler is being prosecuted in absentia.
Based on materials from the Security Service of Ukraine, the court found an agent of Russian military intelligence, who was detained in 2024, guilty and sentenced her to up to 15 years in prison. She was charged under Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (high treason committed under martial law), UNN reports citing the SBU.
Details
As noted by the Security Service of Ukraine, the defendant was a local unemployed woman recruited by the enemy who was in direct contact with an employee of the Russian GRU. According to the investigation, she searched for and recruited potential perpetrators of Russian assignments in Ukraine.
It was established that the woman gave direct instructions to the defendants on making homemade incendiary devices, which they were supposed to use to destroy the vehicles of Ukrainian soldiers. During the investigation, the Security Service also documented the crimes of the agent's handler. According to the investigation, he remotely coordinated her activities: he assigned her to "replenish" the Russian agent network and monitor the commission of arson attacks
Her Russian handler was served in absentia with a notice of suspicion under Part 4 of Article 27 and Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (incitement to commit high treason). The punishment provides for 15 years or life imprisonment, with confiscation of property.

New EU border system triggers hours-long queues at Brussels Airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:40:56 UTC
23:40:56 KST

Non-European travellers arriving at Brussels Airport faced waiting times of up to three hours at border control during peak morning hours on Thursday due to the rollout of the EU's new Entry/Exit System (EES) and a seasonal surge in returning holidaymakers.
Airport spokesperson Jeffrey Franssens confirmed the delays to Dutch-language public broadcaster VRT, noting that non-European passengers experienced three-hour queues upon arrival. By contrast, European citizens using automated passport-control gates experienced shorter wait times, generally between 30 and 60 minutes.
The delays stem largely from the implementation of the EES, a digital border-management system that electronically registers non-European nationals entering and leaving the Schengen Area.
The system replaces physical passport stamps with biometric checks, including fingerprints and facial scans.
"The registration requires more steps and time per passenger. As a result, waiting times build up rapidly during busy periods," Franssens said.
Although the Belgian government deployed additional Aviation Police personnel ahead of the summer season to staff all available control booths, the airport reported that the extra workforce has proven insufficient during high-volume periods.

Lives on hold: Young Iranians watch their futures slip away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
14:40:11 UTC
23:40:11 KST

Share & more
The past six months of bombs, geopolitical tensions and the looming threat of a wider conflict have created a suffocating sense of uncertainty for many Iranians. And it’s not just about the airstrikes. Young people say the period since the US and Israel first struck their country in late February has been one of anxiety-inducing limbo, with their futures put on hold indefinitely.
The New Humanitarian spoke to five young Iranians in the capital, who shared what it feels like to be trapped, watching their best years slip away. From cancelled weddings and crushing unemployment to never-ending news updates and the vanishing of simple pleasures, their stories offer a window into what it is like to live through a war that has taken away their ability to plan for tomorrow.
In Tehran and across the country, fresh US and Iranian strikes this week were a stark reminder that, after half a year of bombing and a war of words between the US and Iran, ceasefire talks remain stalled. The Strait of Hormuz remains largely shut, while the core issues driving the conflict remain unresolved.
Iranian citizens have been left bracing for hostilities to resume at any moment. In the 40 days after the US and Israel launched attacks in late February, more than 3,500 people – including hundreds of civilians – were killed, according to the Iranian government.
While Iran’s economy has struggled for years amid sanctions, US economic pressure and the war have compounded the pain. Iranian officials have put the economic damage from the war at more than $270 billion, though the figure is a preliminary estimate. Inflation reached nearly 88% year-over-year in July with the rial hitting a record low on 2 September, while sweeping corporate budget cuts have triggered mass layoffs; more than a million people in a country of 87 million are believed to have lost their jobs.
Even when the skies over Tehran are quiet, the five young people whose words are featured here – Ziba, Nima, Fatema, Sima, and Amir Ali* – say the agony has shifted beyond the bombing itself. What weighs most heavily now is the paralysis of not knowing what comes next.
Names have been changed due to security concerns, and words have been translated, condensed, and edited for clarity.
Ziba, 27, watched her wedding plans fell apart
“Every major milestone in my life has been frozen”
My morning routine now begins before my feet even touch the floor. The very first thing I do when I wake up is grab my phone and open my main news channels. I have to scroll through everything posted overnight. The news cycle here changes by the minute. You might go to bed reading that a diplomatic agreement is imminent, only to wake up and find out that infrastructure was bombed while you were sleeping. I have to know exactly what reality I am waking up into.
The initial shock we felt when this first started has morphed into something else, but there are still moments that completely rattle me. It’s terrifying when I go outside and see massive lines of people panic-buying fuel at the petrol stations. I look at them and think, “What will happen to the city if they strike tomorrow?”
My nights are consumed by a different kind of anxiety. A few months ago, I didn't even know what [the live online flight tracker] Flightradar was. Now, before I can attempt to sleep, I am on the app monitoring the airspace over the Middle East. I check to see if civilian planes are still flying over Iran, or if flights are still landing in Israel. If I see commercial planes in the sky, I tell myself it's safe enough to close my eyes.
Even our family group chats offer no escape; they are a constant stream of terrifying rumours. Someone will forward a fake message claiming a nuclear strike is coming tonight, alongside advice to hoard food or buy power generators.
To cope with the overwhelming dread, I downloaded half a dozen mindless puzzle games on my phone. But the stress gave me such severe insomnia that I used to wake up multiple times a night just to check the news. Now, I have to take sleeping pills. When the anxiety becomes too heavy, I put on a podcast and play the puzzle games for hours, waiting for the medication to finally make my eyes heavy enough to sleep.
Every major milestone in my life has been frozen. My fiancé and I got engaged exactly 40 days before this recent wave of conflict began. We were deep into planning the wedding, but it completely fell apart. How can you book a venue, buy a wedding dress, or put down deposits when you don’t know if a war will break out tomorrow? We have stopped all planning and will probably just move into our apartment quietly without a celebration. It breaks my heart because I had to let what was supposed to be one of the best nights of my life go.
Even my smallest daily joys have vanished. I used to be obsessed with online shopping and skincare routines. I haven't bought anything in months. I am literally scraping the last drops out of my old makeup containers. Every time I think about restocking, I stop myself. I need to hoard every rial in case the economy collapses and I get laid off. And honestly, what is the point of a skincare routine if a war breaks out?
When I hang out with my friends, the panic has been replaced by a heavy numbness. Six months ago, we took every threat seriously. Now, if someone reads a headline out loud about an impending attack or a peace talk, we just laugh. We have become completely desensitised. Underneath that numbness is a profound grief. The prime years of our youth — the years we should be growing and experiencing life — are being destroyed by the egos of global powers who do not care about regular people.
Nima, 21, fears his attempt to leave Iran has set him back
“The sheer terror of being completely left behind”
For the past two years, my life has been defined by a single, obsessive goal: to emigrate from Iran by the time I turn 21. I took a massive risk and dropped out of university to make this happen. I work in video production and editing now, and every decision I’ve made since leaving school – every late night staring at editing deadlines, every rial I’ve desperately managed to save, every expensive language class I’ve paid for – has been dedicated to preparing for a visa interview at the French embassy and securing a way out. But since the conflict escalated last year, and with this endless, agonising cycle of ceasefires and new threats, my carefully constructed roadmap has been thrown into absolute chaos.
The uncertainty we are living through isn't just an abstract political talking point on the news; it is a solid brick wall standing between me and my future. I am supposed to be finalising my paperwork right now, but I wake up every morning paralysed by questions I cannot answer. If I am finally ready for my visa interview next month, will the foreign embassies in Tehran even be open? Are they quietly evacuating their diplomatic staff right now? Will any country even issue visas to young Iranians right now, or are we considered too high-risk? You just don’t know, and that not-knowing is suffocating.
The uncertainty we are living through isn't just an abstract political talking point on the news; it is a solid brick wall standing between me and my future.
Beyond the geopolitical anxieties, there is the grinding financial exhaustion of trying to survive here. Every single day, just staying afloat becomes harder. The economic fluctuations are tied to the military news cycle. You walk into a local shop and suddenly a pack of cigarettes is exponentially more expensive because of a headline about a potential strike; tomorrow the tension might ease and the price drops slightly, only to shoot up again the next day. We live completely at the mercy of breaking news alerts.
My absolute deepest fear is the very real possibility of losing on both fronts. I sacrificed my university degree for this emigration dream. I held back from fully committing to long-term career progression in the local video industry because I was saving all my energy and resources for a life abroad.
If this state of violent limbo drags on, what happens to me? I won't have my degree, I won't have advanced my career here, and I won't have successfully emigrated either. It’s the sheer terror of being completely left behind, stuck in a void. That is the heaviest burden I carry right now: the creeping realisation that while I wait for the world to decide our fate, my youth is just slipping through my fingers.
Fatemeh, 26, is being squeezed by inflation, job losses, and rising rents
“Watching the prices skyrocket day by day has been terrifying”
The first direct hit I took when the conflict escalated was deeply personal. My partner and I used to work together, but as the economic panic set in, our company began downsizing, and he was laid off. Almost overnight, we were forced into a long-distance relationship. The emotional toll of losing that daily proximity, combined with the crushing stress of his sudden unemployment, put a massive strain on both of us. But that was only the beginning.
Then came the hyperinflation. Watching the prices skyrocket day by day has been terrifying. To give a specific example: During the height of the tension, I wanted to buy a pair of sneakers that cost around four million tomans ($20). Before I could save enough, the price shot up to nearly seven million.
Food prices have increased by 100%. I’ve had to completely eliminate things from my grocery basket that I used to buy without a second thought. Something as simple as a tub of ice cream or snacks? I don’t even walk down those aisles in the supermarket anymore. I just can't justify the cost.
But the absolute hardest blow has been the threat to my basic security: my housing. The inflation resulting from these cycles of war and peace has forced everyone into survival mode. I am working much more now than I was before the conflict just to stay afloat. My roommate realised that staying in a fixed-salary job like she had was financial suicide, so she decided to pivot to doing skincare and facials because service prices and wages inflate and shift alongside the economy.
We live in central Tehran, in a neighbourhood filled with students and bookstores. It’s not the right demographic for premium beauty services. So she decided to move to west Tehran, to a neighbourhood where people have more disposable income. Her plan is to rent a one-bedroom apartment and convert half of it into a skincare studio.
Her decision left me completely stranded. The relentless inflation has wiped out my ability to save anything. I am left hovering between the earth and the sky. I don't have enough money for a new deposit. If I want to find a place of my own, I will have to drown myself in loans and borrow from everyone I know. Even then, my monthly rent will increase by 100%.
The scariest part is the logic behind my roommate's move. From the outside, taking such a massive financial risk in this unstable economy seems insane. But she firmly believes that if she doesn't make this leap this year, she will never be able to do it. The future looks so overwhelmingly dark and unpredictable that her mentality is literally now or never. She is convinced things are going to get so much worse that soon, even taking a risk will be impossible.
Sina, 20, lost the job he hoped would lift his family out of poverty
“A relentless exercise in overthinking”
I come from a lower-income, working-class family. My father is a labourer who has done gruelling physical work his entire life just to feed the family. For a brief moment, I truly thought I was going to be the one to break our family's cycle of poverty.
I had worked hard and managed to land a great, professional job. It was my golden ticket to pull myself up, build a real career, and finally change my social standing. But when the threat of war escalated and the economic shock hit, budget cuts followed immediately. I was one of the first people laid off, and my entire trajectory collapsed.
For the past five or six months, my existence has been reduced to desperately searching for work. I have sent out between 150 and 200 résumés. I’ve gone to countless interviews, but the answer is always the same. Because of the geopolitical situation and the shrinking economy, companies aren't hiring; they are completely frozen or downsizing.
Waking up every day as an unemployed 20-year-old in Tehran is a relentless exercise in overthinking. You wake up with nothing to do but obsess over what is going to happen next. Will prices go up again? You set a goal to save money to buy something basic, and by the time you reach that amount, the item has become drastically more expensive.
But the absolute hardest part is the sheer humiliation and guilt of losing my financial independence. I try to strip my expenses down to the bare minimum so I don't run out of the little money I have left. But sometimes, when I hit absolute zero, I have to ask my father for cash just to get by. At 20, with the pride of a young guy who thought he had finally made it and was supposed to start helping his family, it is a crushing feeling. Having to ask a tired, aging labourer for money just so you can buy a coffee? It completely destroys your dignity. I look at how hard he works, and the guilt eats me alive.
My biggest fear for the next year is that the inflation will spiral so far out of control that we won't be able to afford breathing. The most normal routines from a year ago are now impossible luxuries. Going out for dinner or to a cafe is something you can maybe do once every 10 days now; if you did it every night, your entire month's salary would vanish in two weeks.
People ask if I am afraid of a war breaking out. Honestly, no. I am not afraid of things coming to a head and our fate finally being decided. What genuinely terrifies me is this endless, paralysing limbo where my youth is wasted, and I am dragged right back to the bottom.
Amir Ali, 26, has seen his ambitions shrink after losing his job
“My only strategy is to do absolutely nothing”
At first, I told myself I wasn't bothered by the sound of missiles or the endless talk of war. But slowly it crept into my psyche and took over everything. My baseline level of stress has skyrocketed. I find myself becoming aggressive, snapping at things that used to be completely normal. There is this constant, heavy feeling that my basic safety is under threat.
But honestly, the hardest part isn’t the threat of war itself; it’s the absolute uncertainty. It’s the sheer paralysis of not knowing. You wake up in the morning and ask yourself, “What will happen today?” You check your phone and the news says things are calming down. Half an hour later, a new headline breaks, warning that everything is about to get worse. That relentless whiplash strips the life out of you because it makes it impossible to make a single long-term decision.
“The hardest part isn’t the threat of war itself; it’s the absolute uncertainty.”
The most immediate blow I took from the conflict was to my livelihood. I lost my main job and the steady income I relied on. That single event derailed every plan I had for the future. I had been diligently saving money for months just to upgrade my car. I wasn’t going to buy something luxurious, just a normal step forward. But with the economic shock and my lost wages, that plan evaporated. I couldn't pull the trigger.
Now, just changing my car feels like the absolute ceiling of my ambitions. Buying a house? That is a total pipe dream. Unless you have some miraculous exception, no one can buy property here on a normal salary anymore. Even the thought of getting married has been completely taken off the table. The inflation is so aggressive and the costs are so astronomical that you just give up. I genuinely don't know what to do anymore.
People ask if I have ideas to start a business or invest if things ever quieten down. The truth is, our economic environment is so deeply unhealthy and unpredictable that starting a business feels like walking into a trap.
In this climate, my only strategy is to do absolutely nothing – just freeze, keep my head down, and try to protect the little I have. You can't get a bank loan, because how can you commit to monthly repayments when you don't know if you'll have a job next week? That shadow hangs over every daily routine. I am terrified of being laid off again because no position is secure. And the saddest part is that it’s not just me. Look at anyone in my friendship circle. We are all deeply exhausted, trapped in this exact same limbo, totally clueless about what to do with our lives.
This journalist who authored this piece writes under a pseudonym due to security concerns.

Two new British support ships named at Appledore
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:38:46 BST
23:38:46 KST

The second and third ships in the Royal Fleet Auxiliary’s new Fleet Solid Support programme will be named RFA Reliant and RFA Resourceful, with the names revealed as the keel was laid for first-of-class RFA Resurgent at Appledore in North Devon, the Royal Navy has said.
The three ships are being built to provide ammunition, stores and other supplies to Royal Navy vessels at sea, including the UK’s aircraft carriers. Sections of the vessels are being constructed at Navantia facilities in Appledore and Cadiz, as well as in Belfast, before being transported to Harland & Wolff’s Belfast facility for final integration.
Commodore Sam Shattock, head of the Royal Fleet Auxiliary, announced the names of the remaining two ships during the keel-laying ceremony for RFA Resurgent, which took place on Merchant Navy Day.
He said: “Today represents the moment when vision becomes reality, when plans and drawings come to life, effectively becoming the ship’s birthday.”
On the name of the first vessel, he added: “RFA Resurgent’s name speaks of renewal, resilience and the ability recover stronger from challenge.”
“Those qualities are reflected not only in the ship itself, but also in the people who will design, build, support and ultimately sail her.”
As part of the keel-laying ceremony, a coin was welded to the keel of RFA Resurgent by a Navantia UK apprentice, continuing a shipbuilding tradition marking the formal start of construction.
Each Fleet Solid Support ship will have a core RFA crew of 101, with accommodation for a further 80 personnel when required. Those additional personnel could include teams operating helicopters and boats or carrying out other specialist roles.
The vessels are intended to replenish Royal Navy ships with munitions, supplies and provisions while at sea. The Royal Navy says they will also be able to support wider operational activity, including counter-piracy and counter-terrorism missions and operations alongside allied forces.
The design also includes energy-efficient technologies intended to reduce power consumption. The ships are being built with the ability to use low-carbon, non-fossil fuels and future sustainable energy sources, with the Royal Navy saying the design is intended to allow the vessels to achieve Carbon Zero status by the end of their planned 30-year operational lives.
RFA Resurgent revives a name previously carried by a merchant vessel converted into a fleet replenishment ship in 1957. That ship remained in service until 1979 and supported a Joint Services scientific expedition to the Indian Ocean in 1975.
The name RFA Reliant has previously been used by three vessels, including stores and air stores support ships and a helicopter support ship. The most recent Reliant was a merchant vessel taken into naval service in 1983 and used during the multinational deployment to Lebanon in 1984, including during evacuation operations. She was sold in 1986 after being replaced in the helicopter support role by RFA Argus.
RFA Resourceful is a new name for the RFA, selected to follow the adjective-based naming convention of the class. The Royal Fleet Auxiliary previously operated an armament stores ship named RFA Resource, which served between 1966 and 1997 and received battle honours for the Falklands and Kuwait.
The Fleet Solid Support programme is also intended to support investment in UK shipyards, apprenticeships, skilled employment and domestic supply chains, while combining work in Britain with construction and expertise from Navantia’s Spanish facilities.

Russian Strategic Bomber Chief Reportedly Shot in Engels, Home to Tu-95 and Tu-160 Fleet

14:35:46 UTC
