How 9/11 Shaped My Life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:00:06 UTC
21:00:06 KST

Twenty-five years later, Sept. 11 remains a watershed moment, one with both personal and global implications. To mark the anniversary, TIME spoke to people with very different connections to the day, to hear about what they experienced at the time as well as the ripple effects. For some, the legacy of the date is one of profound loss. Others know about the tragedy mostly from history class. One thing is clear: The attacks that changed the world also changed lives.
I was 4½ when my dad died. I have only brief memories of that day. I remember my mom taking my twin brother and me out of preschool. I remember watching the TV at home and then going over to one of her friends’, whose husband was also a firefighter, and watching it there. We were so young, we didn’t really grasp what was actually going on. But as you get older, you start to realize what you’ve missed out on. It’s not quite the same as being sad because you miss someone close to you. It’s more like you’re sad because you didn’t really get to be close to them.
My dad was a cop for 12 years and a firefighter for only 18 months, but joining the FDNY was always his plan. For as long as I can remember, I also wanted to be a firefighter. I did the entry exam when I was 18, even though they don’t take anyone until 21. I went to college, but I think I was just killing time. I dropped out after two years, as the process ramped up. My mom kept encouraging me to consider other things, but she knew I had put all my eggs in that basket. I loved the routine and discipline of the academy, and I really tried to earn my spot; I didn’t want to feel like I was getting special treatment.
A lot of things about the fire department don’t change, and I remember thinking my dad might have stood right where I was standing, worrying about getting yelled at by some drill instructor for having a button undone. I don’t have many shared memories with him, but that came close. He worked in Brooklyn, just on the other side of the tunnel from the World Trade Center. I wanted to go to a different firehouse, to let the guys make up their mind about me without having known his reputation, so I’m in the Bronx. The firefighters I meet that knew him, I feel like they're happy to see that I'm on the job.
On 9/11 I usually go to Mass at my firehouse and then drop by Ladder 101, where Dad worked. Last year for the first time I met someone who was actually riding that day, and he gave me the full rundown. They were staged at the mouth of the tunnel right under the towers, and as they sat there on the rigs, they watched the second plane come in. They could feel the impact and then they went straight in. From what I understand, his group went up a way, came back down, and were in the lobby when the building collapsed.
Dad was also a lifeguard at Overlook Beach in Long Island, and the lifeguards there put up a little memorial for him. My mom is not big on going to the firehouse or the ceremonies in the city on the anniversaries. I think it’s just too overwhelming. So we do a more casual gathering in the afternoon. It’s less somber, more a reason for everyone to just get together.
Sometimes the attention that comes with being a legacy firefighter is uncomfortable, but not for the reasons you might think. I don’t have trouble talking about it; it was something that happened when I was young, but I had a happy childhood and a very fortunate life. I’m not looking for sympathy—I feel lucky to have had that role model of selflessness and self-sacrifice. On the other hand, I do miss having had a real relationship with my dad.
Do I wish he was still alive? Of course. I sometimes wonder if I’d be different if I’d known my dad. But that event shaped my way of thinking and shaped me. I’m very proud of what he did, and I think it’s a very admirable and honorable way to die. And I wouldn’t want someone else to have been in his place because I don’t think that’s what he would have wanted. –As told to Belinda Luscombe
Kelsey Griffin
My journey of becoming a pilot started when I was 14, when I went to a youth summer camp sponsored by the Organization of Black Aerospace Professionals (OBAP). When I first told my parents that I wanted to be a pilot, of course they were a little bit concerned about the dangers that come with flight training at a young age, but they were also very supportive.
I took my first discovery flight with an instructor in 2022. At first I was definitely nervous, because there was so much going on in the plane at once. But once we were at around 2,000 feet, everything became incredibly peaceful. Looking down at the scenery gave me a sense of freedom that I never really experienced anywhere else. I knew at a young age that I never wanted to work a traditional nine-to-five job. I was also really big on traveling, and that discovery flight showed me that being a pilot was something I could do every day and enjoy. I took my first solo fight in 2024.
Flight training is expensive, but my parents made sacrifices to support me financially as I sought out scholarships and opportunities. I was drawn to the LeRoy W. Homer Jr. Foundation Scholarship, because of their mission to empower future aviators. He was an African American pilot, and a first officer for United Airlines on Flight 93. I wasn’t alive when 9/11 happened, so my understanding comes from learning about it through documentaries and conversations with my parents and grandparents and others.
The tragedies definitely impacted not only the lives of everyday people, but also caused major disruption in the aviation industry. When my mentor just started his career as a pilot, he got furloughed soon after 9/11 because the airline industry was completely devastated over Americans’ fear of flying. I have a family member that is still afraid to fly on aircrafts.
Before I went to college, I became a private pilot and a licensed drone pilot. I briefly stopped my training after one of my friends passed away, but getting the scholarship lifted my spirits and gave me an extra push to continue my goal. The scholarship exists because of somebody who lived with courage, professionalism, and commitment to serving others. Knowing that I’m representing his legacy motivates me to work harder and fly with integrity, and never take opportunities for granted.
At Middle Georgia State University, I'm enrolled in aviation courses to finish out my remaining ratings and license and also to, as we call it in the industry, time build. I have to get at least 1,000 flight hours before I can go to a regional airline. It will probably take me about six more years of training to become a major airline pilot. African American women make up less than 1% of professional pilots in the U.S. I have had the privilege of connecting with several of them through organizations such as Sisters of the Skies, OBAP, Aviation Career Enrichment, Pink STEM, and Youth in Aviation. Having this support gives me a sense of comfort and understanding that through hard work, I can also achieve it. –As told to Philip Wang
Alka Pradhan
I was infamous as an undergraduate at Johns Hopkins for choosing classes in the afternoon so I could sleep all morning. My more diligent roommate would try to wake me so she’d have someone to talk to. On 9/11, I thought that’s what she was doing. Maybe a minute or so after she got me to the TV, the second plane hit. It was terrifying.
Even at 19, I was on track to study the intersection of human-rights law and international humanitarian law. When it became clear in early October that we, the U.S., were going to strike Afghanistan in a way that seemed not entirely targeted and seemed to conflate the Taliban with al-Qaeda, that began my interest in all this. But to me, our actions didn't seem to comply with the law of war that I had been studying. I really did not anticipate that I would eventually use my specialization to litigate as hard as I possibly could against my own government. But that is what I have done for the past 13ish years in my work at Guantánamo.
I was already working with Guantánamo detainees when, in 2015, I got a call from a friend at the Department of Defense, who said the military commissions, which are prosecuting those actually alleged to have organized the attacks on 9/11, were hiring civilians. He asked if I’d be interested in representing Ammar al-Baluchi, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed’s nephew. I thought, well, there's nothing I can do that is deeper in the heart of this morass than the military commissions, because the CIA torture programs are at the heart of these cases. So I've been a defense attorney for Ammar al-Baluchi’s 9/11 case since 2015. It has been in pretrial hearings for 14 years.
For 9/11, the actual fact allegations against al-Baluchi are that he transferred money to people who ended up being the hijackers. We have never contested the fact that he transferred money. He was in Dubai, he was asked to transfer money, he transferred money. The $10,000 question is: What did he know at the time? And the government has no evidence that is not derived from torture that indicates he had any knowledge of what was happening on Sept. 11.
The 9/11 case really is all day, every day. It is the biggest criminal case in U.S. history. I hold a top-secret security clearance, and I still don’t have all the information I need about the torture at the black sites that impacted how Ammar is today and the statements he gave later. The trial has just been scheduled for June 2028, but I don’t know if it will ever happen, and I think that is a very hard truth, particularly for the victims’ family members. Witnesses have passed away, evidence has been destroyed by the government. The men themselves are deteriorating because the U.S. refuses to give them the medical care they need as undisputed torture victims. Millions and millions of dollars have been wasted on this exercise so far. It’s the Jarndyce v Jarndyce of the United States.
However I also think this is one of the most important things I will ever do because it shows fellow Americans that this is what dissent looks like, and I know it sounds trite, but this is also what patriotism looks like. I am both grateful for and have great contempt for what the Department of Defense has done over these 25 years. On 9/11 I will reach out to the victims’ family members who I am in touch with and convey my very deep sadness and anger over what happened. I will watch the commemorations. I will contemplate. Then I will start speaking again about everything that we are continuing to do wrong. –As told to B.L.
Jukay Hsu
I was student-body president at Stuyvesant High, three blocks from the World Trade Center. I had an early meeting that day with the principal about the plans for the year. So normally I’d be walking to school when the first plane hit. We evacuated, I think, just as the first tower fell, and I remember looking through these two-story plate-glass windows at this billowing black-gray kind of fog coming from one way as we went out the other way into a sunny sky.
I grew up in Queens. My mother was a social worker. I was lucky to get full financial aid to Harvard, and signed up for ROTC, then went to Iraq. I always thought service was public service. I was a second lieutenant leading a platoon of 40 men in Salahuddin province, kind of at the mid-end of the surge. Even with combat patrols, I ended up doing a lot around civil governance because counterinsurgency involves that. It was a very different kind of learning.
When I got out of the military, all my classmates were going into tech. I was like, If New York is going to become a tech sector, how can more people be included in that? All the soldiers I worked with never went to college. That's the difference between officer and soldier. Even though my platoon sergeant was 20 years older than me, I was in charge because I went to college. It really got you thinking: All these companies and jobs and wealth are being created, but two-thirds of Americans and two-thirds of New Yorkers don’t have a four-year college degree. In 2011, I ended up creating Pursuit. Our idea was to train working-class people in the skills tech companies tell us they need. The average student arrived making $16,000 and a year later has a job paying $94,000.
I left Pursuit to start a research organization called Bright Future to focus on AI alignment for the benefit of humanity. There’s this idea that AI is going to be so dominant, so superpowerful, not just tools, but creating a being—we’re trying to create like a god, essentially, right? It's kind of crazy. So what does that mean for humans? This year I also joined the New York City Economic Development Board, which oversees and shapes AI policy.
Perhaps the future is not college versus noncollege. Perhaps it’s going to be AI and non-AI. But hopefully, there’s a way to democratize that and enable cooperation. We're creating these new digital minds, so you have to consider their power and impact. Early on in high school, it was imprinted on me that what’s most important is what happens to all of us. And the ability to have agency in that. 9/11 helped cement that. Important critical junctures really can bring out the best in humanity, if we choose to respond.
Marc Rivera
I was born in Puerto Rico but have lived all but the first three months of my life on the Lower East Side of Manhattan. Next year, it will be 50 years that I'm pastoring down here. Primitive Church is within eyeshot of the towers. On 9/11, I saw the towers fall and then didn’t set foot outside lower Manhattan until March the following year.
I had just dropped my younger son at high school a block away from the Trade Center and I was going into the church office when I saw my secretary outside. She simply says, “Look.” Sure enough, there was a gaping hole in the north tower. I could see what I thought was debris falling. Later on, I discovered it may have been people. I turned around to get my son, but the police wouldn’t let me through, so I went back to the church, and all of a sudden, a sea of people filled with soot and stuff came walking down our street. We opened the church to them. We had four landlines that were somehow still working. Eventually my son walked in with a bunch of friends, all covered in soot. My older son also arrived from midtown. That was a rebirth moment for me. I was able to shift my attention to helping the helpers and healing the healers.
By day two after the collapse, I was doing what I've always done: galvanizing people and starting to help individuals, raising money to pay people's rent and medical bills and for funerals. We established the Ground Zero Clergy Task Force, which was simply clergy of different faiths, denominations, and traditions who gathered together to help at the site and to coordinate churches with FEMA and the New York City government. Every day, anywhere from 15 to 50 clergy would meet in the sanctuary, and then go down to the hole, to ground zero, to see what we could do. About a year afterward, I established a Northeast Clergy Group, which was broader and longer-standing. It tried to run the same program for people at the Pentagon and in Pennsylvania.
We closed those organizations eventually, but through them I saw the importance of not being so rigid or immovable in my theological training. Many religious people, regardless of faith tradition, tend to think that we have the patent on truth. This event broadened my perspective and really challenged me to make that change intellectually and also in my practice. When tragedy strikes, no one cares how much training you have, how many books you have written, how large your congregation is. Because the bottom line is love. I saw a fireman who looked so tired and I asked if I could pray for him. I didn’t ask what he believed first.
The most painful consequence for me personally was that my oldest son, Tim, was diagnosed with Stage IV colorectal cancer, one of the cancers that is covered by the 9/11 fund. He fought it courageously for three years, but this September will mark one year since his passing. He would have been 46. We believe he probably got it because we live down here.
One of my greatest concerns today is that there are still people in our congregation and in this community who may qualify for assistance through the 9/11 fund that the federal government set up, but some remain reluctant to apply. They’re more afraid of the system than they are of getting sick. So, more than two decades later, part of our ministry is still helping people understand that the consequences of Sept. 11 did not end on Sept. 11. We are still caring for people. We are still encouraging people to seek the help that is available to them. And we are still learning what that terrible day taught us from the very beginning: when people are hurting, our first responsibility is to love them.
Connie Stevanus
That day, I was working at a bank, and as I went from department to department, they were bringing this up on their computers. On my way home, it’s just a two-lane country road, and there was so much traffic. Cars were passing me in either direction. They were state police cars. When I finally got home, I see my husband picking things out of the yard, and I didn’t know what he was doing until I went to pull into our driveway. It was black, totally black, with small pieces of burnt debris. And it just hit me then what I was looking at. Flight 93 carried mail. We had mail in our trees, in our yard. The neighbor across the road from us had a piece of the United Airlines magazine in her yard.
We started volunteering at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Shanksville, Pa., after my husband had retired from work, like five years after 9/11. People come from all over—Europe, Australia, different countries. They like to tell you where they were and their experiences of that day. And then they always ask, “Where were you when this happened?” We get a lot of school students, and they're very alert to what happened here, so they're usually very quiet and very respectful. My 21-year-old grandson wasn't born yet. And when he was in eighth grade, I think it was, his school came out.
I never get tired of talking about it. Probably 99% of them still feel the pain and show their emotions easily when we're talking. Sometimes it’s a little hard to be there, because I’m that person—I might not be able to say the right thing to you, but I can cry right alongside of you. At the Visitor Center, we have those three phone messages. You know that some of the passengers on Flight 93 had to leave messages because they didn’t get an answer? Those are very powerful.
Can I share one little story with you? This was just after they were done with the excavation and the road opened up. So it was about two weeks later. My husband and I stopped there after work one evening. And it was just like the day of 9/11. Sunny, bright blue sky, not a cloud in the sky. There was nobody around, just me and my husband. We looked down through the field, and you could just see where the crash site was, the fresh soil that covered that area. And we just stood there. And all you could hear were birds, the rustling of the high grass, and just silence. And there wasn't a flag. There was nothing where you would think something like this happened. You could see the little fence that they had around the debris field. But that is a moment that I'll never forget. –As told to Karl Vick
Shams Frough
I was going into fifth grade when 9/11 happened. I remember, because it was two days after a famous Northern Alliance commander was assassinated. Obviously, there was no TV in Kabul, but our ears were wide open and we did hear about it on the radio. (From a very young age, I was listening to BBC Persian.) Then came the bombings, and life in Kabul became a bit hard, so for a short period, I went back to my village, Kapisa, which is 100 km from Kabul, where I had shepherding duties. I remember very well the big difference when we returned to school; girls were going too, and we no longer had to wear black turbans. Everybody wanted the Taliban to go, but we didn’t know that eventually all these American soldiers would come and there would be a hot war again. We all thought the Northern Alliance would take over.
My mother died when I was young, and my father really worked to make sure his children did not have to work on the farm. I went to an elite Turkish-run high school; out of 6,000 applicants, only 100 were accepted—and some of those places were reserved for the children of government ministers. Most lessons were in English, but we also learned Turkish. I wanted to go to medical school, but I was young and male and I believed the hype, and in the last year of school I began working with the U.S. Army. I was sent to Kandahar as an interpreter. After I was nearly killed twice, I was transferred to the Department of Procurements in Kabul and ended up doing simultaneous translation for colonels and generals who were advising the Afghan military and police. I reported what looked like corruption in the Afghan procurement process, and then I knew I had to leave. It took three years, until 2014—a week or so after I resigned—for my Special Immigrant Visa to be processed.
My wife and I were initially assigned to Albuquerque, N.M., which was funny, because my Army friends always made fun of the mud huts in Afghanistan and there they were in America, only it was called adobe. When we moved to Chicago, I went to community college and so I took up driving taxis and Ubers. I’d study all week and then sleep in my taxi at the airport, because there was always a three-hour wait for a fare. Then in 2021, I started a business called Kapisa Rugs; it was rebranded as Rugistan in 2024, and we directly source hand-knotted rugs from Afghanistan. It’s not easy with Amazon and other competition, so to keep prices down, I’m here seven days a week. Right now we have two locations, but this is not the goal.
I love rugs. I'll always cherish them. But hopefully, in about a year, it will be profitable enough, and my wife will have taken over and I will be able to fire myself. Some of my high school friends who didn’t join the Army are already doctors here, so I sometimes feel like I haven’t lived up to my capacity in the way I could have in Afghanistan. I am currently completing my master’s of public health at Southern Illinois University Carbondale, and I hope to start medical school in 2028. I joke with my wife that I’ll probably graduate alongside our sons. –As told to B.L.
Sari Beth Rosenberg
My first day of student teaching was supposed to be 9/11. I was 26, in grad school, planning to observe a teacher teaching U.S. history at LaGuardia High School. My alarm-clock radio played Z Morning Zoo, a show known for its goofiness, but the hosts were talking about a plane crashing into the Twin Towers and I thought, “That’s not funny.” I turned on the TV, and that’s when I was like, “Oh my, no, this is actually real.” I got a phone call from one of my best friends who worked on Canal Street near the Twin Towers, and when I saw the first tower buckle, I yelled to her, “You have to run!”
The next semester, I was placed at Stuyvesant High School by what was once the Twin Towers. The air was constantly being tested in the cafeteria. And yet 9/11 never came up in the classroom. In the years that followed, I would have students interview a friend or family member about that day as a lesson in how history is remembered, showing them that they just collected primary sources.
Nowadays, students are more clued into current events on their devices and TikTok, so they’re asking really interesting questions about 9/11, like “Why did we attack Afghanistan?” Many students don’t understand the difference between why we went into Afghanistan in the early 2000s versus Iraq. Many adults don't know the difference if they don't really pay attention to the news or recent current events. How do you understand what’s going on in Iran now if you don’t understand the history of Iraq, Iran, the Middle East?
Kids don’t talk about the fear of terrorists coming from the Middle East. The thing that kids are more scared of today is what they see as domestic terror coming from ICE agents. I’ve had to explain that ICE was created in 2003 as part of the new Department of Homeland Security, which was established in response to 9/11, and now it’s being used to, in my opinion, terrorize communities.
I’m definitely going to bring up the 25th anniversary in class this year. They were born so long after 9/11, it’s history to them. We need to find ways to cover more recent history. In a U.S. history class—or any history class—there’s so much to cover, and we don’t get to the recent history, from 1980 to the present, because it’s not emphasized on tests and also you run out of time. –As told to Olivia B. Waxman
Allison Turkel
On Sept. 11, I was outside of Albuquerque, N.M. I worked for a not-for-profit then called the National Center for Prosecution of Child Abuse, and we were running a conference. And the receptionist where we were holding it said a plane just hit the World Trade Center, and you could go into our break room to watch it on TV. I went in just in time to see the second plane hit. Luckily I was able to reach my dad, who had a meeting downtown that day. I got him right before the phones went out in New York, and then we started driving back. We looked on our map. We tried to avoid missile silos because we thought that those might be under attack or shooting things. We had no idea. I drove crying. Not the whole time, but a lot. It’s a skill.
I lived in the D.C. area at the time, but I grew up in Manhattan, up in Washington Heights. I worked down in the Manhattan district attorney’s office, which was actually in the zone. So all of it translates well into how and why I’ve been the Special Master of the September 11th Victim Compensation Fund for the last 3½ years.
We want as many people as possible to know, one, we’re still here. We are in business until 2090. We have as much funding as is necessary to pay every eligible claimant. And two, we serve people beyond first responders. We serve people that lived, worked, went to school in the New York exposure zone, who were at Shanksville and at the Pentagon. We really encourage people if they were there, to register with the VCF. In order to file a claim, folks need to get certified that they have a 9/11 illness from the World Trade Center Health Program, which is our sister program that runs out of HHS. We are receiving over 700 new claims a month.
Since 2011, when we reopened, we have received over 110,000 claims. We've paid out $18.5 billion compensation. [The original VCF closed in 2004 after paying out the $7 billion appropriated for those killed or physically injured on 9/11.] The CDC estimates that in New York alone, over 400,000 people may have been exposed to the toxins.
Remember “America Strong”? “Let everybody return”? “Let's begin to live, work, go to school, start over again”? People went back into the New York zone, and the consequence, of course, is they were exposed to these toxins that have made them ill. And people have died from it. On that day, 2,977 people perished at all three sites and on the planes. Since we reopened, we’ve had 6,100 of our claimants die from exposure to the toxins. And unfortunately, every year there are more people becoming ill. Today, 63% of our claimants have a cancer, and those cancers, because of the unique nature of what people were exposed to, may have long latency periods.
Every Sept. 11, the memorial and museum in New York City does the reading of the names of the victims, and there’s always six moments of silence, to mark the four moments of impact and two tower collapses. This year, they’re adding a seventh, to honor the people that have become ill from the toxins. I think that’ll help spread awareness that so many are still suffering and that the 9/11 VCF is here to help.
Christopher Ashley
I actually didn't behave that great that day. I almost got into a fistfight.
It was the first day of rehearsal for the play Wonder of the World, which I was directing. We canceled rehearsal for that day and the next, and I ended up walking back home to the West Village. Late that night, there was a very drunk man who put himself in front of me and asked if I was an Iraqi. He kept putting himself in front of me, and I kept trying to get away. Then he took a swing at me, and I punched him in the face.
It’s not automatic that people are their best selves in these moments. I think one of the things people do with traumatic situations is move on, so it was really meaningful to me to dig back into the feelings that that day created while directing Come From Away, a musical about 38 planes grounded in Gander, Newfoundland, and the people who took care of strangers at this moment of real terror. Telling that story around the world, onstage, on Apple TV helped me heal.
In 2011, the play’s authors, David Hein and Irene Sankoff, went to a 10th anniversary event reconvening a lot of the people who had been diverted there on 9/11. They expected to be there for a couple of days and ended up staying for weeks and weeks. Claude Elliott, the mayor of Gander, used to joke, "Wait, you guys are making a musical about making sandwiches?”
In the current world we're living in, it almost seems mythical that people would take this good care of each other because there are just so many things that pull us apart and make us suspicious of each other. We're all vulnerable. Nobody’s safely apart behind a wall. We're all going to have to figure out how to share the world and the space together. The world keeps changing, but the show remains about the responsibility we have to each other and the value of kindness and connection. Twenty-five years ago, if more people thought like the people in Gander—“these people are my problem, my responsibility, and I will take care of them, despite the fact that I didn't meet them until today”—I think we'd be in a better place. –As told to O.B.W.
Nancy Gibbs
Moments after 8:46 a.m., attention fixed on one incomprehensible event. As first responders scrambled and survivors fled, the rest of us skidded to a stop and watched.
At TIME, editor Jim Kelly launched a reporting army: correspondents around the world tracked the attacks and reactions in real time. White House correspondent Jay Carney was with President Bush in the press pool; writers and editors in the New York City headquarters headed downtown, or to city hospitals and command centers. My job was to curate and condense it all into a single story for a special issue of the magazine. “I just want you to tell the story of today,” Jim told me. “Think of it as a time capsule.”
In one sense we all saw something different. If you lived in New York City, not only did you see the smoke, you smelled it, tasted it. You heard the sirens, felt the fear. Elsewhere, the alerts jolted large towns and small. Local landmarks shivered and then shut down: Disney World and the Sears Tower, Congress and the Supreme Court, the Space Needle. Also, the entire airspace of the United States.
But at a deeper level, we all saw the same thing, a once unimaginable attack on what we soon started calling the Homeland, as though we were all residents of the same reality. No matter how different our individual experiences of that day, we lived through it together and emerged more united: By October, 60% of people said they trusted the government to do the right thing all or most of the time, a three-decade high.
It’s easier to put a jigsaw puzzle together when you can see the whole picture on the lid of the box. Yes, there were toxic rumors and conspiracies even without the yet-to-be-invented Facebook and X. But compared with what has transpired since then, the information landscape looks practically pristine. The demolition of the business model for traditional news sources corresponded with sinking institutional trust across the board. Journalism’s self-inflicted wounds and technological upheaval radically changed how people make sense of the world. Trust in government now sits around 17%. Trust in the media has hit an all-time low.
If you had told me 25 years ago, as we color-coded the threat level, cast a wide surveillance net, launched a Global War on Terror, that we would manage to avoid further terror attacks, I would have found it hard to believe. But I also couldn’t have imagined the maceration of the media as our news channels filled with content of all kinds streaming in from all corners. This year for the first time, more people globally rely on social and video platforms for news, rather than TV or news websites. As audiences migrate from broadcast and cable, print and radio, to creators on TikTok and YouTube, the very notion of a shared reality feels quaint. Eight in 10 of us say Democrats and Republicans can’t even agree on basic facts, which makes reasoned discussion of everything from security threats to education reform all but impossible.
Twenty-five years ago, like journalists everywhere, I focused on how to tell this story, in the belief that stories are stickier than bloodless fact. But what has happened since makes me wonder if I missed the actual war. Sept. 11 did not cause 21st century truth decay, but it coincided with it. Jolted out of the snug 1990s, people went searching for answers they could trust, tribes they could join, distraction as an antidote to alarm. We no longer hear the same stories and too many leaders are counting on that. We can each collect the puzzle pieces, but it's harder to see the full picture. Even when the country is broadly united around key values—reject political violence, protect the safety net, get money out of politics, regulate AI—the sense of division abides and people on both sides see mainly a caricature of their opponents.
Strong societies need good information; communities benefit from shared stories. On Sept. 11, many of those stories were of quiet, reflexive heroism, sacrifice, service. First responders and random strangers modeled courage under fire, and the rest of us were swept up in a wave of gratitude that helped drain the fear. Those are stories worth retrieving now. –Nancy Gibbs
Keira Unterzuber, Eric Johnson, and Freya Johnson
Keira: My first child was due on Sept. 3, and my doctor was going to induce me on the 13th. So the 11th was any other day, really. I was getting ready for work when my husband, who is a pilot and was home on family leave, said, “Keira, come here.” He explained that a plane had crashed in the World Trade Center, and I said, “But it's so sunny!” He's like, “Yeah, that's really weird.” And while we were watching the TV, the second plane hit. As the morning went on, I started to feel unwell. But then I don’t think anybody felt well that day.
Eric: We live near the Pentagon, and suddenly, it was like somebody pushed over a piano in the room next to us. It shook the whole house. The cats jumped off the bed and hid. I went outside and saw smoke. Sometime in there, Keira said, “I’m having the baby today.” I drove 80 to 90 miles an hour all the way  to the hospital. There was zero traffic. It was eerie, like driving somewhere in the middle of the night. 
Keira: Because of construction, we had to go through the emergency-room entrance and I remember all these emergency medical staff just waiting, and not for me. In the delivery room, Eric started to say he was ready to join the military and go fight the terrorists and because of the mood that he was in, he suggested several new names for the baby: Phoenix, America, Freedom, Liberty. I just said no, no, no. Eventually he picked Freya, who is goddess of war and love and a very strong woman. 
Freya: When I was young, I didn’t really understand the significance of the day. But around the 10th anniversary, I realized, “Oh, this is huge,” and then it became very depressing. On the morning announcements at school, they’d show a video tribute, and those videos were obviously very sad. In middle school, some kid told me that I was the reincarnation of Osama bin Laden. So I used to wish I was born on the 10th or the 12th. I actually didn’t celebrate my birthday from ages 10 to 13. It just felt inappropriate and weird to be so happy when everyone else was not. I can’t tell you how many times I’ve told people my birthday, and it becomes a whole conversation. When I need ID at a bar or when I have to pick up a prescription, and they ask me for my birthday, they’re like, “Really?” I’ve even had people ask me, “What was that like for you?” And I have to say, “Well, I was not even born yet so I was not aware of anything.” I’ve learned to just say my birthday is in September. However, as I’ve gotten older, I’ve realized that I like my birthday. It’s such a beautiful time of year. I’m at the point where I can acknowledge that it was sad, but I can also celebrate myself. All my friends tell me that when they think of 9/11, they think of me as their first thought. 
Keira: When something tragic happens, it’s a beautiful thing to be around a newborn baby. My brother’s wife lost her first husband on the 10th, and his funeral was on the 13th. She adores Freya because, in her world, she’s a bright light at a dark moment. We have a lot of friends who say that year after year: She was the shining light that day. –As told to B.L.

External involvement fuelling Sudan war, new report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Outside forces fuel Sudan war, new report finds
Foreign recruitment and external support networks are fuelling the brutal conflict in Sudan, independent UN human rights investigators said on Thursday in a new report, calling for accountability as fighting continues between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
This action is strengthening the military capabilities of the warring parties and enabling increasingly sophisticated military operations with devastating consequences for civilians, according to the report by the UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan.
The report documented the involvement of transnational entities operating in several countries in recruiting, training, and deploying foreign personnel to support the RSF, as well as facilitating the transfer of weapons, ammunition, and military technology, and providing logistical support.
It also concluded that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the SAF used foreign-supplied drones in operations that harmed civilians and civilian objects.
Civilians bearing the brunt
The mission pointed to the "strict international legal obligations" incumbent upon States linked to these supply chains, which require them to exercise due diligence, investigate and stop illicit mercenary and supply networks operating from or through their territories, prevent violations, and enforce the UN arms embargo.
“The consequences of this external support are being felt most acutely by civilians,” said Mohamad Chande Othman, Chair of the Fact-Finding Mission.
“This external support has not brought greater protection for civilians. Instead, civilians are paying the price through attacks on homes, hospitals, schools, markets and places of refuge.”
The mission said it had documented the deployment of up to 2,000 former Colombian military contractors who were directly involved in operating combat drones, artillery and advanced weapons alongside RSF units in Darfur and Kordofan.
The report concluded that there are reasonable grounds to believe that private entities, logistical facilitators, and recruiters operating from countries including Colombia and the United Arab Emirates used transit points in Chad, southeastern Libya, and the Somalian city of Bosaso to facilitate the delivery of personnel, training, weapons, and logistical supplies to the RSF in Sudan.
Drone capabilities expanded
Mona Rishmawi, an expert member of the mission, said it had identified “a transnational chain of networks spanning several countries” that provided the RSF with foreign personnel, training, weapons and logistics.
“This support fed into RSF operations in Zamzam camp and later during the takeover of El-Fasher, where the Mission documented grave human rights and international humanitarian law violations and international crimes, including conduct displaying hallmarks of genocide,” she said.
The report also found that foreign suppliers have substantially enhanced the drone capabilities of both the RSF and the SAF, enabling them to strike far beyond front lines.
Translate warnings into action
The investigators called on States to enforce the arms embargo on Darfur, halt military transfers where there is a substantial risk of contributing to serious violations, investigate individuals and entities involved in illicit support networks, and strengthen accountability measures.
They also urged the Security Council to extend the arms embargo to cover all of Sudan.
Mr. Osman recalled that the international community has received repeated warnings about the violations in Sudan.
“Those warnings must now translate into action,” he said.
"Protecting civilians in Sudan requires taking action not only against those waging this war, but also against the individuals, entities, and networks that enable its continuation."

Gloria Steinem: A voice for women, to the very end
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Gloria Steinem: A voice for women, to the very end
Gloria Steinem, the journalist and women's rights campaigner who became one of the most influential voices of the feminist movement, has died at the age of 92. In an announcement on Instagram, her family said she had passed away on Wednesday at her home in New York City, surrounded by some of the many who loved her.
Following news of her death, UN News revisits a powerful moment from Ms. Steinem's appearance at UN Headquarters in New York in 2016, when she took her message about violence against women to the global stage.
In her landmark speech ten years ago, the pioneering activist warned that violence against women is inseparable from questions of peace, security and democracy.
“The single most important element or determinant of whether a country is violent within itself or whether it will be willing to use military violence against another country is not poverty, not access to natural resources, not religion or even degree of democracy. It’s violence towards females.”
‘This is a world issue’
Ms. Steinem pointed to the many forms violence against women can take, from sexual violence in war – to trafficking, female genital mutilation (FGM) and violence in the home.
She also spoke about the consequences of cultures where sons are prioritised over daughters, and the resulting long-term impact on societies.
“This is not a women’s issue…Hello. This is not a children’s issue. This is a world’s issue.”
Violence against women remains a pervasive global public health and human rights concern.
According to the latest data from the gender equality agency UN Women, an estimated 840 million women – almost one in three – have been subjected to physical and/or sexual intimate partner violence, non-partner sexual violence, or both at least once in their life.
Legacy and inspiration
Ending violence against women and girls is central to the global effort to achieve gender equality and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
For Ms. Steinem, the treatment of women offered a revealing measure of the societies in which they lived.
“The easiest way to figure out how democratic and peaceful any group is, is to see: are there women there and how are they being treated?”
A lifetime of challenging inequality
Ms. Steinem became one of the most recognizable voices of the feminist movement in the United States during the 1960s and 1970s.
She helped highlight issues including reproductive rights, discrimination, political representation and violence against women – bringing them into the mainstream. She was also a co-founder of Ms. magazine and worked with generations of activists seeking greater equality.
Hope for humanity
Underlining that “each of us has some part of the knowledge, the solution, the insight, the understanding that will contribute to the whole”, she said that listening was key.
“You know, there’s nothing more important than listening to each other.”
In her later years, Ms. Steinem continued to write and to bring people together, including in her own New York home, creating regular “Talking Circles” – a tradition she wanted to continue beyond her lifetime, according to her family.

Lebanon–Israel tensions escalate as Gaza sees major aid delivery

Lebanon–Israel tensions escalate as Gaza sees major aid delivery
Peacekeepers in Lebanon have reported a marked deterioration in the security situation along the Blue Line of separation, with Israeli forces intensifying their military footprint in violation of a landmark Security Council resolution, UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said on Thursday.
Meanwhile, in Gaza, humanitarian teams collected hundreds of pallets of aid – including infant food and school bags – as the World Health Organization (WHO) revealed that more than 13,000 patients have now been evacuated from the enclave for urgent medical care.
Rising violence in Lebanon
UN peacekeepers with the UNIFIL mission say that while hostilities eased after the signing of a Framework Agreement in late June, the calm has proven fragile.
Violence rose sharply in August, with the mission recording 56 projectiles from the Israeli military on 1 September alone, a figure that climbed to 84 the following day.
No projectile launches by Hezbollah militants – who have continued to clash with Israeli forces in southern Lebanon despite a US-brokered ceasefire – have been detected since 21 June, Mr. Dujarric said.
Peacekeepers continue to record daily Israeli violations of Lebanese airspace, along with airstrikes, ground activity and naval operations.
Of particular concern, Mr. Dujarric said, is the “continued consolidation and fortification of Israeli positions” north of the Blue Line, including new infrastructure and engineering works.
Peacekeepers have also observed individuals who appear to be Israeli civilian personnel carrying out demolition work in support of military operations.
“There is extensive Israeli military presence north of the Blue Line, which constitutes a violation of Security Council resolution 1701 and of Lebanon’s sovereignty and territorial integrity,” Mr. Dujarric said.
He reiterated the UN’s call “for the Israel Defense Forces to withdraw from all positions north of the Blue Line, and that will be in full accordance and respect with resolution 1701.”
Despite the tensions, UNIFIL continues its humanitarian coordination work, facilitating 20 humanitarian missions between Monday and Wednesday, 16 of them in the Mission’s western sector.
Gaza aid push continues
In Gaza, UN teams on Wednesday collected hundreds of pallets of supplies from the Kerem Shalom-Karem Abu Salem crossing, Mr. Dujarric said, including adult diapers, school bags and food for infants and young children.
Separately, WHO reported that it and its partners have supported the medical evacuation of more than 13,000 patients from Gaza since October 2023, including over 6,000 children.
WHO stressed, however, that thousands more still urgently need specialized treatment unavailable in the enclave, and called for the reopening of the West Bank referral pathway, including to hospitals in East Jerusalem.
The UN’s Special Coordinator and humanitarian chief in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, Dr. Ramiz Alakbarov, concluded a three-day visit to Gaza on Thursday, including a visit to the Emirati Field Hospital in Rafah.
Another bitter winter ahead
Throughout his visit, Mr. Alakbarov stressed that preparing for the rainy season and winter remains a top priority, requiring urgent donor support and the lifting of Israeli restrictions on equipment such as engine oil needed to run facilities including sewage treatment plants.
Ambulances and medical equipment remain among the items currently restricted from entering Gaza, Mr. Dujarric said, adding that these “must be urgently allowed in.”

Misuse of informal money-transfer networks is growing worldwide, global watchdog says
PARIS, Sept 3 - Criminal use of informal banking networks has become a global problem and is growing, the Financial Action Task Force said on Thursday, urging companies and governments to do more to combat professional money-laundering services.
Here's what the global money laundering and terrorist financing watchdog FATF said in a report:
• Criminal misuse of non-bank settlement methods, including hawala and other similar service providers (HOSSPs) - which move payments through agents rather than regulated financial institutions - is "a widespread global phenomenon".
• Illicit networks, once used mainly to launder the proceeds of cash-based crime such as drug trafficking and smuggling, now also process funds from fraud, cybercrime, terrorist financing, illegal gaming and gambling, as well as international organised crime.
• Professional service providers are increasingly involved in facilitating the schemes, including lawyers, accountants, auditors, consultants and real estate agents, FATF member states who contributed to the report said.
• Encrypted communications, fintech, anonymity-enhancing tools and the growing use of crypto and other new technology - have transformed informal money-transfer networks, and can make them faster, more opaque and more resilient.
• Underground banking and HOSSP-based money laundering have become increasingly professionalised, with some operating like sophisticated businesses. REUTERS

Bats carry dangerous viruses without getting sick. This may be why
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:56:01 UTC
20:56:01 KST

Bats carry dangerous viruses without getting sick. This may be why
- Date:
- September 3, 2026
- Source:
- Tulane University
- Summary:
- Scientists discovered that more than 500 species of vesper bats possess two separate sets of antibody genes, an immune arrangement never before found in mammals. The surprising system could help explain how bats tolerate so many viruses without becoming seriously ill.
- Share:
Scientists have long been intrigued by a question surrounding bats: how can these flying mammals carry viruses capable of causing severe disease while rarely becoming seriously ill themselves?
Researchers at Tulane University, working with collaborators at Stanford University and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, may now have identified part of the answer.
A study published in Science Advances found that the world's largest family of bats carries two distinct copies of the genes involved in producing antibodies. These specialized proteins help the immune system identify and fight infections. Every other known mammal has only one such set of genes.
The finding gives scientists a new way to think about how immune systems evolved and how different animals respond to disease.
"We've never seen anything like this in a mammal before," said Hannah Frank, associate professor of ecology and evolutionary biology at Tulane University School of Science and Engineering and corresponding author of the study. "This completely changes our understanding of how mammalian immune systems can be organized and raises exciting new questions about why bats have been so evolutionarily successful and how they respond to viruses."
A Unique Antibody System in Vesper Bats
The discovery was made in vesper bats, a group that includes more than 500 species living on every continent except Antarctica. Scientists have long been interested in the extraordinary evolutionary success of these bats, and their unusual antibody system may provide part of the explanation.
Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins built from two heavy protein chains and two light protein chains. In humans and all other known mammals, the heavy chains are produced using a single set of genes.
Frank and her colleagues found that vesper bats are different. They have two separate heavy-chain gene systems, potentially giving them another way to create a wider variety of antibodies.
Researchers studying bat immunity have traditionally paid more attention to the innate immune system. Frank said the new findings show why the adaptive immune system -- the part responsible for producing antibodies -- also deserves closer study.
"We think this discovery is an important piece of the puzzle," Frank said. "It doesn't fully explain why bats are such effective viral reservoirs, but it reveals a level of immune variety we didn't know existed and gives us an entirely new direction to explore."
Why Bat Immunity Matters
Bats play important ecological roles as pollinators, seed dispersers and natural pest controllers. At the same time, they are natural hosts for many viruses, Frank said.
Learning how bats can live alongside those viruses without becoming ill could eventually help researchers better understand immune responses in other species. That knowledge may also contribute to improved strategies for reducing the risk of disease spillover.
"We've learned an enormous amount about immunity by studying humans and laboratory mice," Frank said. "But the natural world is far more varied than that. Every time we study a species that has evolved differently, we have the opportunity to discover something entirely new."

Ukraine gets first Skyranger 35 systems on Leopard 1 tanks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:53:41 UTC
20:53:41 KST

- Ukraine's 1020th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment has reportedly received the first Rheinmetall Skyranger 35 air defense systems mounted on Leopard 1 chassis.
- The contract, signed in the second half of 2025, is financed by an EU country using proceeds from frozen Russian assets.
Ukraine’s Armed Forces have shown footage of what appears to be one of the first Skyranger 35 short-range air defense systems mounted on a Leopard 1 tank chassis to reach Ukrainian units.
GAU, an account that tracks German military assistance to Ukraine, identified the unit in the footage as Ukraine’s 1020th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment, part of the Ground Forces. The account said the regiment appears to have taken delivery of the first Leopard 1-based Skyranger 35 systems built by Rheinmetall.
Rheinmetall announced the contract for the systems in October 2025, saying an unnamed European Union country would finance the deal using proceeds from frozen Russian assets under the EU’s Windfall Profit Mechanism. The company put the order’s value in the hundreds of millions of euros and said production and integration would take place at Rheinmetall Italia’s headquarters in Rome. Ukraine had already fielded earlier Skyranger 35 systems mounted on truck chassis; the Leopard 1 version is a separate, tracked variant.
The Skyranger 35 is built around a KDG 35/1000 revolver cannon firing 35x228mm ammunition at a rate of 1,000 rounds per minute, with an effective range up to 4,000 meters (2.5 miles). The system fires airburst rounds that detonate near a target and scatter tungsten sub-projectiles, a design intended to improve hit probability against small, fast-moving threats such as Shahed-type drones and FPVs. Rheinmetall has said the turret shares a high degree of commonality with the company’s Oerlikon Revolver Gun Mk 3 and could eventually be fitted with guided missiles.
Rheinmetall first showed the Leopard 1-based Skyranger 35 publicly in September 2024, at a demonstration event at the Erprobungszentrum Ochsenboden test site in Switzerland. That demonstrator used a Leopard 1A5BE hull with an unmanned turret carrying 252 rounds, with the two-person crew, a commander and a gunner, seated in the front of the hull. Representatives from defense ministries and industry in 26 countries attended.
Germany’s own military has ordered 19 Skyranger systems and has discussed acquiring several hundred more, following reports of unidentified drones appearing in European airspace. Ukraine’s version reaching the field ahead of Germany’s own fielding was noted at the time the October contract was announced.
Rheinmetall has previously delivered Skyranger 35 units to Ukraine mounted on wheeled truck platforms. The Leopard 1 chassis gives the new variant tracked mobility and armor protection not available on the truck-based version, allowing it to operate closer to the front line. Ukraine has received roughly 170 Leopard 1 tanks from Germany and other partners since 2023, with about 25 confirmed damaged or destroyed, according to the open-source tracking project Oryx.

IN BRIEF: Russian Deputy Prime Minister Novak’s key statements on sidelines of EEF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:51:10 UTC
20:51:10 KST

VLADIVOSTOK, September 3. /TASS/. Russia’s oil production will fall modestly by the end of 2026, while exports remain stable, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters on the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF).
He noted that Russia has the capacity to repair 100% of its refineries. The country is stepping up fuel imports to saturate the domestic market, drawing supplies from both neighboring countries and nations further abroad.
TASS has compiled the Deputy Prime Minister's key statements.
Situation on fuel market
The fuel supply situation on the Russian market has improved, with authorities noting positive changes this week: "We are constantly monitoring the regions and holding regular coordination meetings with local authorities," Novak said.
Things have gotten better due in part to refineries stepping up production: "A number of refineries have delivered extra volumes to the market."
The situation with diesel and jet fuel in Russia is currently stable, with minor deviations observed only in gasoline supplies: "As I said earlier, the situation with diesel and jet fuel is stable right now. There are some fluctuations and shortages in gasoline. The primary task in this area at present is to fully supply the market with motor gasoline."
The Russian government is observing minor fuel shortages at filling stations, particularly in the Siberian and Ural Federal Districts: "Overall, the situation has partially stabilized and improved over the past week, although we certainly still observe a minor deficit at gas stations, especially in the regions of the Siberian and Ural Federal Districts. This is purely a logistics issue," Novak said.
Authorities’ measures
Authorities intend to balance fuel supply and demand in Russia by increasing refinery output and drawing additional imported gasoline supplies: "We will continue to monitor and balance the market, relying not only on scaling up domestic production but also on securing additional supply volumes from foreign markets."
The government is discussing a reduction of the oil cutoff price within the fiscal rule, with one option being a decrease to $50 per barrel: "This figure is currently under discussion. Naturally, we will provide more precise details once all the figures proposed and reviewed by federal executive bodies are officially approved at a government meeting. Strategically, however, we do plan to lower the cutoff price to ensure a more stable budget, support its replenishment, and top up the National Wealth Fund."
This approach reduces the risk of global price volatility, making it an entirely correct path from a strategic planning perspective.
Russia is engaged in fuel imports to satisfy domestic demand, sourcing petroleum products from both neighboring countries and nations further abroad: "We are also working with companies to arrange fuel shipments from abroad, including both neighboring states and more distant foreign markets, focusing primarily on gasoline supplies."
Ensuring power grid security
Securing Russian electric power facilities remains a top priority for the government: "Our grid and energy companies work around the clock to maintain the security of key power facilities, such as large thermal power plants and major substations. This matter remains under the government’s close supervision and special control."
Refinery maintenance
Russia has sufficient capacity to repair 100% of its refineries: "Of course, for all repairs carried out on the basis of domestic technologies and domestic equipment, there are no issues whatsoever. Our companies and our industry fully provide the necessary resources and equipment."
Oil production
Russia’s oil production will decline slightly by the end of 2026 due to the underutilization of refineries caused by unscheduled maintenance:
"We are currently seeing a partial decline in production volumes compared to forecast figures, which is partly due to the underutilization of refineries due to unscheduled maintenance."
At the same time, exports remain stable, with export infrastructure capacity being utilized to its maximum potential: "Exports are stable, and the full capacity of our export infrastructure, which has been expanded in terms of maritime transport over the past few years, is being utilized to the maximum."
The decline in Russian oil production is a temporary phenomenon: "This is a temporary phenomenon, and in principle, as refineries return to operation and the situation stabilizes, production will increase."
OPEC's role and impact of Middle East conflict
OPEC plays a vital role in the global oil market, with the alliance accounts for a major share of global exports, though the Middle East conflict and the potential closure of the Strait of Hormuz will continue to exert a strong influence on global markets: "We maintain that this [the closure of the Strait of Hormuz - TASS] is actually a localized challenge that affects the supply and demand balance. Nevertheless, OPEC's role remains highly significant because the production volumes of OPEC member states are very large and account for a significant share of global exports. Therefore, it will undoubtedly continue to have a major impact on global markets."
Investment situation
The decline in investments in the first half of 2026 is objective: "This year, we are seeing a decline [in investments], which is clearly objective. There was a slight decline in the first half of the year, by 9.9% on average. The new investment cycle will focus on creating conditions for long-term financial allocations, developing the stock market, and ensuring the availability of long money in the economy."
Overall, the decline in investments for the year is not critical: "By the way, looking at the figures, our total investments in the first half of the year reached 16.2 trillion [rubles]. Last year, total investments during the same period stood at 15.9 trillion [rubles]. That represents an increase of 300 billion, but this is in nominal terms. If we adjust for inflation, it is slightly lower in real terms than last year. However, the decline is not critical."
Power of Siberia 2
The route and commercial terms of gas supplies under the Power of Siberia 2 project will be discussed tomorrow at a meeting of the intergovernmental commission on trade and economic cooperation: "As for the second major project you mentioned, discussions are currently underway between our companies - Gazprom and the China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) - regarding the terms for supplying 50 billion cubic meters of gas, the route, which is also being negotiated today, and, naturally, the commercial conditions. Tomorrow, we will hold a meeting of the intergovernmental commission on trade and economic cooperation between our countries with the PRC, represented by Vice Premier of the State Council Mr. Ding Xuexiang. We will also address this topic, doing our utmost to facilitate a swift agreement."

NEW YORK, September 3. /TASS/. Dutch authorities warn of rising threat from young Western cybercriminals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:48:24 UTC
20:48:24 KST

Dutch police and prosecutors warned on Thursday about an emerging generation of young cybercriminals operating through loosely connected online networks in Western countries, local media reported.
The suspects are generally aged between 11 and 25 and are primarily motivated by money and status rather than political or ideological objectives, public broadcaster NOS reported, citing the Netherlands' annual Cybercrime Overview.
"These are individuals between the ages of 11 and 25," said Stan Duijf, the police official responsible for tackling cybercrime.
"They mainly come from Western countries, speak English, work in a sort of online network, and primarily commit data and crypto thefts," he added.
Duijf said law enforcement agencies had previously focused largely on cybercriminals based in countries such as Russia, where Western authorities have limited access.
"Now we see that there are genuinely Western criminals on the way who are collaborating online and committing serious forms of cybercrime," he said.
The report cited an attack earlier this year against Dutch telecommunications provider Odido, allegedly carried out by criminals operating under the name ShinyHunters.
The hackers demanded a ransom after stealing personal information belonging to six million customers. After Odido refused to pay, the data was offered for sale online.
Authorities warned that young people could be drawn into cybercrime through online games such as Roblox, Fortnite and Minecraft, initially engaging in minor misconduct before progressing to more serious offenses.
An estimated 2.5 million people in the Netherlands fell victim to cybercrime in 2025.
Police also warned that artificial intelligence was making cyberattacks easier to conduct while making scams, including phishing emails, increasingly difficult for the public to recognise.

"Passing ball to new Duma convocation" and Far East’s development: Putin’s speech at EEF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:43:36 UTC
20:43:36 KST

VLADIVOSTOK, September 3. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin said at the plenary session of the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) that he wants to "pass the ball to the new convocation of the State Duma," adding that he expects deputies to play an active role in improving the country’s business climate.
The Russian leader also announced the move to the next stage of the development of the Far East, a renewed strategy for the coming decade.
TASS has compiled the key statements by the head of state.
Far East’s development
Russia’s strategic policy is to turn the Far East into an area for cooperation and dynamic change: "Russia is an active participant in investment and trade cooperation in the Asia-Pacific region. We interact on an equal footing with our partners and the region’s leading integration associations. Our strategic policy is to make the Far East an area for cooperation and dynamic change in the economy and infrastructure, technological development, workforce training and, of course, the social area."
Around 25 trillion rubles ($287 bln) in capital investments have been invested in the Russian Far East over the past 11 years, while the region's gross product has more than tripled: "I would like to point out that about 25 trillion rubles in capital investments have been attracted to Russia's Far Eastern regions over 11 years. The rates of investment activity, industrial growth, and construction here consistently surpass the national average. As a result, the gross regional product of the Far East has more than tripled over 11 years, which is a very rapid pace."
Unemployment in the Far East has recently fallen fourfold to 2.2%, reaching the national average: "Unemployment in the Far East has decreased fourfold. This year it has been at 2.2%, which is the level of the national average. This unemployment figure is a record low for the region."
The Russian Far East is currently experiencing growth, with high economic activity recorded in nearly all of its constituent entities: "High economic activity is recorded across practically all Far Eastern regions of the [Russian] Federation. This is particularly noticeable in small and medium-sized businesses, which employ approximately one-third of the working population. This is a strong indicator. What does it show? It shows that the Russian Far East is on the rise. Businesses and entrepreneurs see clear prospects for developing and expanding their enterprises. Whereas citizens understand that their in-demand knowledge and competencies can yield tangible results, both for the region and for the country as a whole, and for people individually."
Russia is moving into the next stage of the Far East’s development, an updated development strategy for the next 10 years: "We are moving to the next stage - implementing an updated development strategy for the Far East, the Far Eastern Federal District, designed for the next 10 years, through 2036. The key task is to maintain the strong pace of development achieved so far and launch new investment cycles in the region."
Quantum communication networks must be expanded to all regional capitals in the Far East by 2030: "As of today, the length of the main quantum network in Russia already exceeds 7,800 kilometers. It connects 27 constituent entities of the Russian Federation, including 13 cities with populations of over one million. I would like to draw the attention of the government and my colleagues at Russian Railways to the fact that quantum communication networks must be extended to the Far East by 2030, reaching all its regional capitals, thereby integrating them into a high-speed information and data exchange network."
Infrastructure loans repaid by Far East regions may be reinvested into the implementation of master plans in those constituent entities.
Unified preferential treatment
Unified preferential treatment for the Far East and the Arctic will take effect on January 1, 2027: "We are launching a business support system that is unprecedented in scale and scope. A unified preferential regime will begin operating across the entire Far East and Arctic starting as early as January 1 of next year."
The concept behind preferential treatment is to ensure that support tools are not tied to a specific special zone or priority development area, but are instead carefully and effectively tailored to specific types of activities across the entire region: "In other words, an investment project anywhere in the Far East or the Arctic will have access to its own specific menu of incentives."
The full range of available mechanisms will include reduced insurance contributions, tax and customs incentives, and assistance with infrastructure connections and constructing production facilities, among other things.
Existing benefits for residents of existing priority development areas in the Far East will remain even after the introduction of the unified preferential regime: "At the same time, existing benefits for current residents of priority development areas and the Free Port of Vladivostok will be preserved in full, of course."
The system of preferential regimes has already been successfully implemented in the Far East and the Arctic zone: "They include priority development areas, the Free Port of Vladivostok, the special administrative region on Russky Island, and special tax treatment on the Kuril Islands."
These tools have already made it possible to attract trillions of rubles in investment and generate 200,000 new jobs.
"Passing ball to new Duma convocation"
Putin would like to "pass the ball to the new convocation of the State Duma," counting on deputies to play an active role in improving the business climate: "I want to pass the ball, so to speak, to the new convocation of the Russian State Duma, which will be elected soon, in September. I am expecting deputies to take an active stance and engage in fruitful legislative work to improve the business climate."
It is important to continue establishing favorable and predictable conditions for investors, relying on requests from entrepreneurs and needs of regions, being guided by Russia’s national interests.
Need to remove barriers for business
It is necessary to remove bureaucratic barriers for business and avoid excessive control and "tightening the screws": "We need <...> to consistently lift bureaucratic barriers for entrepreneurs and reduce the administrative burden. It even makes no sense to introduce tax incentives while simultaneously, so to speak, tightening the screws through additional inspections and excessive control and oversight. I am saying excessive in particular. <...> I believe colleagues from relevant ministries and agencies will hear the message."
It is important to eliminate the risk of double taxation for businesses in the Far East: "I’m asking to adjust the legal framework accordingly. It is important to continue creating favorable, predictable conditions for investors, relying on the requests of entrepreneurs and the needs of the regions, being guided by Russia’s national interests."
Extraction of resources
Russia will continue to expand mineral extraction in the east and north of the country, including oil, gas, and gold: "For industrial growth and the development of high-tech industries of the future, we need to strengthen our foundation, our resource base. <…> We will continue developing mineral extraction in the east and north of the country, including oil, gas, coal, gold, and rare earth metals. Of course, [we will do so] using clean technologies, as is already being done at a number of our enterprises."
Natural resources extracted in the Far East and the Arctic should increasingly be processed locally: "This refers to metallurgical, gas, and petrochemical facilities, fertilizer production, etc. ensuring that value chains are established, jobs are created, and regional and municipal budget revenues grow right here, in the Far Eastern and Arctic constituent entities of the Federation."
Special legal regime
A special legal regime designed to rapidly test advanced technologies, including UAVs for use in the civilian economy, is set to launch in the Russian Far East starting January 1, 2027: "Its essence lies in the rapid, unhindered testing of cutting-edge technologies, such as agricultural drones, industrial robots, telemedicine, or artificial intelligence for medical diagnostics."
Eased public procurement system
A streamlined public procurement system, including through marketplaces, will launch in Russia on October 1 as a pilot project: "A new federal law enabling more active use of platform-based solutions for procurement at regional and local levels, initially on a trial basis, comes into force on October 1. This applies not only to the Far East and the Arctic but to all constituent entities of the Russian Federation. Their educational institutions, such as kindergartens, schools, and colleges, will be able to purchase goods directly, so to speak, from the shelf of domestic marketplaces."
Transportation
Russia plans to make navigation along the Northern Sea Route year-round.
Authorities expect the volume of freight traffic along the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor to reach at least 70 mln tons per year: "This means it will at least double from the current level."
It is planned to link the Arctic marine terminals with rail and inland waterway networks to ensure cargo flows from Central Russia, the Urals, and Siberia: "We also plan to connect Arctic marine terminals with rail and inland waterway networks so that cargo flows from Central Russia, the Urals, and Siberia could gradually be tied to this route, and to facilitate the delivery of imported goods, of course."
Transportation of civilian cargo using low-altitude drones needs to be tested in the regions of the Far East and the Arctic: "As unmanned aviation develops, low-altitude airspace is becoming a transport artery as busy as railways and waterways. It is essential to establish standards for autonomous transportation of civilian cargo using drones already now."
Vostok Oil
The first oil from Vostok Oil will be shipped shortly: "I would like to note a milestone event that will take place soon. At Vostok Oil, one of our largest Arctic projects located in the Krasnoyarsk Region, a trunk oil pipeline to the new Bukhta Sever terminal will be put into operation. The first oil will also be loaded and delivered to buyers via our Arctic sea routes."
Creation of modern financial center on basis of Eastern Exchange
The government and the Central Bank must carefully consider the creation of a modern financial center based on the Eastern Exchange: "To expand the participation of international capital in our Far Eastern and Arctic projects, we need to leverage the potential of the Eastern Exchange. As I said earlier, we plan to establish a modern financial center on its basis. I’m asking the government and the Bank of Russia to thoroughly address all these issues."

Russia remained India’s top oil supplier in August

Russia remained India’s top oil supplier in August
Russia remained India’s largest supplier of crude oil in August, selling around 2.1 million barrels per day (bpd), or 45% of the country’s total imports, data from maritime intelligence firm Kpler shows.
Russian shipments were down from a record 2.8 million bpd in July, when they accounted for more than half of India’s crude purchases. However, India’s overall imports also declined to around 4.6 million bpd in August, nearly 8% below the more than 5 million bpd bought the previous month.
Indian refiners ramped up purchases in May, June, and July to guard against potential supply shortages amid the conflict in the Middle East. The August decline reflected some normalization after months of heavy buying, scheduled maintenance at Indian refineries, and lower availability of Russian crude, according to Kpler.
“August was less a story of India voluntarily stepping away from Russian oil than of Russia having fewer barrels to offer,” Abu Dhabi-based commodity analyst Natalia Katona told the Financial Express. Lower Russian seaborne exports and stronger competition from Chinese refiners for available cargoes also weighed on supplies to India, she said. 
The United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, and Venezuela were among India’s other leading oil suppliers during the month. Venezuelan shipments rose sharply, reaching their highest level since 2020, according to Kpler data. 
Russian oil has remained an important part of India’s energy mix as it seeks to secure supplies amid disruptions affecting shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. India imports around 90% of the crude oil it consumes.
The purchases have continued despite the prospect of new US tariffs targeting major buyers of Russian oil. The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which cleared the US Senate last month, would allow tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the five biggest buyers of Russian oil. The bill has US President Donald Trump’s backing but still has to pass the House. 
India maintains that its oil purchases are guided by affordability, availability, and national energy security rather than geopolitical considerations.
