Neuroqueering on the lawn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
22 minute listen
The English countryside in the mid-19th century could be an idyllic retreat. It is breakfast time and you are Charles Dickens, respectable author and exemplar of etiquette, sure that today will be safe and uneventful. Searching the house for your daughters, you also find your overstayed houseguest from Denmark, Hans Christian Andersen – famed author of fairy tales like The Little Mermaid and The Ugly Duckling – face down on the grass, in the middle of a complete meltdown on your lawn, after receiving news of a bad book review. The Victorian era remains the measuring stick for (ostensibly) respectable domesticity, where emotions are repressed and ankles sequestered in attempts at control. Nonetheless, here lies Andersen, actively proving that even great authors were one lawn tantrum away from tearing at this veneer of respectability.
And indeed, Andersen has since been headcanoned, with great enthusiasm, as a 19th-century ‘disaster bi’. A disaster bisexual is less an identity or a diagnosis than a way of reading scenes that spill over. Messy. Earnest. Intensely sincere to the point of social detonation. Seen in modern drama from Bridgerton to Saltburn, they are characterised by living, loving and feeling in a perpetual crescendo, then come to a full stop when they melt down.
The term circulates now as affectionate shorthand, especially online, for people and characters who come in too hot, overshare, and punctuate the resulting social chaos with wit. To the chronically online, Andersen’s correspondence, travels and attachments now read as exasperating yet endearing. But Dickens, that poor man, did not have Tumblr. What he had was a lawn.
As Dickens in 1857, you offer Andersen reassurance. Gentle reason. Perspective. After all, you understand the impact of a bad book review (the criticism of your 1844 novel Martin Chuzzlewit still stings). Nonetheless, your words barely clear the air before Andersen begins to weep. Not quietly. Not briefly. Not in a way that can be absorbed and moved past. A full-throated sob and a heavy stream of tears, earth streaked on his face and shirt. He stays there. The scene does not resolve. The emotional alarm bell keeps ringing, time stretches. Dickens’s daughter Katey stares, struggling to reconcile this sobbing spectacle with her assessment of their Danish guest as ‘a bony bore’. Dickens, the great manager of feeling in fiction, realises, with dawning horror, that he – despite priding himself on being the ‘Inimitable’ – has lost control of the atmosphere entirely.
We have all encountered an Andersen. Some of us have loved one. Some of us have been asked whether we really have the capacity to care for them. Some of us are an Andersen. We could treat Andersen’s collapse as a personality problem: a man who simply felt too much and too openly. But what makes the lawn tantrum intolerable is that the Victorian sense of propriety relied on tightly managed bodies, disciplined masculinity, and a strict division between private interior and public display. These expectations – the norms and scripts that still govern our modern social lives – buy into the fantasy that collapse can be avoided if only the most vulnerable behave better. The question is, when these scripts fail, whose collapse will we tolerate – and how many people will we lose by demanding composure?
The lawn, and situations like it, expose an impasse: what happens when feeling exceeds the social scripts meant to contain it. Neuroqueering – the practice of challenging norms about how bodies, minds and emotions should behave – makes that impasse visible, while neuroqueer excess offers a way to understand what spills beyond those norms.
Seeing Andersen and Dickens through the lens of neuroqueer excess is not an attempt to retrospectively diagnose or categorise them, but to use their scenes of overflow to consider how norms are enforced, resisted, and broken. Neuroqueering, as we use it here, is not an identity to be claimed so much as a verb, a doing.
On Dickens’s lawn, these rules are not theoretical. They show up as expectations: speak proportionately, recover quickly, be gentlemanly. Dickens thus acts not merely as a distressed host but as an enforcer of the Victorian norms that Andersen breaks.
This is where a neuroqueering approach changes the terms of the encounter. Instead of asking why Andersen cannot control himself, it asks why Dickens’s preferred forms of speech, feeling and recovery are treated as natural, proper and morally superior. Scholars such as Nick Walker and M Remi Yergeau examine how these often-invisible rules govern the ways bodies, minds and feelings are permitted to move through the world. Drawing on queer theory and neurodivergent ways of knowing, their work challenges the assumption that acceptable expression must be verbally fluent, emotionally proportionate, reciprocal, and delivered at the correct volume and moment.
Expressed by those on the margins, neuroqueer excess is a demand to be noticed and understood on their own terms
It is from this challenge that we propose the concept of neuroqueer excess. By excess, we do not mean flamboyance alone, nor pathology, nor a failure of self-regulation. Instead, neuroqueer excess is a kind of ‘too muchness’ that emerges when feeling, desire or embodiment refuses to stay within the narrow emotional constraints that society dictates. Unlike camp or queer transgression, neuroqueer excess does not rely on shared codes, irony or legibility; it often fails to be readable at all.
Expressed by those on the margins, it’s a demand to be noticed and understood on their own terms. Those who exist outside established norms of behaviour, dress and mannerisms become hypervisible and surveilled; an example could be effeminate men. Norms like these (for instance, heteronormativity and neuronormativity) can be subverted into an act of disruption and rebellion. Neuroqueer excess provides a way to read these scenes not as personal failures, but as moments where the limits of the social system are exposed.
Andersen’s humiliating and excessive public behaviour subverted 1850s English expectations of masculine restraint, composure and intimacy. Across a very different historical moment, the Australian performance artist Leigh Bowery is a useful parallel. His bold club attire and antics, carried out during the AIDS epidemic in 1980s Britain, troubled a later but no less exacting demand: that queer bodies remain discreet, manageable and quietly grateful for survival. Given that Bowery’s performances included explorations of bodily fluids, simulated birth, outrageous fashions drawn from the grotesque and the aspirational, pushback and containment by institutions was firm and final.
His nightclub, Taboo, was closed after The Mail on Sunday in June 1986 reported widespread drug use there. Later, Bowery’s performance at the Freedom Bar in Soho was reported as pornographic and cancelled by Westminster Council in November 1994. He died of AIDS-related illness five weeks later. It was Bowery’s aesthetic hyperbole – his distorted silhouettes, unapologetic flesh, theatrical filth and refusal of good taste – that proved intolerable because he refused to make himself palatable to those watching.
Seeing Dickens recoil from Andersen, and Britain recoil from Bowery, helps clarify what is at stake in neuroqueer excess across time. Each moment reveals a culture frightened by emotion that refuses to be shepherded back into scripts of propriety, productivity or resilience. Disaster bisexuality simply provides a contemporary name for that old terror: the subject who renders the atmosphere unmanageable. Victorian propriety, AIDS‑era respectability politics, and our present appetite for therapeutic neatness share a common demand: that excess be invisible or else useful. Tracing neuroqueer excess across these moments offers a diagnostic tool, revealing how norms become instruments of oppression, and which bodies and feelings they seek to discipline – on the lawn, in the university, or inside the nightclub.
Dickens was not simply enforcing these norms; he had built his life around them, which explains his discomfort at Andersen’s tantrum on his lawn. Charles John Huffam Dickens was a complicated character, who obsessively sought to control his legacy. Feelings of inferiority had haunted him since childhood, when his father was imprisoned for debt, and ever after Dickens (understandably) worried about money. Over time, as his celebrity as a writer increased, he learned how to control more narratives than those in his novels, selectively editing his life history to provide the illusion of a well-bred gentleman.
In 19th-century England, being a gentleman required more than money; it demanded strict adherence to often-contradictory codes of conduct, wherein family pedigree was also scrutinised. You wouldn’t find Dickens at his exclusive Athenaeum club in London discussing his paternal grandparents’ work in the service industry. No, they were conveniently elided.
Dickens was himself a man of intense emotions, who burned his draft autobiography because he couldn’t bear to recount the trauma of being rejected by his first love. (This painful part of his life was likewise excised. After all, it didn’t align with notions of 19th-century masculinity, which mandated emotional restraint and physical discipline – the so-called English ‘stiff upper lip’.)
Although the public might be secretly pining for scandal, they simultaneously demanded concealment
For an insecure gentleman committed to control, and accustomed to editing out inconvenient truths, Dickens was utterly unprepared for the egregious excess of Andersen’s lawn tantrum – his fellow author’s visceral response to a negative review in the papers. Andersen’s upper lip was quivering and covered in tears – openly exhibiting an ungentlemanly emotional outburst. Dickens’s instinctive response was to contain, quell and return order to his domestic domain. Even his subsequent advice to Andersen (likely intended to reassure) was delivered as a command to repress: ‘Never allow yourself to be upset by the papers …’ Refuse to feel.
Nonetheless, this experience with Andersen foreshadowed the public outrage coming for Dickens the very next year. Given his need for narrative authority, Dickens decided to set the record straight (or, as it turned out, decidedly crooked) when rumours of affairs were swirling amidst his marital breakdown. In June 1858, Dickens published a ‘personal statement’ in The Times, reminding his readers that such rumours were completely false and out of character for him. Unfortunately, the public reacted poorly – the scholar Robert Sawyer suggests that people were perhaps more disturbed by Dickens turning his private issues into public spectacle than by the behaviour itself.
Ironically, Dickens did have a mistress, an actress almost the same age when they met – 18 – as his daughter Katey. He went to great lengths to conceal her because, even though many men had mistresses, it wasn’t something that gentlemen broadcast in polite society. The Victorian veneer of respectability required private matters to remain private. Although the public might be secretly pining for scandal, they simultaneously demanded concealment. This provided a comforting illusion of middle-class Victorian domesticity, where the household functioned as a regulatory machine, grounding respectable society. After all, any unravelling of the domestic sphere would surely send the entirety of England spiralling!
These Victorian anxieties and competing impulses resonate today. At a Coldplay concert in Massachusetts in July 2025, the stadium camera landed on a man with his arms around a woman. The pair were Andy Byron, then chief executive of the data company Astronomer, and Kristin Cabot, its chief people officer. As soon as they realised that their embrace was being projected onto the jumbotron, Byron ducked out of sight and Cabot turned her face away. Coldplay’s Chris Martin joked from the stage that they were either having an affair or were simply very shy. The clip raced across social media, where online detectives identified the pair, investigated their private lives and transformed a few seconds of visible panic into a global morality play about an alleged affair. Both executives subsequently resigned. Yet the fascination lay not simply in what may or may not have happened between them, but in the spectacle of a carefully managed public surface suddenly collapsing. Under today’s norms, public displays of distress threaten to expose the precarious choreography sustaining the fiction that everything is under control.
Back to Andersen’s tantrum on Dickens’s lawn. The problem with the Danish writer’s meltdown is not that he is overwhelmed, nor even that he weeps. It is where this happens. Emotional expression was to be reserved for private spaces, while more public areas required restraint. The lawn bridges these realms – belonging to the domestic sphere, yet publicly visible – carefully designed to be seen and therefore to reflect the moral and emotional discipline of the household within.
A breakdown in a bedroom might be unfortunate but containable. A breakdown on the lawn ruptures the boundary altogether. Perspectives shift uneasily – who is responsible for restoring order? Dickens, as master of the house? Behind the scenes, however, his own household was deteriorating; he would separate from his wife the very next year. We might read Andersen’s meltdown on the lawn as marking the moment when the private secrets of Charles and Catherine Dickens’s home began to seep into public view.
It is tempting to imagine ourselves as more evolved than the Victorians, or more compassionate than Britain at the height of the AIDS crisis. We use gentler language now. We (allegedly) advocate for boundaries rather than etiquette, regulation rather than repression, self‑care rather than self‑command. But these are largely changes in vocabulary, not structure. The underlying demand remains strikingly consistent: that feeling be calibrated, legible, productive and contained. Emotional expression is encouraged, but only when it is proportionate, self‑aware, and oriented toward resolution. Distress must be narrated, not enacted; processed, not performed. Meltdowns are acceptable only in retrospect, rendered tidy through insight and growth. Unresolved or unresolvable excess is still treated as a failure of character.
You almost certainly know someone like this. The one advised to lower their voice. To first calm down. To abstain from mannerisms that are ‘girly’, ‘unladylike’ or ‘weird’. The one whose access to care, work or belonging is conditioned upon composure or obedience. Maybe that person is you.
Excess is not inherently virtuous. It is disruptive, exhausting, sometimes damaging to self and others alike
These norms are to our detriment. Neuroqueer excess is costly and destabilising, but it is also informative. It marks the precise points where our scripts for care, communication and belonging break down.
It is fashionable to treat figures like Andersen or Bowery as delightful radicals, icons of sincerity, or brave affronts to decorum. We must resist this temptation. Excess is not inherently virtuous. It is disruptive, exhausting, sometimes damaging to self and others alike. Andersen, Bowery and Dickens are more complicated than we can do justice to here. None of them emerges from this analysis as a moral exemplar. What they are, instead, are stress tests.
They show us what happens when bodies, affects, desires or ways of communicating exceed what a system can manage. And, crucially, they show us which lives are abandoned when systems fail. Victorian containment scripts did not spare Dickens embarrassment; they contributed to his own scandal. AIDS‑era respectability politics did not merely police aesthetics; they helped determine which queer lives were cared for, treated and mourned, and which were allowed to die amid moralised silence. Bowery’s excess unfolded in a Britain structurally incapable of caring for queer bodies without first demanding obedience, gratitude and discretion.
Our contemporary regimes are no kinder for being therapeutic rather than moral. Today, even with therapeutic discourse, neurodivergent and queer people are still routinely failed by scripts that demand self‑regulation, emotional legibility, resilience narratives, and ‘appropriate’ expression before care will be extended. And those who cannot comply? Like Andersen on the lawn, they become problems to be managed, weirdos to be excluded, and people to rush by in public spaces. Dickens, too, belongs among the failed as a man straining against contradictory societal regimes that lacked healthy emotional outlets. With Andersen, Dickens upheld the norms of his day. Later, the same norms would lead him to a scandalous fall, his missteps converted into public morality tales rather than recognised as the familiar fractures of containment under pressure.
What unites these figures is not heroism, but exposure. They reveal that our systems do not fail accidentally. They fail predictably, repeatably, along familiar lines, for similar people.
Neuroqueer excess teaches us that care cannot rely on scripts of propriety, productivity or emotional neatness. Excess will not always be ethical, enlightening or kind – sometimes, it will be unbearable. But refusing to sit with discomfort, insisting instead on rapid containment, has repeatedly left neurodivergent and queer people without care when it mattered most.
Care, here, is not indulgence. Nor is it discipline. It is something more fragile and demanding: the willingness to remain present when emotions spill past what we know how to manage.
Historically, neurodivergence and queerness were written about by those espousing neither identity, thus displacing the invaluable perspectives of people with lived experience. Recent work of groundbreaking neurodivergent and queer scholars offers the opportunity to redress this gap, seeking to understand people on their own terms. Sometimes referred to as testimonial justice, this emerging realisation requires shifting who speaks, who is listened to, and how we respond when they do. Important work remains, including mourning lost opportunities to empathetically engage with the figures in this essay. Testimonial justice requires us to pause before we interpret, to believe before we correct, and to follow rather than reshape what is being communicated. It requires making space for neurodivergent and queer people to define their own terms, building vocabularies without presuming a deficit, and resisting the impulse to smooth over what feels excessive, contradictory or unfamiliar. Instead, we can respond to excess by sitting alongside the person, resisting the assumption that they are broken, and suppressing our impulse to ‘fix’.
As Dickens, you stifle the instinct for decorum, deciding instead to engage in Andersen’s emotional excess
In other words, we get down on the lawn with Andersen, extending grace without requiring palatability – accepting that we may need to choose comfort within discomfort. Sitting quietly with Andersen, co-regulating on the grass. Engaging with Bowery’s art even amid simulated birth and enema water. The work of care inevitably feels inefficient, unsettling and unresolved – but that does not diminish its importance.
Let us now imagine an alternative lawn.
The same 19th-century morning in the idyllic countryside, and Andersen again undone on the grass, sobbing without measure or end. As Dickens, you stifle the instinct for decorum, deciding instead to engage in Andersen’s emotional excess. Despite still feeling somewhat awkward, you manoeuvre onto the lawn, accidentally leaving a muddy smudge as you pat Andersen’s back. Your friend looks at you, tear-stained and messy, and your initial response is revulsion. Pushing that first feeling away, you instead murmur: ‘It is indeed a most unfortunate review.’
And he replies: ‘I was so proud of it,’ before dissolving into tears again. You are painfully aware of your daughter Katey staring aghast at the scene.
Nothing is resolved. It looks wrong. Yet you stay there together, uncomfortable, and you do not leave. You do not speak over him, or force him inside, or let that moment end your friendship. Grass flattens beneath you both. Mud marks your clothes. The moment remains messy.
Perhaps it’s OK if the lawn is ruined.

Convicted Trump Media-linked fraudster funded pro-Trump film in hopes of pardon, lawsuit says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Convicted Trump Media-linked fraudster funded pro-Trump film in hopes of pardon, lawsuit says
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- A Miami investor convicted in a Trump Media insider trading case bankrolled a pro-Trump documentary in hopes that the flattering film would buy him a presidential pardon, a lawsuit alleges.
- The lawsuit by a Los Angeles studio claims Michael Shvartsman demanded early repayment, threatened its CEO and grabbed a bigger slice of profits after the film’s Mar-a-Lago premiere.
- His failed bid for clemency highlights a booming, high-dollar cottage industry around Trump’s pardon power, where wealthy fraudsters bankroll political projects and influence campaigns in pursuit of freedom.
A Miami investor who pleaded guilty to making insider trades connected to the parent company of Donald Trump’s Truth Social platform helped fund a pro-Trump documentary film in hopes of securing a presidential pardon, according to a lawsuit by an L.A. studio that accuses him of threats and extortion.
Michael Shvartsman pleaded guilty in 2024 to insider trading associated with the Trump Media & Technology Group, which federal prosecutors said netted him $18.2 million in ill-gotten gains.
Four months later, Shvartsman helped fund the documentary “The Man You Don’t Know” in an effort to obtain a pardon, according to the lawsuit filed last month in Los Angeles. He denies the allegations.
A company controlled by Shvartsman provided a $425,000 loan in August 2024 to help fund the film, according to the suit. The film featured interviews with Trump’s sons Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. and painted a flattering portrait of the president.
Shvartsman attended the film’s premiere that October at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Fla., where he revealed, according to the lawsuit, that he had provided financing for the movie and “was hoping his participation would enable him to get a pardon.”
The event featured a who’s who of Trump-world insiders, including former New York Mayor Rudolph W. Giuliani, the late pro wrestler and media personality Hulk Hogan, Eric and Donald Trump Jr., as well as the former and soon-to-be president.
Shvartsman and his associates “arranged meetings” with “contacts and stars” associated with the movie in the hopes of achieving his goal of a pardon, the lawsuit said, though it doesn’t state specifically whom he targeted.
Shvartsman had good reason to seek their help.
Days before the event, he had been sentenced by a federal judge in New York to two years and four months in prison for insider trading connected to the announcement of a merger that would make Trump Media & Technology Group a publicly traded company.
Shvartsman, who is a Canadian citizen, also faced the prospect of deportation after his sentence.
Shvartsman said he “disputes all facts and allegations” in the lawsuit and plans to file a countersuit.
“We are not going to litigate this matter through the press,” he wrote in a message to The Times. “We intend to address the issues through the appropriate legal process, where the relevant facts and documentation can be properly presented and considered.”
Shvartsman’s efforts to mitigate his penalty weren’t limited to the documentary film. A day before his sentencing, the Aleph Institute, a Jewish criminal justice reform group, filed a letter to the federal court in New York laying out a proposed community service plan for Shvartsman to follow. The group had been instrumental in helping secure clemency during Trump’s first term for Philip Esformes, a south Florida man who was serving a 20-year prison sentence for his role in a $1.3-billion Medicare fraud scheme.
But Shvartsman’s story didn’t have a Hollywood ending: He failed to secure a pardon.
He went to prison in January 2025 and was held in federal custody until May 29, 2026, according to Bureau of Prison records. It isn’t clear whether he remains in the U.S.
Though Shvartsman was unsuccessful, dozens of other wealthy convicted individuals have been able to win clemency during Trump’s time in office by spending big bucks on influence campaigns to secure their freedom.
Many of them have ponied up millions of dollars to lobbyists and political insiders who have built a cottage industry out of helping monied convicts secure their freedom.
Some pardon chasers have also made big donations to pro-Trump super PACs as part of their efforts.
Scammers have even tried to get in on the action.
Trump’s pardon czar, Alice Marie Johnson, recently took to social media saying that people have been impersonating her and asking for a “processing fee” to help smooth the path to clemency. She said that neither she nor her office would ever ask for such a payment.
The lawsuit against Shvartsman, brought by the Los Angeles film production company Global Ascension Studios and its chief executive, Joshua Macciello, alleges that Shvartsman and his associates demanded immediate repayment of the loan the day after the 2024 Mar-a-Lago event — nine months before it was due — and threatened Macciello’s “physical safety” if the film company didn’t pay immediately or transfer control of the company to Shvartsman.
The lawsuit alleges that Macciello modified the loan agreement under duress and agreed to give Shvartsman and his company a greater share of the film’s potential proceeds.
It isn’t clear whether the loan has yet been repaid.
The proceeds from the film would prove to be middling.
The film was released days before Trump’s 2024 election victory, but its producers blamed political bias for the movie’s lackluster box office performance after fewer theaters than expected agreed to show it.
“In 37 years, I’ve never seen creative work get censored by theaters in this country,” Arthur Sarkissian, Global Ascension Studios’ former head of production, who was involved in the project, told Deadline at the time.
Sarkissian, best known as a producer of the “Rush Hour” franchise, is also being sued by Global Ascension and Macciello, who accused him of fraud and breach of contract in a lawsuit filed last year in Los Angeles.
Sarkissian has filed a counterclaim against Global Ascension, Macciello and others connected to the film production company, also accusing them of fraud and breach of contract.
The case is ongoing.

Hidden China risks are emerging in America’s multibillion-dollar AI data center boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:59:27 UTC
18:59:27 KST

American reliance on China for key components used to power data centers is coming under increasing scrutiny as Washington and Beijing battle for AI supremacy, raising the prospect of higher costs and worsening supply chain shortages for the AI buildout.
U.S. hyperscalers are racing to build multibillion-dollar data centers for AI, and Chinese firms supply large portions of the parts needed to develop these facilities. These include transformers, switchgear, batteries and optical tech, analysts told CNBC.
President Donald Trump signed an executive order last week declaring a national emergency around the "extraordinary foreign threat" to the U.S. involving bulk-power system equipment produced abroad. The order authorized the Energy Department to prohibit or impose conditions on certain transactions involving some components used in the grid and data centers.
Tensions between the U.S. and China over AI have ratcheted up as Chinese AI models become more advanced and their adoption grows across the globe. While American companies produce the most advanced chips and hardware used for AI, Chinese influence on the tech used to power data centers is considered a strategic vulnerability for the U.S.
"Scrutiny over China's presence in the U.S. data centre power stack has only risen over the past eight months or so, this is a shift from the previous focus that centred solely on the compute stack," Laveena Iyer, senior analyst at The Economist Group, told CNBC.
Dependencies
The power stack in a data center is critical to keeping the facility running with minimal downtime. It includes transformers, which change high-voltage electricity from the grid to lower levels needed for servers and cooling equipment. Switchgear are centralized systems that feature switches, fuses and circuit breakers and batteries are needed for backup power.
"There are a few key areas that the AI infrastructure buildout is increasingly dependent on Chinese imports," Ben Boucher, senior analyst, supply chain for Wood Mackenzie, told CNBC. "The most notable ones include substation transformers, which hyperscalers typically have on site to step transmission voltage down."
"The mid-term exposure is concentrated in grid connectors: transformers, switchgear, and batteries," Yury Dvorkin, associate professor at Johns Hopkins University, told CNBC.
"China's share of certain transformer and switchgear categories runs near 30%, and it accounts for over 40% of U.S. battery imports," he added. "Our analysis shows that there is also a deeper exposure upstream: copper, electrical steel, and battery cathode materials."
Optical technology, which uses light through fiber-optic cables instead of electrical signals through copper wires to transmit huge quantities of data, is also an area where China dominates.
Companies including Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink lead global data center optical transceiver revenue, with Chinese firms collectively accounting for roughly two-thirds of global unit supply, according to research firm Counterpoint.
Trump said that "transformers, transmission lines and conductors, substations, high-voltage circuit breakers, power control electronics" were "essential to the national defense" in April as part of a Presidential Determination.
Reducing reliance
Washington is scrambling to reduce reliance on Chinese suppliers as it rapidly develops the infrastructure needed to power AI.
"Since my first term, the threat to the United States regarding foreign supply of bulk-power system electric equipment has become even more acute," said Trump in a statement connected to the executive order published last week.
"The rapid growth of advanced manufacturing, data centers, artificial intelligence, and defense production has increased the Nation's dependence on abundant, reliable electricity and magnified the consequences of a successful attack or supply disruption on the bulk-power system," he added.
"We oppose overstretching the concept of national security to go after foreign enterprises," a spokesperson for the U.K. embassy of the People's Republic of China told CNBC. "We hope relevant countries will provide a fair, just and non-discriminatory business environment for Chinese companies."
U.S. data center capacity is forecast to grow from 62 GW in March 2026 to 152 GW by 2030 due to high-density AI workloads, S&P Global said in June.
"Reshoring manufacturing that's critical to our national and economic security has been a top priority for President Trump, and the Administration continues to deliver with a robust and nimble agenda of tax cuts, tariffs, and deregulation," a White House spokesperson told CNBC. "Trillions in investments across key sectors – from steel to semiconductors to autos – prove that the Administration's strategy is paying off."
Hitachi Energy announced in September 2025 it would invest $1 billion to expand production of critical grid infrastructure in the U.S., including $457 million for a new large power transformer facility to meet demand from the AI buildout. Siemens Energy also said in February it would invest $1 billion in U.S. production for grid and gas turbine equipment for AI infrastructure and data center expansion.
Power inverters produced in foreign countries, which help connect energy sources for AI facilities, were added to the Federal Communications Commission's (FCC) Covered List in July, which features equipment and services the U.S. government has determined pose an unacceptable risk to national security.
The Trump administration is also reportedly drafting a ban on U.S. imports of new Chinese optical transceivers, which allow data to travel at high speed over fiber optic cables between data centers. The FCC, which oversees the telecoms industry, did not respond to a request for comment and the White House did not address the report.
While any restrictions on Chinese optical tech companies could boost U.S. firms like Lumentum and Coherent — both of which received $2 billion in investment each from Nvidia in March — analysts cautioned that scaling manufacturing to meet new demand could come with challenges.
"Western competitors like Coherent and Lumentum possess advanced photonic designs, but currently lack the cleanroom capacity, automated packaging infrastructure, and yield scale required to absorb Innolight and Eoptolink's volume within a 12-to-24-month horizon," Neil Shah, VP research at Counterpoint said in an August report.
Fallout from restrictions
An optical transceiver ban would mean that U.S. hyperscalers will have to look for alternatives locally, potentially pushing up costs, said The Economist Group's Iyer.
Power transformers and substations are already in an estimated market shortage of 15% and 8%, respectively, in 2026, and restrictions on the use of units made in China are set to further exacerbate the supply chain challenges, according to Wood Mackenzie research.
"A bulk of the impacts will be centered around data centers who have been using Chinese units to minimize lead times," Wood Mackenzie's Boucher said in a blog from August.
"The 100 MVA+ segment is where the shortage is already most acute, and it is precisely where data centers have been turning to Chinese manufacturers to manage lead times," he added.
But political will in Washington to reduce dependencies on China in the power stack is rising, Iyer added. "The U.S. administration appears keen to de-risk its AI infrastructure before Chinese tech is fully embedded in it, quite like the 5G rollout where removing Chinese telecoms gear later on led to network rollout delays and rising costs for telecoms companies."

RVC deputy commander plotted assassination of Russian opposition leader — SSU
Unknown

RVC deputy commander plotted assassination of Russian opposition leader — SSU
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by the Security Service of Ukraine (SSU).
As part of its systematic counter-sabotage efforts, the SSU worked to prevent the assassination, which had been planned by the Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) to take place on Ukraine’s Independence Day.
The SSU obtained the relevant information through operational channels.
In particular, contacts were uncovered between the deputy commander of the Russian Volunteer Corps of the International Legion under the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense and Russian special services. The individual in question was to prepare an assassination attempt against one of the leaders of the Russian opposition movement, who was scheduled to arrive in Ukraine at that time, the SSU emphasized.
According to available evidence, during his communications with representatives of Russian special services, this servicemember was tasked with eliminating other members of the Ukrainian Armed Forces in exchange for monetary compensation.
Thanks to the SSU’s proactive efforts, the preparation of the crime was stopped in time, the statement said.
Subsequently, a series of counterintelligence verification measures was carried out with the participation of the aforementioned servicemember.
“In the process, this individual admitted to having contacts with the FSB of the Russian Federation and provided the SBU with relevant information. This allowed the Ukrainian security service to identify the entire chain of individuals involved in the planned crime. The Security Service documented the suspect’s correspondence with an FSB representative on his phone,” the SSU emphasized.
Given this military serviceman’s admission of contacts with the FSB of the Russian Federation and his cooperation with the investigation, no preventive measure was applied against him.
“While SSU officers were conducting urgent investigative actions to collect and document evidence of the aforementioned criminal offense, a completely unacceptable conflict arose, which led to gunfire. This definitely should not have happened,” the Ukrainian security service stated.
The State Bureau of Investigations is currently investigating this incident.
The Security Service of Ukraine is providing maximum assistance to the investigation to ensure an objective and impartial determination of all the circumstances surrounding the incident.
As previously reported, the SSU stated that, together with the Main Intelligence Directorate (DIU), it had thwarted a terrorist attack that Russia’s FSB was planning against one of the leaders of the Russian opposition political national movement, who had arrived in Ukraine to mark Independence Day.
Meanwhile, according to Ukrainska Pravda, a shootout occurred in the Dnipro district of Kyiv between representatives of the SSU and the DIU. According to the publication’s sources, three DIU representatives were wounded.
President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that following the shootout between the SSU and the DIU, the heads of these agencies must take appropriate personnel decisions regarding those involved in the incident.
The head of state also dismissed Oleh Khramov from his position as head of the SSU’s Department for the Protection of State Secrets and Licensing.

Andreas Keil, Social Democrats, Mayor of Employment, Integration, and Business, wrote this in a letter to the mayors.

He further writes that it will simultaneously be a concrete contribution to the redistribution among municipalities that Minister for Immigration and Integration Morten Bødskov (Social Democrats as well) has previously requested.
“I understand it to mean that the five Jutland municipalities would like more settlement, labor, and have more opportunities to accommodate the newcomers, while we, conversely, in Copenhagen are challenged to find accommodation for more than the 3,800 Ukrainians we already accommodate now,” he stated.
The letter has been sent to the mayors of Hjørring, Lemvig, Vesthimmerland, Skive, and Brønderslev Municipality, respectively.

Germany's far-right AfD aims for breakthrough in state election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:56:22 UTC
18:56:22 KST

Germany's far-right AfD aims for breakthrough in state election
BERLIN, Sept 3 - Voters in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt go to the polls on Sunday in an election where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is hoping to win power for the first time and mark a historic shift in German politics.
State Premier Sven Schulze from Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) says the election in Saxony-Anhalt is "a decision that will set the course for Germany."
Opinion polls in the state have put support for the AfD, which wants to restrict immigration, restore ties with Russia and quit the euro, at more than 40%, 15 to 20 points ahead of the CDU, which rules in a coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) and pro-free-market Free Democrats (FDP).
Most other parties running have refused to cooperate with the AfD, designated by the local office of Germany's domestic intelligence service as extremist right-wing, meaning that a CDU-led coalition may keep it from power in Saxony-Anhalt.
But the size of its support, fuelled by disillusion with Chancellor Friedrich Merz's unpopular government in Berlin, has laid bare how far German politics has moved in the decade or so since the party's formation in 2013.
'MY BEAUTIFUL, OLD, SAFE GERMANY'
Ulrich Siegmund, the 35-year-old hoping to become the first AfD state premier, has campaigned for months, drawing crowds to packed rallies in village halls and town squares across the state.
"I want my beautiful, old, safe Germany back," he tells supporters at his rallies.
Formed in western Germany at the height of the euro zone debt crisis, the AfD has increasingly drawn its support from the formerly communist states in the east, where surveys show a lingering sense of dissatisfaction with the results of reunification in 1990.
Siegmund, who rejects the far-right label, says he speaks "the language of the people" with a smiling approach that avoids the rhetoric of party colleagues like Bjoern Hoecke from the neighbouring state of Thuringia, who has been twice convicted for using Nazi slogans.
He has shrugged off criticism that his policies would deepen the problems of a state with a declining population, which economists say will depend on immigration to fill a shortage of workers in sectors from healthcare to tourism and the state's large chemicals industry.
The region has suffered along with the rest of Germany during the recent downturn, with unemployment running at around 8%. But economists say Saxony-Anhalt, a heavily rural state, has done relatively well in recent years, with the establishment of new industrial sectors, including logistics and renewable energy.
"Taking a broad view over the past 10 to 15 years, economic development in Saxony-Anhalt has been more than satisfactory. I would even say it has been quite good," said Thomas Brockmeier, head of the Halle-Dessau Chamber of Industry and Commerce.
Instead, Siegmund has focused on issues ranging from "culturally alien" immigrants and asylum seekers to leftist teachers, gender ideology or the cost to German industry of losing access to cheap Russian oil and gas through support for Ukraine.
Germany's most influential news magazine, "Der Spiegel", dubbed Siegmund "Germany's most dangerous man" in a cover story last month. Siegmund himself, a practised social media user, saw the headline as "good advertising" and posted footage of himself signing the cover on his Instagram account.
DECISIVE ELECTION
Across Europe, anti-establishment parties have made gains and Sunday's vote will be a test of whether the far-right can form a government in the continent's largest economy.
The AfD sees Saxony-Anhalt, which will be followed by two other state elections in the northeastern region of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and in Berlin this month, as a stepping stone to victory in national elections due in 2029.
Although its support is strongest in the east, the party scored around 20% in elections in the western states of Baden-Wuerttemberg and Rhineland-Palatinate earlier this year, underlining its growing nationwide appeal.
State governments in Germany make up the upper house of parliament, the Bundesrat, and have wide powers over education, culture and domestic security and an AfD state government would complicate everyday politics for Merz.
This week, the SPD interior minister of Thuringia warned that an AfD state interior minister would be a "flagrant security risk for the Federal Republic" because of the possibility of security information leaking to extremist groups.
"The consensus-driven model we have been used to within Germany over the last decades is now threatened," said Janos Richter, an analyst with the Verfassungsblog, a public law forum for constitutional and public law.
Siegmund has promised to recruit politically sympathetic officials from other states to help an AfD government to push through changes to schools, law enforcement and asylum centres, pointing to probable clashes with the federal government and other states. REUTERS

1 in 5 children in 21 countries face sexual abuse linked to online contact: UNICEF
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:56:11 UTC
18:56:11 KST

An estimated 20 million children aged 12 to 17, or nearly 1 in 5, experienced at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation and abuse in a single year across 21 countries, UNICEF said on Thursday.
The findings are included in a new report titled Through Children’s Eyes: How Digital Technologies Enable Child Sexual Abuse, which combines survey data with testimonies from children who experienced abuse.
“The report reveals a painful reality. More than 20 million children across the countries studied were subjected to unwanted explicit sexual content or exploitation online, often in the digital spaces where they learn, play, and connect with friends,” UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell said.
“Many children suffer in silence, unsure where to turn for help. We cannot look away,” she added.
The report estimates that more than 15 million children were exposed to unwanted sexual content, while nine million were asked to engage in sexual conversations or share sexual images against their will.
Around four million had sexual images of themselves shared without their consent.
Most cases occurred on social media platforms
Nearly 60 percent of cases occurred on social media platforms including Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok and WhatsApp, while 14 percent took place in online games, according to the report.
The report found that 57 percent of cases involved someone the child already knew, including peers, romantic partners, friends and family members. At the same time, 38 percent of children first encountered the perpetrator online, with abuse facilitated through tools such as fake accounts and private messaging.
The experiences had a significant impact on children’s emotional well-being, sense of safety and trust in others, with research participants describing feelings of fear, shame, confusion and isolation, according to the report.
Children who experienced technology-facilitated exploitation were four times more likely to report suicidal thoughts or behaviours and self-harm, and also reported significantly higher levels of anxiety, the analysis found.
In Mexico and North Macedonia, the risk of suicidal thoughts or behaviours was more than eight times higher among children who experienced abuse, while in Pakistan the risk of self-harm was more than seven times higher, according to the report.
Children suffer in silence
More than 40 percent of cases were never shared with anyone, while fewer than one percent were reported to authorities including police, social workers or helplines.
The most common reason children remained silent across the countries surveyed was not knowing where to go or whom to tell, UNICEF said.
The report calls on governments, technology companies and other stakeholders to strengthen protections for children online, including stronger privacy safeguards, restrictions on unsolicited contact from adults, safer recommender systems and improved detection and reporting of abuse.
It also calls for stronger laws and enforcement measures, improved reporting and support systems, and greater support for families, schools and communities.
“All of us, including governments and technology companies, must do more to protect children online,” Russell said.
The report draws on nationally representative surveys of approximately 21,000 internet-using children aged 12 to 17 across 21 countries, alongside in-depth interviews with 100 young people who experienced abuse in childhood.
UNICEF said the survey findings are representative of internet-using children rather than all children, particularly in countries with lower internet connectivity.

AI generated
VLADIVOSTOK – Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Sept 3 there was a chance of reaching an agreement to end the war in Ukraine, while Kyiv said it expected a “new dynamic” in peace efforts.
Putin, speaking at an economic forum in Russia’s Far East, said a number of countries, including the United States and China, were ready to support a peace settlement.
“Ultimately, however, the problem must be resolved by the countries involved in the conflict — Russia and Ukraine,” he said. “We are grateful to everyone attempting to contribute to a settlement. Is there a chance? In my view, yes, there is.”
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told reporters in Kyiv: “I believe that we will now have a new dynamic in the peace efforts, with the return of this active phase of political and diplomatic engagement in many capitals around the world.”
He did not elaborate further, telling reporters to “follow the news”.
After more than four years of Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II, it is rare for either side to offer an upbeat assessment of peace prospects. They last met for US-mediated talks in February.
Since then, with the US distracted by the Iran war, both Russia and Ukraine have ramped up long-range air attacks deep inside the other’s territory. Hostilities at sea have escalated sharply with attacks by both sides on ports and commercial shipping, pushing up global grain prices.
However, neither Putin nor Sybiha cited specific reasons to expect progress. On the contrary, Putin said Ukraine’s latest actions presented an obstacle.
In response to a question, Putin said Ukrainian attacks on civilian merchant ships and “reported threats of attacks on civilian aircraft” were “acts of state terrorism”, which he said “complicates the prospects for bilateral peace talks”.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned airlines and insurance companies this week that the presence of Ukrainian drones had made Russian skies dangerous, although he said Ukraine would target only Russian military facilities and not threaten civilian aircraft.
On Aug 2, Ukraine urged the UN’s aviation agency to ask members to ban operations in Russian airspace. Ukraine has been cut off from international civil aviation because its own airspace is considered unsafe since Russia invaded in 2022.
Putin said contacts with Ukraine were still taking place.
“It is difficult for me to say right now to what extent these contacts are leading to a peace agreement, given the statements we have heard recently from Ukraine’s top leadership,” he said. “However, contacts do exist and are continuing on an ongoing basis, again, primarily through intelligence channels.”
Speaking alongside Sybiha in Kyiv, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar said: “If India can be of any help, in any manner, we are there.”
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi told Putin on Aug 31 that the war in Ukraine needed to end for humanity’s sake and that New Delhi would support every effort to stop the fighting. REUTERS

Greater Taipei buses free for World Car-Free Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:56:03 UTC
18:56:03 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Greater Taipei's transport departments announced Thursday that bus rides will be free on Sept. 22 for World Car Free Day to encourage use of public transport.
CNA reported the free rides will cover 719 city bus routes served by 5,842 buses across Taipei and New Taipei. Officials said the program is aimed at people who usually drive or ride scooters, encouraging them to use public transport instead.
Taipei Deputy Mayor Chang Wen-te (張溫德) said the city has taken part in International Car-Free Day for 25 years. He said this year's campaign is intended to encourage people to consider alternatives to their usual way of getting around.
Bus operators will deploy as many vehicles as possible to meet higher demand, the Taipei City Bus Joint Management Committee said. Staff will also be assigned to major stops and transfer stations to help passengers, per Rti.
Taipei Transport Commissioner Hsieh Ming-hung (謝銘鴻) said that about 3,500 bus drivers work across the two cities. Operators will increase service while complying with working-hour rules, and officials hope daily bus ridership will rise 5% to 10% from the current 2 million passenger trips a day.
New Taipei Transport Commissioner Chung Ming-shih (鍾鳴時) said the two cities estimated the program would cost about NT$50 million (US$1.64 million) in subsidies. New Taipei is expected to provide about NT$20 million, while Taipei will provide about NT$30 million.
Participating buses will display signs showing that rides are free, Chung said. Card readers and fare boxes will also be covered to prevent passengers from paying by mistake.
CTEE reported that intercity and highway buses are not included in the program. Passengers using those services will still have to pay the normal fare.
World Car Free Day is held each year on Sept. 22 to promote alternatives to driving. It grew from European car-free campaigns in the 1990s and later spread worldwide.

"Song of Youth: Brushing the Sun"

Selected from nearly 2,000 submissions by 500 applicants nationwide, this open-call exhibition presents nearly 60 works by 21 emerging Taiwanese artists born after 1985. The show highlights the dynamic interplay between heritage and experimentation in contemporary Taiwanese art.
The exhibition title draws from ancient poetry and Qu Yuan’s (屈原) classic Li Sao, blended with poet Rainer Maria Rilke’s mandate to “live the questions.”
Among the highlights are Wu Shang-wei (吳上瑋) and Lin Po-yang (林博揚). Li Hsiao-sheng (李曉昇) and Tsai Ming-tsan (蔡名璨) break traditional ink conventions. Chen Kuan-ray (陳寬睿) uses chemical pigments to generate natural rust on canvas.
Location: Bluerider Art Taipei Dunhua
Date: Aug. 1 – Oct. 4
"Objects of Desire: Where Micro and Macro Open in All Directions" and "Shelter Island"
Double Square Gallery is staging a compelling dual solo exhibition. Spanish artist Ana de Alvear, winner of the Edge Artist Award at Taipei Dangdai 2025, presents "Objects of Desire: Where Micro and Macro Open in All Directions."
Drawing inspiration from Susan Stewart’s cultural analysis “On Longing,” Alvear uses hyperrealistic colored-pencil trompe-l'œil techniques in series like “Moss and Void Labyrinth” to challenge spatial perception.
Sharing the gallery space, Taiwanese artist Chang Shan-hsueh (張善學) presents "Shelter Island," an inquiry into natural ecosystems and Taiwan’s historical role as a glacial refugium. Elevating flora from background motif to primary subject, Chang delivers vertical botanical portraits alongside his Datun Volcano Group landscape triptych.
At the center of the gallery sits a live installation of ferns cultivated on the artist's apartment balcony, transforming the concrete urban residence into a living sanctuary.
Location: Double Square Gallery
Date: Aug. 15 – Sept. 26
"A Pair of Underwear, A Pair of Socks"
A favorite in fashion and street-culture circles, Taiwanese artist Sangna Take (桑拿大可) makes his return to Eslite Gallery with his second solo show, "A Pair of Underwear, A Pair of Socks."
Named after fundamental daily garments, the exhibition reflects the unvarnished vulnerability and relaxed state of returning home and shedding societal roles. Featuring 34 new paintings and six ceramic sculptures, the exhibition reveals heavy stylistic influences from Nara Yoshitomo and Jean-Michel Basquiat.
Sangna Take departs from traditional centered compositions, intertwining his signature slacker boy figures with new characters such as fairies and anthropomorphic plants.
The exhibition also debuts Sangna Take's first official self portrait.
Location: Eslite Gallery
Date: Aug. 15 – Oct. 10
"Professional Amatures"
Curated by TKG+ Projects exhibition planner Huang Chung-li (黃仲笠), "Professional Amatures" emerges from an insider's critique of institutional art structures. The exhibition brings together five artists to examine how art market mechanisms define concepts of professionalism and value.
Lin Guan-ming (林冠名) uses photography to document stylized public visuals and labor. Hsu Chia-chen (許家禎) reinterprets Taiwanese sculpture history through public monuments and traditional molding.
Cheng Po-tsung (鄭帛囱) crafts intimate micro-paintings using everyday stationery, while Yang Hui-ching (楊惠青) showcases "blind drawings" cultivated from her background in art education and theater. Curator Huang Chung-li (黃仲笠) reclaims his identity as a painter with works that question formal canvas orthodoxy.
Location: TKG+ Projects
Date: Aug. 22 – Oct. 31
"Art of Miku"
Making its overseas debut at Whitestone Gallery, the "Art of Miku" contemporary art exhibition has entered its second stage, introducing a refreshed roster of artworks and international artists.
The showcase gathers more than 20 creators across diverse cultural contexts, including Auto Moai, Clasutta, Fabien Verschaere, and more. Through painting, sculpture, and multidisciplinary visual formats, the participating artists deconstruct and reframe the virtual idol Hatsune Miku, exploring the possibilities of virtual existence within contemporary art.
Online ticket reservations are required, with exclusive Taipei-edition merchandise available on-site.
Location: Whitestone Gallery
Date:Aug. 29 – Sept. 20
"The Binding Strand of" and "While Everything Falls Away"
Mind Set Art Center presents two concurrent solo exhibitions investigating materiality and sensory awareness.
Portuguese artist Rui Miguel Leitao Ferreira presents "The Binding Strand of," displaying 14 abstract paintings executed since 2020 that layer acrylics, repurposed canvases, and found objects.
Ferreira builds on geometric grid frameworks before allowing fluid paint application and exposed canvas seams to subvert the traditional flatness of modernist painting.
In dialogue with Ferreira's work, Taiwanese artist Huang Kuan-chun (黃冠鈞) presents "While Everything Falls Away."
Drawing on his background in sculpture and fiber arts, Huang stacks acrylic paint layers on glass before peeling them off to create freestanding "paint bodies." Inspired by Marcel Duchamp’s concept of subtle nuance, works like “Sky” are applied directly onto gallery windowpanes, allowing natural sunlight to filter through translucent paint films and dynamically evolve throughout the day.
Location: Mind Set Art Center
Date: Aug. 29 – Oct. 8

In the case involving the director of a language center in Khmelnytskyi, there are now nine child victims
Kyiv • UNN
Law enforcement officers have identified nine girls who were victims in the case involving the director of a language center. He is charged with 14 crimes committed between 2004 and 2025.
The number of child victims abused by the director of one of the foreign language learning centers in Khmelnytskyi has risen to nine. This is reported by the Office of the Prosecutor General, according to UNN.
Details
Under the procedural guidance of the Khmelnytskyi Regional Prosecutor’s Office, a pretrial investigation is ongoing into the director of one of the foreign language learning centers in Khmelnytskyi, who is suspected of committing criminal offenses against the sexual freedom and sexual inviolability of children (Part 1 of Article 156 and Part 4 of Article 153 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine)
According to the available information, when the man was notified of the suspicion in August this year, there were two female victims, aged 13 and 14.
During the further investigation, law enforcement officers identified seven more underage and minor girls who had suffered from the suspect’s unlawful actions. At present, nine victims have been identified in the criminal proceedings, against whom 14 criminal offenses were committed between 2004 and 2025
This concerns the satisfaction of sexual desire with regard to minors (Part 2 of Article 153 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, in the versions in force at the time the criminal offenses were committed), sexual violence against persons under the age of 14 (Part 4 of Article 153 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine), engaging in sexual acts with a person under the age of 16 (Part 1 of Article 155 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine), and the sexual abuse of minors (Part 1 of Article 156 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).
Investigators and prosecutors are currently verifying the circumstances of each episode and carrying out the necessary investigative and procedural actions. Other persons who may have suffered from the suspect’s actions are also being identified. Within the criminal proceedings, at the prosecutors’ request, a preventive measure in the form of detention without the right to bail was imposed on him.
Reminder
The 58-year-old director of the language center is suspected of sexually abusing 13- and 14-year-old female students during classes. The actions took place in 2018–2020 and 2023–2025.

Military recruitment and retention continues to improve as new statistics show yearlong improvement
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:54:29 BST
18:54:29 KST

Military recruitment and retention continues to improve as new statistics show yearlong improvement
More people joined the Regular Armed Forces than left for the fourth consecutive quarter, the longest such run since 2021.
New stats revealed today show that more people have joined the Armed Forces than left for an entire year. Regular strength increased across all three Services over the past year, with the Royal Navy/Royal Marines up 440, the Army up 170 and the RAF up 840.
Alongside rebuilding workforce numbers, the Armed Forces remains one of the UK’s leading routes into skilled careers, with opportunities across engineering, healthcare, cyber and digital roles, supporting growth in every postcode. The Armed Forces are also among the country’s leading apprenticeship providers, with The Times Apprenticeship Rankings consistently placing the Army, Royal Navy and Royal Air Force among the top five employers.
The Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has welcomed the progress on recruitment and retention, which comes after pay rises, £9bn funding to improve forces housing and a range of recruitment and retention reforms since 2024.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP, said:
  There has never been a better or more important time to join our Armed Forces. Under this government, those serving and joining up now can be certain of increased investment in defence and our people. That means better equipment, better housing and better support for them and their families.
I am determined that serving our nation gives people the skills and opportunities to thrive during their service and beyond, no matter their background.”
Today’s statistics also show other improvements, including:
- The number of full-time military personnel available to support Defence operations rose by 1,450 since 1 July 2025.
- The number of fully trained Tri-Service personnel available to support operations increased for the third consecutive quarter. An increase in fully trained personnel was first recorded as of 1 January 2026, the first such increase in trade trained strength since late 2021.
- Regular strength increased across all three Services over the past year, with the Royal Navy/Royal Marines up 440, the Army up 170 and the RAF up 840.
- Intake has increased steadily while outflow has continued to decline since late 2023, helping drive a net gain of 1,460 personnel in the year to 30 June 2026.
The government in 2024 inherited deep recruitment and retention challenges, with targets missed every year for the past 14 years. While rebuilding the workforce after years of declining personnel numbers will take time, the latest figures show signs of improvement, with more people joining than leaving the Armed Forces, strength increasing across all three Services and trained strength rising for a third consecutive quarter.
The Government is continuing to improve recruitment and retention through a range of measures, including:
- More money in the pockets of Service personnel, delivering a cumulative 14.1% pay rise since July 2024 and ensuring every full-time member of the Armed Forces earns at least the National Living Wage.
- Better homes for Service families, with over £7 billion being invested in military housing this Parliament, the biggest renewal of Forces accommodation in a generation.
- Improved recruitment practices, with the scrapping of more than 100 outdated recruitment policies, including rules that blocked applicants with hay fever, eczema, acne or fully healed injuries, while introducing novel entry routes into the military, such as the Cyber Direct Entry Scheme for high-demand specialist roles.
Whether joining straight from school, university or later in life, recruits can build careers in everything from engineering and healthcare to cyber and digital roles, developing skills and progressing on merit regardless of background.

‘Military production can't be the answer’: Critics oppose Volkswagen’s defence plan with Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:54:02 UTC
18:54:02 KST

Volkswagen's revived plan to produce military equipment at its Osnabruck factory with Israel's Rafael has drawn fresh opposition after reports that the state of Lower Saxony could step in to help overcome objections that had stalled the project.
The proposal comes as Volkswagen undergoes a sweeping restructuring amid falling profits, weaker demand in China and growing competition from lower-priced Chinese brands in Europe, with vehicle production at the Osnabruck plant set to end after 2027.
Thorben Peters, co-chair of the Left Party in Lower Saxony, said thousands of jobs at the factory, along with its industrial expertise and know-how, must be preserved without a shift to arms production.
"Replacing civilian production with military production cannot be the answer to the automotive industry's current crisis," Peters told Anadolu.
"The state of Lower Saxony, in particular, should not use public funds to participate in an arms-related joint venture. We reject the false claim that the only alternatives are unemployment or arms production."
Volkswagen confirmed in March that it was in talks with several defence contractors about the Osnabruck plant.
A blocked plan and a new workaround
The proposal has faced opposition from peace groups, labour movements and opposition parties for months, particularly over potential cooperation with Israel's state-owned defence firm Rafael.
In July, Qatar's sovereign wealth fund, Volkswagen's third-largest shareholder, blocked the plan.
Now, management has revived the idea with a structure that could overcome that obstacle.
According to recent German media reports, Volkswagen would transfer parts of the Osnabruck site to the state of Lower Saxony, which could then form a joint venture with Rafael to manufacture military equipment. 
The project could manufacture key components for Israel's Iron Dome air defence system, including launchers, transport vehicles and power generators.
The Hannoversche Allgemeine Zeitung reported that Lower Saxony could invest at least €200 million ($232 million) in the project.
The Left Party argues that if the state is prepared to spend public money to preserve production and jobs at the site, it should instead invest in civilian alternatives.
Peters said those could include special-purpose and environmentally friendly vehicles for public transport.
Volkswagen's supervisory board is due to meet on September 4.
Peters said his party opposes converting civilian industrial capacity to military production as a matter of principle, regardless of the nationality of the company involved.
In the case of Israeli defence company Rafael, however, he said the war in Gaza raises additional concerns.
"Given the massive human rights violations and serious allegations regarding breaches of international law in connection with the war in Gaza, there must be particularly rigorous scrutiny,” he said.
"The guiding principle for public investment must be that human rights and international law are non-negotiable."
'City of Peace' pushes back
The debate has particular resonance in Osnabruck, a city that has long promoted itself as a "City of Peace" because of its role in the negotiations that led to the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, ending the Thirty Years' War.
The prospect of military production at the Volkswagen plant has sparked repeated protests in recent months, bringing peace activists, anti-war groups and local initiatives onto the streets.
The Osnabruck Peace Initiative argues that Lower Saxony should use any public money earmarked for the plant to support a socially responsible and environmentally sustainable transition rather than subsidise weapons production.
"Production for an Israeli arms company amounts to de facto support for the wars the state of Israel is waging against the Palestinians, Lebanon and Iran," Marie Dominique Guyard, spokesperson for the initiative, told Anadolu.
"Defence equipment for the Iron Dome plays a role in Israel's aggressive, offensive military activities, as it provides the protective shield enabling Israel to act aggressively toward its neighbours."
Speaking on behalf of the Osnabruck Peace Initiative, Guyard said the group's position is also informed by international legal proceedings concerning Israel's conduct.
She pointed to a 2024 International Court of Justice advisory opinion that found Israel's continued presence in the Occupied Palestinian Territory unlawful and said states must not provide aid or assistance in maintaining the situation created by that presence.
She cited International Criminal Court arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant on war crimes and findings by a UN commission of inquiry and Amnesty International accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza.
But she also pointed to Osnabruck's own history to explain the depth of local opposition.
The city was repeatedly bombed during World War II, when it was home to arms-related industry. About 65 percent of Osnabruck was destroyed, including 95 percent of its historic old town.
For Guyard, the prospect of military production returning to the city some eight decades later makes the debate about more than the future of one Volkswagen factory.
"When arms factories are once again established in the city some 80 years after the last war, one can only despair at the decision-makers' disregard for history," she said.
“We do not wish to support such a disastrous development and will continue to build opposition to ensure that work in the city serves peace rather than war.”

Ukraine fits Abrams tank with Russian-style hedgehog armor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:50:31 UTC
18:50:31 KST

- Ukrainian forces have fitted an M1 Abrams and a BMP-1TS with "hedgehog" anti-drone armor made of unwound steel cable.
- The design, dubbed Yozh or Oduvanchyk in Ukraine, was pioneered by Russian forces in the fall of 2025.
Ukrainian forces have begun fitting their own armored vehicles with the same “hedgehog” anti-drone armor that Russian units pioneered last year, according to photos and video circulating from Ukrainian military channels.
The images show a Ukrainian M1 Abrams from the 225th Separate Assault Regiment and a BMP-1TS operated by the 58th Motorized Infantry Brigade, both covered in dense frameworks of unraveled steel or aluminum cable.
The armor, known also as “Yozh” (Hedgehog) or “Oduvanchyk” (Dandelion), is built from industrial cabling cut into uniform lengths and unwound into individual wire strands. The strands are bundled and welded onto a metal frame that is then bolted or welded to the vehicle’s hull and turret, producing a bristling covering that can extend a foot or more from the armor underneath.
The design first appeared on Russian tanks in the fall of 2025 and has since spread across the front. Iryna Rybakova, a press officer with Ukraine’s 93rd Mechanized Brigade, told RFE/RL that the covering is meant “to get drones tangled and not detonate, or detonate at a distance” from the vehicle’s hull. Most first-person-view kamikaze drones carry a fuse that protrudes from the warhead and triggers on impact. The wire strands are intended to snag or deflect a drone before that fuse reaches the armor plate underneath.
Ukrainian drone operator Yevhen, who fights under the call sign “Krym,” described a related mechanism to RFE/RL: when a shaped-charge warhead detonates away from the hull rather than flush against it, the resulting blast jet is less likely to penetrate. He said the same wire covering can also break up a vehicle’s silhouette, making it harder for reconnaissance drones to identify from the air.
Ukrainian troops initially mocked the appearance of Russian hedgehog vehicles, which have been compared to a vehicle “wearing a bulky, badly made wig.” One heavily armored Russian vehicle reportedly absorbed around 25 mine and drone strikes near Siversk before a 26th munition disabled it, according to Euromaidan Press. Despite the criticism, Ukrainian units have adopted the same approach for their own vehicles over the past several months, a pattern that has repeated with earlier Russian innovations such as “cope cage” and “turtle” armor.
Ukraine has fitted the covering to at least one M1 Abrams before. In February, an ex-Australian M1A1 Abrams belonging to Ukrainian forces appeared in Zaporizhzhia Oblast wearing a hedgehog frame of unwound aluminum cabling. That tank was later struck and disabled by a Russian FPV drone while stationary.
The tradeoffs of the armor are well documented on both sides of the front. The added weight strains vehicle gearboxes and drivetrains, and heavily covered vehicles have reportedly become stuck attempting to cross rivers and streams. One Russian tank crew member told a reporter that a hedgehog-equipped tank “didn’t even make it 10 kilometers before one of the drivetrain components failed.” Carlo Masala, a military expert at the Bundeswehr University in Munich, told RFE/RL the broader shift toward this kind of improvised protection “seems to be a new tactic to bring maneuver back into warfare,” as cheap FPV drones have made large armored assaults increasingly costly for both militaries.
The extent of Ukraine’s adoption of hedgehog and dandelion armor across its vehicle fleet has not been disclosed, and neither the 225th Separate Assault Regiment nor the 58th Motorized Infantry Brigade has released details on how many vehicles in their formations have received the modification.

TASS has compiled the foreign minister’s key statements.
West’s position on Ukraine
The West’s position on Ukraine is disgraceful, as it disregards key provisions of the UN Charter: "The UN Charter states in its first article that everyone must respect human rights regardless of race, sex, language or religion. Moreover, Ukraine’s constitution still states that the state guarantees the rights of Russians and other national minorities. Nobody cares about that. They passed laws that contradict the UN Charter and the constitution, and everyone says these are supposedly European values. I consider the West’s position absolutely disgraceful."

Germany is once again trying to "place everyone else under its control" and prevent individual EU countries from maintaining normal relations with Russia: "Germany is again trying to bring everyone else under its control and suppress any moves toward normal relations with Russia that still exist in some EU countries, even though there are only a few of them."

Russian Teachers Instructed to Identify Disloyal Students During Weekly Patriotic Classes
Russian educators leading the mandatory “Conversations about Important Things” classes have been directed to track students who display "lack of understanding or disagreement with value orientations," avoid discussions, or ask provocative questions.
Updated guidelines from the Ministry of Education of the Russian Federation for the 2026/2027 academic year instruct teachers to record these incidents in specialized forms following lessons, as reported by The Moscow Times on September 2.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Teachers are also required to complete a self-assessment section where they answer "Were there situations when students demonstrated lack of understanding or disagreement with value orientations? How were they resolved?", while also tracking student passivity.
The official document states that the objective is to provide educational staff and school administrators with data to evaluate the impact of lessons, adjust teaching practices, and assess the "formation of value orientations" and "personal results."
Schools are required to measure these personal outcomes twice a year, at the beginning and end of the term. Individual institutions can choose their own schedule and tools, with school psychologists, deputy directors for guidance, and homeroom teachers tasked with gathering and evaluating the collected data.
In late May, the Ministry of Education released 3 surveys for school students, pedagogical university students, and teachers under 35 years old. These surveys examined views on civic, patriotic, and moral standards, traditional values, the mandatory weekly classes, and willingness to participate in patriotic activities.
Students were asked to evaluate historical figures like Lenin, Stalin, and Brezhnev on a 4-point scale, as well as answer questions about social media usage and their ability to verify information, including content from foreign agents.
University staff were required to submit their completed surveys through the state messenger app Max, while school surveys were distributed directly by teachers.
Conversations about Important Things became a required part of the school curriculum in September 2023, with officials framing the weekly sessions as a way to build patriotism and love for the country.
The lessons cover Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and regularly feature guest speakers, including combatants, former prisoners, and private military company fighters. Schools have also implemented a mandatory Family Studies course that encourages students to have large families and emphasizes sacrifice for the nation.
Previously, an injured Russian serviceman, identified as former machine gunner Alexander Klaus who fought in Moscow’s war of aggression against Ukraine, addressed students at Lyceum No. 11 in Krasnoyarsk during a September 1 school opening ceremony.
