Britain wants laser armed ground vehicle drones
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:39:27 BST
18:39:27 KST

Britain is seeking counter-drone technology that could lead to autonomous laser weapons mounted on Army vehicles and, later, uncrewed ground vehicles, with £5 million available immediately through a new Ministry of Defence competition, the department has said.
Project PANOPTES, launched by UK Defence Innovation on behalf of the MOD, is intended to develop an integrated Counter-Uncrewed Aerial System force-protection capability able to deal with massed and low-cost aerial threats without rapidly exhausting conventional ammunition stocks.
The MOD stated: “Defence seeks additional capacity to detect, track, identify, decide and defeat mass and low-cost threats in a cost-effective manner and without being overwhelmed or exhausting stockpiles. This is particularly acute for deployed land forces, but the problem is applicable to the protection of defence fixed infrastructure in the homeland.”
Although the competition is open to a range of technologies, laser directed-energy weapons are specifically identified as an area of interest. The MOD said: “Based on research, the Authority is particularly interested in capabilities centred on Laser Directed Energy Weapon (LDEW) effectors but is open to submissions relating to credible alternative novel approaches.”
The intended configuration would place the counter-drone capability on a military ground platform. According to the procurement documents: “To address the challenge described above we are looking to deliver an integrated C-UAS force-protection capability capable of autonomous operation, mounted on an Army vehicle.”
The system is intended to protect deployed forces against complex and saturation attacks involving small uncrewed aircraft, including simultaneous threats designed to overwhelm local air defences or force troops to expend comparatively expensive missiles and ammunition.
The MOD stated: “The capability should protect deployed troops against complex and saturation attacks designed to overwhelm existing defences or deplete conventional munition stocks. It should deliver more affordable combat mass against emerging air threats than legacy systems, and should exploit open architectures, platform-generated power, modular design and capable of autonomous operation.”
The initial threat focus covers representative Class 1 UAS and other small aerial targets. These could include individual drones as well as repeated, sequential or simultaneous attacks used for surveillance, targeting, disruption or attempts to exhaust defensive systems.
A later objective would move the capability onto an unmanned ground platform. The MOD stated: “Integration of the capability onto a future uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV) is a planned objective. The solution should provide a scalable pathway towards future Army and Joint Ground-Based Air Defence (GBAD) capabilities as well as considering possible export opportunities.”
UK Defence Innovation has confirmed that Project PANOPTES is open to UK-based innovators and that a share of £5 million is available immediately. Stage 1 will act as an initial screening process, with applicants outlining their proposed technology before successful teams are invited to develop more detailed proposals.
The first phase is not intended to produce a complete operational counter-drone system. The MOD said: “The scope of Phase 1 is to identify and support organisations to accelerate development of their existing technology towards a final deployable system. It is not intended for the Phase 1 competition to seek delivery of a complete operational C-UAS system.”
Successful technologies could then be matured through later phases into demonstrable Minimum Viable Products before selected systems are developed into Minimum Deployable Capabilities for an initial operational user group.
The notice states: “Capabilities that demonstrate operational benefit may subsequently be developed further for wider adoption as part of a future Programme of Record.”
The wider procurement has an indicative value of £125 million excluding VAT, rising to £150 million including VAT. That figure is not an approved programme budget. The MOD stated: “The stated figure in this notice of £150,000,000 inc. VAT is aligned to the current understanding of the Strategic Defence Review, but this does not mean that this funding has been approved and is an indicative figure only.”
Stage 1 submissions are due by midday on 23 September. A launch webinar will be held on 9 September to provide potential suppliers with further information on the operational requirement before the competition moves into its subsequent stages.

Dutch central bank moves gold bars out of U.S. and Canada, citing ‘crisis preparedness’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:38:05 UTC
18:38:05 KST

The Dutch central bank (DNB) has transferred approximately 86 metric tons of gold out of the U.S. and Canada to the U.K., seeking to shore up its contingency planning in view of "increasing geopolitical unrest."
Just over one-quarter of the central bank's gold reserves held in New York and Ottawa had been shifted to London between March and August, DNB said Wednesday.
The transferred gold is now stored with the Bank of England because gold stored there must meet international trade standards and is recognized as "the world's most easily tradable gold," DNB said, adding that the move strengthens its "crisis preparedness."
By contrast, DNB said the gold bars held in the U.S. and Canada could not be utilized as quickly and directly in a crisis situation.
"With this relocation, we have improved the tradability of our gold reserves. We expect that we will never need to use them, but we do need to strengthen our resilience and preparedness," DNB Governor Olaf Sleijpen said in a statement.
The move comes amid a blockbuster rally in gold prices and continued U.S.-Iran geopolitical tensions over the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz, with a comprehensive settlement agreement far from certain.
The price of gold, which is typically considered a safe-haven asset at times of financial uncertainty, has jumped nearly 25% over the past 12 months. The yellow metal is currently trading at $4,429.61 per ounce, up nearly 1% for the session.
The move from the Dutch central bank comes after the French central bank replaced 129 metric tons of gold held at the New York Federal Reserve between July 2025 and January 2026.
Bank of France Governor Francois Villeroy de Galhau said at the time that the move was not politically motivated.
In light of the latest transfer, DNB said the geographical spread of its gold reserves was "more balanced," with London now holding 32.1%, the central bank's cash center in Zeist in the Netherlands holding 30.8% and New York and Ottawa holding 18.5%, respectively.
Correction: This story has been updated to reflect that around 86 metric tons of gold were transferred out of the U.S. and Canada to the U.K.

China Focus: Typhoon Saudel makes third landfall along east China coast
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
17:33:30 CST
18:33:30 KST

Police officers set up cordons and traffic cones to guide traffic on a road in Zhangzhou City, southeast China's Fujian Province, Sept. 3, 2026. Typhoon Saudel, the 18th typhoon of 2026, made its third landfall in Fujian Province on Thursday, with maximum sustained winds of 23 meters per second near its center, according to the provincial meteorological observatory. Local authorities have quickly carried out rescue and flood drainage operations as persistent heavy rain battered parts of the province. (Photo by Zhan Zhaoyu/Xinhua)
FUZHOU, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- Typhoon Saudel, the 18th typhoon of 2026, made its third landfall in east China on Thursday morning, prompting tens of thousands of people to be evacuated amid warnings of strong winds and heavy downpours.
Saudel made the latest landfall in Zhangpu County under the city of Zhangzhou, Fujian Province, at around 6:30 a.m. with maximum sustained winds of 23 meters per second near its center, according to the provincial meteorological observatory.
Previously, Saudel had made landfall twice along the coast of Zhejiang Province, also in east China, on Aug. 28, prompting the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of people across the east of the country.
Authorities in Fujian had evacuated more than 83,000 people by 7 a.m. on Thursday as persistent heavy rain battered parts of the province.
Heavy rain prompted the suspension of work, business activities and school attendance in parts of the city of Zhangzhou. Schools were also closed in other cities in Fujian including Fuzhou, Quanzhou and Ningde, provincial authorities said.
As of 7 a.m., eight sections of major roads had been closed, 657 transport services suspended, work halted at 152 construction sites, and over 150 major tourist attractions shut across Fujian.
The province raised its flood-control emergency response on Wednesday while maintaining a response for the typhoon.
China's National Meteorological Center (NMC) issued a blue alert for the typhoon on Thursday morning.
Saudel is forecast to move westward at 15 to 20 kilometers per hour and gradually weaken, the NMC said.
From Thursday afternoon to Friday afternoon, heavy to torrential rain is forecast across most of Fujian, eastern and northern Guangdong Province, southern Jiangxi Province, southern Hunan Province and much of Taiwan.
Two to three more typhoons are expected to make landfall in or significantly affect China in September, mainly along the country's eastern and southern coasts, said Gao Rong, deputy director of the National Climate Center.
Gao added that there is a risk that some relatively strong typhoons could move northward and affect northern China.
Monitoring data showed that 24 typhoons had formed over the northwestern Pacific and the South China Sea as of Sept. 1 this year, 10.4 more than the historical average for the same period. Seven made landfall in China, 2.1 more than average.
Typhoon activity was particularly high from June to August this year, with prolonged and widespread strong winds and heavy rain.
The period also saw above-average rainfall across China and frequent extreme precipitation. The country was hit by 15 widespread rainstorm events, with daily rainfall at 44 national meteorological stations breaking historical records, according to the data.
Gao urged relevant regions to closely follow short-term typhoon forecasts and updated risk warnings, and guard against mountain torrents, urban waterlogging, heavy rain, strong winds and storm surges. ■

The militaries and navies of various countries had their own laws, both for their conduct in peacetime and for the conduct of military operations. Today, everything is jumbled, everything is thrown off, everything is mixed up. They have simply resorted to real piracy. ====================================================================================================

Feature: Ancient Chinese dragon boat racing thrives in inland Xinjiang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
17:32:47 CST
18:32:47 KST

by sportswriter Sun Zhe
URUMQI, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- In a county on the edge of the Taklamakan Desert, the world's second-largest shifting sand desert, where annual rainfall averages just 47.7 millimeters, water is a precious resource.
But every summer, the sound of drums and splashing paddles fills a small pond in Yutian County, as dozens of villagers climb into dragon boats and race across the water.
Dragon boat racing, an ancient sport born on the rivers and lakes of southern China, has found an unexpected home in the arid landscapes of northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region.
Crews race long boats decorated like dragons, rowing in unison to a drummer's beat, with teamwork and coordination key to reaching the finish line.
For participants like Adiljan Abduegni, the sport opened a window to a world they had rarely seen.
"Most of us used to play football or basketball," the 25-year-old said. "Before we tried dragon boats, we didn't know how to row. Some people couldn't even swim."
Yutian is a typical desert county, far from China's major rivers and coasts. For generations, residents dreamed of water sports but had few opportunities. That began to change in 2022, when the county launched its first annual summer dragon boat race.
Yusupjan Erkin, an official with the local sports department, said nearly 20 townships soon formed teams to take part. Participants were not professional athletes but ordinary people from different walks of life, including taxi drivers, construction workers and, most commonly, farmers.
"At the beginning, people made the boats themselves," Yusupjan recalled. "It was a funny scene because the dragon boats were of different lengths and the paddles came in all kinds of shapes."
The competition was held on a small local fishpond, one of the few available venues. Limited space did not dampen enthusiasm as crowds gathered around the water, eager to watch the novel spectacle.
Races were far from professional. Many crews lacked rowing technique, some boats lost direction and others capsized, but laughter, not frustration, filled the pond.
"The purpose of holding the race was to bring happiness to villagers and let them experience the unique charm of the sport," Yusupjan said.
As interest grew, local authorities purchased standard dragon boats and paddles, and the sport gradually became more organized.
Last year, the county selected more than a dozen paddlers to compete in China's national Dragon Boat Super League in Miluo, a city in central China's Hunan Province, widely recognized as the birthplace of dragon boat culture and the place associated with ancient Chinese poet Qu Yuan.
After a month of hard training, Adiljan and his teammates arrived in Hunan but quickly felt the gap with more experienced competitors.
"Adapting to the environment was one challenge, but the biggest issue was the equipment and experience," Yusupjan said. "Our team still used wooden paddles, while other teams used carbon fiber ones. They lent some to us."
Despite the challenges, dragon boat racing has continued to spread across Xinjiang.
In places without suitable waterways, organizers have introduced land-based races, where teams carry a simulated boat along roads. In northern Xinjiang, even frozen lakes have become places for winter dragon boat competitions.
At Sayram Lake, boats were fitted with blades underneath and brakes at the rear so teams could race safely on ice.
"We installed ice skates under the boats and added brakes at the back," said referee Huang Jin. "After crossing the finish line, teams can use the brakes to slow down."
The sport reached a new milestone in August, when dragon boat racing made its debut at the Xinjiang Ethnic Traditional Sports Games in Kashgar. Twelve teams from across the region took part, including Adiljan's squad.
"We came here aiming for the championship," he said. "But we finished only fourth in the 200-meter race on the first day. There are many strong dragon boat teams in Xinjiang."
For Adiljan, however, victory is not the only measure of success.
"The result is not the most important thing. What matters is feeling the charm of the sport," he said. "One person may paddle fast, but cannot go far alone. Only when everyone works together can we move faster and farther." ■

====================================================================================================

Smart Toilets Are Already Using AI to Analyze Your Poop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

It was only a matter of time before wellness trackers—already out there trying to optimize our heart rate, sleep, stress, steps, blood sugar, and menstruation—came for perhaps the most private biosignal of all: our poop.
The global gut health market is expected to reach nearly $106 billion by 2029, and a handful of companies are betting they can use stool data to provide in-depth health insights, nudge people to change their diets or lifestyles, and advise them to see a doctor if their bathroom habits seem amiss. But gastroenterologists are skeptical that products that rely on AI to analyze images of what’s going on in your toilet bowl are worth the price just yet, and data-privacy advocates warn that people can get locked into long-term subscriptions just to access their own health data.
Among the companies touting smart toilets are Kohler Health—an offshoot of the eponymous plumbing giant that sells its device for $449 plus $130 for an annual family membership—and Throne, a startup that raised $10 million in July. Its product is $399 plus $70 for an annual membership.
Both companies’ stool trackers are sleek white devices that clip to the toilet and have cameras facing down into the bowl. (They are adamant that the cameras cannot turn skyward.) When you sit down, the device uses a light sensor to record a video of your deposits, then feeds them into an algorithm that analyzes your urine and stool consistency and color, as well as other metrics. A few minutes later, you get your bathroom-break report card care of an AI-powered app that tracks gut health and hydration scores.
The companies say they are taking a completely different approach from at-home gut microbiome test kits. Those kits, which claim they can use stool samples to identify food sensitivities, provide dietary guidance, and more, come with thin to nonexistent evidence of their efficacy. The new stool trackers aim to identify what's normal for an individual rather than issuing a binary healthy-or-not verdict.
“This is all deeply personal and very individual—digestive patterns are very different,” says Nora Tophof, Kohler Health’s managing director.
Even so, for healthy people with regular bowel movements, stool trackers may not offer much in the way of new insights, says Daniel Freedberg, a gastroenterologist in New York and a spokesperson for the American Gastroenterological Association.
“It kind of seems like overkill,” he says. “If you want to look at your stool, you can just look at it yourself. I don't know that the AI is bringing a lot of new science to this.”
Tophof says that for healthy people, the real value comes from long-term tracking to identify patterns they can act on—for example, if they realize they’re always dehydrated over the weekend or that a particular food or medication tends to upset their stomach.
Scott Hickle, Throne’s cofounder and chief executive officer, says people with inflammatory bowel disease or other digestive conditions can benefit from regular, automated stool monitoring. “Their physicians ask them to track, or keep stool logs … and compliance for that is basically zero,” he says. “No one wants to journal about their poop.”
Throne plans to offer more than helping users track their gut health. Rates of colorectal cancer have risen among younger adults over the past decade, and it is now the leading cause of cancer death among those under 50. Doctors don’t quite know why, but exposure to ultra-processed foods, microplastics, and antibiotics are prime suspects. Screening for colon cancer typically involves a colonoscopy—or a stool-based test that looks for hidden blood in feces.
Hickle says the next generation of Throne’s device will be capable of detecting blood in fecal matter using multispectral imaging that is much more sensitive than the naked eye. Early tests with a prototype are promising, he says, and the updated device could launch within two years. The company has yet to determine a price, but Hickle says Throne's goal is “to make it as accessible as possible so that this can benefit as many people as possible.” He hopes that blood-based data will eventually help detect colorectal cancer, though it’s not clear whether this approach would be as good as testing in medical labs.
“We don't want to be in the business of making diagnoses,” Hickle says. “Looking for those patterns of bleeding over the course of weeks and months should be enough to get someone to at least escalate the conversation they have with their physician.”
Kohler Health says its tracker already alerts users when it detects blood in the toilet. While often harmless—common examples include menstrual blood and hemorrhoids—it can also be a sign of serious health conditions.
“We really want to help people and ultimately save lives,” Tophof says.
Even if the trackers’ blood-detection technology bears out as a clinically meaningful signal, they are still too expensive to be widely used as screening tools for cancer or other health risks, says Gianluca Ianiro, an assistant professor of gastroenterology at the Catholic University of Rome.
“A screening test should be non-invasive but also cheap—and this is not cheap,” Ianiro says.
Would-be buyers should also consider how much personal data they’re willing to give up for what they get out of using the device—especially because “you’re having to pay time and time again in order to access and analyze your own information,” says Lauren Hendry Parsons, a digital rights advocate at the Mozilla Foundation. If customers keep re-upping their subscriptions, “it may feel harder to detach yourself if you've got years and years of data and information about yourself inside that particular service,” she adds.
In addition to the contents of your toilet bowl—and any details you tell the app about your health, such as diet or medication—Throne and Kohler Health both collect the usual litany of personal data, including name and demographics. Kohler Health also tracks your precise location, while Throne does not.
Both companies say they don’t share user health information for targeted advertising purposes, but they can still share this data with law enforcement, another company in a merger or sale, and third-party service providers for things like IT, customer service, and engagement, according to their privacy policies.
Tophof says Kohler Health doesn’t plan to sell users’ health data. Throne also says it will never do so without express permission. Eventually, Hickle wants to share user health data with universities doing gut health research—but people will have to opt in, and refusing will not affect their ability to use the app or device, he says.
Hendry Parsons has advice for privacy-minded buyers: “Be informed. Know what the trade-offs are, know what you're sharing, know what your data is being used for, and weigh that up against the benefit that you are deriving from the product.”
That calculus might be different for someone “suffering from Crohn’s disease, and this is something which will materially improve your day-to-day life,” she says, compared with a “health optimizer who's casually thinking it might be fun to understand the impact of your homemade kombucha.”

It has become possible to get a divorce online through &quot;Diia&quot; - how to do it
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
12:29:47 EEST
18:29:47 KST

It has become possible to get a divorce online through "Diia" - how to do it
Kyiv • UNN
Spouses without joint minor children can get a divorce through «Diia» after a video conference. The electronic record will appear within 24 hours.
Divorce in Ukraine became available online in the "Diia" app starting September 3. UNN reports this, citing the Ministry of Justice and "Diia".
We are launching online divorce in the "Diia" app. The service is available to couples who have jointly decided to end their marriage
Who can use the service
According to the Ministry of Justice, couples can use the service in the "Diia" app if both spouses are Ukrainian citizens, are at least 18 years old, and meet the following requirements:
-  mutual consent of both spouses to the divorce; 
-  no minor children in common; 
-  each spouse has a verified taxpayer registration number (RNOKPP) and "Diia.Signature"; 
-  possession of an ID card or biometric international passport; 
-  a marriage record in the State Register of Civil Status Acts (DRATS). 
"It is important that without the consent of both parties, it will not be possible to submit an application for divorce," "Diia" stated.
How it works
Previously, the mutually agreed divorce procedure generally involved personal visits to a DRATS office: to submit a joint application and, after the one-month waiting period had expired, to register the divorce with the state.
From now on, the main stages can be completed online in the "Diia" app:
-  Application creation: one of the partners submits an application through the "Diia" app and chooses a convenient date and time for a video conference with the registrar (no earlier than one month and two days from the date of submission). 
-  Confirmation and signing: the other spouse receives a notification and, within 12 hours, confirms the necessary information  and signs the application using the "Diia.Signature." 
-  Application verification: information about both partners is checked against state registers. 
-  Video conference: at the specified date and time, the spouses join a video conference with an employee of the DRATS office, during which the partners confirm their intention and certify it with their "Diia.Signatures." 
-  Receiving the result: an electronic display of the divorce record is generated in "Diia" for each spouse within 24 hours after the video conference. Paper divorce certificates are sent by JSC Ukrposhta to each spouse at the address specified in the application. 
"The marriage will be dissolved in a month. If you change your mind during this time, you can withdraw the application — no later than four hours before the video conference," "Diia" stated.
If the spouses have children
If the spouses have minor children in common, the divorce, as before, takes place through the court. Those who do not use "Diia" can still submit an application in person at a DRATS office.
"Marriage Online" extended for another two years10.08.26, 11:57 • 5672 views

No evidence Morocco orchestrated Ceuta border surge: Spain's PM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:24:01 UTC
18:24:01 KST

Spain has found no evidence to conclude that July's deadly border rush from Morocco into its enclave of Ceuta was orchestrated or carried out by Moroccan authorities, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez told lawmakers on Thursday.
Sanchez's comments in the lower house of parliament followed a police report that emerged this week saying that the mass entry into Ceuta was not a spontaneous migration event but a planned and phased operation designed to overwhelm border controls.
"I can assure you that no institution — not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, nor any international body — has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever," Sanchez said.
However, he said Morocco's Gendarmerie police did allow crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on July 30, when migrant arrivals peaked. Spanish authorities had yet to determine whether this was due to inaction or inability to contain the influx, Sanchez added.
The police report, seen by Reuters, alleged that Moroccan security forces were initially deployed in smaller numbers than usual near the Tarajal breakwater separating the enclave from the North African country and did not make a serious attempt to disperse the crowds.
Some uniformed Moroccan officers gave directions towards the crossing point, while other unidentified people appeared to guide or monitor the flow of people, the report said, but it did not identify individual officers or provide independently verified evidence of orders from Moroccan authorities.
Moroccan officials have denied enabling the crossing.
On the other hand, Spanish politicians and commentators have accused Israel of helping inflame the migration crisis in Ceuta amid deteriorating relations over Spain’s stance on Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. The claims intensified after Israeli UN Ambassador Danny Danon attacked Madrid over its immigration policy and questioned Spain’s control of Ceuta and Melilla.
Transport Minister Oscar Puente responded that the events were becoming “quite clear,” without elaborating further. Lawmaker Gabriel Rufian also echoed claims that the crisis was serving Israeli interests.

18:23:32 KST

Families in flood-hit areas of Nepal are holding symbolic funerals for missing loved ones as the death toll from last week's flash floods rose to 1,252, with more than 4,200 people missing, official data showed on Thursday.
In neighbouring China, 21 people were killed and 541 remained missing, including 261 foreigners, according to local authorities.
The combined death toll from both countries stood at 1,273, while 4,757 people remained missing, including 844 foreign nationals.
In Rasuwa, one of Nepal's hardest-hit districts, families created funeral effigies using kaas-kush, or sacred grass, and performed final rites to "liberate the souls" of missing relatives after losing hope of finding their bodies, the Kathmandu Post reported.
On Wednesday, dozens of such effigies were cremated in a mass funeral at Pashupati Aryaghat temple in Kathmandu on the banks of the Bagmati River.
In Chitwan, another badly affected district, authorities buried unidentified bodies after collecting DNA samples because the number of remains made individual identification and storage difficult.
Many flood victims have been left without places to observe mourning rituals after floodwaters swept away both family members and homes in several districts.
Those who lost everything and travelled to Kathmandu seeking shelter have also been unable to find space at public facilities for the rituals.
Military personnel, police and others continued search and rescue operations in flood-hit areas on Thursday.
Rescuers, however, faced difficulties as roads, power supplies and communications remained disrupted across wide areas.
They were also working to deliver relief supplies and maintain hygiene in shelters to prevent the spread of infectious diseases.
The disaster struck on August 26 when a glacier on Nepal's Mount Langtang Lirung fractured at an altitude of about 5,200 metres, triggering an ice-rock avalanche that developed into a massive debris flow and swept through valleys along the border.
Floodwaters and mudslides devastated Nepal’s Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Kavre districts, as well as the Kathmandu Valley, while also burying the Gyirong border crossing in China’s southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region, also known as Tibet.

Nigeria confirms US troop withdrawal
Nigeria has confirmed that around 200 US troops deployed to support its fight against armed groups will begin leaving the West African country, with most expected to withdraw by late September.
A smaller advisory and intelligence team will remain, while cooperation in training and information sharing will continue, Nigerian military spokesperson Major General Samaila Uba said on Tuesday. “The deployment of United States personnel was tied to specific operational and counterterrorism objectives,” Uba said, according to AP.
The troops arrived in February to provide intelligence, targeting, and training support. Washington subsequently deployed MQ-9 Reaper surveillance drones to Bauchi Airfield in northeastern Nigeria. The mission came after US President Donald Trump accused the Nigerian authorities of failing to protect Christians and threatened military action.
Nigeria rejected claims that Christians were being systematically targeted, saying jihadist violence, banditry, and communal conflicts affect citizens of different faiths.
The two countries conducted coordinated airstrikes against alleged Islamic State fighters in Sokoto State in December 2025. In May, Nigeria’s Defense Headquarters and US Africa Command said a joint operation in the Lake Chad Basin killed senior Islamic State figure Abu-Bilal al-Minuki. Trump described him as the group’s second-highest-ranking leader globally.
US Africa Command chief General Dagvin Anderson announced in July that most of the American troops had been withdrawn, saying the campaign had successfully degraded Islamic State’s leadership and disrupted its wider network. Samuel Memeh, chairman of Nigeria’s Democratic Leadership Alliance, disputed that assessment. Memeh told RT that the deployment had produced no significant improvement in security and argued that foreign forces alone could not defeat the country’s armed groups.
Nigeria continues to face overlapping threats from Boko Haram and its Islamic State-affiliated offshoot in the northeast, armed bandits operating across the northwest and central regions, and intercommunal violence. More than 40,000 people have been killed since the insurgency began in 2009, UN News reported in January.
Major attacks continued during the US deployment. On August 21, gunmen attacked several communities in Niger State, reportedly killing 30 people and abducting hundreds of worshippers from a mosque. Residents put the number of captives as high as 600, although the authorities said the figure had not been verified. At least 2,000 people reportedly fled into neighboring Benin.
Lagos-based security consultancy SBM Intelligence said in a report last month that at least 7,825 people were abducted across Africa’s most populous nation between July 2025 and June 2026, a 66% increase from the previous 12-month period.

Ukrainian ground robot survives five FPV strikes, finishes mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:16:47 UTC
18:16:47 KST

- A Ukrainian Droid TW-12.7 ground robot survived five FPV drone strikes and completed its mission before a sixth strike disabled it.
- The system, built by DevDroid and armed with a 12.7 mm M2 Browning machine gun, has previously held a frontline position for 45 days.
A Ukrainian armed ground robot survived five FPV drone strikes and completed its combat mission before a sixth strike finally disabled it, according to DevDroid, the Ukrainian company that builds the system.
Soldiers from the fire support company of Ukraine’s 74th Separate Reconnaissance Battalion remotely operated the Droid TW-12.7 during an operation to clear an area where enemy personnel had gathered, DevDroid said. As the unmanned ground vehicle approached enemy positions, two FPV drones struck it almost simultaneously. One hit damaged its aiming module, but the machine stayed mobile and continued toward its objective, according to the company.
Operators kept firing on the target using the weapon’s barrel direction to aim after the aiming module was damaged, DevDroid said. Two more FPV strikes hit the UGV during the engagement, and it remained operational and completed the mission. A fifth strike hit the system on its way back, and it kept moving. A sixth FPV drone finally disabled the Droid TW-12.7, according to the company.
DevDroid said the enemy troop concentration was cleared and enemy forces took losses. The operation was carried out remotely, without exposing Ukrainian soldiers to direct contact with enemy forces, the company said.
“In this engagement, the enemy was able to stop the Droid only with the sixth FPV drone, but they still failed to prevent it from completing the mission,” said Yurii Poritskyi, CEO of DevDroid. “For us, this is what survivability means in practice: after being hit, a system must not simply remain mobile, it must retain enough functionality for its operators to complete the mission and achieve the intended result.”
The Droid TW-12.7 is a tracked ground robot built around a remotely operated turret carrying a 12.7 mm M2 Browning machine gun. According to specifications published by its distributor, the system can engage targets out to 1 km, reaches a top speed of 7 km/h (4.3 mph) and has an operational range up to 25 km (15.5 miles), with a tactical deployment radius of 5 km (3.1 miles) from its control station. It combines manual control with AI-assisted automatic targeting and communicates over radio, with mesh, LTE or satellite links available as options. Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense has codified the system, clearing it for supply to Ukrainian forces.
The platform has seen extended combat use before this engagement. Ukraine’s Third Army Corps said in November that a Droid TW-12.7 operated by the corps’ NC-13 Strike Company held a frontline position for 45 straight days, standing in for an infantry unit at a contested crossroads while taking no Ukrainian casualties. The unit said the robot left its position briefly every two days for maintenance and to reload ammunition, handled by a crew stationed roughly 2.4 miles behind the front line.
DevDroid said the Droid TW-12.7 combines remote control, an integrated ballistic computer and AI algorithms to detect, track and engage targets while reducing risk to personnel. Beyond engaging infantry fighting vehicles, armored personnel carriers and other armored targets, the company said the system can strike unarmored vehicles and equipment and suppress enemy positions, including platoon strongpoints and firing points. It also carries cameras and data links that let operators maintain situational awareness from a distance, according to DevDroid.

Why Finland is staging Europe's biggest civil defence drill since WWII
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:16:15 UTC
18:16:15 KST

Finland is carrying out one of Europe's largest civil defence exercises since World War II, with more than 2,000 people in the central city of Kuopio rehearsing how to respond to missile strikes, cyberattacks and disruptions to critical infrastructure amid heightened security concerns over Russia.
The two-day exercise, known as Shelter 2026, is taking place from September 2 to 3 at an underground sports and events centre in Kuopio that can be converted into a civil defence shelter for about 7,000 people, AP reported. Authorities, students, volunteers, businesses and other organisations are taking part.
The scenario involves a deteriorating security situation in which critical infrastructure has been disrupted and the threat of military force has increased. Participants are practicing how to move large numbers of people into shelters and how authorities and other organisations would coordinate if normal services were disrupted.
Inside the shelter, Finnish conscripts are practicing radiation monitoring and other emergency procedures. Hundreds of participants are also sleeping overnight in the facility to test how it could function during a prolonged emergency.
The exercise is not being held in response to an immediate threat. Finnish authorities describe it as a planned preparedness exercise aimed at testing decision-making, communications, situational awareness and cooperation during a crisis.
But the scale of the exercise reflects the way Finland has changed its security planning since the Russia-Ukraine war.
Finland's border with Russia stretches more than 1,300 kilometres from the Baltic Sea up to the Arctic Circle. In 2024, along with Sweden, Finland joined NATO, following the Russia-Ukraine war.
Russian aircraft have entered Finnish airspace
Finland's concern about Russia is not purely theoretical.
Drones have entered its airspace this year, although at least one was identified as Ukrainian, while Finnish authorities linked the incidents to the war in Ukraine.
Russia has also tested Finland's airspace.
On August 20, Finland said it suspected a Russian military aircraft had entered Finnish airspace over the Gulf of Finland. The Finnish Border Guard later identified the aircraft as an IL-20 reconnaissance plane and said it had remained inside Finnish airspace for about three minutes.
Finland had reported another suspected violation by a Russian military aircraft in May.
Sweden is also increasing its military presence in Finland, with jets and a naval vessel due to support surveillance and protection of Finnish territory through the end of 2026 as regional security concerns grow.
Sweden will deploy its Gripen jets and a corvette warship to Finland to support the surveillance and protection of Finnish territory through the end of 2026, according to Finland's defence forces.
Swedish Defence Minister Pal Jonson stated that Sweden might assist Finland in repelling any territorial violations.
Finland fought several wars with the Soviet Union
In its wars with the Soviet Union, Finland lost around 11 percent of its territory, and more than 400,000 people, around 12 percent of the population, fled their homes from an area that is now in western Russia.
At Kuopio's veterans’ museum, Risto Moonkkoonen, 95, showed AP a piece of paper on which he had written down the dates the city was bombed and who died.
“I cannot forget it,” he said explaining how, as a child, he and his father ran into a shelter just as a bomb hit, killing five of his father’s friends.
Pirkko Naukkarinen, 102, recalled how, aged 16, she worked in a field kitchen by the front lines, sometimes sharing dugouts with soldiers and diving for cover in ditches as the Soviet air force attacked the retreating Finnish army.
Aili Toivanen, 92, told AP she was forced to leave her home twice over the various wars. Both times, her family was told by Finnish soldiers that they had one hour to pack their belongings.

MOSCOW, September 3. /TASS/. Ukraine's latest drone attack on the Moscow Region was one of the largest in two years, according to TASS calculations based on data from Mayor Sergey Sobyanin.
A drone hit an apartment building in the area of Pavlovsky Posad, shattering windows in eight flats. Drones additionally caused fires at a factory in the Bogorodsky district and in an apartment building in Kubinka.
According to the latest data, two people were injured.
TASS has compiled the key facts about the consequences.
Scale
- Between 8:00 p.m. Moscow time (5:00 p.m. GMT) on September 2 and 8:00 a.m. Moscow time (5:00 a.m. GMT) on September 3, air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 416 Ukrainian aircraft·type unmanned aerial vehicles over Russian regions, the Defense Ministry said.
- It said drones were shot down over the Bryansk, Belgorod, Kaluga, Tver, Smolensk, Kursk, Oryol, Tula, Voronezh, Lipetsk, Tambov, Rostov, Volgograd, and Penza regions, the Moscow Region, the Republic of Crimea, as well as the Black Sea.
- Between 8:00 a.m. Moscow time (5:00 a.m. GMT) on September 2 and 12:00 a.m. Moscow time (9:00 a.m. GMT) on September 3, 548 UAVs were heading towards the Moscow Region, Sobyanin said on Max messenger.
- Most of them were destroyed while still far away; 143 drones were destroyed as they approached Moscow.
- The latest attempt by enemy drones to attack the Moscow Region was one of the largest in two years, according to TASS estimates based on Sobyanin’s data.
Effects
- A drone hit an apartment building in Pavlovsky Posad, Moscow Region, Governor Andrey Vorobyov said on Max messenger.
- There was no fire, but windows were shattered in eight apartments.
- Residents were evacuated.
- Also, in the Bogorodsky District, in the village of Bolshoye Bunkovo, a drone hit the territory of a factory.
- A fire broke out there.
- A fire broke out on the eighth and ninth floors of an apartment building in Kubinka, near Moscow, from a drone strike.
- A balcony on the seventh floor also caught fire.
- According to preliminary information, there are no casualties.
- Residents of the evacuated building in Kubinka are staying at a temporary shelter, said Andrey Ivanov, head of the Odintsovo district, said on Max messenger.
- He assured them that they would receive the necessary assistance.
- According to him, representatives of the Capital Repair Fund of the Moscow Region and the Housing and Communal Services administration of the Odintsovo district have begun to assess the damage.
- The Moscow Region Prosecutor's Office has opened a hotline for prompt reception of complaints and provision of legal assistance, its official told TASS.
- On the instructions of Prosecutor of the Moscow Region Sergey Zabaturin city prosecutors personally monitor the situation, coordinate interaction with the authorized departments and local governments to provide comprehensive assistance to the affected people and assess the damage.
- A fragment of a drone fell on a passing car in the Odintsovo district, Ivanov said on Max messenger.
- As a result, a 44·year·old man was injured.
- He was taken to the Clinical Center for Restorative Medicine and Rehabilitation.
- In addition, a 22·year·old man who was working at a construction site nearby was injured as a result of the UAV falling in Kubinka.
- He sustained a shrapnel wound to the thigh.
- According to Ivanov, the victim is at the Clinical Center for Restorative Medicine and Rehabilitation in Zvenigorod.
- His condition is assessed as satisfactory, and there is no threat to his life.
- Doctors are providing all the necessary assistance.

Maduro, wife seek dismissal of drug trafficking indictment on immunity grounds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:08:00 UTC
18:08:00 KST

Maduro, wife seek dismissal of drug trafficking indictment on immunity grounds
New York — Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife asked a judge on Wednesday to dismiss the drug trafficking indictment against them on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.
In papers filed in Manhattan federal court, lawyers for Maduro said a judge was required by law to reject the indictment because it cannot be brought against a foreign leader.
"No American court has ever presided over the criminal trial of a foreign leader who was recognized by their own country as the sitting head of state at the time the charges were brought," the lawyers wrote. "That is not an accident of history. It reflects a rule older than the common law: heads of state are exempt from the criminal process of any national court but their own."
Maduro and his wife are scheduled to go on trial on drug trafficking charges next June 1. Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein has set oral arguments for Nov. 17 on motions to dismiss the indictment.
Maduro, 63, and his wife, Cilia Flores, 69, have been held at a Brooklyn jail since U.S. forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid in early January and brought them to New York.
In separate papers filed Wednesday, lawyers for Flores said she too has immunity from U.S. prosecution on sovereign immunity grounds.
"It is an attribute of Venezuela's sovereignty, and only Venezuela may surrender it," her lawyers wrote.
Maduro's lawyers said that even if Maduro were not entitled to sovereign immunity as the head of state, the case against him must be dismissed because he is also entitled to conduct-based sovereign immunity.
Meanwhile, the lawyers argued, Maduro "vehemently denies the allegations against him."
"If this case were to proceed to trial, it would be apparent that he has been falsely accused," they said.
Both have pleaded not guilty in a criminal case first brought six years ago against numerous alleged co-conspirators. They face potential life prison sentences if a jury agrees that they were part of a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S.
Federal prosecutors are scheduled to file a response to the arguments later this month.
President Trump's administration has defended the raid to capture Maduro as a "surgical law enforcement operation." Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.
U.S. prosecutors say Maduro carried out a conspiracy to move thousands of tons of cocaine into the U.S. by colluding with Venezuelan law enforcement to help drug kingpins.
Maduro has remained defiant. On Sunday, he posted pictures of himself from prison on social media, saying he was "standing firm."
"I send these photos as a small gift to all my grandsons and granddaughters, to the boys and girls, and to all the noble people who love us," he wrote.
"I want you to know that we stand firm, with our hearts full of your love, that love that reaches us transformed into prayer, into constant action, into solidarity and true support. Infinite thanks for every word, for every gesture, for every blessing," he went on to say.
On the Telegram messaging service, he added, "We will remain strong, calm and confident: God is with us. God will provide. Venezuela will rise again," French news agency AFP reported.

El Niño likely to intensify, may become strongest ever recorded, WMO says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:06:11 UTC
18:06:11 KST

'Supersized' El Niño may become strongest ever recorded, UN says
GENEVA, Sept 3 - The El Niño weather phenomenon is set to intensify further into 2027 and could be the strongest ever, raising risks of extreme weather into next year, the World Meteorological Organization said on Thursday.
The U.N. weather agency said its forecasts showed a near 100% likelihood that El Niño would persist through February 2027, fuelled by exceptionally warm Pacific Ocean temperatures. This is the first time it has expressed such a degree of certainty, the WMO said.
"If this trajectory continues, it may be stronger than anything since our monitoring began. So literally off the charts," WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo told a Geneva press conference.
El Niño is a periodic warming of sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific caused by weakening trade winds. It occurs every two to seven years and tends to last up to 12 months, causing intense rains and droughts across Latin America.
A very strong El Niño can significantly shift rainfall and temperature patterns worldwide, and fuel extreme weather, such as droughts and typhoons.
WARMING OCEAN
While it is a naturally occurring phenomenon and not directly linked to fossil fuel-driven climate change, it can be intensified by warmer ocean temperatures, which are.
"El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: The planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up," said U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.
Sample Pacific Ocean temperatures in this year's El Niño - one of just four categorised in the top "very strong" bracket in records dating back to 1950 - are already more than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) above normal, the WMO said.
The event has already had an impact on soft commodities in tropical areas, causing a severe food crisis across Central America's Dry Corridor.
'PULSE' IN GLOBAL TEMPERATURES
It is set to peak towards the end of this year, the WMO said in a statement. But its effects will continue into 2027 and are set to leave higher global temperatures next year in its wake, WMO officials said.
"Normally after an El Niño event we tend to see a pulse in the global temperatures - a temporary one," Wilfran Moufouma Okia, the WMO's chief of climate prediction services, told reporters, referring to 2024, which was the hottest year so far. "2027 has the potential to be the warmest on record."
The WMO said it was stepping up preparedness and early warning efforts in preparation to allow states to take early action, such as switching to drought-resistant crops in some places.
"WMO is committed to working closely with partners across the United Nations and humanitarian system to provide the climate intelligence and insights needed to support disaster management and climate-sensitive sectors like agriculture, health, energy and water resources," Saulo said. REUTERS

75.8% of flat owners at block unscathed by Tai Po fire agree to sell to authorities
Housing Bureau says 188 households at Wang Chi House have signed sale and purchase agreements as part of buy-back scheme
More than 75 per cent of homeowners at the only block spared the worst of last November’s deadly fire at Wang Fuk Court have agreed to sell their flats to the Hong Kong government, with authorities to press ahead with acquisition procedures.
The Housing Bureau said on Thursday that 75.8 per cent of the flats at the estate’s Wang Chi House, or 188 households, had signed sales and purchase agreements as of Wednesday.
“[The] government confirmed that it will continue to take forward the acquisition work of Wang Chi House and sign assignments with its owners progressively to complete the relevant procedures on title acquisition,” a spokesman said.
In the aftermath of the fire, which killed 168 people and displaced nearly 5,000 others, authorities announced a plan to buy back flats in the eight-block subsidised housing estate in Tai Po.
Under the scheme, the government is acquiring flats at HK$8,000 (US$1,020) or HK$10,500 per square foot, depending on whether the owners have paid their land premiums.
Participants can use the cash compensation to buy a flat on the private open market or join a special sales exercise to purchase new subsidised housing under the government’s “flat-for-flat” arrangement.

Taiwan chip testing suppliers step up expansion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:00:48 UTC
18:00:48 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Testing-interface suppliers are expanding production capacity to keep up with growing orders, CTEE reported Thursday.
Semiconductor makers are facing higher testing requirements as AI and high-performance computing chips become more complex. Their higher cost means defects during packaging or testing can result in greater losses, prompting customers to place greater emphasis on testing quality and validation, according to CTEE.
WinWay Technology Co. is working on more than 10 projects related to co-packaged optics, a packaging technology that integrates light-based components with computing chips in the same package. The company said the need to move large amounts of data at high speeds is driving greater interest in CPO as AI chips become more powerful.
Small-volume production of related testing products is expected to begin in the second half of next year, followed by larger-scale production in 2028. Its work spans several stages of the testing process.
The company is developing socket solutions, which connect chips to testing equipment, as well as probe cards used for wafer-level testing. It is also expanding its capabilities for testing both wafers and packaged chips.
WinWay’s socket production capacity is expected to remain tight through the first quarter of next year. Additional facilities are scheduled to come online gradually in the second and third quarters.
Chunghwa Precision Test Tech Co. is also seeing strong orders from customers in AI and high-performance computing. The manufacturer said its production capacity remains relatively tight, with orders visible through 2027.
As AI chips become more complex, Chunghwa Precision said customers are seeking more services beyond wafer-level and final testing. System-level testing is becoming more important, while burn-in testing, which simulates prolonged operation to identify potential failures, is also seeing greater interest, according to Odi Morgan.
Meanwhile, customer planning horizons are becoming longer. Chunghwa Precision said some customers are no longer discussing capacity requirements for just one year, but are instead planning for two or three years, or even longer. The trend is particularly pronounced among AI and HPC customers, according to Anue.
To support future orders, Chunghwa Precision is expanding its manufacturing footprint. A new plant and additional equipment are expected to be ready in 2029, while several projects are currently under development and validation.

NATO warns Russia over submarine build up ‘We see them’
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
10:00:47 BST
18:00:47 KST

NATO says it is closely monitoring the expansion and modernisation of Russia’s submarine force in the High North, including new-generation nuclear-powered cruise missile submarines operating from the Kola Peninsula, according to Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum.
In a statement published on X, the NATO command drew attention to developments around Russia’s Northern Fleet and said the Alliance was treating the growth of its undersea forces seriously.
Allied Joint Force Command Brunssum stated: “Something is moving beneath the surface. Russia is expanding and modernising its submarine force, with the Kola Peninsula remaining a key hub for the Northern Fleet.”
The Kola Peninsula in north-west Russia contains several of the Northern Fleet’s principal naval bases and provides access to the Barents Sea and wider North Atlantic. The area is central to Russian submarine operations in northern waters and hosts both nuclear-powered attack submarines and strategic ballistic missile submarines.
NATO specifically referred to the development of newer nuclear-powered guided missile submarines, saying: “Among them: new-generation nuclear-powered SSGNs, bringing serious long-range strike and sea-denial capabilities into the High North.”
Something is moving beneath the surface. 🌊
Russia 🇷🇺 is expanding and modernising its submarine force, with the Kola Peninsula remaining a key hub for the Northern Fleet.
Among them: new-generation nuclear-powered SSGNs, bringing serious long-range strike and sea-denial… pic.twitter.com/UneKonlDon

SSGN is the designation commonly used for nuclear-powered submarines equipped primarily for cruise missile operations. Russian boats in this category can be employed against surface ships and land targets, depending on their weapons fit and tasking, while retaining the endurance associated with nuclear propulsion.
The command stated: “They may be invisible beneath the waves. But not for us. We see them, we watch the developments closely and yes, we take these developments seriously.”
The Northern Fleet is responsible for Russian naval activity across the Arctic and High North and operates from bases concentrated around the Kola Peninsula. Its submarines can reach the Norwegian Sea and North Atlantic through waters bordering NATO members Norway and Iceland and areas routinely monitored by allied maritime patrol aircraft, surface vessels and submarines.
Undersea activity in the High North has remained an important part of NATO maritime planning because the region connects Russia’s northern bases with the wider Atlantic. Allied forces regularly conduct anti-submarine warfare training in northern European waters, while maritime patrol aircraft and naval units contribute to surveillance and tracking activity.
Joint Force Command Brunssum is one of NATO’s operational-level joint headquarters and is responsible for planning and conducting activities across part of the Alliance’s northern and eastern area.

Taiwan begins 3rd phase of flexible migrant caregiver pilot program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:00:30 UTC
18:00:30 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Applications for the third phase of a pilot program that allows families to hire migrant caregivers for flexible, part-time care services have opened.
The Ministry of Labor's Workforce Development Agency said the “Diverse Companion Care Pilot Program” is designed to meet urgent and short-term care needs, per CNA. Under the self-paid program, residents can apply to participating nonprofit organizations for care services.
Thirteen nonprofit organizations currently provide services in 16 cities and counties, giving the program coverage for more than 70% of the country. The agency said it has received numerous complaints from residents in areas where the service is not yet available.
Hu Hsin-yeh (胡欣野), deputy director of the agency's Cross-Border Workforce Affairs Center, said applications for third-phase pilot organizations will be accepted through Sept. 24. The program aims to extend services to all 22 cities and counties, she confirmed.
Only nonprofit organizations that have been legally registered for at least five years are eligible to apply, according to the agency. Applicants must submit a care-service plan and documents demonstrating relevant service experience, among other requirements.
The labor ministry will evaluate applications through a selection panel, with proposals scoring at least 70 points considered qualified. Results are expected to be announced by Dec. 4, with new organizations potentially joining the program as early as the beginning of next year.
The program serves people with disabilities, serious illnesses, recent medical treatment or surgery, or long-term care needs at levels 2 to 8, per UDN. Services include assistance with basic daily activities.
As of the end of July, the program had provided more than 100,000 hours of care, with one-time services and once-a-week services the most common, CNA reported. The cumulative number of service users had surpassed 10,000.

====================================================================================================

MAD’s lucas museum of narrative art opens in LA this month: take an early look inside
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:00:22 UTC
18:00:22 KST

After more than a decade in development, the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art is preparing to open in Los Angeles on September 22, 2026. Designed by Ma Yansong of MAD with Stantec, and set within an approximately 52,600-square-meter campus landscape by Mia Lehrer of Studio-MLA, the five-story, 27,870-square-meter institution takes shape in Exposition Park as a continuous, curving volume hovering above the ground. Founded by George Lucas and Mellody Hobson, the museum will be dedicated to narrative art — images that communicate stories, beliefs and collective memory across painting, illustration, comics and cinema.
For MAD, however, the project begins before visitors encounter any of those works. Rather than treating the museum as an isolated object sitting on a conventional plinth, the architecture pulls much of its mass upward, allowing gardens, paths and sheltered public areas to continue beneath and around it. Conceived without a single straight line, the smooth exterior draws on the tree canopy of Exposition Park, producing a building that appears less deposited on the site than caught somewhere between landscape and sky. Its skin is assembled from more than 1,200 uniquely shaped curved panels of fiberglass-reinforced polymer, selected for their ability to produce the building’s flowing geometry while remaining considerably lighter than alternative materials.
That apparent lightness requires some fairly muscular engineering. At the center of the building, a central arch spans 56 meters to form a suspended plaza beneath the museum, creating a shaded gathering space connected to the surrounding park. From here, visitors can enter through north and south lobbies, while an elliptical Oculus hovers four stories above the plaza, opening a view from the ground toward the sky. The gesture turns what could have been the building’s most monumental moment into an absence.
Inside, the architecture becomes progressively brighter and more vertical. Sweeping arches define the main lobby, where daylight enters through large glazed openings and glass elevators carry visitors toward the galleries and restaurant above. The lower floors also contain two theaters, a horseshoe-shaped research library and learning space overlooking the park, ten studios and classrooms, a shop, café and an approximately 930-square-meter gallery. The movement through the museum is therefore not simply from room to room, but from landscape to sheltered plaza, from plaza to luminous interior, and finally upward into the exhibition spaces — a sequence that makes circulation part of the building’s storytelling.
the lucas museum rises above exposition park | image by Iwan Baan, courtesy of Lucas Museum
WHEN ROCKWELL MEETS COMICS
More than 9,290 square meters of the museum are devoted to galleries, drawing from a collection of over 40,000 works assembled by Lucas and Hobson. Its inaugural exhibitions alone will unfold across more than 30 galleries and bring together over 1,300 works. Their range deliberately collapses distinctions that museums have traditionally kept apart: paintings and popular illustration sit alongside comics, children’s books and cinematic art, with figures including Frida Kahlo, Norman Rockwell and Charles White forming part of a much wider history of images made to tell stories. The museum’s proposition is simple but surprisingly disruptive: illustration does not need rescuing from popular culture to qualify as serious art.
The curatorial structure extends that idea. Rather than primarily sorting works through movements, periods or mediums, galleries explore recognizable human themes such as family, love, work, play, childhood and adventure. A dedicated cinema installation, Star Wars in Motion, will examine vehicles from the first six films through concept designs, props and costumes, while another inaugural exhibition turns the lens back onto the building itself, presenting Ma Yansong as a narrative artist through drawings, renderings and photographs of the Lucas Museum and other MAD projects. Two cinematic theaters expand the narrative beyond static images, while a free research library, learning spaces, dining, retail and areas for public programs turn the building into something broader than a sequence of exhibition rooms. Architecture and curatorial strategy arrive at roughly the same conclusion: categories are useful, but stories have a habit of ignoring them.
MAD shapes the museum as a continuous curved volume
A 52,600-SQUARE-METER GARDEN AROUND THE ARCHITECTURE
The landscape by Studio-MLA is therefore less a decorative perimeter than the second half of the project. Gardens and planted spaces extend across the approximately 52,600-square-meter campus and slip beneath the elevated architecture, softening the conventional boundary between museum and park. Replacing what was previously an asphalt parking lot, the landscape introduces more than 300 trees alongside indigenous and drought-tolerant planting, a hanging garden, amphitheater, meadow and a fountain conceived as a dramatic waterfall. Its contoured topography draws on California’s foothills, valleys, mesas and canyons, turning the landscape itself into another form of narrative. In a part of Los Angeles already populated by major civic institutions, including the California Science Center and Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, the project uses its footprint somewhat paradoxically: building something enormous while trying to occupy as little of the ground as possible.
When the Lucas Museum opens on September 22, its collection will inevitably attract much of the attention — particularly the meeting of fine art, illustration, comics and artifacts linked to Lucas’s own cinematic universe. Ten monumental sculptures spread through the freely accessible park extend that collection outdoors, ranging from works by Fernando Botero and Prune Nourry to bronzes depicting Princess Leia, Yoda and Grogu. Yet MAD’s building makes a parallel argument through architecture. If narrative art is supposed to belong to everyday culture rather than remain trapped inside traditional hierarchies, the museum housing it cannot quite behave like an ivory tower either. Here, the tower has effectively been lifted out of the way, leaving a park underneath.
more than 1,200 curved FRP panels form the exterior
WHEN THE PEOPLE’S ART TAKES OVER
The inaugural exhibitions push that argument further, spreading narrative art across subjects and formats that rarely share the same museum floor. More than 30 galleries move between children’s literature, manga, comics and graphic stories, photography, murals, science fiction, romance and myths of the American West, alongside dedicated presentations of artists including Norman Rockwell, N.C. Wyeth, Maxfield Parrish, Frank Frazetta and Thomas Hart Benton. Other rooms turn to everyday life — childhood, family, love, school, sport and work — while works by Judith F. Baca, Diego Rivera and JR bring large-scale public storytelling into the mix. Taken together, the opening program gives architectural form to what George Lucas has described as ‘the people’s art’: images made not simply to be looked at, but to circulate, communicate and tell stories.

Face Recognition Is Becoming the Norm for Dating Apps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

In 2025, AI deepfakes flooded Tinder. According to the company, 98 percent of the content-moderation actions on the app were focused on combating fake accounts, scamming, and spam, pushing the company to expand its moderation efforts for its 60 million global users.
The problem is not unique to Tinder. The spread of AI-generated fake accounts has become a rising concern for dating apps, as things like chatfishing and voice cloning have gotten more widespread across the industry.
Among current online daters in the US, nearly half have been targeted by a dating scam, with US romance scams surpassing $4 billion between 2015 and 2025, according to the FBI.
The issue has forced just about every dating platform to adopt stricter authentication tools to ward off scammers. More and more, apps are asking that you surrender your most unique attribute in order to ensure that you’re a real person: your face.
More than a dozen major dating apps and sites use face recognition to verify users, often relying on liveness checks, 3D authentication, video selfies, or biometric ID to demonstrate humanness.
To combat the issue, Tinder launched the mandatory face-screening tool Face Check for new members in October 2025. “It’s not a feature. It’s a statement about what human connection online should require,” Yoel Roth, head of trust and safety for Match Group, which owns Tinder, said to WIRED in an email. Match Group tells WIRED that it is also starting to require Face Check for existing users in several of Tinder’s core markets, including the US and UK.
As face verification slowly transforms into a prerequisite for participation across the industry, the collective drive to combat bad actors has created a necessary and equally concerning new standard where “proof of human” profiles may soon be the norm.
Underpinning the shift, however, is a grim irony: In attempting to solve the problem of knowing whether someone is real, Big Dating is potentially creating more opportunities for privacy and security risks by forcing users to give up biometric data, while also legitimizing a culture of surveillance.
One company pushing for the use of ID-verification tech in dating apps is Tools for Humanity. The AI company created World ID, an iris-scanning biometric verification system, and partnered with Tinder in April, though it’s still optional for users. The most distinct feature about World ID is that confirmed users receive a “verified human” badge on the app after undergoing the process, which requires them to scan the colored part of their eye using the company’s orb device. They are given an identification number as their official World ID.
“In the near future, any dating app, like most online platforms in general, will need some sort of proof-of-human system like this,” says Tiago Sada, chief product officer at Tools for Humanity, adding that the way the majority of dating platforms handle verification is “super creepy, because you have to give your personal data to every single app that you want to use.” As stipulated by World’s policy, the orb does not share or retain any data; it is able to verify users without ever sending their data to a server. Once your image is confirmed, the orb sends the coded image to your phone before permanently deleting it, the company claims. Likewise, Face Check collects and stores an encrypted map of information about the shape of the user’s face, not the actual picture, Match said.
But even as dating apps claim that your biometric data is safe, security continues to be a significant concern.
Dating apps are subject to occasional data breaches, and while the inherent premise in these ID systems is that verification equals trust, cybersecurity researcher Katie Moussouris says that they are mostly a smoke screen. “Normalizing the idea that a face scan provides any assurance of identity or age is security theater.”
A liveness check requiring face scanning and live video only indicates a person was present at sign-up and does not guarantee that the person was not using AI to alter their appearance in real time. Likewise, an ID scan indicates an ID was presented, not that it belongs to the person who presented it. “Neither should be confused with trust,” Moussouris says. “A verified profile can still belong to a romance scammer who took over an account or created one using AI tools.”
And while passwords and usernames are interchangeable, faces are not, which makes them unique targets for attacks. More than that, biometric verification sets a risky precedent, says Woodrow Hartzog, a technology law professor at Boston University who previously served on the Massachusetts special commission on facial recognition.
“When we get accustomed to having our face scanned for everything we do online, it is really dangerous, not only potentially for the privacy risks but also to acclimate an entire population into thinking that that is normal behavior,” he says. “Facial recognition is the most dangerous surveillance tool ever created.”
Existing privacy laws are not equipped to deal with biometric verification on dating apps, according to Hartzog. He believes policies should ensure that less invasive options are used when they're available. In the case of biometrics, for example, your face, which can be monitored everywhere you go, is much more dangerous to collect than your thumbprint.
Utah’s State-Endorsed Digital Identity law, which went into effect in May, was one of the first major attempts at that. It limits the kinds of data that can be requested to only what is absolutely necessary while establishing a “duty of loyalty,” meaning platforms and providers cannot engage in practices that “conflict with the best interests of an individual” or “result in a disproportionate risk” to them. The law attempts to mitigate situations where people might have to present ID every time they log online, and also includes significant rules on the entity that’s collecting the data. The American Civil Liberties Union called it “the nation’s strongest digital identity bill.”
“Look at how easy it is to channel people's choices into agreeing to have their faces scanned as a condition of a good or service,” Hartzog says. “The more we can lean into policy frameworks that require strong protections from the company—rather than putting the onus on the person whose face is being scanned or who has to reveal their identity—then the better off I think we’ll be.”

Threats to civilian ships and aircraft constitute ‘state terrorism’ – Putin
The seizing and targeting of Russian civilian vessels constitute acts of “state terrorism,” President Vladimir Putin has said, warning that these actions are making peace talks with Ukraine more difficult.
Speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok on Thursday, the Russian president denounced the recent captures of Russian civilian vessels and pointed to Kiev’s threats against passenger aircraft.
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky previously stated that the “safe days” in Russian skies are over, addressing foreign airlines, insurers, and governments whose aircraft continue to use Russian airspace.
“This, of course, is a manifestation of state terrorism,” Putin said, adding that these actions “undoubtedly complicate the possibility of bilateral peace negotiations.”
He also warned that “those who remain silent and do not pay attention to this become accomplices in international terrorism,” referring to Kiev’s Western backers.
Putin’s remarks came a day after the Norwegian authorities seized the Russian research vessel the Professor Molchanov in Svalbard at the request of Ukraine’s state-owned Naftogaz. The ship was detained while docked in the Russian settlement of Barentsburg.
The Professor Molchanov is a Russian state-owned research vessel that operates regular passenger and cargo services between Murmansk and Svalbard, carrying scientists, workers, their families, tourists, and supplies to Russian settlements on the archipelago. Moscow has said the seizure will be challenged in court.
The detention follows a series of Western seizures of Russian-linked vessels accused of belonging to a so-called “shadow fleet,” although the Professor Molchanov itself was seized in connection with a legal claim by Ukraine’s Naftogaz against Russia. Moscow has rejected the “shadow fleet” label as having no basis in international law and accused Western states of using sanctions as a pretext to interfere with civilian maritime trade.
Putin warned last month that attempts to seize Russian ships and sell their cargo amounted to “piracy and robbery,” saying Moscow is prepared to respond in kind in any part of the world.
Kiev has also stepped up attacks on civilian shipping. Putin said earlier this week that around 100 Russian merchant vessels had been damaged over a 40-day period, with sailors killed in the attacks, including Russian and foreign nationals.
