Spy planes swarm Russia’s borders in rare surge
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
09:17:33 BST
17:17:33 KST

Two RC-135W Rivet Joint surveillance aircraft, at least two P-8A Poseidons and American tanker support are operating across the High North in a concentration of intelligence-gathering flights rare in both scale and composition, according to open-source tracking.
The account DefenceGeek, run by one of our team members Jon, logged the aircraft operating from the United Kingdom and Iceland, watching across the border into Russia. Among them were the Royal Air Force Rivet Joint ZZ666 using the callsign ASCOT 7202, an American RC-135W as JAKE 17, and a KC-135R tanker as RAKE 67 providing refuelling.
A United States Air Force Rivet Joint is operating within the European Command area for the first time in a while, flying near Russia’s naval base complex at Murmansk. It is likely to be operating with fighter escort given an active tanker bridge in the area. A second Rivet Joint, this one British, was tracked along the border between Russia and Finland, with a Poseidon monitoring the Baltic at low altitude. American Rivet Joint aircraft have concentrated elsewhere in recent years, which is what makes an appearance over the Barents notable.
NATO Eyes on Russia Continues
Two RC-135 “Rivet Joint” SIGINT platforms and at least 2 P-8A “Poseidon” aircraft are operating out of the UK & Iceland today in the high north, watching across the border into Russia, supported by US tankers:
🇬🇧 RC-135W “ASCOT7202” ZZ666 #43C39D… pic.twitter.com/dqKU3KIQuv
— DefenceGeek 🇬🇧 (@DefenceGeek) September 2, 2026
What they are looking at
Murmansk and the wider Kola Peninsula hold the Russian Northern Fleet, including the ballistic missile submarines that carry the sea-based portion of the Russian deterrent, along with the attack boats that transit south into the Atlantic. It is the single most concentrated collection of Russian naval power anywhere, and the point from which any submarine deployment towards the Greenland, Iceland and United Kingdom gap begins.
The RC-135W does not take photographs, no, it is an electronic surveillance aircraft, and its crews survey the electromagnetic spectrum to collect communications, radar emissions and other signals, building a picture of what is switched on, where it is, and how it behaves. Flying a track along a border allows the aircraft to map air defence radars and communications networks without entering the airspace they cover.
The P-8A Poseidon does a different job, of course. It hunts submarines, using sonobuoys dropped into the water and its own radar and acoustic processing, and the Royal Air Force operates nine of them from RAF Lossiemouth in Moray. A Poseidon working the Baltic at low altitude is looking at what is on and under the surface.
Britain operates three Rivet Joints from RAF Waddington in Lincolnshire, converted from KC-135 airframes under a co-operative programme with the United States Air Force, which flies a larger fleet of the type from Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska.
The flights come at the end of a fortnight of unusually heavy allied air activity along the Russian frontier. Around 25 aircraft from several nations operated over the Baltic region on 18 August in a package overseen by the United States, including an EA-37B Compass Call electronic attack aircraft and an ARTEMIS II intelligence platform, with further flights on the two days following. NATO E-3A Sentry aircraft and Multinational MRTT Fleet tankers have been operating over Lithuania and Poland since.
Germany formally attributed the attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport to Russian intelligence on Tuesday, announcing the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn along with new sanctions and entry restrictions, in a step Estonia’s prime minister described as Russia taking its hybrid attacks in Europe to a new and dangerous level.
Surveillance flights of this kind are deliberately visible, as readers will know. Aircraft on these missions generally transmit, and their tracks appear on civilian monitoring platforms, which is a choice rather than an oversight.
The Russian Navy has meanwhile had no presence in the Mediterranean since June, with a NATO official telling us last week that allied warships outnumber Russian vessels in European waters by roughly three to one.
Neither the Ministry of Defence nor United States Air Forces in Europe comments on individual intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance sorties.

AEVEX, Divergent team up on new autonomous aircraft

- AEVEX Corp. and Divergent Technologies announced a collaboration to build a new autonomous aircraft using Divergent's 3D-printing manufacturing platform.
- Neither company disclosed a contract value, funding source, or timeline for a prototype.
EVEX Corp. and Divergent Technologies said Tuesday they will jointly develop a new autonomous aircraft platform, combining AEVEX’s unmanned systems work with Divergent’s 3D-printing based manufacturing process.
The companies did not disclose a contract value or say which government customer, if any, the resulting aircraft is intended for. AEVEX, based in Solana Beach, California, builds unmanned aerial systems and unmanned surface vessels and trades on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker AVEX. Divergent, headquartered in Torrance, California, manufactures parts and structures using a platform it calls the Divergent Adaptive Production System, or DAPS, which combines 3D-printed metal components with AI-assisted design and robotic assembly.
“Working with Divergent allows us to evaluate next-generation manufacturing concepts that could improve responsiveness and bring new flexibility to how future unmanned systems are developed and delivered,” said Manan Patel, Chief Technology Officer at AEVEX.
“We’re proud to collaborate with AEVEX to deliver mass at the pace of need,” said Lukas Czinger, Co-Founder and CEO at Divergent. “Divergent is a force multiplier for our customers’ programs, and we’re excited to integrate DAPS with AEVEX’s field-proven expertise to set a new standard for delivering capability at speed and scale.”
The two companies said early work will focus on adaptable airframe designs, faster integration processes and production methods intended to cut part counts and shorten development timelines.
This is not Divergent’s first partnership built around DAPS with a larger aerospace player. As The Defence Blog reported in June, Lockheed Martin’s Skunk Works division used the platform with Divergent to build a 2.7-meter (9-foot) wingspan drone called Replicator, taking it from concept to a first physical article in under a year. Lockheed Martin made a $25 million strategic investment in Divergent in 2024 to explore applications across advanced munitions and unmanned aircraft. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth viewed the Replicator during a stop at Divergent’s facility as part of his “Arsenal of Freedom” tour of American defense manufacturers.
Divergent also holds a spot on the US Air Force’s Eglin Wide Agile Acquisition Contract, a multiple-award vehicle with a ceiling of $46 billion for developing and fielding weapon systems. The company is building a 430,000-square-foot (40,000-square-meter) factory in Long Beach, California, meant to house 64 of its Monolith One metal printers and eventually produce tens of thousands of missile airframes and warhead casings a year. Divergent raised $290 million in a Series E funding round earlier this year at a $2.3 billion valuation, led by Rochefort Asset Management.
AEVEX has delivered unmanned systems to national security customers, including intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance aircraft, electronic warfare equipment and unmanned surface vessels. The company completed an initial public offering in April, raising roughly $312 million and listing on the NYSE. AEVEX had operated as a portfolio company of Madison Dearborn Partners before the offering. It employs about 650 people across manufacturing sites in the United States.

Leasing or royalties: The Finance Ministry may resolve the issue over which the BEB is pursuing airlines
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
11:14:47 EEST
17:14:47 KST

Leasing or royalties: The Finance Ministry may resolve the issue over which the BEB is pursuing airlines
Kyiv • UNN
The Finance Ministry plans to unify the taxation of airlines’ lease payments to non-residents. The UTP will not change the law, but may affect unresolved BEB disputes.
The Ministry of Finance of Ukraine may use a general tax consultation to establish a unified approach to applying legal provisions that state bodies interpret ambiguously. This is the mechanism planned for resolving the issue of taxation of Ukrainian airlines’ leasing payments in favor of nonresidents. UNN examined the legal force of a general tax clarification, whether regulatory authorities must take it into account, and whether it can affect the existing claims of the Economic Security Bureau against representatives of the aviation business.
Why is the Finance Ministry’s clarification needed on the issue of aviation leasing?
The issue of taxing aircraft leasing became the subject of a dispute between the aviation business and state authorities. It arose after the Economic Security Bureau decided to interpret aviation leasing not as the rental of vehicles, but as the use of equipment. According to the investigators’ version, Ukrainian air carriers should have paid royalties for leasing aircraft and helicopters.
The ESB is investigating criminal proceedings against at least 5 air carriers, including MAU, "Constanta Airline," "Urga," H3Operations, and "Skyline Express." The cases were opened despite the fact that almost all air carriers had successfully passed tax audits, and the tax authorities’ comments concerning leasing applied to only one company.
Representatives of the aviation industry insist that the problem arose because of an ambiguous interpretation of legal provisions and requires the establishment of a unified state approach. They call the Bureau’s approach to interpreting aviation leasing, without amending tax legislation, pressure that could destroy an entire sector of passenger and freight transportation. After all, according to the State Register of Civil Aircraft of Ukraine, 86% of the aircraft fleet of Ukrainian companies is leased.
That is why the issue of aviation leasing was submitted for consideration by the tax committee of the Public Council under the Ministry of Finance. Following the first meeting, it was decided to initiate the establishment of a working group under the Finance Ministry, which is to develop a draft general tax consultation regarding the taxation of leasing payments in favor of nonresidents.
In response to a request from UNN, the Ministry of Finance reported that the taxation of aircraft leasing transactions is carried out in accordance with the Tax Code and international treaties of Ukraine. It is worth noting that tax legislation in this area has not changed for several decades and, until 2024, had raised no questions either among tax authorities or law enforcement agencies.
The aviation industry hopes that the general tax clarification will settle all questions regarding the taxation of aviation leasing. But is that really the case?
What is a general tax consultation?
As lawyer Yuliia Panasiuk of Prykhodko & Partners Law Firm explained to UNN, a general tax consultation is an officially published position of the Ministry of Finance regarding the practical application of certain provisions of tax and other legislation, compliance with which is monitored by regulatory authorities.
"It is formulated on the basis of a generalization of individual tax consultations provided to taxpayers, or in cases where the Finance Ministry identifies ambiguity in the application of certain legal provisions," Panasiuk explained.
According to her, such a clarification is approved by an order of the Ministry of Finance.
Tax policy expert Danylo Monin noted that the Finance Ministry usually generalizes the practice of applying legislation with regard to a specific problem or topic.
"As the body that formulates state financial policy, the Finance Ministry has the right to generalize the practice of applying legislation concerning disputed issues and, on this basis, issue a general tax consultation. Usually, this is done regarding a specific problem or a particular topic," Monin explained.
Thus, the situation involving differing interpretations of the taxation of leasing payments is precisely the kind of case in which the mechanism of a generalized tax clarification can be used to establish a unified approach.
Can the Ministry of Finance establish new rules for airlines?
As experts explain, a generalized tax consultation does not amend legislation. Through this mechanism, the Ministry of Finance cannot create a new tax, change its rate, or impose on airlines an additional tax obligation that is not provided for in the Tax Code.
"Such a consultation does not create new tax rules and cannot amend the provisions of the Tax Code of Ukraine. Its task is to provide an official position on how an already effective provision should be applied in practice," Panasiuk emphasized.
In the context of aviation leasing, this means that the task of the generalized tax clarification will not be to establish a new taxation regime, but to clarify how the current provisions should be applied to payments for the leasing of aircraft from non-residents.
At the same time, according to the lawyer, if an individual tax consultation contradicts a generalized one, the provisions developed by the Ministry of Finance apply, pursuant to paragraph 53.1 of the Tax Code.
Should state authorities take the Ministry of Finance's position into account?
Controlling authorities must take into account the position formulated by the Ministry of Finance in a generalized tax consultation when applying the relevant legislative provisions.
At the same time, for a taxpayer, the clarification does not become a new provision of law. Businesses must primarily follow the Tax Code, while conduct that complies with a generalized consultation provides the taxpayer with the legal guarantees stipulated by law.
This may be of fundamental importance for airlines if the position formed by the Ministry of Finance differs from the approach previously applied by controlling or law enforcement authorities to leasing payments.
"If the Ministry of Finance has published a GTC that interprets the relevant provision differently from the way a controlling authority previously did, the taxpayer may refer to such a consultation both during a tax audit and at the stage of administrative or judicial appeal," Panasiuk noted.
Going forward, a taxpayer's compliance with the provisions of tax consultations may constitute grounds for exemption from financial liability. The legislation also provides for cases in which no penalty interest is accrued or already accrued penalty interest is subject to cancellation.
What will happen to aviation leasing cases?
One of the key questions in this situation is whether the Ministry of Finance's clarification will be able to affect disputes and proceedings that arose before its adoption.
According to Panasiuk, a new generalized tax consultation does not in itself automatically change the tax consequences of transactions carried out previously. In other words, the appearance of the consultation will not mean the automatic termination or review of all disputes related to the taxation of leasing payments.
However, for cases that have not yet been finally resolved when the document appears, its significance may be substantial.
"If a tax dispute has not yet been concluded, the taxpayer may refer to the new GTC as the Ministry of Finance's official position on the interpretation of the relevant legislative provision," the lawyer explained.
According to her, in such a case the court will assess the consultation together with the provisions of the Tax Code, the circumstances of the specific case, and current judicial practice.
Under the provisions of the Tax Code, generalized tax consultations must be published on the Ministry of Finance's official website within five calendar days of their issuance.
"The Tax Code does not establish a separate period after the expiration of which controlling authorities may begin taking a GTC into account. Therefore, in practice, primary attention should be paid to the date on which the Ministry of Finance's order approving the relevant GTC enters into force," the lawyer warned.
If the Ministry of Finance develops an unambiguous position on the application of the relevant provisions of the Tax Code and international treaties, it could serve as a guideline for the further practice of the supervisory authorities and as a strong argument for airlines in cases handled by the Economic Security Bureau, where aircraft leasing is interpreted as royalties. That is why the development of a UPT may become one of the key stages in resolving the situation.

Later, in an Instagram post, the prime minister claimed that IDF officers deliberately did not wake him for over an hour because they knew he would prevent the massacre.

Foreign support, drones fuel Sudan war and possible war crimes, UN probe says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:14:11 UTC
17:14:11 KST

Foreign weapons, military technology, fighters and logistical networks are helping sustain Sudan's conflict and expanding the warring parties' ability to strike deep into civilian areas, a United Nations fact-finding mission said in a report published on Thursday, warning that some attacks may amount to war crimes.
Sudan's war erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between Sudan's military and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) ahead of a planned transition to civilian rule. The conflict has devastated the country, displaced more than 14 million people and created what the United Nations has described as one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
The UN mission said investigators found reasonable grounds to believe that a transnational network involving individuals and entities in the United Arab Emirates, Chad, Libya and Somalia supplied the RSF with weapons, military equipment, logistics, training and foreign personnel.
The UAE, Chad, Libya and Somalia, the RSF and Sudan's military did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters.
UAE, Chad deny allegations
The UAE rejected allegations that it had provided military, logistical, financial or political support to the RSF, and Chad said it remained neutral in the war and denied knowledge of weapons transfers through its territory, according to the report.
The UN mission also said it obtained evidence that Colombian contractors played a significant role in operating and maintaining drone systems and other advanced weapons used by the RSF. It estimated the total number of Colombian contractors involved could approach 2,000 and said some were present during operations around al-Fashir in Darfur.
Colombia told investigators it opposed mercenarism and was taking steps to address the participation of Colombian nationals in foreign conflicts.
Mass killings of non‑Arab communities when the RSF captured al‑Fashir bore hallmarks that point to genocide, the UN mission said in a previous report in February.
In the past, the RSF has denied such abuses, saying the accounts have been manufactured by its enemies and making counter-accusations against them.
The mission said its investigation into external support for Sudan's military was at an early stage but had found evidence that foreign-supplied combat drones and loitering munitions, which can hover over an area before striking a target, had expanded the army's long-range strike capabilities.
It said some of those weapons were used in attacks on civilian locations, including Yabus Market in Blue Nile State.
Drone warfare violated international human rights law, UN says
The report found both sides committed serious violations of international human rights law and international humanitarian law in their drone operations, with some conduct amounting to war crimes. Both sides have previously denied allegations of human rights abuses.
Expanded range, persistence and increasingly sophisticated capabilities enabled Sudan's military and the RSF to strike far beyond immediate front lines, and evidence points to both sides carrying out drone attacks that killed civilians and hit hospitals, schools, markets and displacement sites.
More than 1,000 civilians were killed in drone strikes between January and May 2026, according to figures cited by the report.
Between May and July 2026, repeated RSF drone attacks damaged electricity and fuel facilities in the North Kordofan capital of El Obeid, which was under SAF control as RSF pressure intensified in June this year. Strikes disrupted water supplies, healthcare, transport and other basic services in a city already under severe strain and partial siege, the mission said.
Among the cases highlighted in the report were SAF strikes on Ad-Da'ein Teaching Hospital in East Darfur that investigators said killed at least 70 people and left the facility non-functional.
The mission reiterated calls for enforcement of the Darfur arms embargo and urged the UN Security Council to extend it across all of Sudan.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:14:02 UTC
17:14:02 KST

Iran has warned the United States that it would respond forcefully to an Israeli offensive on a mountainous ridge in southern Lebanon where Iranian military personnel are holed up alongside Hezbollah terrorists, three officials briefed on the message told Reuters.
The message, delivered last month, highlights Iran's continued direct involvement in the ground fighting in southern Lebanon and its readiness to retaliate against Israeli attacks there as the regional war enters its seventh month.
Hezbollah is believed to have built an underground command center and weapons stores within the Ali al-Taher ridge, which has a commanding view of southeastern Lebanon, according to Lebanese security sources, and has become one of the most contested pieces of ground in the Israel-Hezbollah war.
Hezbollah has said in public statements that it controls the hill and will confront any Israeli advances. Its officials have referred to a "facility" there, but have declined to provide details.
The IDF has occupied swathes of territory to Ali al-Taher's south and has identified the ridge as one of its "primary operational focuses" in public statements.
In its message to Washington, Tehran threatened that any full-fledged Israeli offensive on the ridge would be met with a large-scale Iranian attack, said the three officials in the region, who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity.
Hezbollah declined to comment on whether Iranian forces were present in Ali al-Taher. In response to Reuters questions about the message, or whether the US had put pressure on Israel not to attack Ali al-Taher, a White House official said, "this is not accurate." There was no immediate comment from Iran's permanent mission in Geneva, the US Defense Department, or Oman's foreign ministry. The Israeli military declined to comment.
IRGC forces holed up, officials say
Two of the officials said the message was delivered via Oman, which has played a mediating role. Those two regional officials, briefed by Tehran, said over a dozen members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, including at least two senior officers, were with Hezbollah fighters.
The third source, a foreign official with direct knowledge of the message, said it was delivered around mid-August and that as a result of US pressure, Israel had put off storming Ali al-Taher.
Contacted by Reuters, Hezbollah's media office neither confirmed nor denied Iran's message but said it was a "natural conclusion" that such a warning would have been sent about the ridge.
"Iran considers any Israeli move on the ground in southern Lebanon, especially territorial expansion, a major violation of the Islamabad Agreement," Hezbollah's media office said, referring to the June US-Iran memorandum of understanding that included a Lebanon ceasefire.
Iran fired missiles towards Israel in early June in retaliation for attacks on Hezbollah on the Lebanese capital's outskirts.
Israel seeks to besiege Hezbollah fighters
Despite a ceasefire announced in June, the Israeli military has said Hezbollah is still operating around the ridge and twice over the last week launched explosive drones towards Israeli troops near the ridge.
In July, it said it had launched an air strike on a Hezbollah fighter near an access shaft to the underground site at Ali al-Taher and vowed not to allow Hezbollah to operate in the area or pose a threat to Israeli soldiers.
An Israeli military official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told Reuters in June that Hezbollah fighters were stuck underground without food or water. Israeli newspaper Maariv, citing a military source, said on Thursday that the Israeli military assessed there were no IRGC forces in Ali al-Taher and that some Hezbollah fighters had died without food and water.
The third official said Israel's military was trying to smoke out Hezbollah and IRGC personnel by besieging them, shooting down attempted drone deliveries of food and water to the ridge.
"What we have seen over the past month is Israeli pressure to besiege Ali al-Taher in order to impose a reality within this facility that renders it uninhabitable. This approach, and the absence of a large-scale attack, means that it is possible a message was conveyed through several countries -- this is a natural conclusion," Hezbollah's media office told Reuters.
Hezbollah threatens retaliation
A Lebanese source briefed by Hezbollah said the group's fighters can still access their positions through the ridge's northern side.
Reuters could not independently confirm the military situation at Ali al-Taher, which Israel's military has included in a self-declared security zone occupied by its troops and off-limits to Lebanese.
Despite Iran's warning, the Lebanese source and a senior Lebanese security official said an Israeli military operation to capture the ridge was still possible in the coming weeks.
Hezbollah said any large-scale attack on Ali al-Taher would mean a return to full-blown war, and could see missiles landing on northern Israeli communities.

India, Sri Lanka, and Israel’s overlooked Indian Ocean opportunity  - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:13:43 UTC
17:13:43 KST

While Sri Lanka is not an obvious priority in Israel’s Asian policy, with India, Japan, and Singapore receiving far more strategic attention, it has considerable potential because of its location, its development needs and the direction its relationship with India is heading.
During my recent visit, this became particularly clear. The island sits close to major sea lanes and within India’s immediate maritime security environment. For New Delhi, Sri Lanka is not simply another neighbor. Access to its ports and maritime infrastructure carries significance beyond bilateral relations.
Indian concerns about China’s research and survey vessels illustrate this sensitivity. The issue is not simply Chinese commercial investment. New Delhi is also attentive to the possibility that external actors could gain access to ports, infrastructure, or oceanographic information with potential dual-use applications close to India’s coastline.
Sri Lanka should not be reduced to another arena of India-China competition. Colombo has strong reasons to maintain relations with multiple partners, including China. Any Israeli strategy framed primarily around containing Beijing would misunderstand Sri Lanka’s interests and risk narrowing the space for cooperation.
India’s own approach has become broader. During Sri Lanka’s economic crisis in 2022, New Delhi provided some $4 billion in assistance. Since then, the relationship has moved beyond emergency support toward longer-term cooperation in energy, infrastructure, digital connectivity, trade, and security.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s April 2025 visit marked an important step. The two countries signed agreements on electricity interconnection, digital transformation and development, and, for the first time, a formal memorandum of understanding (MoU) on Defence Cooperation.
India, Sri Lanka and the United Arab Emirates also agreed to cooperate on developing Trincomalee as an energy hub.
The defense agreement did not create bilateral security cooperation: India and Sri Lanka already had substantial ties in training, naval visits, exercises, and capacity-building. Yet the MoU gave this relationship a more formal framework. Cooperation includes joint exercises, maritime surveillance, hydrography, capacity-building, and the provision of defense platforms and assets.
SLINEX is a regular bilateral naval exercise, and in April 2026 the two navies conducted their fourth bilateral diving exercise in Colombo, including complex underwater operations. Sri Lankan personnel have also participated in India’s wider IOS Sagar initiative.
Taken together, these developments suggest that India is progressively embedding Sri Lanka within a wider Indian-led maritime security architecture. This does not mean that Colombo is surrendering its strategic autonomy or that India is constructing a formal alliance system. India continues to prefer flexible partnerships. But New Delhi increasingly sees regional security as something built through training, maritime domain awareness, interoperability, capacity-building, and institutional cooperation.
For Israel, this creates an opportunity that deserves attention.
For years, Israel-India relations have been viewed primarily through defense cooperation, technology, and an expanding strategic convergence. Those ties remain important. But as India’s regional role grows, Israel should consider whether that partnership can also provide a basis for selective cooperation with third countries.
Sri Lanka offers a useful test case; there is evidence of Sri Lankan interest in expanding relations with Israel. In August 2026, Sri Lanka’s new ambassador to Israel identified agricultural technology, defense, and trade as areas in which Colombo would like to deepen cooperation.
Agriculture is an obvious starting point. India and Israel have spent years developing Centers of Excellence that combine Israeli agricultural technology with Indian institutions, local adaptation, and training. A similar trilateral initiative could bring together Israeli technology, Indian implementation experience, and Sri Lankan development priorities.
The potential goes further.
Maritime security is one area where Israeli capabilities could complement rather than compete with India’s regional role. Israel has relevant experience in sensors, electro-optics, unmanned systems, and maritime infrastructure protection. Cybersecurity and artificial intelligence are also important as ports, energy facilities, and digital systems become connected and vulnerable.
Israel’s comparative advantage lies not in establishing a military presence in Sri Lanka but in providing niche capabilities, technology, and practical solutions. India brings geographical proximity, political weight,and military-to-military engagement. Israel can contribute specialized expertise in maritime surveillance, cyber defense, AI, and critical-infrastructure protection.
This does not require a formal India-Israel-Sri Lanka strategic triangle. A more realistic model would be functional trilateralism: concrete projects addressing Sri Lankan needs. The India-UAE-Sri Lanka cooperation around Trincomalee provides a useful precedent, illustrating that third-country participation can complement Indian interests rather than challenge them.
Israel must also recognize Sri Lanka’s political sensitivities. Colombo has historically supported the Palestinian cause and continues to support a two-state solution. Treating Sri Lanka merely as another market for defense technology would therefore be politically shortsighted. A broader relationship combining agriculture, water, technology, trade, and carefully calibrated security cooperation would be more sustainable.
The larger lesson extends beyond Sri Lanka. As India becomes more influential across the Indian Ocean, Israel should think about India not only as a bilateral strategic partner but also as a platform for regional cooperation.
For decades, the focus has been on what India and Israel can do together. The next question is what their accumulated experience and complementary capabilities might allow them to do together elsewhere.
Sri Lanka may be one of the best places to begin.

Taiwan drones yet to see steady foreign demand

17:13:29 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – There has been no long-term foreign demand for drones despite export spikes in recent years, a DSET report published on Wednesday said.
Author Cathy Fang said exports grew from 3,472 units in 2024 to 122,726 in 2025 and 191,373 in the first half of 2026. She added that the main export markets are Poland, the Czech Republic, and the US, with a NT$1.5 billion (US$47.18 million) shipment to Saudi Arabia in June.
Fang said that European demand is tied to the war in Ukraine, which is unsustainable. She added that government contracts outside the US are also limited.
On cooperation, Fang said that instead of signing agreements with allies on one-time exchanges, Taiwan should seek joint development and licensing to gain ownership of software and hardware. She noted future purchases and collaborations should stem from operational experience.
Fang also mentioned technological gaps in flight controls, communications, and positioning, as core components and flight software are sourced overseas. Although the economics ministry has approved NT$326 million (US$10 million) for domestic development, firms could take up to two to three years for testing before mass production.
On materials, Fang said most batteries and rare minerals used to make components are imported from China, despite government efforts to establish a non-China supply chain. She urged working with allies to mine or develop alternative sources.
On testing, Fang suggested more flight tests with signal cutoffs, electronic interference, and long-distance patrols. She said ministries should coordinate on flight zones, test sites, and safety.
DSET is a government-funded research institute. Its full name is Democracy, Society, and Emerging Technology.

German startup TYTAN debuts new rocket-boosted interceptor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:11:10 UTC
17:11:10 KST

- TYTAN Technologies said it showed German Cabinet officials a new rocket-boosted interceptor drone during the government's August retreat in Brandenburg.
- The company has not disclosed the new system's speed, range, or a timeline for testing or production.
Munich-based counter-drone company TYTAN Technologies said it demonstrated a new rocket-boosted interceptor drone to the German Federal Cabinet last month, presenting what the company described as a new category of system built for greater range and speed against aerial threats.
TYTAN said the demonstration took place during the Cabinet’s annual retreat at Schloss Neuhardenberg in Brandenburg. The two-day retreat, held August 25 and 26, brought together Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Vice Chancellor and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and other Cabinet members to discuss economic growth, competitiveness and technology policy, according to the German government. TYTAN said Merz, Klingbeil and Pistorius were the first officials to see the new interceptor.
The company said the system uses rocket boosters to extend its range and speed compared with TYTAN’s existing interceptor line, and that it was developed in response to changing drone threats observed in Ukraine. TYTAN has not disclosed the new interceptor’s speed, range, altitude ceiling, or a timeline for testing or delivery.
TYTAN’s existing product line includes the EOS, a short-range multicopter interceptor built for NATO Class I drones weighing up to 150 kg (330 pounds), and the METIS, a long-range fixed-wing interceptor for Class II drones between 150 and 600 kg (330 and 1,320 pounds). The company has said METIS can reach speeds of 350 km/h (217 mph), fly out to 25 km (15.5 miles) and operate at altitudes up to 5,000 meters (16,400 feet). TYTAN’s smaller interceptor drones use computer vision to track and ram hostile drones rather than carrying an explosive warhead, with a reported top speed above 250 km/h (155 mph), a range beyond 15 km (9.3 miles) and a weight around 5 kg (11 pounds).
TYTAN raised €30 million ($34.8 million) in a Series A round in February 2026, co-led by Armira and the NATO Innovation Fund. In January, the company signed a cooperation agreement with German sensor maker HENSOLDT to integrate TYTAN’s interceptors with HENSOLDT’s Elysion Mission Core command-and-control software.
The company said it was founded by two international engineering students two and a half years ago and has grown to around 200 employees. TYTAN opened a serial production line in Bavaria this year with capacity for 3,000 interceptor drones per month, with production activity scheduled to begin in August, CEO Balázs Nagy told Defense News in June.
TYTAN said its interceptors are already deployed in Ukraine, along with Germany and Baltic states listed among its customers. The company said frontline feedback from Ukrainian operators is incorporated into its systems through software updates rather than hardware redesigns, which it said lets it shorten the gap between identifying a capability gap and fielding a fix.
Nagy has said the company’s pricing model is built around cost, telling Defense News in June that TYTAN aims to protect the same airspace “200 times cheaper than with legacy systems.”

Security Is the Key to Resolving the Thai-Cambodia Border Conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:10:00 UTC
17:10:00 KST

With UNCLOS conciliation proceedings between Thailand and Cambodia now formally under way, Thailand is preparing to engage constructively. We would have preferred to resolve the matter directly with Cambodia. Direct diplomacy is usually faster, less cumbersome and, when there is sufficient political will, more effective. But Thailand is a State Party to UNCLOS, the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea. We accepted the process and will take part in good faith, with the interests of the Thai people and our sovereign rights firmly in view.
That willingness to engage through international law should not be mistaken for a willingness to treat every dispute along the Thailand-Cambodia border as if it existed in a vacuum. They do not.
A boundary is not drawn on a blank sheet of paper. It is surveyed on actual ground, by actual people, in communities that need to be safe enough for technical work to take place.
This is the point that risks being lost in Cambodia’s push to convene the Joint Boundary Commission, because no technical or legal process can be separated from conditions on the ground. Before survey teams can do their work, the border must be sufficiently safe, stable, and properly managed.
That means implementing the commitments already agreed by both sides on ceasefire and de-escalation, joint demining, and cooperation against transnational crime. These measures are what make credible border discussions possible in the first place.
Consider demining. Thai soldiers have repeatedly been injured by landmines along the border, including incidents involving mines that have been identified as newly laid. Just a couple weeks ago, yet another Thai deminer lost a limb. Whatever political narrative one prefers, a mine does not become less dangerous because a meeting has been scheduled. Nor can a Joint Boundary Commission survey team be expected to work in an area potentially littered with mines.
Joint demining is a practical prerequisite to constructive talks. It is also an obligation rooted in the commitments that both Thailand and Cambodia have undertaken bilaterally and internationally, including under the Ottawa Convention. If both sides are genuinely committed to resolving border problems peacefully, making the ground safe for the people expected to do that work should hardly be controversial.
The same logic applies to transnational crime. A border is not secure if criminal syndicates can exploit weak enforcement, traffic people across it, and operate industrial-scale scam networks with impunity.
The scale of the problem is well known. The global online scam industry generates more than $1 trillion a year, while the International Organization for Migration estimates that more than 300,000 people from over 80 countries have been trafficked into illicit call-center networks in Southeast Asia. Reports have identified operational bases in our neighboring countries, but Thailand is not exempt from responsibility. We have a duty to act on our side of the border as well, and we have been doing exactly that.
Thailand has helped tens of thousands of Thai and foreign victims return home. We have expanded intelligence and information sharing with foreign partners, strengthened cooperation on prosecution, and pushed for wider international partnerships. These efforts intensified after last year’s clashes with Cambodia, when Thai authorities uncovered large scam operations along the border, including in areas previously used by Cambodian forces as military positions. The discoveries helped expose the scale of the networks, their methods, and the extraordinary degree of impunity in which they had been operating.
This matters to the border question because lawlessness does not politely stay in its own policy silo. Areas affected by mines, military tensions, or organized criminal activity are also areas where communities cannot return to normal life, while cross-border commerce suffers, and any serious effort to resolve contested claims becomes harder.
The sequence is therefore important. The first step is security: uphold the ceasefire, reduce military risks, clear mines, strengthen law enforcement, and cooperate against criminal networks. Then technical border work can proceed on firmer ground, literally and politically.
These security issues are already reflected in the Joint Statement painstakingly negotiated and signed by both sides on December 27, 2025. What is needed now is implementation.
Thailand will continue to do what it can and what it must. We will engage international mechanisms seriously and uphold our legal obligations. We will continue to advocate for a rules-based international order in which law is not treated as an à la carte menu. States cannot insist on rules they find useful while treating inconvenient obligations as optional.
That principle applies to Thailand as much as to Cambodia. A durable settlement will not come from public posturing, legal theater, or technical talks detached from realities on the ground. It will come from concrete steps that reduce risk, protect communities, and create the conditions in which both countries can address difficult boundary questions peacefully and credibly.
Thailand is ready to turn that page. We hope Cambodia is ready to do the same. But first, we must make sure the proper foundations are in place.

====================================================================================================

Denmark’s looming leadership void
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:05:16 UTC
17:05:16 KST

On November 10, 1982, Soviet state television interrupted its programming to play Tchaikovsky’s Swan Lake. Viewers had learned to recognize the cue: somewhere in the Kremlin, another old man had died.
It was Leonid Brezhnev, General Secretary for eighteen years, dead at 75. His successor lasted fifteen months before he too was gone. The man after him made it barely a year. Three state funerals, three general secretaries, in under three years. By 1981, the average age of the men running the Soviet Union was 69 – thirteen years older than Ronald Reagan’s own cabinet. It took that string of deaths, and the arrival of a 54-year-old outsider named Mikhail Gorbachev, before the pattern finally broke.
It’s tempting to file that away as a curiosity of late-Soviet dysfunction. It’s less comfortable to notice that a quieter, more mundane version of the same pattern is now playing out in one of the world’s most functional economies: Denmark.
In 2024, more than one in three Danish managers – approximately 35.8% – were aged 55 or above.1 A decade earlier, in 2014, that figure was 26.7%. That’s a 9.1 percentage-point rise in ten years, and with roughly 125,000 managers in Denmark, it works out to about 44,800 people approaching retirement in a single leadership generation. With Denmark’s retirement age at 67, most of these 44,800 managers will leave the workforce within the next decade – not gradually, but as a single, unusually large cohort retiring at roughly the same time.
The natural question is whether this is just what happens to any aging population – a Nordic story, not a Danish one. So I turned to Eurostat’s harmonized labor force data, which lets managers across ten Northern European countries be compared using the same occupational classification, the same age band (55–64), and the same methodology.
The results say otherwise: Denmark’s trend still holds even under this stricter, internationally comparable measure – the sharpest rise of the ten countries screened.2 Norway and Germany also rose, but by less. Sweden, Ireland, Belgium, the Netherlands, Estonia, and Finland all rose only modestly. And Iceland – a much smaller Nordic welfare state, but one facing the same demographic and economic pressures – went the other way entirely: its share of managers aged 55–64 fell, from 28.2% to 22.8%.
It would be easy to explain this away with a simple story: Danes are just retiring later, so of course more managers are staying on past 55. And there’s something to that – Denmark’s early-retirement age has climbed from 60 to 64 since 2014, and the state pension age from 65 to 67, part of a reform that ties retirement age to life expectancy, automatically rising as Danes live longer. Iceland’s retirement age, by contrast, has stayed flat at 67 for years, with no such escalator built in – so if rising retirement ages were the whole story, Denmark and Iceland should never have been comparable to begin with. But when I looked closer, the story didn’t hold up as neatly. That same rise in effective retirement age has been roughly three times steeper for less-educated workers than for university-educated professionals – and managers overwhelmingly fall into the latter group.3 If anything, managers are the workers least affected by the reform, yet they’re the group whose numbers shifted the most. Something else is doing the real work here.
While the full answer is subject to further inquiry, the best place to start looking is a handful of sectors.1 In the metal industry, the share of managers 55 and older rose from 28.6% to 48.2% in ten years – among the steepest increases anywhere in the Danish economy. Textiles, electrical equipment, and food and beverage manufacturing all rose nearly as sharply. Education is the one clear exception: its share of older managers actually fell over the same period, the only sector in the Danish data to get younger. Whatever is driving the leadership void, it is concentrated in specific corners of the economy.
Denmark built its prosperity on being able to renew itself – a small country punching above its weight through the quality of its institutions and the people running them. If more than a third of its managers are now over 55, and its closest Nordic peer is trending the opposite way, that gap deserves more attention than it’s gotten so far. Perhaps it’s time to take a closer look at our Nordic neighbor, and ask what it is doing differently.
Ebba Hansen is a Copenhagen-based Advisor at Voluntas, where she advises on leadership strategy and executive succession, and former Head of Office at Voluntas India in Mumbai. She is currently writing a book on the global leadership succession crisis.

- Analysis based on Eurostat’s EU Labour Force Survey (lfsa_egais), harmonised across countries by occupation, age band, and year.
- Denmark’s retirement-age reforms stem from a 2011 law tied to the 2006 “velfærdsaftale,” which indexes retirement age to life expectancy. The finding on the uneven effect by education level is based on analysis by Arbejderbevægelsens Erhvervsråd (AE), a Danish economic think tank.

Middle East’s biggest shipping hub at risk amid Hormuz blockade — FT

LONDON, September 3. /TASS/. Jebel Ali, the largest shipping hub in the Middle East, has come under its most serious strain in decades amid the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, the Financial Times (FT) reported.
According to the British newspaper, in the early weeks of the conflict around Iran, shipping through the port that has driven Dubai’s transformation into one of the world’s great commercial hubs declined more than 90%. Volumes plunged as 17 vessels a day on the average transited in the week to August 28, compared to 135 a day before the United States launched the war on Iran, the FT wrote.
The port and free-trade zone alone is responsible for more than a fifth of the emirate’s GDP. Last year, Jebel Ali accounted for 30% of the revenues of state-owned DP World, the newspaper added.
The UAE is looking for alternatives beyond the Hormuz Strait. DP World is planning to build two port terminals in Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman coast. However, experts doubt those could replicate the system built around Jebel Ali as its advantage includes not only port capacity but also the network of businesses and transport links, the newspaper argued. "Dubai as we know it would not exist without Jebel Ali," the FT quoted Jim Krane, a fellow at Rice University in Texas, as saying.

U.S. Army taps AZAK’s wheel-centric robot for fielding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
08:01:01 UTC
17:01:01 KST

- AZAK signed an Other Transaction Agreement with the Army's G-TEAD directorate after soldiers tested its wheel-centric unmanned ground vehicle.
- The company has demonstrated a 227 kg robot towing a 24,040 kg Army truck, more than 100 times its own weight.
Denver-based robotics company AZAK has signed an Other Transaction Agreement with the U.S. Army’s Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate, the company said in a statement. AZAK said it is one of the first companies selected for the program directly by soldiers who tested the system in the field.
G-TEAD, established in late 2025, is an Army directorate built to move new technology from demonstration to fielded units in as little as 180 days, using Other Transaction Agreements and soldier-led evaluations instead of the service’s traditional acquisition process. The directorate has already fielded counter-drone systems including the Merops interceptor, built by Perennial Autonomy, and the FD One quadcopter, according to prior reporting.
AZAK builds unmanned ground vehicles around a wheel-centric, chassis-free design. Each wheel functions as a self-contained power unit, housing the motor, motor controller, gearbox, control electronics, battery management system and battery. AZAK CEO Ben Meager has said the design keeps those components below the wheel’s center point, giving the vehicle a low center of gravity and allowing it to climb obstacles rather than route around them.
The Army evaluated AZAK’s platform through 2025 at events including the xTechOverwatch competition and a rotation at the National Training Center. Army and special operations units have looked at the system for resupply runs, casualty evacuation, counter-drone payloads and drone-launch platforms, the company has said.
In a demonstration released in July, AZAK showed a 227 kg (500 pound) robot towing a 24,040 kg (53,000 pound) Palletized Load System truck, plus an additional 454 kg (1,000 pounds) of ammunition, a combined load more than 100 times the robot’s own weight.
AZAK said the new OTA will let the mobility systems it has been testing move into the field on G-TEAD’s timeline. The company did not disclose the contract’s value, the number of systems involved, or a delivery schedule.
G-TEAD Director Col. Christopher Hill has said the directorate is built to compress that kind of transition. In one case involving a counter-drone system in Europe, Hill has said the Army went from identifying the operational need to a signed contract with industry in about 148 days.
AZAK’s demonstrations have centered on the S26 wheel, first shown publicly at DSEI 2025. Meager has said each wheel carries all the components needed to operate independently, letting the company scale a vehicle’s torque by adding wheels rather than redesigning a drivetrain. The company has said this allows the same wheel system to be configured into different vehicle types without a full redesign.

Global South must ensure AI sovereignty – expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:59:23 UTC
16:59:23 KST

Global South must ensure AI sovereignty – expert
The Global South cannot merely remain consumers of artificial intelligence but should also author the norms governing the technology, to avoid it being used against their sovereignty and security, an Indian cyber and AI law expert has said.
China, India, and Russia will become integral to this norm-making process, Pavan Duggal told RT on the sidelines of the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok.
The Global South can no longer be a mere spectator, but must be “an actual author of the norms for AI before they get crystallized,” Duggal told the gathering on Wednesday. He added that China, India, and Russia represent the collective thought leadership and vision of the Global South and will play a major role in creating the governance framework for AI.
Duggal said that a country’s sovereignty now extends beyond its traditional territorial boundaries and encompasses cyberspace and emerging technologies such as AI. Countries need to create stricter laws for providers of AI services anywhere in the world, as long as the services are delivered within their respective territories.
Nations of the Global South also have to ensure that their data does not fall into other countries’ hands, so it is not used to “prejudicially impact their sovereignty, security, and integrity.”
“We don’t want to be just consumers of AI services provided by someone else and governed by their respective norms,” he told RT.
Duggal’s arguments come at a time when emerging economies are taking a harder look at how to protect their security and economic interests in a turbulent world. A meeting of the national security advisers of the BRICS group in July took a wider view of the security challenges they face, including cybersecurity and emerging technologies that could be exploited by extremist organizations.
Security cooperation is also expected to remain on top of the agenda for the BRICS summit later this month in India.
It is a strategic requirement of sovereign countries that AI must ultimately be accountable, Duggal said. However, he said existing legal frameworks are not adequate to deal with these emerging technologies, because they were drafted keeping in mind the acts of a human versus another human.
Current AI regulations across countries focus on the risks of the technology but don’t deal with making it accountable, he added.
Duggal said countries like India are beginning to see a new trend of “cognitive colonialism,” where people are ready to become “cognitive slaves” of big tech companies so long as their day-to-day work is done by AI.

Taylor's claim teachers push 'political agenda' prompts backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:55:06 UTC
16:55:06 KST

Teachers hit back at Nationals claim about 'anti-boy' ideology in schools
In short:
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says teachers are pushing political agendas to students, while his counterpart rallied against anti-boy ideology in the classroom.
A teachers' union has labelled the remarks "ignorant".
What's next?
It remains unclear how the government intends to give Australians more control over their content amid pressure to back an algorithm opt-in model.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says teachers are pushing agendas in the classroom, while his Nationals counterpart believes the school curriculum is teaching "anti-boy" ideology.
The comments have sparked a backlash from teachers, who labelled the views "fundamentally incorrect".
Nationals leader Matt Canavan rallied against the "lecturing" of young men in schools, alleging that a state-funded Respectful Relationships curriculum could be turning them to harmful online content.
He said the program provided opportunity for "young boys to reflect on their male privilege and power", and while well-intentioned, could be having an adverse effect.
"I think this anti-boy ideology has no place in our schools," he told reporters on Thursday.
"They have counter-productive results and then drive young boys to toxic voices online because they're looking for someone to provide them with respect and support."
The Respectful Relationships national framework, established to teach both primary and secondary students about respectful relationships, gender equality and consent, does not mention male privilege.
Its inclusivity outcome instructs teachers to help students, without specifying gender, "to consider how their identities and experiences — including those related to power and inequality — affect their relationships and lives, in ways that suit their age and development".
It also sets out to help "boys and young men to explore concepts of masculinity in healthy ways".
The debate was initially stirred up on Wednesday, when Senator Canavan blamed the "feminisation" of the curriculum for driving young men towards "manosphere" content online.
He said programs like Respectful Relationships were "essentially a recruitment ground for Andrew Tate", a self-proclaimed misogynist with a large online following.
Teacher fury over 'agenda push' remarks
Asked about Senator Canavan's comments on Thursday, Liberal leader Angus Taylor pushed back against the "politicisation" of the curriculum by teachers.
"The idea that we have a balanced curriculum being run at the moment, that there are not agendas being run by some teachers, I think is wrong," he told the ABC.
"We do see those agendas being run."
Mr Taylor insisted teaching consent was important, while calling for a "degree of balance".
The Australian Education Union has fired back at the criticisms, labelling them a "fundamentally incorrect portrayal" of the education system.
"These comments are either a malevolent mischaracterisation of Australia's education system for political gain, or a display of complete ignorance of how the teaching profession operates," the union said in a statement.
The teachers' union said the remarks by Senator Canavan, Mr Taylor and One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, who claims schools are "brainwashing students", further fueled the "aggression and disrespect" towards teachers, which was already on the rise.
Last week, a national survey of 2,600 teachers, conducted by Monash University, found that 78 per cent had observed or experienced sexism or misogyny in school.
One in three teachers said that the presence of gendered violence made them "occasionally" consider leaving the profession.
The report's author, Stephanie Wescott, said for many teachers, schools had become "unbearably hostile places to work, with levels of sexism, misogyny and sexual harassment that have made their jobs untenable".
A separate government-funded study into misogyny and youth radicalisation found one in three teenage boys express "misogynistic attitudes, mistrust of women and a belief in traditional gender roles".
Almost a quarter of generation Z males believed feminism "should be resisted with violence if necessary".
Call for more male teachers
While Senator Canavan did not offer any alternatives for respectful relationship and consent education on Thursday, he doubled down on a call for more male teachers.
"Maybe we should look at getting more male teachers in. That used to be an agenda, I don't know what's happened to that. But maybe we should have more male role models in schools," he told Nine.
"I just know young boys often feel that they don't get any kind of instruction, leadership. They're not cherished there."
Currently, only one in four teachers are male.
While Education Minister Jason Clare agreed that students would benefit from more male teachers, he said ultimately, it was a discussion about respect.
"Teaching boys to respect girls isn't woke, it's common decency," he told reporters.
Mr Clare said the focus should not be on teachers, who he labelled "heroes".
“The bad guys here are the big tech companies, they're the ones poisoning our kids with algorithms that are shovelling shit into their heads."
On Wednesday, sexual consent advocate Chanel Contos called on the government to mandate an opt-in model for social media algorithms, to allow teenagers to avoid harmful messaging including manosphere content.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has flagged support for giving Australians more control over their online content but has stopped short of backing the algorithm opt-in model proposed by Ms Contos.

LeVanta Tech shows off its unusual HALIA drone at sea test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:53:51 UTC
16:53:51 KST

- LeVanta Tech demonstrated its unusually shaped HALIA float-and-fly drone with partner STR at ANTX Coastal Trident.
- HALIA can land on the open ocean, float for weeks, then relaunch at speeds LeVanta Tech has reported above 100 knots.
LeVanta Tech said it demonstrated its HALIA unmanned system at ANTX Coastal Trident last month, showing how the platform can link air, surface, subsea and seabed assets over long distances.
Photos of HALIA show an unusual design. The drone sits low in the water with a dark, angular hull riding hull-down, mostly submerged. Two cylindrical engine pods sit side by side on top of the fuselage, feeding what appear to be ducted fans, while swept white wings and twin tail fins jut out near the back, just clear of the waterline. A small sensor mast pokes up from one wing root. Little about the shape resembles a conventional aircraft or boat.
HALIA is a “float-and-fly” drone: it flies to a location, lands directly on the open ocean, and can sit there for weeks in a low-power floating mode before relaunching to reposition or leave the area, according to LeVanta Tech, which profiled the company in September 2025. The company said HALIA does not require a dedicated ship or fixed infrastructure to operate, since it can move between the air and water on its own.
At Coastal Trident, LeVanta Tech worked with STR, a defense technology firm with undersea systems and sensor work based near Boston, to demonstrate a communications architecture connecting air, surface, subsea and seabed systems. STR provided what the companies called a “rapidly repositionable” command-and-control air-water gateway, using what the companies described as high technology readiness level components to deliver over-the-horizon, real-time command-and-control links to subsea and seabed systems.
ANTX Coastal Trident is an annual exercise run by the Naval Surface Warfare Center Port Hueneme Division at the Port of Hueneme, California, bringing together Navy, other government agencies, academia and industry to test maritime and port security technology in an operational setting.
LeVanta Tech, founded in 2023, started out building real-time maritime monitoring tools for the offshore wind industry before shifting to a defense-first focus. The company’s leadership includes CEO Kelly Echols, an engineer and patent attorney by background; Chief Aviation Officer Jon Smith, a former P-3C Orion instructor pilot and Navy unmanned aircraft test project manager; and CTO Johnny Doo, who has more than 40 years in aircraft and hovercraft development, according to Defense Tech Signals.
The company was one of six finalists selected from 260 applicants for the 2024 Gulf Blue Navigator accelerator. A demonstration that year drew interest from the Air Force, which led to a $1.8 million Direct-to-Phase II Small Business Innovation Research award. The Air Force Research Laboratory followed with a Phase II SBIR contract worth $1.76 million running through December 2026, covering a project titled “Floating and Loitering Ocean Advanced Technology Sensing,” according to federal contract records cited by Defense Tech Signals. LeVanta Tech has also raised more than $1.1 million in early funding, including an $800,000 credit investment from Leonid Capital Partners in April 2025.
LeVanta Tech is developing HALIA in two configurations: a battery-electric version for tactical missions and a hybrid-electric version built for longer range. Both are designed to scale into larger platforms, the company has said. HALIA uses variable buoyancy combined with a hovercraft-assisted launch and recovery system, intended to let it take off and land in rough seas. Its top speed has been reported at more than 100 knots (185 km/h), with loiter times of weeks in its powered-down floating mode.
The platform carries a modular payload bay that LeVanta Tech says can support intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance sensors, electronic warfare packages, kinetic payloads and communications equipment, feeding into wider command-and-control networks. The distinctive hull shape and twin engine pods are part of what LeVanta Tech describes as a design built specifically for surviving repeated transitions between air and water, rather than adapted from an existing aircraft or boat.

Germany Identifies Russian-Backed Suspects in Leipzig Drone Sabotage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:52:11 UTC
16:52:11 KST

- Category
- World
Germany Identifies Russian-Backed Suspects in Leipzig Drone Sabotage
German law enforcement agencies have identified two suspects involved in an attempted FPV drone sabotage operation at Leipzig Airport, according to Bild.
The incident took place on August 5, when explosive-laden drones were discovered near four Ukrainian Antonov An-124 cargo planes.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Investigators determined that the planned attack was carried out by a native of Russia holding a Latvian passport and a Belarusian citizen who also holds Russian citizenship. Authorities are currently searching for at least four individuals whose movements and phone numbers were tracked using cell tower location data.
German Federal Minister of the Interior Alexander Dobrindt stated that Russia directly organized the attack, with the perpetrators acting on instructions from Russian intelligence services.
The Federal Criminal Police Office suspects that more unmanned aerial vehicles may have been deployed than initially thought, as remnants of three devices have been recovered so far.
The first suspect, a Russian native, acted as a logistical coordinator and instructor while maintaining direct ties to Russian intelligence. He arrived in Germany at the end of July via Berlin Brandenburg Airport, traveled toward Leipzig in a rental vehicle, and departed the country by plane two days before the attack was executed. The second suspect, a citizen of Belarus, was identified through DNA evidence left at the scene.
Traces of his genetic material were recovered directly from one of the drones, from the inner side of a tin can containing explosives, and from a signal amplifier antenna mounted on a tree near the airfield. Matching these genetic traces against European databases revealed prior records in Lithuania and Finland, where the individual had previously been prosecuted for other offenses.
He entered the Schengen zone using an Italian tourist visa issued in Minsk in late April. The sabotage attempt unfolded on the night of August 5, when a shuttle bus driver spotted the first explosive drone at 00:42 near four Ukrainian An-124 heavy transport aircraft.
Following the discovery of a second device, air traffic over the airport was completely suspended. During the airspace closure at 01:03, a inbound DHL cargo plane was forced to abort its landing approach and collided with another flying object, likely a second drone, at an altitude of 400 meters. A third drone was discovered on August 14 in a field in the municipality of Kabelsketal, bordering the western side of the airport.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described the drone incident at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport as an attack carried out by Russian intelligence operatives using military-grade materials on European Union territory.
Speaking in Brussels ahead of a meeting with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, von der Leyen stated that the EU would not tolerate such actions and expressed full solidarity with Germany. She noted that if Russia had intended the incident to make European countries reconsider their support for Ukraine, it had instead strengthened their determination to continue backing Kyiv.
Von der Leyen characterized the sabotage operation as a new escalation on EU territory directly linked to Moscow, forming part of a broader pattern of increasingly dangerous hybrid activities. Consequently, she pledged that the EU would maintain and intensify pressure on Russia until it ended its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, emphasizing that the bloc remained prepared to introduce additional sanctions and close existing loopholes.

Dhesi presses PM on pathway to three per cent

16:50:54 KST

The Prime Minister has told the Commons that he has already committed to a pathway to spending three per cent of gross domestic product on defence, in response to a question pressing him to do so urgently rather than waiting for a future fiscal event.
Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi, the Labour MP for Slough and chair of the Defence Committee, put the question at Prime Minister’s Questions on Wednesday.
He said: “The British people should be under no illusion that the nation faces a significantly increased threat level, especially from Russia, but also that we have a US leadership for whom European security is no longer a focus or a priority. That is why it is imperative that we invest in our armed forces in the here and now, rather than being sorry later. Indeed, defence is definitely one area where vibes alone just will not be enough.
“Rather than kicking the can down the road, waiting for a fiscal event in a future year, will the Prime Minister urgently commit to charting a pathway to reaching 3% of GDP being spent on defence by 2030? As his Chancellor rightly noted, that is critical to keeping our country safe.”
Andy Burnham replied: “I have made that commitment, I have made it very clearly, and I have done so for a considerable time. I was in Ukraine last week for a very specific reason: to repeat it on the world stage. My hon. Friend can be absolutely sure of that.”
He went on: “Alongside our commitment to defence, we also have to build the resilience of Britain. We need to ensure that the maximum amount of the funding committed to the defence investment plan goes back into the reindustrialisation of our communities. We should do more to maintain sovereign manufacturing and production capability here, and that will be a theme of my Government. We will make sure that British taxpayers’ money goes to supporting industry in our own country, to make us more resilient going into the future.”
The exchange turns on a distinction between committing to a figure and setting out how it will be reached. Dhesi’s question asked for a pathway, and specifically for one that does not wait on a future fiscal event, which is the point on which the government has previously declined to be drawn.
Wes Streeting, the Defence Secretary, has argued that announcing a spending figure without setting out how it will be funded invites a loss of market confidence and rising borrowing costs. He has said he has every confidence the Defence Investment Plan will be fully funded, and has not ruled out tax rises as part of the answer.
The Office for Budget Responsibility has previously put the cost of reaching three per cent at an additional £17.3 billion in 2029-30. Behind the domestic argument sits NATO’s push towards 3.5 per cent of GDP on core defence by 2035, agreed at the alliance summit in The Hague.
The second half of Burnham’s answer picks up a theme the government, current and former, has been developing through the Defence Industrial Strategy and the Defence Investment Plan, which commits £298 billion to defence over four years.
The department has pointed to figures published last month showing that spending with industry supported 274,000 jobs across the United Kingdom in 2024/25, with £31.9 billion spent, including 12,200 direct jobs in Scotland where shipbuilding and submarines account for 7,900 of them. Jobs supported by spending on weapons and ammunition manufacturing rose 51 per cent across the country over the same period, an increase the department attributes to the drive to rebuild what it calls an always on pipeline of munitions supply.

Meta is imposing its new AI agent on employees
Kyiv • UNN
Meta has canceled employee evaluations based on the frequency of AI use. At the same time, employees are actively testing the Hatch agent, increasing token consumption.
Meta no longer plans to evaluate employee performance based on how frequently they use artificial intelligence tools, but employees are still being encouraged to test the company’s new AI agent called Hatch. Wired reports this, according to UNN.
Details
In an internal announcement this week, the social media giant told employees that evaluations of their performance would no longer depend on how often they used artificial intelligence tools, three employees who received the announcement told WIRED. But as Meta employees are simultaneously beginning to test a new agentic artificial intelligence tool known as Hatch, they say their token consumption continues to grow
Previously, Meta linked employee evaluations to how much they used AI to improve their daily work. Employees even received labels such as "AI Native," "AI First," or "AI Enabled."
Now, in new performance evaluation guidelines, the company said it would assess employees primarily based on their contributions, rather than how they achieved them.
The new performance evaluation guidelines presented this week replace references to evaluating employees based on criteria such as "AI usage" and their designation as "AI Native" with looser wording suggesting that "these results may be supported by AI or other means." This shifts Meta’s focus back to evaluating employees based on their impact, with less emphasis on how that impact is achieved. Some Meta employees told WIRED that the changes are minor but welcome, freeing them from feeling pressured to use AI in situations where it does not make sense
Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton said that this merely emphasizes the approach the company had used previously.
According to the publication, despite the relaxed requirements, Meta employees are actively using the new agentic AI tool Hatch. As a result, employees say, token consumption continues to grow.
For months, according to some Meta employees, their colleagues repeatedly—or, as they saw it, frivolously—suggested that artificial intelligence tools maximize internal usage metrics, such as the number of tokens or AI units consumed. The Tokenmaxxing era peaked when one Meta employee created an internal leaderboard to track how many employees were using AI, giving them titles such as "Token Legend." After details of the dashboard leaked online, the employee deleted it in April. A few months later, Meta began rationing employees’ use of artificial intelligence
Recall
Meta reported that its AI model unintentionally gained access to data from another system. This is the third such case in recent weeks, following incidents involving Anthropic and OpenAI.
