More teachers, better access, fewer pupils: India’s government school paradox
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:49:04 UTC
16:49:04 KST

Schools are back in focus. In larger policy discussions and political debates. The Opposition, emboldened by its NEET protest victory, is looking to up the ante by exposing ramshackle school infrastructure in different states, starting with Rajasthan. TOI ground reports, too, have found gross inadequacies in government schools across different parts of the state. Particularly jarring is the fact that in Kota, widely called the coaching capital of India, many government schools are in a dilapidated state.A wider ground report by TOI reporters across the country found that Rajasthan was hardly an outlier. In Bihar, nearly 200 children from four classes were sharing a single room at one school while cattle occupied two others. In Uttarakhand, leaking roofs meant buckets and umbrellas had become classroom fixtures. In Madhya Pradesh, TOI found schools struggling with teacher shortages and unsafe buildings. Keralam was a prominent exception to this broader picture.However, the fact remains that in a country of 1.4 billion people, structural gaps are perhaps expected, if certainly not desired. A good metric of how much the school system has improved over the years is to look at the data furnished by the central government and its allied agencies.
The pan-India numbers make for interesting reading. Rajasthan had 7,200 single-teacher schools in 2025-26, while only 36.4% of schools reported ramps with handrails and 26.3% had toilets tailored for Children with Special Needs (CwSN).The country has nearly a lakh fewer government schools than it did a decade ago, and those schools are losing pupils. It also has more teachers, far fewer children in single-teacher schools, more teenagers reaching higher secondary and internet access in about two-thirds of schools. Fewer than half of schools, however, report a toilet designed for children with special needs. Yet despite improvements in many metrics, government-school enrolment is falling.
From buffaloes and buckets to what the national numbers say
Most of what is known about India's schools comes from UDISE+, the Unified District Information System for Education Plus. It is an annual, census-like administrative database covering schools across management types. Schools report on their pupils, teachers and infrastructure, from enrolment and staffing to toilets, electricity, ramps, computers and internet access, and they are incorporated into the Union education ministry's national school statistics.The system grew out of UDISE, created in 2012-13 by merging separate elementary and secondary databases. UDISE+ became its online successor from 2018-19. The government uses it to locate infrastructure gaps, and states draw on it when seeking support for classrooms, toilets, drinking water, electricity, libraries and digital facilities under schemes such as Samagra Shiksha.A school can figure in the database as open and equipped with a particular facility, but reality can be very different. TOI's visits across states repeatedly brought out that distinction.
Nearly 1 lakh fewer govt schools, but access improves on paper
India had 11,04,796 government schools in 2015-16. Ten years later, UDISE+ records 10,05,245, a difference of 99,551 schools or 9%. The rider is that a school leaving the UDISE count can reflect closure, merger, rationalisation, reclassification or other administrative change.The decline is stark in some states. Madhya Pradesh had 1,21,976 government schools in 2015-16; by 2025-26 the count was 91,199, a reduction of 30,777. Uttar Pradesh fell from 1,62,645 to 1,37,103, a reduction of 25,542. Together, the two states account for about 56.6% of the national net decline over the decade.
Nearly 1 lakh less government school in 10 years
There have also been changes in school mapping and verification, with UDISE+ replacing the older UDISE system from 2018-19. Questioned in Parliament, the Centre has said that decisions on opening, closing and rationalising schools lie largely with states and Union territories, while the Right to Education framework requires elementary schools to remain accessible within prescribed neighbourhood limits.Between 2018-19 and 2024-25, the Gross Access Ratio rose from 88.24% to 95.35% at the secondary level and from 65.05% to 94.97% at higher secondary. GAR measures the proportion of habitations or villages with a school available within the prescribed distance; it is not an enrolment ratio. So although there are fewer schools, the measured access ratio has improved. This is also part of the government's defence.
Govt schools are losing pupils even as the system improves
Government-school enrolment fell from 12.75 crore in 2023-24 to 11.89 crore in 2025-26, nearly 85.9 lakh fewer pupils in just two years, a decline of 6.7%. Over the same period, enrolment in private unaided schools rose from 9.00 crore to 9.89 crore, an increase of about 88.3 lakh, or 9.8%. The thinning out is also visible over a decade with average enrolment per government school falling from about 132 pupils in 2014-15 to 120 in 2024-25, a decline of roughly 9%; the latest UDISE+ figures put it at about 118 in 2025-26.One figure from the government's own parliamentary reply captures the scale of it. In 2024-25, government institutions accounted for 68.9% of all schools in India but 49.2% of all enrolment.
The changing mix
A movement this large might be expected to have triggered a substantial investigation. On July 29, 2026, the government was asked why government-school enrolment had fallen from about 12.8 crore to 11.9 crore while private enrolment rose from around 9 crore to 9.9 crore.The ministry confirmed the numbers but did not cite or summarise such an assessment in its reply. Instead, it listed the interventions being made to strengthen government education.NITI Aayog's 2026 UDISE+-based review says the broader decline in enrolment through 2024-25 is partly attributable to demographic shifts, particularly falling fertility and a smaller school-age population, alongside school consolidation and challenges in retaining pupils at higher levels.Ranabir Bhattacharyya, teacher-in-charge of the English-medium primary section of Chetla Boys' High School in Kolkata, points to some of the practical issues with UDISE+ and also offers context for the dwindling numbers. He says the data had many issues at one point, but the pipeline has increasingly been made more robust as the government seeks to bring all students onto the platform to roll out various developmental schemes aimed at schoolchildren.He alleges that there was earlier an incentive in certain quarters to inflate pupil numbers, but says tighter vigilance has reduced that tendency and the numbers now being reflected are closer to reality. Ranabir, however, flags other problems like the website can be difficult to use and often suffers technical glitches, while the absence of additional staff increases the workload of those responsible for keeping the data updated. As a result, underreporting can happen too, according to him.
More teachers nationally, TOI finds the gaps locally
India had 96.96 lakh teachers in 2020-21 and 102.73 lakh in 2025-26, nearly 5.77 lakh additional teachers in five years. Single-teacher schools fell from 1,10,971 in 2023-24 to 1,00,843 in 2025-26, and the number of children enrolled in them dropped more steeply still, from 39.94 lakh to 29.12 lakh. Nearly 11 lakh fewer children are now in such schools.But the national improvement hides striking state differences. Andhra Pradesh alone has 16,357 single-teacher schools; Jharkhand has 9,827, Maharashtra 9,269, Karnataka 8,042 and Uttar Pradesh 7,874. Those five states together account for just over half of India's 1,00,843 single-teacher schools.And this is one area where the statistical picture intersects sharply with what TOI reporters saw. In Madhya Pradesh, TOI found 70 children and one teacher operating from a single dilapidated room at a school in Bhopal's Kolar, while students in Classes XI and XII at a PM SHRI school in Mandla had gone without teachers for newly introduced streams for a year.
Single teacher school decreasing
Uttarakhand has 2,655 single-teacher schools, about 11.8% of its entire school network, alongside its unusually high proportion of very small schools. The Centre acknowledges the problem. It has told Parliament that recruitment and postings are primarily state responsibilities; and that it repeatedly presses states on faster recruitment and redeployment while supporting them under Samagra Shiksha.Ranabir highlights another issue involving children of migrant labourers. He says that when a student shifts from one school to another, the subsequent UDISE+ entry does not always move smoothly as it requires manual intervention. West Bengal School Education Minister Dipak Barman, speaking to TOI, says many private schools in the state have not uploaded their student lists. Barman says the state is working to get the figures updated. It is hard to know whether similar anomalies exist elsewhere, but if they do, they could significantly undermine the purpose of what the central government is trying to achieve with the UDISE+ platform.
More children stay on, but Class X remains a fault line
The encouraging part is that reported dropout rates are falling. In many states, girl students are incentivised to continue school education. At the same time, higher-secondary Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) rose from 56.2% in 2023-24 to 61.7% in 2025-26, and the secondary dropout rate fell from 14.1% to 9.5% over the same period. Here too, the national number hides enormous variation. Keralam, for instance, reported secondary retention of 99.1% in 2025-26.
Drop-outs decreasing
For many from financially weaker sections, there is a significant opportunity cost to staying in school after Class X. The government has therefore deployed a range of measures to keep more students in the system. Parliamentary replies point to PM POSHAN, residential schools and hostels, KGBVs, transport assistance, free textbooks and uniforms, enrolment campaigns and vocational education, and more recently to Vidya Samiksha Kendras and APAAR IDs as tools for tracking students who drop out or move between schools.
Digital access surges, but TOI finds a different classroom reality
In step with the government's Digital India push, digital infrastructure has expanded rapidly. In 2020-21, 24.5% of schools reported internet access; by 2025-26, 67.4% did. Computer availability rose from 41.3% to 69.9%. The approved budget for ICT labs, smart classrooms and other digital initiatives rose from ₹381.1 crore in 2018-19 to ₹3,221.1 crore in 2025-26.NITI Aayog's 2026 UDISE+-based analysis of functional smart classrooms shows coverage rising from 14.9% of schools in 2021-22 to 30.6% in 2024-25. In other words, even after rapid expansion, nearly seven in ten schools still lacked one.The interstate divide is striking. Punjab reported functional smart classrooms in 80.1% of schools and Delhi in 75.7%; the corresponding figures were only 4.3% in Meghalaya, 5.7% in West Bengal, 14.9% in Bihar and 19.8% in Uttar Pradesh. Tamil Nadu offers the opposite story: its reported coverage went from virtually zero in 2021-22 to 60.8% in 2024-25.TOI's ground visits underline why infrastructure numbers need context. In Uttar Pradesh, schools visited by reporters had toilets and drinking water, but digital resources were missing; in Himachal Pradesh, strong coverage of basic facilities coexisted with substantially weaker smart-classroom and disability-access indicators.Regarding West Bengal's poor showing, Barman says many of the state's UDISE+ figures have not been properly updated and that the government is working to correct them, and is looking to start 2000 smart classrooms in the next one year. He says Bengal expects to be among the top 10 when the next calculation is made.
Toilets on paper, TOI finds the functionality gap on the ground
India is now close to universal provision of toilet facilities in schools, at least on paper. UDISE+ reports girls'-toilet availability in 98.5% of girls' and co-educational schools in 2025-26. But availability and functionality are not the same.TOI's ground reporting provides a simple illustration of that distinction. Schools visited in Uttar Pradesh had separate toilets for boys and girls, but reporters found many of them unclean, with teachers blaming the absence of sanitation workers. This issue of not having adequate sanitation staff is something Ranabir also flagged repeatedly.The same NITI Aayog analysis, using 2024-25 data, puts national functional girls'-toilet coverage at 94%, up from 85.17% a decade earlier. Yet the state map remains uneven.In 2024-25, Bihar and Odisha were both at 98.1% functional girls'-toilet coverage and West Bengal at 99.6%, while Rajasthan stood at 87.3%. Meghalaya was at 68.7%, Arunachal Pradesh 73.7% and Manipur 74.5%.
The basic-access gap remains
In 2020-21, 24.5% of schools reported internet access and 41.3% computers. About 48.3% reported ramps with handrails and 25.3% toilets for children with special needs. By 2025-26, internet availability had reached 67.4% and computers 69.9%. Ramps with handrails were at 58.2%, while CwSN-friendly toilets stood at only 40.1%.The state contrasts are revealing. Himachal Pradesh reports functional electricity in 99.1% of schools and computers in 87.2%, but internet reaches only 66.2% and CwSN-friendly toilets 34%. At the same time, 18.3% of its schools are single-teacher schools and almost half have 30 pupils or fewer.
Basic access gap remains
Keralam, the prominent exception in TOI's ground reporting, also stands apart on several UDISE measures. Computer availability is 99.5%, internet access 92.6%, and only 67 schools, about 0.4% of its network, are single-teacher schools. Secondary retention is 99.1%. The state is not without gaps, only around 51.7% of schools report CwSN-friendly toilets but the overall contrast with many other states is striking.The Accessibility Code was notified in 2024, and Samagra Shiksha and PM SHRI provide funds for facility upliftment. Ranabir says funds often come in a trickle or are regularly delayed. As a result, he says, many of these metrics do not improve as smoothly as desired. He also highlights that many rural schools have irregular electricity supply, and hence while internet and other digital facilities are present on paper, reality can be different.Taken together, most of these service and outcome indicators have moved positively. Yet government-school enrolment is falling. That may partly reflect an aspirational society where some parents are looking to private schools for stronger English-language exposure, soft skills, peer networks and perceived advantages in college and beyond. Anecdotally, one can also see the mushrooming of English-medium schools in suburbs and mofussils.
But the national data do not by themselves establish why families make these choices. Some of the decline may also reflect cleaner data and ironically even lack of proper uploading of data as pointed out by the Bengal education minister.There is no one-size-fits-all solution for such a large country. The data show substantial progress on several fronts, yet the lived reality may be different in some places. For now, the government will need to tick the boxes on what should be absolutely non-negotiable in terms of core deliverables, including the lacunae exposed in those reports. Winning the larger battle for aspiration may be a challenge for another day, or another decade.

The universe has plenty of hydrogen. So why is star formation collapsing?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:48:14 UTC
16:48:14 KST

The universe has plenty of hydrogen. So why is star formation collapsing?
- Date:
- September 3, 2026
- Source:
- Chinese Academy of Sciences Headquarters
- Summary:
- Star formation across the universe has fallen dramatically over the past 4.5 billion years, but astronomers have uncovered a surprising twist: the supply of neutral hydrogen, a key ingredient for making stars, has barely declined. Using China’s FAST radio telescope and data from roughly 2.5 million galaxies observed by DESI, researchers found that star formation was about 2.5 times higher 4.5 billion years ago, while neutral hydrogen levels were only about 1.4 times higher.
- Share:
The universe is producing fewer stellar "babies." Over the past 4.5 billion years, the rate at which new stars form has fallen to less than half its previous level. Yet the supply of one of the most important types of "fuel" for star formation has changed surprisingly little.
That finding comes from an international research team led by scientists from the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), working with the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) project. Using China's Five hundred meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST), the researchers made precise measurements of cosmic neutral atomic hydrogen across the past 4.5 billion years.
Their results show a striking mismatch. Star formation has declined sharply, while the amount of neutral atomic hydrogen (HI), an important reservoir of gas within galaxies, has decreased only modestly.
The findings were published online in Nature Astronomy on Sept. 1.
Why Is the Universe Making Fewer Stars?
Understanding why star formation has become less active as the universe ages is a major question in research on galaxy formation and evolution. One seemingly straightforward explanation is that galaxies have gradually consumed the cold gas needed to produce stars.
If dwindling supplies of cold gas were primarily responsible, however, astronomers would expect the dramatic fall in star formation to be accompanied by a similarly large decline in the available gas. So far, observations have not shown such a sharp depletion.
HI plays a central role in this puzzle. It is an important cold gas reservoir inside galaxies, connecting the broader cosmic supply of gas with the processes that eventually produce new stars. Astronomers primarily detect HI through its extremely faint 21-centimeter radio emission line.
Detecting that signal from distant galaxies is difficult because it is often overwhelmed by background noise.
FAST and DESI Survey Millions of Galaxies
For years, astronomers faced a major observational challenge. Very deep surveys could achieve the necessary sensitivity but could not examine large regions of the sky. Surveys covering much larger areas, meanwhile, generally lacked the sensitivity needed to detect such faint radio signals.
As a result, scientists have struggled to directly and reliably determine how the universe's total HI mass has changed across the low- to intermediate-redshift universe.
The new research tackled this problem by combining the exceptional radio sensitivity of FAST with the enormous optical spectroscopy data set provided by DESI. The team studied about 2.5 million galaxies spread across nearly one-third of the sky.
The researchers used an HI spectral stacking method to combine radio signals that would have been too faint to detect individually. Using precise measurements of each galaxy's redshift, they aligned the weak signals and stacked them together. This process allowed the average HI signal to emerge from the background noise.
The approach enabled the scientists to track changes in cosmic neutral hydrogen using a sample of unprecedented size and with exceptionally high statistical precision.
Star Formation Fell Much Faster Than Hydrogen
The results exposed a major difference between the evolution of star formation and the supply of neutral hydrogen.
About 4.5 billion years ago, the cosmic star formation rate was approximately 2.5 times higher than it is today. Over the same period, however, neutral atomic hydrogen density was only about 1.4 times higher than its present level.
In other words, star formation dropped dramatically without a comparable disappearance of the universe's HI reservoir. The findings indicate that rapidly exhausting neutral hydrogen cannot by itself explain why star formation has declined so strongly.
The Cosmic Mystery Shifts
According to the researchers, the results change the central question from "whether the gas is depleting" to "why it is increasingly difficult to form stars despite abundant neutral hydrogen reserves."
Stars do not form directly from most neutral atomic hydrogen. They are mainly born inside much denser clouds of molecular gas. Neutral atomic hydrogen occupies an important intermediate position between the universe's larger gas supply and the molecular hydrogen that can ultimately fuel star formation.
The researchers suggest that the most important changes in the more recent universe may involve how gas moves through the baryon cycle rather than how much HI exists overall.
As the flow of gas from the cosmic web becomes weaker and gas densities decrease, galaxies may become less efficient at converting HI into molecular hydrogen. Under this scenario, the overall HI reservoir can remain relatively stable while supplies of the molecular gas directly responsible for creating stars gradually decline.
Why the Universe's Star Factories Are Fading
The implications therefore extend beyond simply determining how much hydrogen exists in the universe. The findings offer an important new clue to why the universe's enormous star-forming engines have been gradually slowing down.
According to the researchers, combining observations from FAST and DESI provides a new observational benchmark for studying the cosmic gas cycle during the universe's later evolution, the long-term decline in star formation, and the broader processes shaping galaxies.
The research was led by scientists from the National Astronomical Observatories of China, the Shanghai Astronomical Observatory of CAS, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University, together with researchers participating in DESI.
Contributors came from research institutions across Asia, North America, and Europe. The collaboration demonstrates the scientific potential of combining highly sensitive radio observations with enormous optical spectroscopy surveys.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Chinese Academy of Sciences Headquarters. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Chuan-Peng Zhang, Hong Guo, Yizhou Gu, Amélie Saintonge, Xiaohu Yang, Dirk Scholte, Ming Zhu, Peng Jiang, Hu Zou, Manasvee Saraf, Wenlin Ma, Yirong Wang, Y. P. Jing, Zheng Zheng, Zhejie Ding, J. Aguilar, S. Ahlen, D. Bianchi, D. Brooks, T. Claybaugh, A. de la Macorra, P. Doel, E. Gaztañaga, G. Gutierrez, M. Ishak, R. Joyce, S. Juneau, R. Kehoe, D. Kirkby, A. Kremin, O. Lahav, C. Lamman, M. Landriau, L. Le Guillou, M. Manera, A. Meisner, R. Miquel, J. Moustakas, S. Nadathur, W. J. Percival, F. Prada, I. Pérez-Ràfols, G. Rossi, E. Sanchez, D. Schlegel, M. Schubnell, H. Seo, J. Silber, D. Sprayberry, G. Tarlé, B. A. Weaver. Weak evolution of cosmic atomic hydrogen over the past 4.5 billion years. Nature Astronomy, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41550-026-02965-9

Pic story of Kazakh businesswoman at China-Kazakhstan Horgos Int'l Border Cooperation Center

====================================================================================================

Study shows men and women follow different aging timelines
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:45:00 CST
16:45:00 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- A new study from China has found that men and women age in strikingly different ways -- and the clues lie hidden in the results of everyday blood tests and health checkups.
The study, recently published in the journal Nature Aging, was jointly conducted by researchers from the China National Center for Bioinformation (CNCB), under the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), the Institute of Zoology of CAS, Xuanwu Hospital of Capital Medical University and other institutes.
Researchers looked at health data from more than 104,000 adults across China, aged 18 to 98. They focused on 172 common measurements, like weight, cholesterol, and blood sugar. From this, they built special "aging clocks" to show when human bodies go through the biggest changes over time.
They found that for men, the most important turning point came between ages 35 and 45. During this decade, their metabolism shifted noticeably -- body mass index went up, along with triglycerides and cholesterol. For women, the big change happened later, between 55 and 65, around the time of menopause. At that stage, women experienced strong hormonal changes, along with rising fat and cholesterol levels. Yet despite these distinct aging trajectories, the physical differences between men and women tended to diminish as they grew older.
The study also showed that certain substances in our blood -- including glucose, lipids, uric acid, and two tumor-related markers called CEA and HE4 -- build up as we age and are linked to faster biological aging. To test this, the scientists exposed human blood vessel cells to higher levels of these substances in the lab. The cells began to show clear signs of senescence, suggesting that these factors are not just markers of aging but may actually help cause it.
But there is some encouraging news. The researchers found that some aging effects might be reversible. For example, a common diabetes drug called metformin helped protect cells from the aging damage caused by high glucose levels. In another experiment, mice that were switched from a high-fat diet back to a normal diet showed clear improvements in liver aging.
"This suggests that lowering metabolic stress -- by improving diet or controlling blood glucose -- could be a potential strategy to slow down aging," said Xiong Muzhao, a researcher from CNCB.
The findings suggest that reducing age-related metabolic burden may be a promising strategy for promoting healthy aging. They also highlight the importance of sex-specific assessment and intervention throughout the lifespan, said Li Jiaming, a researcher from CNCB. ■

Study finds more than 1,200 genetic variants linked to personality traits
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:44:58 CST
16:44:58 KST

SYDNEY, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- An international study involving researchers in Australia has identified more than 1,200 genetic variants associated with personality traits.
The findings showed that genetic variants linked to personality were also associated with a broad range of outcomes, including mental and physical health, educational attainment, career trajectories, longevity and social relationships, according to a statement released Thursday by Australia's QIMR Berghofer Medical Research Institute.
Published in Nature, the study examined the "Big Five" personality traits: openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism, the statement said.
By examining how personality and genetics interact with other health traits, researchers can better understand the underlying causes of disorders and identify the most appropriate treatments and interventions for individuals, it said.
The study found no evidence of a single "personality gene," with personality differences arising from the combined influence of many genetic variants, each having a very small effect.
QIMR Berghofer researchers contributed family-based genetic analyses to help separate genetic influences from the influence of shared family environments. By comparing relatives within families, the team was able to show that many of the observed genetic associations could not be explained simply by growing up in the same household.
The findings provide a new understanding of how biology and environment work together to shape personality, said the study's co-author, Associate Professor Michelle Lupton of QIMR Berghofer.
Common genetic variation could explain up to 16 percent of the variation in personality, with the remainder attributable to environmental factors including life circumstances and experiences, Lupton said.
The study also found links between personality-related genetic variants and a range of behaviors and lifestyle factors, including daytime activity levels and night-owl tendencies. ■

Feature: "I left a part of my heart in China," says retired U.S. teacher
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
15:44:44 CST
16:44:44 KST

Ronald Sakolsky arrives at Washington Dulles International Airport after his trip to China, near Washington, D.C., the United States, on Sept. 1, 2026. "I came back home today, but I left a part of my heart in China." Retired U.S. teacher Ronald Sakolsky told a small group of reporters after landing at Washington Dulles International Airport late Tuesday, reflecting emotionally on his 10-day trip to China. (Photo by Li Yuanqing/Xinhua)
WASHINGTON, Sept. 3 (Xinhua) -- "I came back home today, but I left a part of my heart in China."
Retired U.S. teacher Ronald Sakolsky told a small group of reporters after landing at Washington Dulles International Airport late Tuesday, reflecting emotionally on his 10-day trip to China.
Returning to China for the first time in 26 years, he reunited with Yin Yuzhen, a farmer and a pioneer in combating desertification.
Their friendship began in 1999, when Sakolsky taught English at a school in central China's Henan Province -- more than 11,000 km from his home in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, under a teachers' exchange program between the two countries.
One ordinary evening, a television program caught his eye. On the screen was Yin, planting trees to help hold back the advancing sands of the Maowusu sandy land.
Stretching across parts of Inner Mongolia, Shaanxi and Ningxia, the Maowusu has been one of the front lines in China's fight against desertification in the north -- an effort launched in 1978 and slated to continue through 2050.
"I was so touched that I started to cry," Sakolsky recalled, thinking back to that evening. "I honestly cannot tell you why. Something just happened to me. I just felt like I needed to help."
Moved by her endeavor, he raised 5,000 dollars to help Yin and her husband plant trees and combat desertification. Today, the saplings purchased with the donation have grown into more than 50,000 trees.
In May this year, Yin took to social media to find the American teacher who had once helped her plant the trees. In late August, Sakolsky was invited to return to Inner Mongolia, where he reunited with Yin.
Sakolsky said he had never imagined that trees could be grown in the desert. But Yin's dedication and perseverance turned sand into soil and "made it alive." Sakolsky recalled touching the trees and hearing the soil. "They are my children. Ms. Yin said to me that my children were waving because it was windy and the trees were moving."
After 26 years, Sakolsky and Yin did not need many words when they met again. There were tears, embraces and a sense of familiarity that seemed to bridge the years between them.
Throughout his 10-day trip to China, Sakolsky said, there were many moments when the two understood each other without speaking. "Because we spoke from the heart," he said.
"If a lady that lived in the desert in China, with no telephone, no roads, no television, no electricity, can meet a simple American history teacher, and we can create together a forest ... If one and one can do it, 10 and 10 can do it, 100 and 100 can do it, a million and a million can do it," he said.
For Sakolsky, their story was also a reminder that meaningful change can begin with just two people.
He believes ordinary Americans and Chinese alike want a better relationship between their two countries. Yet fear can grow out of a lack of understanding, he said, while ignorance and prejudice often take root in a lack of education.
That is why he hopes more Americans will learn about China -- by visiting the country, reading about it and opening themselves up to its culture. He likewise encouraged Chinese people to learn about and embrace American culture.
"It is up to the regular common people," he said. "Stop listening to everybody else. Do what you know is the right thing to do."
During his 10-day trip to China, Sakolsky visited Ordos and Hohhot in Inner Mongolia, Luoyang in Henan Province, and Beijing, where he also reunited with some of his former students.
The reunion was among the most memorable moments of his visit. But even as he boarded his flight home, Sakolsky was already thinking about what might come next.
"I would not be here if it was not for a teacher exchange program," he said, adding that to improve relations between the two countries, "start with the children and the students." ■

- Seasats said its Quickfish interceptor USV has entered production, offering 40-plus knot speeds and weeks-long endurance at sea.
- The company deployed Quickfish and four other USVs during the Navy's Silent Swarm 2026 electromagnetic warfare exercise in Alpena, Michigan.
San Diego-based unmanned surface vessel maker Seasats said its Quickfish interceptor-class USV has entered production and is now available at scale.
The company said Quickfish is built on Seasats’ existing technology stack and can sprint at more than 40 knots (74 km/h) while remaining at sea for weeks at a time. It has a large modular payload bay designed to carry a range of mission systems, including unmanned aircraft, according to Seasats. The company said the hull is self-righting and built to survive Sea State 10 conditions, the roughest classification on the World Meteorological Organization’s sea state scale.
Seasats took part in Silent Swarm 2026, a two-week Electromagnetic Spectrum Operations experimentation event run by the Naval Surface Warfare Center, Crane Division. The exercise took place July 13 to 24 at the Alpena Combat Readiness Training Center in Michigan, part of the National All-Domain Warfighting Center, and drew participants including the Michigan National Guard, NOAA, the Army’s C5ISR Center and the Air Force Test Center.
Seasats said it deployed a fleet of five autonomous surface vessels during the exercise, including its Lightfish and Quickfish platforms, to demonstrate coordinated multi-platform operations with a small number of operators. The company said the event also involved integrating maritime sensing and electromagnetic spectrum equipment across the fleet.
A production-run Quickfish completed the full two-week exercise while carrying multiple payloads, Seasats said. The company described Quickfish as built on the Lightfish hull and electronics stack, adding high sea state performance, long range and a payload bay sized for aerial vehicles. Seasats also said the boat includes an on-station patrol mode that allows it to stay deployed for weeks without refueling.
Seasats credited the Naval Surface Warfare Center, Crane Division for the opportunity to test the technology.
The company said Quickfish’s payload bay is watertight and can hold several unmanned aircraft of different types and sizes. That allows a single vessel to be reconfigured for different missions, such as intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, communications relay or strike, without modifying the boat itself, according to Seasats. Because the aircraft ride inside the enclosed bay, the company said a Quickfish on patrol gives no outward sign of what it is carrying.
Seasats linked that capability to the Defense Innovation Unit’s Suitable Warfighting Adaptive Payloads program, known as SWAP-USV, which is seeking mature, affordable unmanned surface vessels that can integrate with unmanned aircraft to counter asymmetric threats at sea. The company said Quickfish is in production now and can be delivered on DIU’s timeline.

U.S. Army awards AV $464.8 million laser weapon deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:31:46 UTC
16:31:46 KST

- The US Army awarded AV a $464.8 million contract for 26 LOCUST X3 laser weapons under its first formal directed energy program of record.
- The Other Transaction Agreement runs five years and follows a June demonstration where Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth watched the system shoot down drones.
The US Army has awarded defense contractor AV a $464.8 million contract to produce high-energy laser weapons under the Enduring High Energy Laser (E-HEL) program, the Army’s first formal directed energy program of record, according to Laser Wars.
Under the Other Transaction Agreement, AV will deliver 26 of its 30 kilowatt LOCUST X3 laser weapons to the Army over the next five years. The systems are meant to counter low-cost weaponized drones.
The X3 was formally unveiled in March and built specifically for the E-HEL program. It is the latest version of AV’s LOCUST Laser Weapon System, which American troops have already used for counter-drone missions from the Middle East to the US-Mexico border.
The Army’s fiscal year 2027 budget request called for the procurement of two E-HEL systems at $17.4 million apiece, with plans to field up to 24 additional units over the following five and a half years, according to a draft request for proposals from the service’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Fires published in January.
“This award marks a defining moment not only for AV, but for the future of modern defense,” said AV Chairman and CEO Wahid Nawabi.
“The transition of directed energy from experimentation to an enduring, fielded capability reflects years of collaboration, innovation, and operational success alongside the US Army. We are proud to deliver these production systems and support the Army’s mission with scalable, modular, and cost-effective defense solutions.”
The Army first announced E-HEL in a July 2024 special notice, describing it as a modular system built on lessons from two earlier LOCUST-based programs. One is the 20 kilowatt Palletized-High Energy Laser, which conducted live-fire testing from the flight deck of the aircraft carrier USS George H.W. Bush (CVN 77) in October 2025. The other is the Army Multi-Purpose High Energy Laser, a vehicle-mounted system tested over the past year from the back of the service’s Infantry Squad Vehicle and Joint Light Tactical Vehicle.
The Department of War has gradually expanded its use of laser weapons overseas to protect troops from drones. The Army sent several Palletized-High Energy Laser systems to an undisclosed location, likely within the US Central Command area of operations, starting in 2022. Four Stryker-mounted, 50 kilowatt Directed Energy Maneuver-Short Range Air Defense systems followed in 2024 for in-theater testing before that program was later canceled. In July, the US Air Force disclosed it had deployed several Boeing Compact Laser Weapon System units across Europe as part of a layered air defense network.
The Army’s requirements for E-HEL call for three distinct engagement profiles: 30 one-second shots per minute against high-density target sets, six nine-second shots per minute against low-density sets, and three 17-second shots per minute against hardened targets. The system must also sustain full power for a full minute, with a recharge cycle capped at four minutes.
The draft RFP also required that an E-HEL system arrive with production capacity already in place. AV said it met that requirement with a $30 million manufacturing expansion in New Mexico announced in March.
The contract follows a June demonstration at White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico, where Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth personally observed AV’s LOCUST shoot down drones, according to Laser Wars, which first reported the event. That demonstration also featured nLight’s “P5 version” of the DE M-SHORAD system and Lockheed Martin’s 300 kilowatt Indirect Fire Protection Capability-High Energy Laser prototype, known as Valkyrie. Weeks later, the Pentagon awarded nLight and Lockheed Martin contracts for the 300-500 kilowatt Joint Laser Weapons System, part of the “Golden Dome for America” missile defense effort.
Earlier Army laser efforts struggled to reach production. The Mobile Test Unit, the first vehicle-mounted laser weapon, was judged “neither scalable nor robust enough for Army standards,” while the Government Accountability Office found the DE M-SHORAD system “not mature enough” for full production.
Separately, the US Air Force’s Recovery of Airbase Denied by Ordnance system, a 3 kilowatt Zeus III laser mounted on a Cougar 4×4 MRAP vehicle, is already in sustained production, with contractor Parsons under contract for 29 units.

Belgium reports about 3,000 excess deaths over summer due to heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03

Belgium reports about 3,000 excess deaths over summer due to heat
BRUSSELS – Heatwaves from June 18 through Aug 16 caused 2,935 excess deaths in Belgium, or 22.6 per cent excess mortality, public health body Sciensano said in a report on Sept 3.
From June 18 through July 3, Belgium recorded its highest excess mortality, with 2,035 additional deaths, or 48.8 per cent above expected levels, Sciensano said.
Starting on June 18, maximum temperatures of around 30 deg C were recorded for 10 consecutive days, including three days of temperatures around 35 deg C, with nights during that period also exceptionally warm.
Sciensano said mortality from June 18 through July 3 was the highest recorded during a heatwave since the start of its analyses in the year 2000.
The two other heatwave periods, from July 4 to 17 and July 28 to Aug 16, saw lower excess mortality, with 535 excess deaths (14.8 per cent) and 365 excess deaths (7 per cent), respectively.
While people aged 65 and older account for most heatwave-related deaths, Sciensano said excess mortality also occurs among younger people.
Europe experienced several heatwaves during the summer, with the UN weather agency in August saying periods of extreme heat are becoming more frequent, intense and longer-lasting as climate change warms the planet. REUTERS

The Kitchen Edge: Service, Storage, and Domestic Boundaries in Compact Interiors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

In compact homes, the kitchen is rarely only a room for cooking. It often operates as an edge: a service wall or a boundary between domestic work and social life. Its importance lies not only in food preparation, but in how it organizes the rest of the home, particularly due to limitations of plumbing and ventilation requirements. Before a living room can feel open, the kitchen often has to absorb the practical intensity of daily life: water, heat, smell, appliances, groceries, and storage.
This is especially visible in dense East Asian interiors, where domestic space is frequently shaped by limited area, changing family structures, hybrid work, and the cultural specificity of cooking. The open kitchen may be framed as a lifestyle feature, but in many apartments it is also a planning problem. It has to negotiate domestic labor, support informal gathering, and sometimes, as space-saving strategies, replace the hallway or foyer. More than a design gesture, the kitchen edge is therefore a spatial agreement between service and living.

Nalsar row: SC strikes down BCI orders, says it has 'no statutory power to regulate conduct of students'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:26:11 UTC
16:26:11 KST

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday held that the Bar Council of India has "no statutory authority to regulate the conduct of law students". The court set aside two BCI notifications issued against students of Hyderabad's Nalsar University of Law.A bench comprising CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana passed the order.
The orders were linked to the students' protest over Chief Justice of India Surya Kant's proposed participation in the university's convocation.The court's observation came after the BCI initially directed state Bar Councils not to enrol Nalsar's 2026 law graduates as advocates following a student campaign opposing CJI Surya Kant's proposed participation as chief guest at the university's convocation.Also read - BCI action, U-turn and SC rebuke: How NALSAR students' protest against CJI kicked up a rowThe BCI later withdrew the directive and allowed the graduates to be enrolled while an inquiry was pending.
How the NALSAR row began
The controversy began after several Nalsar students submitted representations asking the university to reconsider its invitation to CJI Surya Kant. The students referred to remarks attributed to the CJI during a hearing concerning alleged police excesses against protesters during a July 20 march to Parliament.
At least six representations were submitted by students from different batches, with the first being sent on July 23. The students argued that inviting the CJI was inconsistent with the university's stated commitment to constitutional rights, access to justice and reasoned engagement with grievances.One representation cited the CJI's response to an offer to show videos of the alleged police action: "We are not interested in videos; we don’t have time to watch." It also quoted him as telling counsel: "Don’t waste our time, and don’t waste your time".The students maintained that their objection was rooted in constitutional values and not disrespect towards the judicial office."We respect the CJI’s position. But we have been taught the Constitution and constitutional values, and we don’t want to support something that goes against those values," a student who was also part of the Student bar council had told TOI.The dispute escalated when BCI chairperson Manan Kumar Mishra directed state Bar Councils not to enrol Nalsar's 2026 law graduates as advocates until further orders.The BCI sought a report from Nalsar identifying students who had allegedly initiated, organised or mobilised the campaign against CJI Surya Kant's participation in the convocation.The council's initial communication stated, “Till further orders, no student of Nalsar University of Law, who has obtained law degree in the year 2026, shall be enrolled by any state bar council as an advocate.”It also said, “A student of Law, having no regard or respect for the highest judicial office of the country, is not expected to be a responsible or sensible advocate, teacher or a judge. Such persons shall always be a liability on the profession. Such conduct reflects adversely upon the person’s suitability for entry into or association with the legal profession and is inconsistent with the dignity, discipline and ethical standards of the legal profession.”The BCI further alleged that some members of Nalsar's academic staff had been involved in "misleading, instigating and misguiding" students.“As per some reliable sources, there exists groupism and dirty politics among some of the academic staff and they have played a very active role in misleading, instigating and misguiding the students. This is a very serious matter. The teachers, instead of involving themselves in their teaching job, are doing nasty politics in the campus. BCI, being the regulator of Legal Education cannot be a mute spectator of such a serious situation.”The directive drew criticism from sections of the legal fraternity, with Supreme Court bar association president Vikas Singh describing the move as arbitrary, illegal and disproportionate, while maintaining that he did not support the students' opposition to the CJI's invitation.
The BCI withdrew its original directive within hours amid the criticism. In its revised communication, Mishra said the council had “thoroughly discussed and deliberated” on the earlier letter and modified its direction.He said the “vast majority” of Nalsar's 2026 graduating students were innocent and “were not inclined to take part in the move of disrespect”. However, he added, “It has been further reported by some reliable sources that a handful of teachers and outsiders were instrumental in instigating innocent students.”The revised decision permitted the 2026 graduates to be enrolled while the BCI awaited an inquiry report from Nalsar.

Russia preparing new AK-12+ rifle for serial production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:25:20 UTC
16:25:20 KST

- Kalashnikov unveiled a mock-up of its new 5.45mm AK-12+ assault rifle at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, saying serial production is being prepared.
- The rifle, built for special forces, has a thicker barrel, modified sights and removed sling, bayonet and grenade launcher fittings compared to the standard AK-12.
Kalashnikov Concern unveiled a mock-up of its new AK-12+ assault rifle at the Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, presenting a 5.45mm weapon built for improved shooting precision.
The rifle is on display in the Voin Center pavilion at the Far East Street exhibition, part of the 11th Eastern Economic Forum, running September 1-4 on the campus of Far Eastern Federal University.
Kalashnikov, part of the state defense conglomerate Rostec, said the weapon is now being prepared for serial production. The company described the AK-12+ as a high-precision small-arms system built on the existing AK-12 platform, intended primarily for special forces units.
The system was developed under the supervision of Russian Deputy Prime Minister and Presidential Plenipotentiary Envoy to the Far Eastern Federal District Yury Trutnev, the company said.
The AK-12+ carries a thicker barrel than the standard AK-12, with a threaded muzzle designed to accept a flash suppressor or a muzzle brake. Kalashnikov modified the rifle’s mechanical sights and widened the contour of the gas cylinder to match the new barrel profile. Fittings previously used to attach a sling swivel, an underbarrel grenade launcher and a bayonet have been removed. The mock-up shown in Vladivostok featured an extended stock.
The rifle will also carry electro-optical sights. Kalashnikov said the sights are meant to improve accuracy at medium range in both daytime and nighttime conditions.
At the forum, Kalashnikov and the Voin Center signed a cooperation agreement. Under the deal, the two organizations will jointly develop engineering skills among the center’s cadets and expand the material and technical resources at its regional branches.
The Voin Center, formally the Center for Military-Sports Training and Patriotic Education of Youth, was created on presidential order in 2023. It trains teenagers aged 14 to 18 and reservists aged 18 to 35, and now operates branches in more than 20 Russian regions.
Kalashnikov already produces several variants of the AK-12 platform. The baseline AK-12 is chambered in 5.45x39mm, weighs about 3.6 kg (7.9 pounds) unloaded, has a 415 mm (16.3 inch) barrel and fires at a cyclic rate of roughly 700 rounds per minute. The family also includes the AK-15, chambered in 7.62x39mm, and the export-oriented AK-19, chambered in 5.56x45mm NATO.

Chalmers can't avoid questions on house prices, Marles learns from melon saga
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:22:15 UTC
16:22:15 KST

analysis
Chalmers questioned about house prices, Marles learns from melon saga
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.
Jim Chalmers sits alone in a darkened press conference room, selfie camera on, chatting to his social media followers about the latest economic data.
But of course he wasn't asked any questions in his pre-filmed video. It was more an avenue for him to declare the economy was "robust" despite challenges from the Middle East war, point out more people are switching to EVs and that housing construction is up before he had to face reporters half an hour later.
He fronted up to the press conference for a tense back and forth where almost every single question was house prices.
When the government made the U-turn on its promise not to wind back negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount, it did so armed with Treasury forecasts. Growth, the budget papers said, would slow by 2 per cent over a number of years.
Property data firm Cotality this week flagged drops in every capital city in August, and predictions from the Commonwealth Bank that prices could drop as much as 13 per cent have some mortgage holders understandably worried.
Chalmers has largely brushed off movements in price as not unusual and backed in his department's forecast. "Buying a house is a long-term proposition," he said.
The major factor at play here is recent interest rate rises, he argued, not the government's tax changes.
That argument wasn't made easier for him either, after fellow frontbencher Matt Thistlethwaite declared on News24 (formerly Sky News Australia) there was "no doubt" the tax changes contributed to house prices falling.
"I think that's one of a number of reasons," Chalmers told ABC's Sally Sara when asked again this morning.
Opting out of algorithms?
Thistlethwaite may have made the sell a little bit harder for Chalmers, but the treasurer named the "disturbing rubbish" pushed by social media algorithms as the thing making his job more difficult.
"Our society, our social cohesion, the way that we come at big problems including in my part of the shop in the economy is hampered, not helped, by the way algorithms are dominating people's day," Chalmers said.
It's a similar argument that's been put before by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who has said algorithms are fuelling polarisation. Albanese is supportive of the idea that Australians should have more control over what they are shown online.
But that doesn't go as far as what consent advocate Chanel Contos has put forward: an opt-in algorithm for social media accounts. If adopted, it would be a world where we'd return to chronological feeds where our friends' content is shown instead of strangers. It's an idea backed by some of the crossbench and the Greens amid concerns social media is exposing young people to misogynistic content.
There seems to be no disagreement among the leaders of the major political parties that some of the content fed to people is toxic. But for some it's a bit of a chicken and egg argument.
Nationals leader Matt Canavan, for example, this week argued it is the "feminisation" of the school curriculum and a lack of male teachers that pushes boys towards such content. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor also accused teachers of running agendas in the classroom.
Contos argued the algorithm is the missing piece here — young boys are being shown this content whether they seek it out or not.
Coalition focuses on tobacco
Meanwhile, the Coalition finally released its plan to slash the tobacco excise. The plan also included a proposal to legalise and tax vapes and nicotine pouches.
An estimated 80 per cent of the cigarettes and other nicotine products consumed in Australia last year were illegal, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
Last month, One Nation revealed its own plan to slash the excise by 75 per cent. The opposition went one further, revealing a proposal to cut the excise by 80 per cent. It argues it would be enough to tip the scales and redirect customers towards legal tobacco.
The Parliamentary Budget Office costed the policy but the Coalition has not released the costings or the assumptions underpinning them.
It says its plan, paired with a further $200 million spend on law enforcement to support more raids, arrests and closure of illegal tobacco shops, would increase tax revenue by about $8 billion over the first four years — double the current forecasts.
That hinges on the idea that cutting the price would encourage Australians to ditch the black market and that illegal distributers wouldn't also drop prices to compete — something Taylor disagrees with.
Back in the Pacific
While this was all going down at home, Albanese returned to palm tree-lined beaches and crystal clear blue water of Palau for the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF).
It's not the first time the prime minister has visited — he made the trip to the small Pacific nation last year for a pre-wedding holiday with now wife Jodie Haydon.
The early stages of the meeting were overshadowed by tensions between China and Taiwan about Taipei's increased presence at the gathering (Palau has diplomatic ties with Taiwan) and the number of leaders who decided to skip the annual forum.
Albanese said he wasn't distracted by all that as he pressed on with discussions about climate change and tackling the issue of drug trafficking in the Pacific, where Australia and New Zealand's appetite for illegal drugs has caused real issues.
Leaders were also due to discuss the matter of China's test-fire of a nuclear-capable missile carrying a dummy warhead in the Pacific — with host nation Palau indicating it would like to issue a united statement about the test.
Despite escaping PIF without another T-shirt faux pas, it wasn't all smooth sailing for Albanese, who had a tense press conference of his own at the forum about United Nations climate event being held in Fiji and Tuvalu next month.
The pre-COP events are organised by Australia and are part of the compromise Australia struck with Türkiye last year after we bowed out of hosting the climate conference in Adelaide.
But so far just five leaders from outside of the Pacific have confirmed they're making the trip, which was designed to highlight the impact of climate change on Pacific nations. It's not typical that leaders usually attend a pre-COP event.
Asked about this, Albanese said the focus on the non-Pacific leaders was "disrespectful".
Loading
Treaty yourself
And finally, have you been looking for the perfect gift for the Kiwi in your family? Or perhaps you have a long-distance American pen pal you need a stocking stuffer for?
Don't worry, Defence Minister Richard Marles has you covered for inspiration. He presented a framed copy of the full text of the ANZUS Treaty on vellum, and signed by Albanese, to a member of the Trump administration.
Vellum is a thin, translucent material made of calfskin and commonly used by artists.
Why are we presenting Albanese autographed military treaties to our allies? To mark the 75th anniversary. You can't get that at the shops.

====================================================================================================

Iranian-backed militia Badr admits it killed, wounded thousands of protesters in Iraq in 2019
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:19:29 UTC
16:19:29 KST

In October 2019, thousands of protesters were killed and wounded in Iraq. For years, it was known that Iranian-backed militias were likely unleashed by the government to suppress the protests. Yet there has been a lack of confirmation or evidence about the role of the militias.
The head of the powerful Badr militia, Hadi al-Amiri, now appears to have admitted that the group was behind the killings. In Iraq, social media is focused on this story.
In 2019, Iraq was in a transition period. The prime minister was Adil Abdul-Mahdi, who was relatively weak and ineffectual. Powerful Iranian-backed militias that had been empowered by the war on ISIS were increasing their control across Iraq.
Instead of Iraq receiving a kind of “peace dividend” when the war against ISIS largely ended in 2018, the country transitioned to new rounds of violence and economic stagnation. Militias also began targeting US-led coalition forces.
Tishreen movement
In October 2019, this led to protests, which have often been referred to as the Tishreen movement.
“Iraqi authorities continue to persecute activists and protesters while failing to deliver meaningful justice and accountability for the killings of hundreds, and the maiming of thousands of protesters, by security forces and militias; or to reveal the fate and whereabouts of those disappeared,” Amnesty International reported last year.
A video of Amiri, a former member of the Iraqi Council of Representatives, giving a speech began to make the rounds in Iraq on Monday.
“The resistance stood bravely in the face of the October fitna [as it was dubbed] and preserved the state and political system,” he said.
It’s worth understanding the terminology here. Amiri uses the term “resistance” to refer to the Iranian-backed militias. These groups are part of the government’s paramilitary Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF). Some are also formally part of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq.
Most of the militias have been sanctioned by the US as terrorist groups. Badr is among the most powerful, but it has not been sanctioned.
Amiri uses the word fitna, which has a number of meanings but essentially accuses the protesters of sedition and heresy. It accuses the protesters of undermining the state and trying to create civil strife.
He was basically admitting that the Iranian-backed militias, such as Badr, had massacred hundreds or thousands of people. He was accusing the protesters of being traitors who were then put down.
Amiri’s speech comes as Iraq seeks to disarm and rein in the militias. Several of the most powerful militias have said they would not disarm, or they have presented new conditions for placing their arms under state control. They include Harakat Hezbollah al-Nujaba, Kataib Hezbollah, and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada.
Badr is not usually seen as one of the most extreme militias. Amiri has long played a role as a power behind the throne in Iraq, however, with Badr as an enforcer of Iran’s agenda.
Lawyer submits report to Prosecutor General
Amiri’s comments have now led to controversy in Iraq. Some social-media sites have been circulating images from the October 2019 protests, showing the protesters being oppressed.
A lawyer had submitted a report to the prosecutor-general of Wasit Province, demanding an investigation and lawsuit into Badr and the comments by Amiri, according to a report on Wednesday.
The lawyer as seeking to sue Amiri pursuant to his statements, Iraq’s Al-Sharqiya news channel reported.
Currently, there is debate in the region’s Arabic media about what Amiri said. Did he reveal the “true face” of the “resistance” by appearing to take responsibility for the mass killings?
“Was it a slip of the tongue by Hadi al-Amiri, head of the Badr Organization and one of the most prominent leaders of the Coordinating Framework that runs the sectarian power structure in Iraq?” asked another report.
Another question is whether his statement is actually a threat that the militias could again use force against protesters or against a government that would seek to disarm them.
“The wave of anger and popular criticism against the head of the Badr Organization, Hadi al-Amiri, continues, following statements in which he admitted the involvement of what he called the ‘resistance’ in the events that accompanied the ‘October Movement’ of 2019, which lasted for about two years and during which more than 600 demonstrators were killed and over 20,000 others were wounded,” Arabic-language newspaper Asharq Al-Awsat reported.
Families of victims now say lawsuits will follow, and there are calls to prosecute Amiri.
This is important because unlike some of the other militia leaders, Amiri has always been able to avoid sanctions and controversy.
Badr has been the main Iranian-backed militia in Iraq that is not sanctioned by the US, which considers most of the others as Foreign Terrorist Organizations or Specially Designated Terrorist Groups.
As such, Badr has a unique role. It continues to have major influence in the Interior Ministry and other parts of Iraq.
The role of the militias in the massacres is very similar to involvement by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in killing protesters.
This past January, Iran was accused of massacring tens of thousands of people. It has done this before, and it has exported this model to Iraq and other countries.
The militias have kidnapped journalists and assassinated people. They have also attacked Americans and targeted the autonomous Kurdistan Region in northern Iraq.

US, China arm for space warfare, raising stakes in race for military control of orbit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-03
07:18:42 UTC
16:18:42 KST

In June, a secretive unmanned Chinese spaceplane closely monitored by US military analysts released a small satellite hundreds of miles above Earth in an orbital region crowded with commercial and military satellites. The object then looped around another Chinese satellite before returning towards the spaceplane, according to US space-tracking firm LeoLabs.
Little is known about the satellite or the mission. But the US military operates a similarly secretive spaceplane resembling a small shuttle, also with no crew. Both programs reflect the rapidly evolving field of military space operations as Beijing and Washington prepare for the possibility of conflict extending into space, according to a Reuters review of documents, space-tracking data and interviews with current and former military officials.
Chinese researchers linked to the military are developing technologies ranging from satellites designed to pursue and even capture other spacecraft to systems that could extend fuel supplies while doing so, according to a Reuters review of patent-related documents, procurement notices and academic papers. And the United States and Britain conducted their first joint military operation in space in the path of a suspected Chinese spy satellite, according to commercial space-tracking data.
"The Chinese are rapidly developing capabilities," including ground- and space-based weapons designed to interfere with or destroy targets, US Space Force’s Chief of Space Operations General Chance Saltzman said in July. The threat from China is "substantial," added Saltzman, who is retiring.
Satellites have become indispensable to modern warfare, as conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East have demonstrated. For decades they have provided communications, navigation and intelligence services to armed forces on Earth, and once placed in orbit typically remained on fixed paths. Increasingly, however, militaries view them as active weapons platforms capable of launching attacks by disrupting a satellite’s operations through jamming or laser dazzling, or even capturing enemy spacecraft.
Disruption of US space capabilities would "cripple our massive military in the terrestrial sphere," affecting everything from surveillance to missile defense, said Everett Dolman, a former professor at the US Air Force's Air War College. Spaceplanes, because they are agile and capable of deploying satellites or carrying cargo, could appear to opponents as potential "space fighters," he said.
Allies join the US effort
The growing competition comes as Earth's orbit becomes increasingly crowded. SpaceX, which recently debuted on public markets, operates about 11,000 Starlink satellites and plans a constellation of larger AI-enabled data centers in space. China is building rival networks, while US President Donald Trump's Golden Dome missile defense program envisions space-based interceptors.
The United States is also refining capabilities that could prove important in a future conflict.
In the joint US-British operation in September last year, US space forces working from a base in Colorado directed a US military satellite to swoop in close to a U.K. one as China's Shiyan 12-01 satellite passed about 83 kilometers beneath them, according to space intelligence company Slingshot Aerospace. At that altitude, specialists consider the distance relatively close.
Three space experts with military backgrounds told Reuters it appeared intended as a signal to Beijing, including at space-tracking firm COMSPOC. Andrew Turner, a retired senior British air force officer who is now a space consultant, said it was “almost certainly a strategic signal to China” to demonstrate allied unity, capability and a warning to not interfere with the UK satellite.
The US and Britain publicly announced the operation, the first known one between two members of the "Five Eyes" intelligence alliance, but did not disclose its proximity to a Chinese spacecraft. Much of what occurs in space remains classified because of its intelligence implications.
US Space Command told Reuters the mission demonstrated the ability to work with allies in space. Britain's defense ministry said space is increasingly important to military operations and the UK and its partners were conducting advanced orbital operations to protect their national and military interests. Neither commented on the operation’s proximity to the Chinese satellite.
The US Space Force’s next chief of space operations, Lieutenant General Douglas Schiess, had been involved in the operation. In an interview shortly after, he said operating close to another spacecraft could help verify whether an allied satellite is functioning properly or determine whether an adversary is "doing something it shouldn't." He declined to say at the time whether another country's satellite had been nearby.
Britain recently disclosed that the mission was conducted alongside a maritime deployment to the Indo-Pacific region.
Using space not only to support military operations on Earth but also to influence their outcome is "really, really important," then U.K. Space Command chief Major General Paul Tedman said in April at a conference. He has since retired from the military.
China's foreign ministry said it was not familiar with the specific details of the US-British operation. More broadly, Beijing opposes the weaponization of space and supports its peaceful use, the ministry said, while accusing Washington of stoking an arms race through efforts including the missile defense system Golden Dome and potential space-based weapons.
Asked about Shiyan 12-01 and the Chinese spaceplane, the ministry said it had no information. State news agency Xinhua has described Shiyan 12-01 as conducting space environment surveys, and the spaceplane as an experimental craft supporting the peaceful use of space.
US Space Force says its own spaceplane is carrying out a range of tests and experiments.
Space Weapons
US Space Command head General Stephen Whiting has repeatedly emphasized the importance of space to modern warfare, warning that adversaries are developing capabilities to deny the United States access to key systems and reduce military effectiveness. He has said adversaries would likely seek to target US space assets early in a conflict.
To counter such threats, the US must adopt a more active warfighting posture in space, Whiting argues. That means not only protecting US systems but also being prepared to threaten or strike hostile assets if necessary. He has called for orbital interceptors and other weapons.
"We must be well-prepared for conflict in space. And if deterrence fails, we will fight and win," he told a conference in April.
Western officials warn of a range of threats, including ground-based lasers, electronic jammers, cyberattacks and anti-satellite missiles.
In orbit, the United States, China and Russia all operate maneuverable satellites capable of approaching and inspecting other spacecraft. Such systems could be adapted to carry weapons, including lasers or projectiles. Western officials say Beijing and Moscow have demonstrated technologies that could be used to threaten US and allied satellites.
The US has also accused Russia of developing an anti-satellite capability involving a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon. Moscow has denied that it is developing a space-based anti-satellite nuclear weapon.
The U.K.'s Tedman, in an interview last fall, said militaries now see satellites as “weapons systems” that need to maneuver and fight. The West is “working hard to retain our strategic advantage in space,” he said.
Some specialists note that disrupting satellites remains easier from Earth than through spacecraft-on-spacecraft attacks.
In a rare disclosure about its own capabilities, the US Space Force announced in June that it had introduced an earthbound electromagnetic weapon from L3Harris Technologies designed to disable or disrupt adversary satellites.
"Dogfighting" and hunter satellites
Although the United States remains the world's leading space power, China is rapidly expanding both the number of satellites it operates and the complexity of its missions.
Chinese satellites have demonstrated what US officials describe as orbital "dogfighting," which includes multiple satellites moving in a synchronized way in proximity. Chinese spacecraft have also shown the ability to capture a defunct satellite and move it into a different orbit.
Last year, China conducted what was likely an on-orbit refueling attempt, according to a US Space Force official. Refueling would be a major breakthrough because satellites are normally constrained by the fuel they launch with. The ability to replenish fuel could determine whether a spacecraft remains a hunter or becomes the hunted.
Chinese institutions continue to pursue new capabilities. Patent-related documents show the maker of some of China's most advanced military aircraft acquired technology that allows satellites to autonomously calculate fuel-efficient maneuvers while pursuing another spacecraft.
Meanwhile, a technology-transfer notice published by the National University of Defense Technology described a mature system capable of managing hundreds of satellites simultaneously for both defensive and operational purposes.
Researchers at another major Chinese university with close military ties have also been developing pursuit satellites, including concepts involving multiple spacecraft using nets to capture targets, according to patent-related documents.
The institutions and the People's Liberation Army did not respond to requests for comment. On-orbit capabilities such as refueling and capturing another satellite could have non-military uses.
China's official military newspaper, PLA Daily, said in a 2022 editorial that controlling space was essential for safeguarding national security, seizing the strategic initiative and achieving victory in war.

Norway has seized a Russian ship in the Arctic to enforce a $4.22 billion compensation claim won by Ukrainian energy firm Naftogaz over Moscow's seizure of its assets when Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, officials said late on Wednesday.
The vessel, the Professor Molchanov, was seized off the Norwegian Arctic archipelago of Svalbard after a 24-hour standoff with the Norwegian Coast Guard, according to Covington, the US law firm representing Naftogaz.
Russian state news agency TASS quoted a Foreign Ministry spokesperson as saying the Norwegian action was "piracy."
Naftogaz has been pursuing legal action against Russia since 2016 to seek compensation for the expropriation of its property in Crimea.
A tribunal in The Hague in April 2023 ordered Russia to pay Naftogaz $4.22 billion plus interest and legal costs, but Moscow has not done so.
"Russia cannot evade responsibility simply by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award," said Naftogaz Acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko.
Covington tracks the Professor Molchanov for months
Covington, the law firm, said it had been tracking the Professor Molchanov, a Russian-owned vessel that is used for commercial cruises, for months.
Anticipating the ship's arrival in Svalbard en route to Barentsburg, a Russian mining settlement, Naftogaz's lawyers applied to a Norwegian court for the vessel to be arrested there and subject to a compulsory sale.
The application was approved by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court on Monday. In its ruling, it required the governor of Svalbard to enforce the order, supervise the vessel, and ensure that it is not moved.
The governor's office issued a statement confirming that the ship had been seized and would be held in Svalbard.
Naftogaz has said it is coordinating enforcement measures across multiple jurisdictions, including the United States, France, the United Kingdom and Finland, where Russian assets have been frozen. Russia is appealing the process, saying no notice was given.
"We will continue to pursue Russian assets around the world until the compensation awarded to Naftogaz and other Naftogaz Group companies is paid," the Ukrainian company said.
Russia calls Norway's seizure of its ship 'piracy', TASS reports
The Russian Foreign Ministry on Thursday called Norway's seizure of a Russian vessel at the request of Ukrainian state firm Naftogaz "piracy."
The Ukrainian company has been pursuing legal action against Russia since 2016 to seek compensation for Moscow's expropriation of Naftogaz property when Russia annexed Crimea in 2014.
Norway seized the ship on Wednesday, after Moscow failed to pay Naftogaz $4.22 billion plus interest and legal costs to compensate for assets it seized in Crimea following a 2023 ruling by a tribunal in The Hague.
Alexei Chekunkov, Russia's Minister for the Development of the Russian Far East and Arctic, said Moscow would challenge the ruling, saying the seizure of the vessel, "Professor Molchanov," was "another example of Western countries' legal nihilism and lawlessness," according to the Interfax news agency.

house-like concrete play structures frame community arc park in chihuahua
